Doses varied up to 20-fold between the lowest and the highest.Source: van der Heijden and Frykholm 2026 (survey of 57 paediatric anaesthesiologists at 14 hospitals in the five Nordic countries, 2024)
  • EEG is not part of the monitoring. EEG is not mentioned among the monitoring methods in the survey. 86 % used gestational age in weeks as the lowest acceptable mean arterial pressure in mmHg. NIRS was used by 40 %, most without a fixed threshold for intervention.Source: van der Heijden and Frykholm 2026
  • Research and evidence-based protocols are needed for this vulnerable group. That is the authors' conclusion from the wide variation. Caveat: the response rate was about 30 %, and the answers reflect what the doctors report, not measured practice.
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): in the youngest and most immature, anaesthesia is currently dosed without looking at the target organ, and the EEG looks different both with age and after preterm birth. An age pattern in the spectrogram therefore cannot be transferred directly from adults or older children.
Poorun 2016 van der Heijden and Frykholm 2026

Isoelectric EEG in infants and toddlers under anaesthesia (Yuan 2020 and 2022)

This card is about how often the EEG becomes almost flat during anaesthesia in children under 3 years. The findings concern anaesthesia for surgery, not sedation in intensive care.Sources: Yuan 2020 (Anesth Analg) and Yuan 2022 (Anesthesiology), same research group

  • An almost flat EEG is common in the youngest, especially under 3 months. Among 648 children under 3 years at 15 hospitals, 32 % had at least one episode: 59 % at 0–3 months and 24–28 % in the older groups. The proportion varied from 9 to 88 % between hospitals. In a smaller pilot study 63 % had at least one episode, but the episodes made up only 0.1 % of anaesthetic time.Sources: Yuan 2022 (Australia, China, Europe and the USA; sevoflurane or propofol); Yuan 2020 (51 children)
  • The episodes occur mostly early in the anaesthetic. They were most common before incision (19 %) and during maintenance (18 %). In the pilot study most occurred between induction and incision.Sources: Yuan 2022; Yuan 2020
  • The studies defined “flat” slightly differently. The pilot study used below 20 µV for at least 2 seconds. The large study recorded frontally with four channels (SedLine) and required below ±10 µV for at least 2 seconds in all four channels simultaneously.Sources: Yuan 2020; Yuan 2022
  • Young age, a propofol bolus and low blood pressure were associated with the episodes. The strongest were young age (0–3 months, OR 4.4 versus 19–36 months) and a propofol bolus after sevoflurane induction (OR 2.9). Moderate and severe hypotension gave 3.5–7 times higher odds, although the difference in mean arterial pressure was only 4–5 mmHg. A tracheal tube rather than a laryngeal mask and slightly higher sevoflurane (about 0.2 percentage points) were also associated with episodes, while neuromuscular blockade for intubation was associated with fewer.Source: Yuan 2022
  • The significance for outcome is unclear. The episodes were not associated with emergence behaviour. Quality of life at 30 days was measured, but the analysis was exploratory and cannot be interpreted with confidence.Source: Yuan 2022
  • Caveats: observational studies, so they show associations, not causes. Frontal EEG does not see the whole brain. The manufacturer supplied the monitors and sensors, and two of the authors have received fees from the manufacturer.
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): in the youngest, anaesthesia may become deeper than necessary when the dose is guided by age, weight and circulation alone. The raw EEG and spectrogram can show this as it happens, and the findings fit with the EEG in infants under 3 months looking different (see the Children sub-tab). Whether avoiding the episodes improves outcome has not been studied.
Yuan 2020 Yuan 2022

A rapidly developing brain: what the textbook says (Vutskits et al. 2025)

  • The brain grows fastest from the third trimester to the first years of life. In this period, very many synapses are formed, and neural activity guides how the networks develop. Drugs that interfere with normal activity in this period may affect brain development.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • Neonates respond to pain, but differently. Preterm and term neonates respond more diffusely and less specifically to noxious stimulation than older children. When pain begins to be experienced is unresolved. Early painful experiences may nevertheless alter later function of the central nervous system, even if they are not conscious, and adequate pain relief can improve outcome.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • Neurotoxicity has been shown in the laboratory but is uncertain in humans. Both inhaled and intravenous anaesthetics cause neurotoxicity and behavioural changes in laboratory studies. Some human studies find an association between anaesthesia early in life and later developmental problems, but this may be explained by other factors.Source: Vutskits et al. 2025
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): In the youngest, both too deep anaesthesia and inadequate pain relief are possible concerns. What the episodes of isoelectric EEG mean in the long term is not known (see the Yuan card above).Sources: Vutskits et al. 2025; Yuan 2022
Vutskits et al. 2025

Drugs: consciousness and amnesia

Each drug is described separately here: where it acts, what it does to consciousness, memory, pain and movement, and how it looks in the EEG. The figures are population averages from the literature with large individual variation, and they are not dosing advice. Why the dose is only a prediction is explained in the “Dose and prediction” sub-tab.

Key points

  • The agents act on different receptors and circuits. Propofol, barbiturates, etomidate and benzodiazepines act via the GABAA receptor. Ketamine blocks the NMDA receptor. Dexmedetomidine and clonidine act on α2 receptors. The EEG signatures are thought to arise because the drugs act on specific receptors in specific circuits.See “Basic concepts: receptors, ion channels and circuits”
  • Amnesia, unconsciousness and immobility need different doses. With propofol, memory is lost at a lighter hypnotic level than response. Preventing movement at incision needs a much higher concentration (16 µg/ml with no other drugs). Midazolam causes anterograde amnesia but does not affect retrograde memory.See
  • Slow waves do not mean the same for every drug. Under dexmedetomidine the EEG resembles NREM 2 sleep, connectivity within the cortex is preserved, and the patient can be roused. Increased delta after clonidine should not be read as just as much deeper hypnosis as the same change after more propofol. Ketamine gives an active EEG with theta and gamma.See
  • When benzodiazepines fail, the NMDA side may explain why. In alcohol withdrawal and prolonged seizures, GABAA inhibition weakens while the NMDA system becomes overactive. Propofol or ketamine has been used when benzodiazepines do not work. The studies are small and retrospective. (interpretation based on the sources)See “Propofol and midazolam: alone, together and in withdrawal”
  • Involuntary movements with propofol can mislead the index. Seizure-like phenomena are rare and occur mostly at induction and emergence. The muscle noise can raise the index. So look at the raw EEG and the patient. Consider full EEG for prolonged or repeated episodes or known epilepsy. (interpretation based on the sources)See “Propofol and involuntary movements: dyskinesia and seizure-like phenomena”
  • Age and opioids lower requirements, but the sources give different figures. MAC falls by 4–6 % per decade, depending on the source. Opioids lower MAC, but with a ceiling. High doses can stop spontaneous breathing without the patient losing consciousness.See
  • The dose is a prediction, not a measurement. The numbers on the pump and in the tables apply to an average patient. With fast induction the pump showed almost double the concentration of slow induction, for the same endpoint. After brief burst suppression the same calculated concentration gave a deeper effect than the model predicted. The brain's response must therefore be observed.See

Each drug has its own sub-tab. The basic concepts of receptors and circuits are below this overview.

Basic concepts: receptors, ion channels and circuits
Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025 Purdon 2015 Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010

Each drug below has its own section on the micro level: which receptors the drug binds to, what happens in the nerve cell, and which circuits are affected. Much of this knowledge comes from animal experiments, cell studies and modelling. The mechanisms are probable, not fully mapped.

  • The GABAA receptor comes in many variants. It is a chloride channel made of five subunits. It can be built from 18 or more different subunits, and the α subunit exists in six variants (α1–α6). Different parts of the brain have different combinations. The drugs bind at the interfaces between subunits, and the combination determines how well, for example, propofol, etomidate or pentobarbital binds.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • When the channel opens, the nerve cell is inhibited. Chloride flows in, the cell membrane is hyperpolarised, and it takes more for the nerve cell to fire. This is why the GABA system is called inhibitory.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • The drugs enhance GABA, and at high doses activate the channel themselves. At clinical concentrations propofol, barbiturates and etomidate enhance the action of GABA, so less GABA is needed. At higher concentrations they can open the channel directly, without GABA. Benzodiazepines only enhance the GABA response.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • The hippocampus has its own sustained inhibition. It has many GABAA receptors with the α5 subunit, which is almost absent elsewhere in the cortex. They give sustained (tonic) inhibition of CA1 pyramidal cells and regulate long-term potentiation (LTP) with stimulation in the theta range. This is linked to amnesia, see etomidate and inhaled agents.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Ketamine blocks the NMDA receptor only when the channel is open. The NMDA receptor is a glutamate-gated ion channel, and ketamine is a channel blocker.Source: Purdon 2015
  • α2 adrenoceptors act via G proteins. They inhibit adenylate cyclase and affect calcium and potassium channels.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Wakefulness is maintained by several arousal centres. These are nuclei in the brainstem, hypothalamus and basal forebrain: locus coeruleus (noradrenaline), raphe (serotonin), tuberomammillary nucleus (histamine), ventral tegmental area (dopamine), basal forebrain and the laterodorsal and pedunculopontine tegmental nuclei (acetylcholine), and lateral hypothalamus (orexin). The preoptic area of the hypothalamus sends inhibitory GABA and galanin pathways to these centres. Activation of these pathways is thought to be a key part of how NREM sleep begins.Sources: Brown 2010, Purdon 2015
  • The EEG signatures reflect receptors and circuits. The signatures are thought to arise because the drugs act on specific receptors in specific circuits. With propofol, thalamus and cortex do not switch off when inhibited. They are tightly connected and instead oscillate in rhythms such as alpha and beta.Source: Purdon 2015
  • Interactions give clues about the site of action. Additivity suggests a shared site, synergy different sites. See the card «Synergy between agents and isoelectric EEG».Source: Hendrickx 2008

Slow waves do not mean the same for every drug

An EEG dominated by slow waves is easily read as deep hypnosis. But its meaning depends on which drug produces the waves, and on what happens in the circuits behind them.

  • Dexmedetomidine resembles sleep. During deep dexmedetomidine sedation the EEG resembled NREM sleep stage 2. The spindles were like those in normal sleep, but lasted longer (1.11 vs 0.88 seconds). The patient could be roused with verbal commands, even at 5.1 ng/ml. Spindles and slow waves are smaller than under propofol, which may explain why the patient can be roused. The study is small, with one channel.Sources: Huupponen 2008 (and an earlier study by the same group), Purdon 2015
  • The cortex stays in contact. During dexmedetomidine-induced loss of consciousness, coupling between the thalamus and the default mode network was disrupted, but coupling between cortical areas was preserved. The authors propose a hierarchy: lighter states (NREM 2 sleep, dexmedetomidine) disrupt thalamocortical coupling. Deeper states (propofol anaesthesia) also disrupt cortical coupling. Caveat: connectivity in fMRI is co-variation, not directly measured communication between nerve cells.Source: Akeju, Loggia et al. 2014
  • The starting point is the locus coeruleus. Dexmedetomidine hyperpolarises nerve cells in the locus coeruleus. Less noradrenaline is then released, and the preoptic area inhibits the arousal centres. In rats, antisense against α2A in the locus coeruleus delayed and shortened loss of righting reflex, while antisense against α2C had no effect (4–5 rats per group). Mice that cannot make noradrenaline are nevertheless hypersensitive to dexmedetomidine. This suggests that other mechanisms also exist.Sources: Purdon 2015, Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025, Mizobe 1996
  • Clonidine gives partly real hypnosis. Propofol and clonidine were additive for hypnosis, and clonidine lowered sevoflurane MAC-awake by 17–21 %, with a ceiling. No spectral study of clonidine combined with propofol or a volatile agent was found. When dexmedetomidine was given under propofol, delta–theta rose from 4.5 to 7.7 dB and PSI fell from 30 to 23, but consciousness was not tested. Interpretation based on the sources: increased delta after clonidine should not be read as just as much deeper hypnosis as the same change after more propofol. Nor should the volatile agent be lowered below what is needed for unconsciousness.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, Zhang 2021, Hight 2020
  • Ketamine goes the other way. Ketamine gives an active EEG with generalised theta, plus alternating slow-delta and gamma. Ketamine also increases cerebral metabolism.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025, Akeju

Dexmedetomidine: from the locus coeruleus to a sleep-like state

Sources: Purdon 2015; Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025

The studies in detail:

Huupponen 2008 Akeju, Loggia et al. 2014 Mizobe 1996 Purdon 2015 Hendrickx 2008 Zhang 2021 Hight 2020 Mashour and Pryor 2025; Vuyk et al. 2025
The studies in detail: Morgan and Mikhail (1 card)

What another textbook says: Morgan and Mikhail 2022 (ch. 8, 9 and 43)

Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 7th edition (Butterworth, Mackey, Wasnick, McGraw Hill 2022). The chapters on volatile agents, intravenous agents and geriatric anaesthesia contain little on EEG, but three things are worth keeping alongside Miller's.

  • MAC-awake (Mashour and Pryor 2025): 0.3–0.4 MAC is associated with awakening when the volatile agent is the only thing maintaining the anaesthetic, versus 1.3 MAC to prevent movement in about 95%. It is the distance between “no movement” and “awake” that allows the EEG pattern to look adequate close to emergence (see neural inertia in Hight 2020, Fundamentals tab).
  • MAC and age: Mashour and Pryor 2025 gives a 6% fall in MAC per decade “regardless of agent”, ch. 43 gives 4% per decade over 40 years (see discrepancies). Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025 gives 6% per decade after 30 years (Mapleson 1996).
  • Barbiturates and EEG (Eikermann et al. 2025): the EEG goes from low-voltage fast activity at small doses to high-voltage slow activity, burst suppression and electrical silence at large doses, in parallel with the fall in cerebral metabolism (up to 50%). Thiopental doses that maintain burst suppression or a flat line give prolonged emergence, delayed extubation and a need for inotropes. Ketamine “dissociates” sensory impulses from the limbic cortex, and the patient can look awake (eye opening, swallowing) without being so.
  • Older patients (ch. 43): the chapter says that “some have suggested” that BIS monitoring may reduce cognitive impairment, and that the mechanism of perioperative neurocognitive disorder is unclear. This is more weakly worded than Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025, which proposes pEEG to avoid burst suppression.
Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 7th ed. 2022, ch. 8, 9 and 43
Propofol
EEG signature (Purdon 2015) Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Half lose response at 2.3–3.5 µg/ml. This applies when no other agents are given. In volunteers, half were unresponsive at BIS 63 and 95% at BIS 51.
  • Memory goes before response. 95% had no recall at BIS 77. Amnesia thus sets in at a lighter level of hypnosis than loss of response. Unstimulated volunteers needed an infusion of at least 2 mg/kg/h for amnesia.Sources: Glass 1997; Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Much more propofol is needed to prevent movement. Half did not move at incision at 16 µg/ml without other agents (Sleigh et al. 2025: at least 15). With opioid, markedly less is needed. Muscle tone is reduced, but movement in response to surgical stimulation may occur. Aitkenhead gives lower figures (see Discrepancies).Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025; Aitkenhead ch. 3
  • Awareness can occur shortly after induction. Propofol is rapidly redistributed and metabolised. The risk may increase during intubation after a non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking agent, or at the start of surgery, unless an inhaled agent or more propofol is given.Source: Aitkenhead ch. 3
  • The EEG shows alpha-delta during maintenance. See the Spectrogram tab.
  • Blood pressure falls later than the EEG changes. The half-time for equilibration between blood and effect is about 2.5 minutes for the EEG and about 7 minutes for haemodynamic depression. Hypotension may increase some minutes after loss of consciousness.
  • Older patients need much less, but the numbers differ. The sources disagree on how much less patients aged 80 years or more need than 20-year-olds: about half the dose (Vuyk et al. 2025) or a 65% lower dose (Kim et al. 2025, Schnider 1999).Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Kim et al. 2025; Schnider 1999

The BIS values above are from healthy volunteers. Individual patients can become conscious at BIS values from 40 to 90.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Propofol acts mainly via the β subunit of the GABAA receptor. Sites on β1, β2 and β3 in the part of the receptor that crosses the cell membrane are crucial. The α and γ2 subunits also seem to contribute.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Propofol enhances GABA, and at high concentrations it opens the channel itself. The enhancement shifts the concentration–response curve to the left. At higher concentrations propofol activates the channel directly.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Propofol also acts at many other sites. It inhibits NMDA receptors widely (through modulation of sodium channel gating) and acts on GABAA and glycine receptors in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. It increases dopamine in the nucleus accumbens (well-being), reduces serotonin in the area postrema (antiemetic) and inhibits release of acetylcholine in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. The α2 system seems to play an indirect role in sedation.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • More inhibition in cortex and thalamus gives alpha, beta and slow-delta. In the cortex, propofol enhances the inhibition of pyramidal cells by inhibitory interneurons. In the thalamus, propofol enhances GABA inhibition in the reticular nucleus, which controls what the thalamus passes on to the cortex. Because thalamus and cortex are tightly connected, this produces oscillations in beta and alpha. Propofol also enhances the inhibitory GABA pathways from the preoptic area to the arousal centres, and release of histamine from the tuberomammillary nucleus is inhibited. Less excitatory input from thalamus and brainstem hyperpolarises the cortex and gives slow-delta.Sources: Purdon 2015, Brown 2010
  • After a bolus, propofol probably acts rapidly in the brainstem. Slow-delta appears within seconds, together with loss of response, loss of the oculocephalic reflex, apnoea and atonia. This is interpreted as action on cranial nerve nuclei III, IV and VI (eye movements), the respiratory centres in the medulla and pons (apnoea) and reticular nuclei in the pons and medulla (atonia).Source: Purdon 2015
  • Alpha and slow waves disrupt communication in different ways. Frontal alpha is highly coherent and may arise in circuits between thalamus and frontal cortex. The slow waves are not coherent. Recordings with electrodes in the cortex show that they bracket brief periods of firing. The proposal is that alpha prevents normal communication between thalamus and cortex, and that the slow waves prevent communication within the cortex.Source: Purdon 2015
  • Paradoxical excitation has two proposed explanations. One is GABAA-mediated inhibition of the inhibitory pathways from the globus pallidus to the thalamus, so that the thalamus drives the cortex more. The other (from simulation studies) is transient blockade of slow potassium currents in cortical nerve cells.Source: Purdon 2015
  • Propofol prevents new learning in the hippocampus, but does not weaken what is already learned. When we learn something new, the connections between nerve cells in the hippocampus become stronger and stay strong. This is called long-term potentiation (LTP) and is regarded as a cellular mechanism of learning. Propofol prevents such strengthening from getting started, but does not weaken strengthening that has already taken place. Connections becoming weaker (long-term depression, LTD) is not affected. The effect acts via the GABAA receptor, because it disappears when the receptor is blocked with picrotoxin. In one study, LTP was inhibited only at doses that produce anaesthesia, not at lower doses that only cause memory loss. In addition, the cortex and hippocampus stop oscillating together in the theta rhythm (4–8 Hz), via the β3 subunit of the GABAA receptor. This fits with words learned before propofol being remembered normally in Veselis 2004, while words learned while propofol was acting were lost faster (interpretation based on the sources, see the card on Veselis 2004).Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Physostigmine has reversed propofol-induced unconsciousness. This has been shown in clinical studies. Physostigmine increases cholinergic activity throughout the cortex.Source: Brown 2010
  • Propofol can both suppress seizures and produce epileptiform changes. It suppresses seizures through GABA, NMDA inhibition and slow calcium channels. GABA agonism and glycine antagonism can also produce epileptiform changes, especially at induction and emergence.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
Propofol and involuntary movements: dyskinesia and seizure-like phenomena
Walder 2002 San-juan 2010 Lee 2020 Bilotta 2006 Reddy 1993
  • Seizure-like phenomena with propofol fall into five groups. Generalised tonic-clonic seizures, focal motor seizures, increased tone with twitching and rhythmic movements, opisthotonus (arched back) and involuntary movements. The first three most resemble epilepsy.Sources: Walder 2002, as reported in San-juan 2010
  • It happens mostly at induction and emergence, rarely during maintenance. Among published cases without known epilepsy, 34% came at induction, 40% at emergence and 23% delayed after anaesthesia. Only 2 of 70 came during maintenance. Patients with epilepsy had them mostly at emergence. That it is rare during maintenance may be because neuromuscular blockade hides the movements.Sources: Walder 2002, as reported in San-juan 2010; Kumar 2021
  • Serious events are rare, but movements at induction are more common. In adults, 5.5% had movements with propofol, versus 86.6% with etomidate. In children, 3 mg/kg gave spontaneous movements in 90%, versus 20% at 4 mg/kg.Sources: Reddy 1993, Borgeat 1997
  • Repeated boluses for sedation give more movement than infusion. During ERCP, 21% had involuntary movements with boluses, versus 3.5% with continuous infusion. The authors link this to the peaks and troughs in concentration that boluses produce.Source: Lee 2020
  • There are several possible explanations. Glycine antagonism in structures below the cortex, enhanced GABA inhibition giving uncoordinated oscillations, or an imbalance between acetylcholine and dopamine in the basal ganglia triggered by a rapid change in propofol concentration. In the laboratory, propofol is mainly anticonvulsant but also has a weaker pro-convulsant effect.Sources: San-juan 2010, Jeon 2007, Voss 2015
  • Patients with Parkinson's disease can develop dyskinesias. Patients operated on off levodopa developed dyskinesias resembling their levodopa dyskinesias. One patient had severe dyskinesia about 20 minutes after a small propofol dose.Sources: Krauss 1996, Nakajima 2022
  • Lidocaine, fentanyl and infusion can reduce movements. Lidocaine 2 mg/kg before propofol in 358 children gave movements in 2.5% versus 29% with saline, but more coughing (62.5 versus 17.5%). Fentanyl 1.5 µg/kg gave fewer excitatory events (1 of 32 versus 13 of 32). For sedation, continuous infusion can be used instead of boluses.Sources: Bilotta 2006, Middle East J Anesthesiol 1996, Lee 2020
  • It usually resolves on its own. In the case reports it lasts from a few hours to 21 days. Benzodiazepines have had variable effect.Source: Tam 2009
  • The EEG is usually normal, but that does not exclude seizures. Of 24 patients who had an EEG after the episode, 5 were abnormal. Another study found no seizure activity with propofol. But a normal scalp EEG does not exclude epileptic activity deeper in the brain, and in one patient polyspike-and-wave complexes coincided with the jerks.Sources: Walder, as reported in San-juan 2010; Reddy 1993; Voss 2015; Jeon 2007
  • The movements can make the patient look light on the monitor (interpretation based on the sources). Muscle artefact raises the index. Look at the raw EEG and the patient. For prolonged, recurrent or delayed episodes, or known epilepsy, a full EEG should be considered.
Midazolam (benzodiazepines)
Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Hypnosis and amnesia during surgery need 100–200 ng/ml in plasma. Patients usually wake below 50 ng/ml.
  • Midazolam does not remove memories from before the dose. The amnesia is anterograde, and retrograde memory is not affected. After an anaesthetic dose the amnesia lasts about 1–2 hours.
  • The patient can seem awake and still not remember. During benzodiazepine sedation patients can be awake and coherent and still not remember the procedure. This is scenario 1 in the Components tab.
  • Flumazenil reverses sleep and respiratory depression more than amnesia. This is usually the case. It is a pharmacological example of how amnesia and sedation can be separated.
  • Different subunits may underlie amnesia for different agents. For benzodiazepines, sedation and anterograde amnesia are linked to GABA-A receptors with the α1 subunit. For etomidate in mice, amnesia is linked to α5 subunits. These are not necessarily contradictions.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Older patients need less.Source: Jacobs 1995
  • Poisoning can cause “beta coma”, which usually resolves. In poisoning with and withdrawal from benzodiazepines and barbiturates, beta (12–16 Hz) is seen, mostly frontal, mixed with spindle-like activity, alpha or delta. It is largely reversible with a good prognosis. Alpha coma and spindle coma can also be seen in poisoning. See the simulator in the Spectrogram tab and the alpha coma case in the Intensive care tab.Source: Sutter and Kaplan 2012
  • Midazolam at sedative doses is associated with beta, which can resemble ketamine. A child who received ketamine and midazolam as premedication had beta and gamma at the start. The authors think this probably reflects both drugs together. What the EEG looks like at higher doses of midazolam is not described in the sources here.Source: Brandt 2020

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Benzodiazepines enhance GABA at the GABAA receptor. They facilitate opening of the chloride channel, and the cell is hyperpolarised. The benzodiazepine site is different from the site where propofol, barbiturates and etomidate act.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025, Hendrickx 2008
  • Each subunit accounts for different effects. α1 is linked to sedation, anterograde amnesia and anticonvulsant effect, α2 to anxiolysis and muscle relaxation. α2 and α3 are linked to the rewarding effects and thus addiction.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Where the receptors are: highest density in the olfactory bulb, cerebral cortex, cerebellum, hippocampus, substantia nigra and inferior colliculus, lower in the striatum, lower brainstem and spinal cord.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Lorazepam is the most potent, diazepam the least. Affinity is lorazepam > midazolam > diazepam. Midazolam is about 3–6 and lorazepam 5–10 times as potent as diazepam.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Midazolam alone cannot abolish movement, propofol alone can. Midazolam alone cannot fully abolish movement to noxious stimuli, whereas propofol alone can. This is one argument that the drugs act differently, even though both act through GABAA, and that the combination is therefore synergistic.Source: Hendrickx 2008
  • The effect of flumazenil depends on how much agonist occupies the receptors. Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist with high affinity and almost no intrinsic effect. After a very high agonist dose, a small dose of flumazenil attenuates the deep CNS depression (unconsciousness, respiratory depression) without reducing the effects that need only low receptor occupancy (drowsiness, amnesia). Large doses of flumazenil with little agonist reverse everything. Flumazenil is cleared rapidly, so sedation can return.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Remimazolam is broken down quickly and does not accumulate. It resembles midazolam and binds selectively to the benzodiazepine site. Tissue esterases rapidly break down a carboxylic ester side chain to an inactive metabolite (CNS7054), not via CYP. Clearance is about 70 l/h, and long infusions do not cause accumulation. Pharmacokinetics were unchanged in end-stage renal failure, but caution is advised in hepatic failure, and lower doses should be considered in the frail elderly. Flumazenil reverses it in about 1 minute (10.5 minutes with placebo) without resedation. For endoscopy, sedation success was comparable to propofol and better than midazolam.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Remimazolam and propofol gave broadly similar EEGs at induction in older patients. In a randomised substudy of 52 patients over 65, patients received remimazolam 6 mg/kg/h or propofol TCI 3.5 µg/ml, both with remifentanil. Remimazolam produced alpha and delta, and there were no significant differences in spectral power or BIS. Both produced alpha anteriorisation and reduced frontal-to-parietal feedback connectivity. Only induction was measured, and no patient had burst suppression. The study was partly funded by Hana Pharmaceutical, which according to the article had no role in the analysis. Interpretation based on the sources: that remimazolam produced alpha and delta, whereas midazolam is linked to beta, may reflect dose (anaesthesia vs sedation) and is not necessarily a difference between the drugs.Sources: Kim 2024, Brandt 2020
Propofol and midazolam: alone, together and in withdrawal
Vuyk et al. 2025; Kim et al. 2025 Hendrickx 2008 Olsen and Liang 2017 Lorentzen 2014 Shah 2018 Zhou 2014
  • Midazolam needs GABA to work, and its effect has a ceiling. It binds the benzodiazepine site on the GABAA receptor and enhances the response to GABA by facilitating chloride channel opening. Alone, it cannot fully abolish movement to noxious stimuli.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025, Hendrickx 2008
  • Propofol can open the channel without GABA. It binds the β subunit, a different site. At clinical concentrations propofol enhances GABA. At higher concentrations it can open the channel directly. Propofol also inhibits NMDA receptors.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • The sources disagree on whether the combination is synergistic or additive. Because the drugs bind different sites, several studies found synergy for hypnosis, and midazolam often acts synergistically with other hypnotics (Vuyk et al. 2025). Kim et al. 2025 instead calls the interaction «primarily additive», see Discrepancies.Sources: Hendrickx 2008 (Short and Chui 1991, McClune 1992, Short 1992); Vuyk et al. 2025; Kim et al. 2025
  • The drugs also raise each other's blood concentrations. A sedative midazolam concentration (200 ng/ml) raises propofol concentration by about 25 %, probably via altered circulation and hepatic perfusion. Propofol raises midazolam concentration by 27 %. Propofol also inhibits CYP3A4, which metabolises midazolam (about 37 % lower activity at 3 µg/ml). Interpretation based on the sources: both synergy and higher concentrations point towards lower dose requirements when the drugs are given together.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • In the ICU, switching from midazolam to propofol before waking gave faster extubation and less agitation. Benzodiazepines give amnesia and haemodynamic stability, but accumulate (active metabolite, especially in renal failure) and cause more delirium than dexmedetomidine. Propofol gives fast awakening but more hypotension. In a randomised, open-label, single-centre study (n=124 ventilated patients), time to extubation was 45 hours with midazolam alone, 3 hours with propofol alone and 2 hours after switching. Hypotension: 23 %, 52 % and 21 %. Agitation after stopping: 49 % with midazolam alone vs 19 % after switching. The authors suggest propofol may mask midazolam withdrawal. Note: this was switching, not simultaneous use, and patients with alcoholism were excluded.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025, Zhou 2014

Micro level: why benzodiazepines can fail in alcohol withdrawal

  • Alcohol enhances GABAA and inhibits NMDA. With chronic use GABAA function weakens. When alcohol is withdrawn, the NMDA system is left unopposed.Sources: Lorentzen 2014, Shah 2018
  • Repeated alcohol remodels the receptors (rat). A «subunit switch» occurs: extrasynaptic δ-containing receptors (tonic inhibition) and α1 are down-regulated, while α4, γ2 and α2 are up-regulated. The rats became tolerant to the sedative effect of alcohol, benzodiazepines and neurosteroids, while anticonvulsant and anxiolytic effects showed little tolerance. After repeated cycles the changes lasted at least 120 days. In humans this is a hypothesis.Source: Olsen and Liang 2017
  • Clinicians explain the resistance by «saturated» receptors and an overactive NMDA system. GABAA receptors become «saturated», and benzodiazepines have no effect on the overactive NMDA system.Sources: Lorentzen 2014, Shah 2018
  • Propofol acts on both systems. Propofol has a «dual effect»: GABAA via a different site and NMDA inhibition. Interpretation based on the sources: since propofol at higher concentrations can open the channel without GABA, it is biologically plausible that it works where benzodiazepines have reached their ceiling. This is not tested in the sources.Source: Lorentzen 2014
  • Propofol successfully treated 12 of 15 with benzodiazepine-refractory delirium tremens. The study was retrospective. The patients had not responded to up to 2000 mg benzodiazepines. They received propofol a mean 4.22 mg/kg/h over 48 hours (max 5.65), RASS −4 to −5, ventilated. 7 of 15 developed pneumonia, none developed propofol infusion syndrome, and mean ICU stay was 4.67 days.Source: Lorentzen 2014
  • Ketamine is an alternative, but most patients were intubated. Retrospective study, n=30 with benzodiazepine-resistant withdrawal (more than 40 mg diazepam per hour). Ketamine blocks NMDA directly. Lorazepam requirement fell by 4 mg/h at 24 hours, but 73 % were intubated.Source: Shah 2018
  • Caveats: the studies are small, retrospective and uncontrolled. Deep sedation with propofol requires a secured airway. The sources here concern alcohol withdrawal. Other poisonings (mixed overdose, stimulants, GHB) are not covered. EEG in benzodiazepine poisoning and withdrawal (beta coma) is described in the midazolam card.
Ketamine
EEG “gamma burst” (Akeju, 12 patients) Vuyk et al. 2025; Patel et al. 2025
  • Ketamine gives dissociative anaesthesia, not sleep. The patient may have open eyes and some reflexes left. Do not assume that the reflexes are protective.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Pain is dampened at far lower levels than those causing unconsciousness. The pain threshold is raised from 0.1 µg/ml. General anaesthesia requires at least 0.6–2 µg/ml.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • The patient does not recall surgery, but the amnesia is weaker than with benzodiazepines.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Ketamine increases brain metabolism. Both CMRO₂ and blood flow increase.Sources: Patel et al. 2025; Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Theta is the shared finding in the EEG under ketamine. Miller's describes generalised theta and seizure-like (petit mal) activity in the hippocampus, but not gamma or slow-delta. Akeju also describes alternating slow-delta and gamma. The sources thus differ in scope rather than conflict.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Akeju

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Ketamine blocks the NMDA receptor. Ketamine is a channel blocker. The channel therefore has to be open for ketamine to act.Source: Purdon 2015
  • At low to moderate doses the inhibitory interneurons are hit first. Their NMDA channels are generally more active than those of pyramidal cells. The pyramidal cells then become less inhibited. This may explain increased metabolism, and that cortex, hippocampus and amygdala keep communicating but without coordination in time and space. The result is hallucinations, dissociation, euphoria and dysphoria. At higher doses the NMDA receptors on the excitatory nerve cells are also blocked, and consciousness is lost.Sources: Purdon 2015; Brown 2010
  • The hallucinations are probably enhanced by disrupted dopamine transmission in the prefrontal cortex. This is partly due to increased glutamate activity at glutamate receptors other than NMDA.Source: Purdon 2015
  • Ketamine also acts on several other receptors. These include opioid receptors and monoaminergic receptors. At high concentrations sigma receptors are also affected, muscarinic receptors are blocked and GABA transmission is facilitated. S(+)-ketamine has some μ-opioid activity. Experiments in μ-knockout mice suggest that the μ system contributes to respiratory depression and supraspinal antinociception. Increased activity in the locus coeruleus appears to contribute to the anaesthetic effect.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Ketamine dampens pain already in the spinal cord. The spinal analgesia is linked to inhibition of wide dynamic range neurons in the dorsal horn. Ketamine also inhibits central sensitisation and opioid-induced hyperalgesia. Purdon 2015 places the analgesia at «the dorsal root ganglia, the first synapse of the pain pathway in the spinal cord».Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Purdon 2015
  • Ketamine causes functional disorganisation, not uniform depression. Parts of the cortex (especially association areas) and the thalamus are depressed, while limbic areas, including the hippocampus, are stimulated. Many anaesthetics reduce metabolism in the thalamus, but ketamine is the exception.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • The active EEG fits with the disinhibition. At a low dose of ketamine alone, beta–gamma at about 25–32 Hz is seen. No specific antagonist reverses all the effects of ketamine.Sources: Purdon; Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Ketamine also inhibits the HCN1 channel. HCN1 is activated by hyperpolarisation and is important for rhythmic activity. Mice lacking HCN1 do not lose the righting reflex with ketamine. Propofol also inhibits HCN1. The proposal is that frontal gamma results from NMDA-mediated disinhibition (counteracted by the GABA effect of propofol), while the shared HCN1 inhibition may explain why occipital alpha falls further when propofol is added. See the card in the Components tab.Source: Tian 2023
  • Under ketamine, sensory information stops before the motor cortex. In monkeys the signals reached the primary somatosensory cortex but did not pass on to the motor cortex. The directed coupling between neurons in the two areas fell.Source: Schroeder 2016
Ketamine in refractory status epilepticus: when GABAergic drugs lose their grip
Espinosa 2023 Gaspard 2013
  • In continuous seizures, GABAA receptors disappear from the cell surface. After a few minutes they move into the cell («internalisation»), while more glutamate and NMDA receptors move out to the surface («externalisation»). Inhibition weakens and excitation increases. This has been shown in animal models.Source: Espinosa 2023
  • Benzodiazepines work less well the longer the seizure lasts. It is not GABA that is missing, but the receptors the drugs act on. Sensitivity to GABA agonists declines with prolonged seizures, whereas sensitivity to NMDA antagonists does not.Source: Gaspard 2013
  • Ketamine targets the part of the system that is up-regulated. Ketamine blocks the NMDA receptor and causes little respiratory or cardiovascular depression.Source: Gaspard 2013
  • Ketamine may help control seizures, but probably only at a high enough dose and if not started too late. In a retrospective study from ten centres (58 patients), 57 % achieved permanent seizure control. Ketamine was always given with other drugs, and the response was judged likely in only 12 % and possible in 20 %. Likely responses required at least 0.9 mg/kg/h and were not seen when ketamine was started 8 days or more after onset, or after 7 or more failed drugs. Mortality was 43 %: 16 % when seizures were controlled within 24 hours of ketamine vs 56 % otherwise. ICP did not rise in monitored patients, except two with anoxic cerebral oedema.Source: Gaspard 2013
  • The evidence does not support ketamine as first choice or monotherapy. A scoping review found about 20 publications, mostly case reports and small series, with widely varying doses (loading 0.5–5 mg/kg, infusion 0.05–10.5 mg/kg/h). Of 19 case reports, 63 % achieved complete seizure control, usually within 12 hours, but seizures recurred in 10–60 % after withdrawal. Adverse effects were arrhythmias, cardiovascular collapse and metabolic acidosis, with unclear causality in patients on many drugs.Source: Espinosa 2023
  • The pattern resembles alcohol withdrawal. Interpretation based on the sources: there too GABAA function is weakened and the NMDA system overactive, and ketamine and propofol are used when benzodiazepines fail (the propofol and midazolam card above).
  • Ketamine does not cause classic burst suppression. Continuous EEG is used to guide treatment and to detect non-convulsive seizures (Intensive care tab). Ketamine produces a more activated EEG with beta and gamma, and not classic burst suppression at clinical doses (see the ketamine card). Interpretation based on the sources: the treatment target should therefore be judged on the raw EEG.
  • Caveats: no randomised trials. Gaspard 2013 is retrospective and may be biased, because the most severe cases more often received ketamine. Several authors disclose ties to the pharmaceutical industry (including UCB, GSK and Pfizer). Espinosa 2023 reports no conflicts of interest.
Dexmedetomidine
EEG (Akeju 2016, 8 volunteers) Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • The patient can be roused. Patients can be roused and follow commands, and fall asleep when not stimulated. The pattern resembles natural NREM sleep.
  • Low concentrations give rousable sedation, high concentrations deep sedation. Rousable sedation at about 0.2–0.3 ng/ml. Above about 1.9 ng/ml the patient cannot be roused.Source: Ebert 2000
  • The patient may remember more than with propofol. In intensive care, patients on dexmedetomidine remembered more of their stay than patients on propofol. In an experimental low-dose study, memory encoding failed. The findings are not directly comparable.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Hysteresis: dexmedetomidine increases neural inertia.Source: Sleigh et al. 2025

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Receptor: α2 agonist. Dexmedetomidine acts at G-protein-coupled α2 adrenoceptors. Inside the cell, adenylate cyclase and L- and P-type calcium channels are inhibited, and calcium-activated potassium channels conduct more easily.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Subtypes: α2A, α2B and α2C. α2A is mainly peripheral, α2B and α2C are in the brain and spinal cord. Analgesia in the dorsal horn is linked to α2C and α2A. In rodents, removing α2A receptors from the locus coeruleus prevents dexmedetomidine-induced loss of righting reflex (see Discrepancies in the Sources tab).Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Circuit: less noradrenaline from the locus coeruleus. Dexmedetomidine binds presynaptically on nerve cells from the locus coeruleus and hyperpolarises them, so that less noradrenaline is released. This removes the inhibition of the preoptic area. The preoptic area then inhibits the arousal centres with GABA and galanin, including histamine release from the tuberomammillary nucleus. In addition, the basal forebrain, the intralaminar thalamic nuclei and the cortex lose their noradrenaline supply.Sources: Purdon 2015, Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Animal studies point to the locus coeruleus, but not only there. Microinjection of dexmedetomidine into the locus coeruleus lowers the level of consciousness, and the α2 antagonist atipamezole prevents this. Mice that cannot make noradrenaline are hypersensitive to dexmedetomidine. This suggests that other mechanisms also exist.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • To the EEG: spindles and slow-delta, but weaker than with propofol. The spindles (9–15 Hz) probably arise, like propofol frontal alpha and sleep spindles, in loops between thalamus and cortex, but they are brief and episodic. Slow-delta arises because the cortex receives less excitatory input. Both spindles and slow waves are smaller than under propofol. Purdon interprets this as less disruption of nerve cell activity, and as a possible explanation for why the patient can be roused.Source: Purdon 2015
  • Cognition may be better preserved. Data suggest that reduced expression of α5-GABAA receptors after anaesthesia may contribute to better preserved cognition with dexmedetomidine.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Reversal: atipamezole, but not in humans. The α2 antagonist atipamezole reverses the effect, but is not approved for humans.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • α2A in the locus coeruleus matters for loss of consciousness in rats. Antisense against α2A in the locus coeruleus delayed and shortened loss of righting reflex after dexmedetomidine. Antisense against α2C had no effect. See the card below and Discrepancies.Source: Mizobe 1996
  • The thalamus disconnects, while the cortex stays connected. During dexmedetomidine-induced loss of consciousness, coupling between cortical areas was preserved. Coupling between the thalamus and the default mode network was disrupted. See the card below.Source: Akeju, Loggia et al. 2014
  • The spindles resemble NREM 2 sleep, but last longer. During deep sedation, spindles had the same density, amplitude and frequency as spindles in normal NREM 2 sleep. See the card below.Source: Huupponen 2008
Clonidine
Vuyk et al. 2025; Patel et al. 2025; Fukuda 2025 Hendrickx 2008 Hight 2020 Giovannitti 2015 Zhang 2021
  • Clonidine is an α2 agonist that is less selective and less potent than dexmedetomidine. The ratio of α2 to α1 binding is about 220:1, versus 1600:1 for dexmedetomidine.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Patel et al. 2025
  • Clonidine paved the way for dexmedetomidine. Experience with patients taking clonidine showed that α2 agonists could be used in anaesthesia. One study found lower halothane MAC in such patients.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Clonidine lowers MAC, but the effect has a ceiling. In humans, MAC fell by about 30% for isoflurane and 17–34% for sevoflurane. MAC-awake fell by 30% (isoflurane) and 17–21% (sevoflurane). In children, doubling the dose did not further reduce sevoflurane MAC-awake. Clonidine alone does not produce immobility at clinically used doses.Source: Hendrickx 2008
  • Clonidine enhances other hypnotics. With propofol the effect was additive in humans. With midazolam it was synergistic in rats. Fentanyl and clonidine produced hypnosis together in animals even though neither did alone. The infusion dose should be reduced when clonidine is combined with propofol.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Clonidine does not enhance opioid respiratory depression. This applies to fentanyl and other opioids. Intravenous clonidine abolished the sympathetic activation from μ blockade in opioid-dependent patients, and α2 agonists can suppress fentanyl cough.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • The EEG resembles sleep, and hysteresis is more marked. α2 agonists such as dexmedetomidine and clonidine produce a slow-wave-dominant EEG with intermittent spindles, sharing features with sleep stages 2 and 3. Take care when lowering the inhaled agent concentration below that needed for unconsciousness.Source: Hight 2020
  • EEG when clonidine is added to propofol or a volatile agent: more hypnosis or just a different EEG? A question from the author of the app. The sources give a split answer.
    • Part of the effect is real hypnosis: propofol and clonidine were additive for hypnosis in humans, and clonidine lowered MAC-awake for sevoflurane by 17–21 %. The infusion dose should be lower when clonidine is combined with propofol.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, Vuyk et al. 2025
    • The EEG change in combination has only been studied for dexmedetomidine: there is no study of clonidine plus propofol or volatile agent with spectral analysis. When dexmedetomidine was given under propofol, the alpha peak fell (but the confidence interval crossed zero), delta–theta rose, and PSI fell from 30 to 23. The authors interpret this as deeper anaesthesia, but consciousness was not tested, because the patients were already unconscious.Source: Zhang 2021 (21 patients)
    • Slow waves from α2 agonists do not mean the same as from propofol: under dexmedetomidine alone the patient can be roused even though the EEG is dominated by slow waves and spindles (see dexmedetomidine).Source: Purdon 2015 Part I
    • Ceiling: doubling the clonidine dose gave no further fall in MAC-awake for sevoflurane in children.Source: Hendrickx 2008
    • Interpretation based on the sources: the answer is probably both. Part of the alpha loss and delta increase reflects a real, additive hypnotic effect, and the propofol or volatile dose can then be reduced somewhat. But increased delta after clonidine should not be read as just as much deeper hypnosis as the same change after more propofol. The hypnotic should not be reduced just because the index falls, and the volatile agent should not be lowered below what is needed for unconsciousness when clonidine has been given. Remember also that alpha loss can have other causes, such as nociception.Sources: Hight 2020, García 2021
  • Clonidine is long-acting: the half-life is 12–16 hours. Clonidine is the original α2 agonist. It is used mostly for hypertension, but also for anxiety, ADHD, chronic pain, withdrawal and postoperative shivering. About 50% is metabolised in the liver, and 40–60% is excreted unchanged in the urine.Source: Giovannitti 2015
  • Abrupt withdrawal can cause rebound hypertension. After long-term use, blood pressure can rise up to 20 hours after the last dose. An early case report described a hypertensive crisis when one dose was withheld before anaesthesia. At initiation, blood pressure may rise transiently because peripheral postjunctional α1 receptors are stimulated.Source: Giovannitti 2015
  • As premedication in children, clonidine gives better mask acceptance than midazolam, but acts later. Clonidine improves mask acceptance at induction and reduces anaesthetic requirements by 40–60% (see Discrepancies). In a study of 45 children (2–8 years), oral clonidine gave better sedation, separation and mask acceptance and less shivering than midazolam. Onset was after 60 minutes, versus 30 for midazolam.Source: Giovannitti 2015

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Receptor: α2 adrenoceptors, like dexmedetomidine. The receptors are G-protein-coupled and inhibit adenylate cyclase (see dexmedetomidine). The circuit mechanism (locus coeruleus and preoptic area) is described for dexmedetomidine, not specifically for clonidine.
  • Imidazoline receptors may contribute to bradycardia. Clonidine and dexmedetomidine both belong to the imidazole subclass. The clinically available α2 agonists have an imidazole ring that also activates imidazoline binding sites, and they do not discriminate between α2 subtypes. Bradycardia may partly be due to imidazoline receptors in the brainstem.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025, Mizobe 1996
  • Neuroprotection in animals. Clonidine lowered plasma catecholamines and improved outcome after incomplete ischaemia in rats.Source: Patel et al. 2025
  • Signalling pathway: less noradrenaline gives sedation and lower heart rate and blood pressure. All three α2 subtypes inhibit adenylate cyclase. In the locus coeruleus, lower cAMP leads to potassium efflux through calcium-activated channels, calcium cannot enter the nerve terminal, and firing is suppressed. Less noradrenaline and less activity in the ascending noradrenergic pathways give hypnosis and sedation. The same negative feedback lowers heart rate and blood pressure and dampens the stress response.Source: Giovannitti 2015
  • Subtypes: α2A and α2C act centrally, α2B in the vessel wall. α2A and α2C are found mainly in the central nervous system and probably account for sedation, analgesia and sympatholysis. α2B is found mostly on vascular smooth muscle and causes vasoconstriction.Source: Giovannitti 2015
  • Most of the analgesia happens in the spinal cord. α2 receptors in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord inhibit nociceptive neurons and reduce substance P release. There is also evidence for supraspinal and peripheral sites.Source: Giovannitti 2015
Dexmedetomidine and clonidine compared
Mashour and Pryor 2025; Patel et al. 2025; Vuyk et al. 2025 Giovannitti 2015 Hendrickx 2008 Walsh 2025 (A2B)

Both are α2 agonists (they stimulate the receptor); atipamezole is an example of an α2 antagonist. Even so, they are quite different.

  • Dexmedetomidine is much more selective for α2. Dexmedetomidine binds α2 over α1 in a ratio of about 1600:1, clonidine about 220:1. Clonidine is also less potent. Clonidine's α1 effect can cause a transient rise in blood pressure at the start.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Patel et al. 2025, Giovannitti 2015
  • Both act in the locus coeruleus. Dexmedetomidine being “more specific” refers to the receptor type (α2 over α1), not the brain region. The animal studies linking loss of consciousness to α2A receptors in the locus coeruleus were done with dexmedetomidine. The sources do not describe a separate circuit mechanism for clonidine.Sources: Mashour and Pryor 2025, Mizobe 1996
  • Both have an imidazole ring. They can therefore also activate imidazoline binding sites, which may contribute to bradycardia.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025, Mizobe 1996
  • Clonidine lasts much longer and is harder to titrate. The half-life is 12–16 hours for clonidine (the A2B protocol gives about 13 hours), versus about 2 hours for dexmedetomidine. Clonidine therefore takes longer to wear off.Sources: Giovannitti 2015, A2B protocol
  • Clonidine has a ceiling, dexmedetomidine can give deep sedation. Clonidine lowers MAC-awake for sevoflurane by 17–21 %, but no further. Dexmedetomidine gives rousable sedation at 0.2–0.3 ng/ml and non-rousable sedation above about 1.9 ng/ml.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, Ebert 2000
  • Both give a sleep-like EEG. The pattern has slow waves and spindles. Spectral studies exist for dexmedetomidine, but not for clonidine in the sources here.Sources: Hight 2020; Akeju, Purdon, Huupponen
  • In intensive care, neither gave faster extubation than propofol. Both caused more agitation (RR 1.54 and 1.55) and more severe bradycardia (RR 1.62 and 1.58). Clonidine is not licensed for ICU sedation in the UK, but is much cheaper.Source: Walsh 2025 (A2B)
Dexmedetomidine in children: maturation, circulation and pallor
Chrysostomou 2014 Morse 2020 Janse van Rensburg 2025 Potts 2010 Yuen 2008, 2010
  • Newborns break down dexmedetomidine more slowly. The younger the child, the lower the clearance and the longer the half-life. The half-life is 7.6 hours in preterm infants and 3.2 hours in term infants. Term newborns have about 42% of adult clearance, and by 3 years it is about 80%. The half-life is about 2.3 hours under 2 years and 1.6 hours at 2–11 years.Sources: Chrysostomou 2014, Morse 2020, Janse van Rensburg 2025
  • The liver enzymes are not fully developed at birth. Dexmedetomidine is broken down in the liver, partly via CYP2A6 and partly by direct glucuronidation (UGT1A4 and UGT2B10). On cardiopulmonary bypass, clearance falls by about 95%.Sources: Precedex prescribing information, Janse van Rensburg 2025
  • Intranasally, it works after 20–30 minutes. The dose is 2–3 µg/kg, and the effect lasts about 85 minutes. 0.5 and 1 µg/kg gave more sedation at separation from the parents than midazolam.Sources: Janse van Rensburg 2025, Yuen 2010, Yuen 2008
  • Blood pressure and heart rate fall slightly. In a meta-analysis of 13 RCTs, intranasal dexmedetomidine lowered systolic blood pressure by 6.7 mmHg and heart rate by 6.8 beats/min compared with control. A review reports hypotension and bradycardia in 10–20%, and transient hypertension via peripheral α2B receptors.Sources: Can J Anesth 2017, JPPT 2010
  • Low concentrations lower blood pressure, high concentrations raise it. In children, low concentrations lowered blood pressure (half effect at 0.10 µg/L, maximum −12.3 mmHg). Higher concentrations raised it (half effect at 1.1 µg/L, maximum +50.3 mmHg). Above about 1 µg/L, mean arterial pressure rose about 20%. The rise comes from peripheral vasoconstriction.Source: Potts 2010
  • Pallor is not documented as a side effect. No peer-reviewed source describes pallor as a side effect of intranasal dexmedetomidine in children. The closest is a case report of local vasoconstriction in a newborn after a block with dexmedetomidine. A possible explanation is that α2B receptors in skin vessels constrict, while a lower heart rate gives a lower cardiac output. This is an interpretation based on the sources, not a documented explanation. In practice: check heart rate, blood pressure and capillary refill. If the circulation is otherwise good, the pallor is probably harmless, but that is not documented either.Source: Guensch 2023 (only the title was read)
  • Whether maturation of the noradrenaline system affects sensitivity has not been studied. No studies link the maturation of the locus coeruleus or the noradrenaline system in children to how sensitive they are to dexmedetomidine. The experiment with mice lacking noradrenaline concerns genetically modified animals and cannot be transferred directly. In 7-day-old rats, dexmedetomidine was not neurotoxic and reduced cell death from isoflurane, but long-term outcome data in children are lacking.Source: Sanders 2009
  • The EEG in children is sleep-like, but infants may lack spindles. Of 107 children given intramuscular dexmedetomidine, 55 reached N3 and 51 N2. Spindles are not synchronous in infants: at 3 months it is normal to lack spindles, and they become synchronous around 2 years of age. Missing spindles under dexmedetomidine in an infant are therefore not a sign that the drug acts differently (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Mason 2012, Yune 2026
The studies in detail: dexmedetomidine and sleep spindles, dexmedetomidine and the thalamus, the α2 receptor (3 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Dexmedetomidine and sleep spindles: like NREM 2 sleep (Huupponen 2008)

Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2008;52:289–294. Eleven healthy young men (20–28 years) received dexmedetomidine as a target-controlled infusion, first 0.5 ng/ml for 25 minutes and then 3.2 ng/ml for 30 minutes. Measured plasma concentration during deep sedation was 5.1 ng/ml (SD 1.0). EEG was recorded from a single frontal channel with the Entropy Module. The control group was ten other healthy people (seven men, 21–43 years) during normal night sleep, with the first sleep cycle analysed.

  • Visual: the EEG during deep dexmedetomidine sedation resembled NREM sleep stage 2, with slight to moderate slow activity and abundant spindles. The low dose (0.5 ng/ml) did not induce sleep in everyone and was excluded from analysis.
  • Quantitative: spindle density (1.17 vs 1.26 per minute), amplitude and frequency (11.5 vs 12.0 Hz) did not differ between groups. Spindles lasted longer under dexmedetomidine (1.11 vs 0.88 seconds, p = 0.0014). The authors mention that longer spindles might mean stronger sleep protection, but call this only one possible explanation.
  • Frequency and origin: frontal spindles are slower than central ones (11–12 Hz frontally vs 13–14 Hz centrally in normal sleep). The authors believe the frontal spindles are probably generated in the mediodorsal thalamic nucleus, and that the same pathway is active under dexmedetomidine.
  • Arousal: in an earlier study by the same group, participants could be roused with verbal commands and possibly light shaking, even at 5.1 ng/ml (see Discrepancies).
  • Caveats: different people in the two groups, morning versus night recording, a single channel and small groups. The number of spindles per person ranged from 1 to 174. Three of the authors are from GE Healthcare, which makes the Entropy Module, and one author does contract research and consulting for Orion Pharma, which manufactures dexmedetomidine.
Huupponen et al. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2008;52:289–294

Dexmedetomidine and the thalamus: cortical coupling preserved, thalamocortical disrupted (Akeju, Loggia et al. 2014)

eLife 2014;3:e04499. Healthy volunteers (18–36 years, ASA I) received dexmedetomidine 1 µg/kg over 10 minutes followed by 0.7 µg/kg/h. Loss of consciousness was defined as sustained eye closure and no response to a request to open the eyes. Glucose metabolism was measured with FDG-PET (ten participants, two visits each), and blood flow (ASL) and functional connectivity (BOLD) were measured simultaneously with MRI (17 participants, complete BOLD data in 15). Not the same study as «Akeju 2014» on sevoflurane elsewhere in the app.

  • Metabolism and blood flow: glucose metabolism and blood flow fell most in the thalamus, the default mode network (DMN) and both frontoparietal networks. Blood flow and metabolism fell together, so the coupling between them was preserved.
  • Connectivity: coupling between cortical areas within the DMN and frontoparietal networks was preserved. Coupling between the thalamus and the DMN was disrupted, especially towards the posterior cingulate, precuneus and inferior parietal lobule. The thalamic region corresponded to intralaminar, midline, mediodorsal and ventral anterior nuclei, but the method could not resolve the nuclei precisely.
  • Recovery: coupling between the thalamus and the DMN, especially the posterior cingulate, returned when participants again responded to commands, while blood flow did not rise. The authors interpret this as coupling being restored before metabolism normalises, and recovery happening gradually.
  • A hierarchy of unconsciousness: the authors propose that lighter states (NREM 2 sleep, dexmedetomidine) involve disrupted thalamocortical coupling with preserved cortical coupling, while deeper states (propofol anaesthesia, some disorders of consciousness) also disrupt cortical coupling. Preserved cortical coupling may explain why the patient is easily roused.
  • Caveats: loss of consciousness was defined by failure to open the eyes on request. Functional connectivity in fMRI is co-variation in slow BOLD fluctuations, not directly measured communication between nerve cells. No conflicts of interest declared. Funded by the NIH and FAER.
Akeju, Loggia et al. eLife 2014;3:e04499

Which α2 receptor produces hypnosis? α2A in the locus coeruleus (Mizobe 1996)

J Clin Invest 1996;98:1076–1080, from the Maze group. Rats received antisense oligonucleotides (short DNA strands that prevent a specific receptor from being made) against α2A or α2C directly into the locus coeruleus, followed by dexmedetomidine 7 µg into the same area.

  • Cell studies: antisense against α2A reduced α2A receptors by about 30%, and antisense against α2C reduced α2C by nearly 40%, without affecting the other subtype.
  • Rats: after α2A antisense, loss of righting reflex came later and lasted shorter, and the effect was gone eight days after the last dose. α2C antisense, scrambled control sequences and saline had no effect.
  • Conclusion: α2A is the subtype mediating the hypnotic effect in the locus coeruleus. The authors write that α2A and α2C predominate in the central nervous system, while α2B is sparsely represented.
  • Side effects: the authors write that the rise in blood pressure after a rapid bolus is probably due to α2B (knockout mouse experiments), and that the bradycardia may partly be due to imidazoline receptors in the brainstem.
  • Caveats: 4–5 rats per group, and receptor reduction was measured only in cell cultures, not in the locus coeruleus itself. Funded by Veterans Affairs, the NIH and the Uehara Foundation.
Mizobe et al. J Clin Invest 1996;98:1076–1080
Thiopental and etomidate
Vuyk et al. 2025; Patel et al. 2025
  • Thiopental gives weaker amnesia than benzodiazepines. When the EEG becomes isoelectric, brain metabolism is about 50% of baseline.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Etomidate lowers cerebral blood flow and metabolism without changing blood pressure. At 0.2–0.3 mg/kg, CBF falls by 34% and CMRO₂ by 45%, without change in mean arterial pressure.Sources: Vuyk et al. 2025; Patel et al. 2025

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Barbiturates act through the GABAA receptor. It is the only proven site of barbiturate anaesthesia. At low concentrations GABA dissociates from the receptor more slowly, and the channel stays open longer. This probably gives sedation and hypnosis. At higher concentrations barbiturates open the channel without GABA, which may explain the anaesthesia itself. They also inhibit excitatory transmission (glutamate, acetylcholine). In rats, thiopental reduced glutamate levels and NMDA currents in the prefrontal cortex.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Barbiturates can only halve the brain's energy use. CMRO₂ falls to about 50% when the EEG becomes isoelectric, and no further. Barbiturates reduce the energy used for signalling, not the energy used to keep cells alive. Only hypothermia can reduce that.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Etomidate acts almost exclusively through GABAA. At clinical concentrations it enhances the GABA effect (positive modulation). At higher concentrations it activates the receptor directly. Two independent binding sites on the α1β2γ2 receptor contribute equally.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
  • Amnesia and hypnosis can run through different receptor variants. In mice, etomidate blocks LTP in CA1, but not in mice lacking the α5 subunit. These mice are resistant to the amnesia but not to the anaesthesia. The effect is reversed by an α5-selective drug with the opposite action (inverse agonist, L-655,708). The β3 subunit does not appear to be involved in the amnesia from etomidate.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Etomidate increases EEG activity in epileptogenic foci. It has therefore been used for mapping before epilepsy surgery.Source: Vuyk et al. 2025
Inhaled agents (sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane)
Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8 Purdon 2015 Mashour and Pryor 2025; Fukuda 2025 Hendrickx 2008
  • MAC is the concentration at which half of patients do not move at incision. It is the alveolar concentration, and only one point on the concentration–response curve (equivalent to the EC50). About 1.3 MAC prevents movement in about 95%.Source: Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8
  • MAC differs between agents. For 30–55-year-olds, MAC is about 2.0% for sevoflurane, 1.2% for isoflurane and 6.0% for desflurane.Source: Morgan and Mikhail
  • Patients wake at around 0.3–0.4 MAC. This is called MAC-awake and applies when the inhaled agent is the only anaesthetic.Source: Morgan and Mikhail
  • Two inhaled agents roughly add up. 0.5 MAC nitrous oxide and 0.5 MAC isoflurane give the same effect as 1.0 MAC isoflurane. There is no synergy between two inhaled agents, but usually synergy with intravenous agents. Opioids reduce MAC, but with a ceiling.Sources: Morgan and Mikhail; Hendrickx 2008; Fukuda 2025
  • MAC falls with age. The fall is about 6% per decade, regardless of agent. Another chapter of the same book gives a different figure (see Discrepancies).Sources: Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8 and 43
  • Desflurane gives very rapid induction and emergence. The effect comes when the brain concentration reaches a therapeutic level, and it follows the alveolar concentration. Desflurane has low solubility in blood and tissues, which makes it fast.Source: Morgan and Mikhail
  • Sevoflurane resembles propofol in the EEG, but adds theta at higher doses. Below MAC, sevoflurane gives strong alpha and slow-delta. At MAC and above, theta appears and fills in between slow-delta and alpha. When the concentration is lowered, theta disappears first. At emergence, alpha gives way to lower-amplitude beta and gamma, like a zipper opening. Isoflurane and desflurane give the same pattern, and high doses give burst suppression. See the Spectrogram tab.Source: Purdon 2015

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • Inhaled agents act on many targets, and no obligatory site of action has been found. They enhance GABAA inhibition, block two-pore potassium channels and HCN channels, and inhibit glutamate release via NMDA receptors. They also enhance the glycine receptor α1 subunit, and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are another target.Sources: Purdon 2015; Morgan and Mikhail
  • Potency follows lipid solubility, but only approximately (Meyer–Overton). This correlation once supported a shared mechanism for all inhaled agents.Source: Morgan and Mikhail
  • Immobility arises in the spinal cord. MAC is unchanged after spinal cord transection in rats (see Discrepancies and the Jinks 2010 card in the Components tab). The muscle-relaxing effect results from action on receptors and channels in the spinal cord. Two inhaled agents show no synergy for MAC, which is interpreted as a shared site for immobility despite different receptor effects.Sources: Morgan and Mikhail; Purdon 2015; Hendrickx 2008
  • Specific circuits modulate isoflurane anaesthesia. Noradrenergic nerve cells in the locus coeruleus modulate both the anaesthesia and emergence from it. In the pontine reticular formation, lower GABA levels are linked to unconsciousness. So GABA does not always inhibit wakefulness.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Memory loss involves several receptors in the hippocampus. Isoflurane and sevoflurane inhibit LTP in the hippocampus, and the effect is abolished by GABAA antagonists. Low, amnestic concentrations enhance tonic inhibition through α5 receptors. Mouse studies point to α4 and β3 for isoflurane and HCN1 for sevoflurane, while α1 and α2 do not appear to be involved. For isoflurane, the α4β2 nicotinic receptor is also implicated. In rodents, impaired memory 24–48 hours after isoflurane appears to be mediated by α5.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • The dose changes which effects matter most. Sevoflurane acts on all its targets all the time, but sensitivity differs. Low concentrations (about 0.5 MAC) enhance both GABA- and glycine-mediated inhibition. At higher concentrations (1.5 MAC) the GABA effect weakens or is blocked, and inhibition runs mainly via glycine receptors. NMDA inhibition increases with dose but is below 30 % at MAC, far less than the potentiation of GABA and glycine. There is no fixed order in which each target comes into play. Caveat: these are cell and animal studies, and none links theta in the human EEG to a specific target.Sources: Eckle 2013; Hapfelmeier 2001; Brosnan and Thiesen 2012 (rats); Hemmings 2019
  • GABA probably explains alpha and slow-delta, while theta may have another mechanism. Below MAC, sevoflurane resembles propofol, which is interpreted as GABA enhancement being the main mechanism. Theta at MAC and above may reflect one of the other mechanisms. The effect of sevoflurane on hippocampal theta may involve TASK-3 channels. Both are hypotheses.Sources: Purdon 2015; Mashour and Pryor 2025
Nitrous oxide
Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8 Purdon 2015 Mashour and Pryor 2025; Fukuda 2025 Hendrickx 2008
  • Nitrous oxide is too weak to give anaesthesia on its own. It is therefore used as an adjunct. MAC is 105%, i.e. above one atmosphere. Trying to give enough nitrous oxide alone for unconsciousness causes nausea and vomiting.Sources: Purdon 2015; Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8
  • Give 100% oxygen after nitrous oxide to prevent diffusion hypoxia. Nitrous oxide is eliminated so rapidly that alveolar oxygen and CO₂ are diluted. Give 100% oxygen for 5–10 minutes after nitrous oxide is turned off.Source: Morgan and Mikhail
  • Prolonged exposure can harm bone marrow and nerves. The side effects are bone marrow depression (megaloblastic anaemia) and peripheral neuropathies.Source: Morgan and Mikhail
  • Nitrous oxide gives beta and gamma in the EEG, and BIS can rise even though the patient is unconscious. When switching from an ether agent to more than 70% nitrous oxide, a transient strong slow-delta can appear.Sources: Liu 2023; Purdon 2015

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • The site of action is not fully clear. The EEG patterns of nitrous oxide are linked to NMDA receptors. At the same time, nitrous oxide is counted among the inhaled agents with a less clear site of action.Sources: Purdon 2015; Hendrickx 2008
  • The mechanism behind the EEG patterns is unknown. Nitrous oxide typically gives beta–gamma. When switching from an ether agent to above 70% nitrous oxide, strong transient slow-delta can appear with loss of power above about 10 Hz. One hypothesis is blockade of NMDA-mediated excitatory signals from the parabrachial nucleus and the medial pontine reticular formation to the basal forebrain and thalamus. The beta–gamma may share its mechanism with ketamine.Source: Purdon 2015
  • The more the theta peak frequency is slowed, the more memory is impaired. Amnestic concentrations of nitrous oxide, isoflurane and halothane suppress hippocampus-dependent fear learning in animals, in proportion to how much the theta peak frequency is slowed.Source: Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Nitrous oxide and isoflurane are possibly infra-additive.Source: Hendrickx 2008
  • In mice, nitrous oxide relieves pain via the κ receptor, not μ. The analgesia runs via the κ receptor and descending inhibitory pathways in the spinal cord. The hypnotic effect does not depend on κ. 70% nitrous oxide is an effective NMDA antagonist that reduced opioid-induced hyperalgesia.Source: Fukuda 2025

The numbers in the textbooks: MAC, age and discrepancies

The figures in this sub-tab come mostly from Miller's. Morgan and Mikhail 2022 contains little on EEG, but gives useful figures alongside. The books do not always agree, and sometimes neither do chapters of the same book.

  • MAC is only one point on the curve. MAC corresponds to the EC50 for movement at incision. About 1.3 MAC prevents movement in about 95 %, while 0.3–0.4 MAC is associated with awakening when the inhaled agent is the only anaesthetic. The distance between ‘no movement’ and ‘awake’ allows the EEG pattern to look adequate close to emergence. Opioids lower MAC, but with a ceiling, and high doses can stop spontaneous breathing without the patient losing consciousness.Sources: Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8; Fukuda 2025
  • Age: MAC falls 4 or 6 % per decade, depending on the source. Two chapters of Morgan and Mikhail give different figures: 6 % per decade “regardless of agent” and 4 % per decade over 40 years. Miller's gives 6 % per decade after 30 years. For propofol the figures also differ: 80-year-olds need about half the dose of 20-year-olds, or the dose should be reduced by 65 %, depending on the chapter.Sources: Morgan and Mikhail ch. 8 and 43; Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025 (Mapleson 1996); Vuyk et al. 2025; Kim et al. 2025 (Schnider 1999)
  • Synergistic or additive? The sources disagree on propofol and midazolam. Studies have found synergy for hypnosis between propofol and midazolam, and midazolam often acts synergistically with other hypnotics. Another chapter of Miller's, however, describes the interaction as “primarily additive”.Sources: Hendrickx 2008; Vuyk et al. 2025; Kim et al. 2025
  • Barbiturates depress the EEG more as the dose rises, and ketamine can mislead. Small doses of barbiturates give low-amplitude fast activity. Large doses give high-amplitude slow activity, burst suppression and electrical silence, in parallel with the fall in cerebral metabolism (up to 50 %). Thiopental doses that maintain burst suppression or a flat line give prolonged emergence, delayed extubation and a need for inotropes. With ketamine the patient can look awake without being so.Source: Morgan and Mikhail ch. 9
  • Morgan and Mikhail are more cautious than Miller's about EEG monitoring in older patients. Morgan and Mikhail only say that “some have suggested” that BIS monitoring may reduce cognitive impairment. Miller's proposes processed EEG to avoid burst suppression.Sources: Morgan and Mikhail ch. 43; Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025

The studies in detail:

Morgan and Mikhail 2022 Kim et al. 2025; Vuyk et al. 2025; Fukuda 2025; Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025 Hendrickx 2008 Schnider 1999 Mapleson 1996
Opioids
Fukuda 2025 Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010 Hendrickx 2008 Balanza 2022

This card describes opioid action from receptor to clinic. Much of the mechanistic knowledge comes from cell studies and animal experiments.Source: Fukuda 2025 (Fukuda)

  • Opioids are not complete anaesthetics. They reduce MAC, but with a ceiling, and must be combined with other drugs. Analgesia is not usually accompanied by loss of consciousness. High doses can abolish spontaneous breathing without unconsciousness, and the patient may breathe on command. Fentanyl alone does not give full hypnosis. This may explain awareness in cardiac surgery with high-dose opioids.Sources: Fukuda 2025; Brown 2010; Hendrickx 2008
  • High doses give slow delta waves, but with a ceiling. Fentanyl, alfentanil, sufentanil and remifentanil give the same pattern. Small doses of fentanyl (2–5 µg/kg) change the EEG minimally, while high doses (30–70 µg/kg) give high-amplitude slow delta waves. After large doses, isolated transient sharp waves (usually frontotemporal) can be seen. In children and adolescents, morphine reduced alpha and beta, while delta and theta were unchanged.
