The spectral edge frequency follows remifentanil concentration with almost no delay, but lags for fentanyl and sufentanil. Frontal theta has also been found with fentanyl (see the card below and Discrepancies).Sources: Fukuda 2025; Montandon 2016; Balanza 2022
  • Respiratory depression is caused by μ receptors in the brainstem. Opioids act directly on the respiratory centres. The preBötzinger complex mediates only part of the effect (timing, not the fall in rate). G-protein-gated potassium channels contribute. Mice lacking the μ receptor do not get respiratory depression from morphine. Analgesia and respiratory depression appear to use different signalling pathways: the A118G gene variant alters analgesia but not respiratory depression from morphine-6-glucuronide. In monkeys, tolerance developed to analgesia but not to respiratory depression.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Opioids can increase pain sensitivity (hyperalgesia). In animal experiments this is linked to sensitisation to glutamate and substance P, NMDA plasticity and AMPA receptors in the dorsal horn. Ketamine, nitrous oxide, magnesium and buprenorphine reduced it in studies. With long-term use the cAMP system in the locus coeruleus is upregulated.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Muscle rigidity is not caused by action on the muscle. Proposed mechanisms are the nucleus raphe pontis, caudate nucleus and fentanyl action in the locus coeruleus on spinal motor neurons. Naloxone reverses the rigidity.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Fentanyl also acts outside the opioid receptors. Fentanyl, but not morphine, bound to human α1A and α1B receptors, dopamine D1 and D4 receptors and VMAT2 (Ki about 0.9–1.7 µM). Noradrenergic effects may therefore contribute to chest wall rigidity, but this is an untested hypothesis. In rats, repeated high fentanyl doses gave a 291 % increase in EMG and respiratory depression without clear tolerance, while time to righting became shorter (50 to 16 minutes). The sources disagree on naloxone: in his lecture at Høstmøtet 2026, Ken Solt said that rigidity with synthetic opioids is resistant to naloxone and probably does not act via the μ receptor. He showed case reports involving haloperidol and Parkinson's disease (see Discrepancies).Sources: Torralva 2020; Obert 2025; Ken Solt, Høstmøtet 2026

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • All opioid receptors are G-protein-coupled receptors. μ, δ, κ and the nociceptin receptor share about 50% amino acid sequence. They have seven segments crossing the cell membrane, and the ligand binds deep within a large pocket. Endogenous ligands are β-endorphin and endomorphins (μ), enkephalins (δ), dynorphins (κ) and nociceptin. The sigma receptor is no longer regarded as an opioid receptor. Morphine, fentanyl, sufentanil, alfentanil and remifentanil are μ agonists.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Opioids make the nerve cell less excitable. The receptor activates Gi/o proteins. Adenylate cyclase is inhibited (less cAMP), voltage-gated calcium channels are inhibited and inwardly rectifying potassium channels are activated.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • In the spinal cord, opioids dampen the pain signal both before and after the synapse. Opioid receptors are abundant in the substantia gelatinosa. Presynaptically, inhibited calcium channels reduce release of glutamate and substance P from primary sensory neurons. Postsynaptically, open potassium channels hyperpolarise the dorsal horn projection neuron, so glutamate excites it less easily.Sources: Fukuda 2025; Brown 2010
  • In the brainstem, opioids inhibit the inhibition. In the periaqueductal grey (PAG), they inhibit GABA release from tonically active interneurons. This releases descending pathways via the medulla, which release noradrenaline and serotonin that dampen pain signals in the dorsal horn.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Opioids also act higher up in the brain. PET with remifentanil showed activation in the anterior cingulate, insula, orbitofrontal cortex and brainstem. In rats, action in the amygdala contributes to analgesia.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Opioids reduce acetylcholine release. In rats, morphine reduced acetylcholine in the prefrontal cortex, given both intravenously and directly into the basal forebrain. This is a possible neurochemical basis for altered consciousness. Fentanyl reduces acetylcholine in the medial pontine reticular formation.Sources: Fukuda 2025; Brown 2010
  • It is unresolved whether G-protein-biased opioids have fewer side effects. The theory of biased agonism is that Gi/o signalling gives analgesia, while β-arrestin gives side effects such as respiratory depression, constipation and euphoria. Mice lacking β-arrestin-2 had less respiratory depression from morphine in one study, but not in a newer one.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • μ and δ agonists are rewarding, κ agonists aversive. Opioids inhibit GABA neurons in the ventral tegmental area and nucleus accumbens, so that more dopamine is released in the nucleus accumbens. Activity in the locus coeruleus is inhibited.Source: Fukuda 2025
  • Several opioids also have other targets. Buprenorphine blocks sodium channels, d-methadone is an NMDA antagonist, pethidine acts at the α2B adrenoceptor (a possible explanation for its anti-shivering effect), and morphine and hydromorphone inhibit the 5-HT3A receptor. In mice lacking the μ receptor, ketamine-induced respiratory depression and antinociception were reduced, and the MAC of sevoflurane was higher.Source: Fukuda 2025

Key points

  • Each effect has its own concentration. Different effects of the same drug have different C50 values. Aim for a 95–99 % probability of effect, not 50 %. Drug displays rely on population models that do not fit everyone.Source: Kim et al. 2025. See
  • A slow EEG is not the same as hypnosis. Fentanyl and α2 agonists give slow activity without unconsciousness. Lidocaine and magnesium appear to act by dampening arousal. Nociception pulls the other way, and no EEG measure shows memory. Look for the hypnotic's own signature, and watch how the picture changes with stimulation.Sources: see “When the EEG slows without hypnosis: direct effect or dampened arousal”
  • Opioids change the EEG little but depress breathing early. With fentanyl, theta and slow-delta increase with concentration. This is clear in the spectrogram but hardly visible in the raw EEG. Breathing falls at far lower concentrations than those that prolong reaction time. The study is small and was done before induction, not during anaesthesia.Source: Balanza 2022. See
  • Drugs from different classes mostly enhance each other. Opioid + hypnotic is synergistic, and propofol + midazolam is synergistic for hypnosis. Two inhalational agents, and propofol + sevoflurane, are only additive. Ketamine showed no synergy with GABAergic drugs in any study.Source: Hendrickx 2008. See
  • A sudden flat EEG after several simultaneous boluses is the extreme end of burst suppression. Older patients are most at risk. Titrate one drug at a time, and look at the raw EEG and suppression ratio after each bolus, not just the index. A clean flat line with normal impedance, appearing right after the doses, distinguishes it from a technical fault.Sources: see “Synergy between agents and isoelectric EEG”
  • Lidocaine and magnesium spare dose, but are not hypnotics. Neither has a known EEG signature of its own at clinical doses. They lower the hypnotic requirement mainly through antinociception, and should be counted as opioid-sparing when weighing synergy. With lidocaine during volatile anaesthesia, MAC was lower but BIS higher. If you guide only by MAC and blood pressure, hypnosis may be lighter than you think. The study measured only the index, not the EEG signature, and the evidence base is small.Sources: Bazin 2018 and others. See

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

Several effects, different concentrations

Each drug has a dynamic range: the concentration at which the effect changes. Below the range little happens. Above it, more drug does not give more effect. Different effects of the same agent have different C50 values.Source: Kim et al. 2025

Hypnotics and opioids enhance each other. The analgesic effect is enhanced markedly, the hypnotic effect moderately. Two GABAergic hypnotics together are largely just additive. Aim for a 95–99% probability of effect, not 50% as MAC does. Drug displays show predicted effect, but are based on population models that do not fit everyone.Sources: Kim et al. 2025 (Hendrickx 2008, Bouillon 2004, Egan 2001)

Kim et al. 2025 (Hendrickx 2008, Bouillon 2004, Egan 2001)

Fentanyl and EEG: frontal theta (Balanza 2022)

  • A small study, done before induction. 25 patients received fentanyl 2 µg/kg (ideal body weight) every 2 minutes, two or three doses, before general anaesthesia. They performed an auditory task and were monitored with frontal EEG, respiratory belts and pulse oximetry. The effect-site concentration is model-derived, not measured. Recruitment stopped early because of covid-19.Source: Balanza 2022
  • Theta rises with fentanyl, but differently from patient to patient. More fentanyl gave more theta (4–8 Hz) and slow-delta (below 4 Hz). Theta is hard to see in the raw EEG, but clear in the spectrogram. Concentration alone explained little (marginal R² 0.15), because patients differed a great deal.Source: Balanza 2022
  • Breathing falls already after the first dose. Minute ventilation fell 30% after the first dose, 55% after the second and 60% after the third. SpO₂ stayed at 95–100%, but patients were preoxygenated. More theta was linked to lower ventilation.Source: Balanza 2022
  • Breathing falls long before reactions slow. Reaction time increased on average 277 seconds after ventilation began to fall. The concentration that gave a 10% fall in ventilation was about 1750 times lower than the one that prolonged reaction time. 16 of 25 stopped responding. All could be roused, and four needed a jaw thrust. Slow-delta tracked loss of response better than theta.Source: Balanza 2022
  • The EEG might warn of respiratory depression, but this has not been tested. It is the authors' hypothesis. The study is small and did not measure during anaesthesia.Source: Balanza 2022
  • The numbers cannot be compared directly with the textbook. Miller's gives fentanyl C50 of about 2 ng/ml for analgesia, 4 for ventilatory depression and 20 for EEG changes. Balanza saw theta rise across the whole range 0–15 ng/ml, but found no threshold. The endpoints and methods differ.Sources: Kim et al. 2025 (Egan 2001), Balanza 2022
  • Caveat – conflict of interest: Purdon reports patents, a licence to Masimo and co-founding of a company developing closed-loop systems.
Balanza et al. PNAS Nexus 2022;1:pgac158

When the EEG slows without hypnosis: direct effect or dampened arousal

Many drugs change the EEG without producing unconsciousness or amnesia themselves. This happens in two different ways, and they mean different things for how much hypnotic the patient needs. At the same time nociception pulls in the opposite direction. You therefore need to know what has been given, and what is happening in the surgical field.

  • Some drugs slow the EEG without producing unconsciousness. Fentanyl gives more theta and slow delta, and breathing falls long before reaction time increases. High opioid doses alone (fentanyl above about 8 ng/ml) give more delta and a lower median frequency. Usual doses together with hypnotics change the EEG little. α2 agonists give slow waves and spindles, but the patient can be roused. Dexmedetomidine under propofol gave more delta–theta and a lower PSI.Sources: Balanza 2022, Sleigh et al. 2025, Hight 2020, Purdon 2015, Zhang 2021
  • Lidocaine and magnesium appear to act by dampening arousal. Lidocaine changed neither BIS nor propofol requirements without surgical stimulation, only during stimulation. During volatile anaesthesia, lidocaine gave lower MAC but higher BIS. Magnesium gave no BIS difference in one study and lower BIS in another. There, less muscle activity may be part of the explanation, but that is a hypothesis. Spinal lidocaine sedated healthy volunteers, probably because less sensory input reached the brain. None of these has a known EEG signature of its own at clinical doses.Sources: Hans 2010, Bazin 2018, Memiş 2003, Walia 2018, Pollock 2000
  • Pain can both lighten and apparently “deepen” the EEG. A noxious stimulus can give beta arousal, delta arousal or alpha dropout. The last two can make the index show deeper anaesthesia, even though the patient is reacting.Source: García 2021
  • The hypnotic requirement follows the stimulation. Opioids and hypnotics enhance each other, and lidocaine spared propofol only while surgery was ongoing. When stimulation falls, or adjuvants dampen it, less hypnotic is needed. When stimulation rises, or the adjuvant wears off, more is needed.Sources: Kim et al. 2025, Hendrickx 2008, Hans 2010
  • No EEG measure shows memory. With propofol, memory is lost at a lighter level than response, but this cannot be transferred to other drugs. Frontal alpha–delta did not exclude response to command.Sources: Glass 1997, Gaskell 2017
  • Look for the hypnotic's own signature, not just a slow EEG (interpretation based on the sources). With propofol and sevoflurane, this is frontal alpha above slow activity. Consider which drugs have been given and when, and watch how the picture changes with stimulation. Do not reduce the hypnotic just because the index falls after an opioid, α2 agonist or adjuvant. When clonidine has been given, the volatile should not be lowered below what is needed for unconsciousness.Source: Hight 2020
  • Reflection from the author of the app: when several drugs affect the EEG without producing hypnosis or amnesia, and nociception at the same time pulls the other way, interpretation becomes harder. The EEG must then be read together with what has been given, when it was given and what is happening surgically.
  • Caveat: the studies are small and use different measures. For lidocaine and magnesium there are almost only index data, no spectrogram studies.

More on this: . The cards on fentanyl, lidocaine and magnesium are in this section, and clonidine and dexmedetomidine under “The drugs”.

Balanza 2022 Kim et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025 Hight 2020 Zhang 2021 Hans 2010 Bazin 2018 Memiş 2003 Walia 2018 Pollock 2000 García 2021 Gaskell 2017

Synergy between agents and isoelectric EEG

A clinical picture many will recognise: several agents are given at the same time in large doses, for example at induction, or because the patient moves during the procedure (more volatile agent, opioid, clonidine and esketamine all at once). The EEG abruptly becomes completely flat, without bursts, and only returns when the bolus effect has worn off. Older patients are most at risk. This is not a separate phenomenon, but the extreme end of burst suppression.

  • A flat EEG is the end of burst suppression, and must be told apart from a technical fault. Suppression is amplitude below 10 µV. Isoelectric EEG is 2 µV or lower. Burst suppression is a continuum: the suppression ratio increases with dose until the EEG is completely flat. The monitor shows this as SR near 100. A loose electrode or a cable break gives noise, an impedance alarm or a lot of artefact. Isoelectric EEG is a clean flat line in all channels, with normal impedance, and appears in relation to the doses.Sources: Guay 2025, Ching 2012
  • Drugs from different classes mostly enhance each other. Opioids are synergistic with both intravenous and inhaled hypnotics. Opioids alone can never produce full hypnosis or immobility, so any reduction of more than 10% counts as synergy. Propofol + midazolam is synergistic for hypnosis, probably because they bind to different sites on the GABAA receptor. Volatile agents are synergistic with intravenous agents, but only additive with each other. Propofol + sevoflurane is additive. The cut-offs: a sum of normalised doses below 0.9 is synergy, 0.9–1.1 additive and above 1.1 infra-additive.Sources: Hendrickx 2008 (systematic review, Anesth Analg 2008;107:494–506), Short and Chui 1991, McClune 1992, Short 1992
  • Ketamine does not enhance GABAergic drugs. Ketamine showed no synergy with GABAergic agents in any study. Propofol + ketamine was additive, and on reanalysis infra-additive for immobility. Midazolam + ketamine was infra-additive for hypnosis. The same is seen in dogs: ketamine before propofol did not change the propofol requirement for intubation, but gave more apnoea at the highest dose.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, Hui 1995, Mair 2009
  • In the example above, the synergy comes from sevoflurane + fentanyl (+ clonidine), not from esketamine. Clonidine + propofol was additive for hypnosis. But clonidine lowers MACawake for sevoflurane by 17–21% and MAC by 17–34%, with a ceiling effect, which counts as synergy. Synergy for side effects such as respiratory depression and hypotension is little studied.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, Higuchi 2002
  • Midazolam halves the propofol dose, and the fall in blood pressure is enhanced just as much. In 200 young women, the combination gave hypnosis in 85% on a dose that gave hypnosis in only 50% with each agent alone. Midazolam 0.13 mg/kg halved the propofol dose for anaesthesia (no response to a tetanic stimulus), from 1.93 to 0.93 mg/kg. Midazolam alone never produced anaesthesia. Blood pressure fell as much with the combination as with each agent at equipotent dose, that is, synergy for the hypotension too.Source: Short and Chui 1991 (BJA 67:539–545)
  • Whether a combination is called synergy depends on the model. Interactions are measured with isobolograms (straight line = additive, curved towards the origin = synergy) or response surface models, where the effect is shown as a surface over two doses. A single parameter cannot capture synergy in one dose range and antagonism in another.Sources: Minto 2000, Lee 2010 (Korean J Anaesthesiol)
  • Older age and low blood pressure make suppression more likely. Older patients are more sensitive to propofol, and MAC falls with age. Hypotension after a bolus can in itself produce suppression. Suppression is linked to reduced cerebral metabolism. Ketamine increases CMRO₂ and does not produce classic burst suppression at clinical doses.Sources: Schnider 1999, Purdon 2015 (BJA), Georgii 2022, Ching 2012 (Burst suppression tab)
  • The EEG does not go straight back to baseline. When the effect wears off, activity returns, often as high-amplitude slow activity before the alpha band is back. At the same calculated concentration, the picture is not the same as before.Source: Sepúlveda 2026 (Burst suppression tab)
  • It has not been shown that a brief flat period gives a worse outcome. Suppression is associated with delirium, but ENGAGES reduced suppression time without reducing delirium. “Cortical collapse” is an image, not a technical term. “Reboot”, on the other hand, is used for the abrupt jump in connectivity between deep brain regions and the cortex at emergence; see the card on hysteresis and neural inertia in the Fundamentals tab.Sources: Fritz 2016 (Burst suppression tab), Wildes 2019, Huang 2021 (Neuroimage)
  • Antiseizure drugs can both enhance and counteract. Chronic use can enhance hypnotics, but raise the requirement for opioids and neuromuscular blockers. See the card “Antiseizure drugs and anaesthetic drugs: do they enhance or counteract?” under Metabolism and tolerance.
  • Movement does not mean that hypnosis is too light. Movement is a spinal response to nociception (see the Fundamentals tab: nociception). Titrate one agent at a time, slowly in older patients, and look at the raw EEG and SR after each bolus, not only at the index. See image 16 in the image quiz.Sources: Obert 2024, Sepúlveda 2020
Hendrickx 2008, Short & Chui 1991, Minto 2000, Lee 2010, Ching 2012, Guay 2025

Multimodal anaesthesia: lidocaine and magnesium in the EEG

Lidocaine and magnesium are used to spare opioid and hypnotic. The question is whether they have an EEG signature of their own, whether they take part in the synergy between agents, and whether they affect the coupling between brain regions. There is little research, and almost all of it deals with dose sparing measured with BIS.

  • Lidocaine dampens the response to surgery, but does not produce hypnosis. Lidocaine lowered the propofol requirement (guided by BIS) only during surgical stimulation. Without stimulation, neither BIS nor haemodynamics changed. The effect is antinociceptive, not hypnotic.Source: Hans 2010 (BJA, 40 patients)
  • With lidocaine and a volatile agent, MAC was lower but BIS higher. In a small, randomised, blinded study in open colorectal surgery, the volatile and fentanyl were titrated to blood pressure and heart rate, and the anaesthesiologists could not see BIS. With lidocaine, age-adjusted MAC was lower (1.0 versus 1.1), while BIS was higher (45 versus 39), especially late in the operation. Either hypnosis was lighter with lidocaine, or BIS does not capture its effect below the cortex. The authors advise caution with low MAC when lidocaine is given and depth is guided by haemodynamics. Only the index number was measured, not the raw EEG or spectrogram. Caveats: 25 patients, volatile agents only, and fentanyl was titrated rather than standardised. No conflicts of interest.Source: Bazin 2018
  • Look at the spectrogram, not just MAC and blood pressure, when lidocaine is given (interpretation based on the sources). Lidocaine can lower the requirement for volatile agent without lowering the index. If depth is guided by blood pressure and heart rate, the patient may end up in lighter hypnosis than the MAC value suggests. What the spectrogram looks like with lidocaine has hardly been studied (only two cases).Sources: Bazin 2018, Firdaus 2026
  • The type of interaction lidocaine has is unclear in humans. In animals, lidocaine lowers MAC for volatile agents, with a ceiling of about 50% MAC reduction, which counts as synergy. One animal study found synergy with propofol for hypnosis, and in rats lidocaine + thiopental was infra-additive. Lidocaine potentiates midazolam in humans, but the type is unknown. No human isobolograms exist, and the studies stopped below 10 µg/mL because of the risk of seizures.Source: Hendrickx 2008
  • Only two cases describe lidocaine on the spectrogram. Two craniotomy patients with TIVA and lidocaine: one kept an alpha–delta pattern, the other developed delta dominance with weaker alpha and episodes of burst suppression. The authors themselves say that no dose–response or causal relationship can be drawn. High plasma levels of lidocaine are proconvulsant, so the EEG effect does not rise steadily with dose.Source: Firdaus 2026
  • Magnesium spares propofol and opioid, but does not always change BIS. MgSO4 30 mg/kg before induction lowered the propofol requirement for BIS 40–50 and gave lower BIS for the first 40 minutes, but less than dexmedetomidine. Mg also spared vecuronium. In intensive care patients, Mg lowered sufentanil requirements without a difference in BIS. Mg does not produce sedation at serum levels below 8 mmol/L when ventilation is adequate.Sources: Walia 2018, Memiş 2003
  • “Propofol sparing” is not the same as an EEG effect. Magnesium crosses the blood–brain barrier poorly. A reasonable reading (an interpretation, not from a source) is that the saving in BIS studies is a mixture of reduced nociceptive response, haemodynamics and less muscle activity. Mg potentiates neuromuscular blockade and thus the EMG contribution to the index. This is a hypothesis.
  • No one knows whether lidocaine or magnesium changes the coupling between brain regions. No human studies on this during anaesthesia were found. What exists on connectivity concerns propofol and sevoflurane (Fundamentals tab), ketamine (Components tab) and dexmedetomidine.Source: Vlisides 2017 (ketamine)
  • Opioid-free anaesthesia with dexmedetomidine gave severe bradycardia and more complications (POFA). 314 patients received propofol, desflurane, lidocaine and ketamine, and either remifentanil or dexmedetomidine, titrated to BIS 40–60. The trial was stopped early after severe bradycardia in five patients on dexmedetomidine, three of them with asystole. Four of the cases occurred during CO₂ insufflation for laparoscopy. Hypoxaemia, ileus or cognitive dysfunction within 48 hours occurred in 78% with dexmedetomidine versus 67% with remifentanil, mostly due to hypoxaemia. Dexmedetomidine gave less morphine use and nausea afterwards, similar analgesia, but later extubation and a longer stay in the recovery unit. Dexmedetomidine was dosed by heart rate, because validated monitors of nociception and depth are lacking, and the mean dose of 1.2 µg/kg/h may have been too high. Caveat: several authors report fees from Orion Pharma, which manufactures dexmedetomidine.Source: Beloeil 2021
  • BIS 40–60 may mean something different with dexmedetomidine than with remifentanil (interpretation based on the sources). Dexmedetomidine can shift the index independently of hypnotic depth (see Fundamentals → Monitoring and artefacts). When no monitor is validated for dosing, the raw EEG and the spectrogram at least give a picture of what the drugs do to the brain, rather than titrating by heart rate and numbers alone.
  • In summary: lidocaine and magnesium are opioid-sparing, not extra hypnotics. Neither has a known EEG signature of its own at clinical doses, as propofol, sevoflurane, ketamine and dexmedetomidine have. They lower the need for hypnotic, mostly via antinociception. The EEG change you see is therefore most often indirect: less arousal response to surgery, or the hypnotic being dosed lower. The evidence base is small, and spectrogram studies of adequate size are lacking.
Hans 2010 · Bazin 2018 · Hendrickx 2008 · Firdaus 2026 · Walia 2018 · Memiş 2003 · Beloeil 2021

Key points

  • Sedation prevents storage, and propofol also makes memories fade faster. Lightly sedated volunteers stored the words, but with propofol they had forgotten more of them hours later than with the other drugs. More deeply sedated volunteers did not store the words at all, whatever the drug.See
  • Amnesia works forwards, not backwards. Midazolam caused dose-dependent memory loss for what happened after the dose, but not reliably for what happened before. What was learned before the drug was remembered as usual.See
  • Dreams mostly belong to emergence and are not a sign of awareness. Dreamers showed a REM-like pattern just before emergence, and dreamers had no more awareness than non-dreamers.See
  • Evidence for choosing a drug to prevent awareness is weak. Benzodiazepines reduced awareness compared with thiopental, ketamine and placebo, but with risk of bias, very few events and differing definitions.See
  • How many recall dreams depends heavily on method. Large clinical studies found 3–8 %, experimental studies often far more. Frequent dreaming at home, priming before induction and immediate interview gave higher recall.See
  • Dreaming can be steered with an emergence bundle. With five measures around emergence, 69 % reported dreams, and 93 % when all five were completed. The study had no control group.See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Never stored or forgotten afterwards: two routes to amnesia

Memory loss under sedation can have two causes: something is never stored, or something that was stored fades faster afterwards. The drugs differ here.Sources: Veselis 2004; Pryor 2010 (laboratory studies in healthy volunteers)

  • More sedation: nothing is stored. The more sedated participants responded to 54 % of the words and recognised them after 15–33 seconds no better than chance, whatever the drug. This is interpreted as failure of encoding. The less alert the participant, the weaker the initial memory trace (r = 0.83).Sources: Veselis 2004; Pryor 2010
  • Propofol: stored, but forgotten faster. Lightly sedated participants stored the words as well as with placebo. After 3.5–4 hours, however, they had lost much more with propofol (38.8 percentage points) than with thiopental, dexmedetomidine and placebo (11.9–22.9). The same pattern was seen with pictures: strong encoding, but a marked, dose-dependent faster loss.Sources: Veselis 2004; Pryor 2010
  • Dexmedetomidine and thiopental act as pure sedation, midazolam is a mixture. With dexmedetomidine and thiopental, the initial trace weakened in step with reduced alertness, but forgetting afterwards was barely affected. With midazolam, faster loss dominated at low dose and reduced alertness at high dose. Faster loss is linked to attenuation of the P2-N2 complex in the EEG at encoding, but this rests on nine group values, and the authors call the measure indirect and preliminary.Sources: Pryor 2010; Veselis 2004
  • Caveats. The authors themselves write that the finding for propofol is not conclusive, partly because the propofol group had a slightly better baseline and there may be a floor effect. The groups were small (12 per drug), and the concentrations were model-derived. These are laboratory data without surgical stimulation, and they say nothing directly about memory in surgical patients.Sources: Veselis 2004; Pryor 2010

The studies in detail:

Veselis 2004 Pryor 2010

Amnesia works forwards, not backwards

A sedative cannot reliably erase the memory of something that has already happened. Three studies tested memory for what was shown or learned before the dose, and none found a reliable retrograde effect.Sources: Bulach 2005; Veselis 2004; Pryor 2010

  • No effect backwards. What was shown or learned before the dose was remembered as well as without the drug. Posters shown 1–4 minutes before midazolam were recognised by 9–10 of 10 in all groups, and venous cannulation and transfer to the operating table were remembered equally well. Words and word tests learned before the drug showed no difference from placebo.Sources: Bulach 2005; Veselis 2004; Pryor 2010
  • A clear effect forwards. A poster shown 4 minutes after the dose was recognised by 8 of 10 in the control group, but only by 0–2 of 10 after midazolam 2–10 mg. One patient in the 10 mg group had a tourniquet inflated to 300 mmHg without remembering it.Source: Bulach 2005
  • The moment of the dose is a grey zone. Only 4 and 3 of 10 remembered the mask preoxygenation that started at the same time as 5 and 10 mg, versus 10 of 10 in the control group. This may indicate a near-immediate retrograde effect, but if so a very short-lived one. In humans there is generally little support for retrograde amnesia. Some findings suggest retrograde facilitation, but it was not found here.Sources: Bulach 2005; Mashour and Pryor 2025
  • Midazolam cannot be used to erase the memory of what has already happened. This is the authors’ clinical conclusion. Caveats: only 10 patients per group, no auditory test, and all received propofol at induction, so a small retrograde effect may have been missed.Source: Bulach 2005

The studies in detail:

Bulach 2005 Pryor 2010 Veselis 2004 Mashour and Pryor 2025

Dreams belong to emergence and are not awareness

Patients who say they dreamt “during the operation” can raise concern about awareness. The dreams mostly occur just before emergence, and dreaming is not the same as being present during the procedure.

  • The dreams come just before emergence. About one in four patients dreamt, as often with propofol (27 %) as with desflurane (28 %). In the last 5 minutes before the interview, dreamers had more high-frequency activity (30 Hz) and fewer spindles, a REM-like pattern. During the operation itself there were no definite differences. When patients say ‘during the anaesthetic’, it therefore cannot be taken literally.Source: Leslie 2009 (300 patients, BIS 40–55)
  • Dreaming is not awareness. None of the patients in two of the studies reported awareness. In five studies there was no difference in awareness between dreamers and non-dreamers. Dreaming should therefore not be read as a sign of too light anaesthesia.Sources: Leslie 2009; Sikka 2026; Sikka, Hu and Heifets 2026
  • But the boundary is not always sharp. Dreams containing elements from the operating room may be memories from before anaesthesia or processing of stimuli during it. Nightmares occurred in only five studies, and two of them may have been awareness. In experimental studies, high recall often went together with high awareness, suggesting lighter sedation.Source: Sikka, Hu and Heifets 2026
  • The content is mostly everyday. Family, friends, work and leisure recur, and pleasant dreams predominate. Propofol and dexmedetomidine dreams were mostly static, whereas ketamine gave vivid, surreal experiences.Sources: Leslie 2009; Sikka, Hu and Heifets 2026
  • Evidence for choosing a drug to prevent awareness is weak. A Cochrane review found that benzodiazepines reduced awareness compared with thiopental, ketamine and placebo. But there was risk of bias, very few events and differing definitions of awareness.Sources: Messina 2016 (Cochrane); Vuyk et al. 2025

The studies in detail:

Leslie 2009 Sikka 2026 Sikka, Hu and Heifets 2026 Messina 2016 Vuyk et al. 2025

How many recall dreams depends on method and can be steered

The proportion who recall dreams ranges from 0 to almost 100 % between studies. Much of the difference seems to be about how and when patients are asked, and the proportion can be steered.

  • Large clinical studies find few. The largest clinical studies and RCTs found 3–8 %, whereas experimental studies often found 40–80 %. All clinical studies with 65 % or more used ketamine (or etoxadrol).Source: Sikka, Hu and Heifets 2026
  • Patient and method explain a lot. Patients who often dream at home more often recall dreams after anaesthesia (OR 3.0). Priming before induction also gives more recall, and an interview immediately after emergence gives clearly more than a later one. The difference between studies “likely” reflects fragile memory and method, not that fewer actually dream. This is an interpretation, not proof.Sources: Sikka, Hu and Heifets 2026; Leslie 2009
  • An emergence bundle increased the proportion who recalled dreams. The bundle had five parts: priming, propofol, EEG guidance towards a pre-emergence state (alpha fading, beta rising, PSI about 40–70), at least 10 quiet minutes and an interview immediately after extubation. Then 69 % reported dreams, and 93 % among the 57 in whom all five parts were delivered. 86 % of the dreams were positive. By comparison, 27–28 % dreamt in Leslie 2009.Sources: Sikka 2026; Leslie 2009
  • Caveats. Sikka 2026 had no control group, and the hands-off period was achieved in only 14 % of cases, so the 93 % figure comes from a small, self-selected subset. The review is a mapping exercise, not a meta-analysis, and everything rests on self-report.Sources: Sikka 2026; Sikka, Hu and Heifets 2026

The studies in detail:

Sikka, Hu and Heifets 2026 Sikka 2026 Leslie 2009
The studies in detail: memory loss over time, retrograde amnesia, dreaming and awareness (7 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Propofol and memory: loss over time (Veselis 2004)

  • Design: 83 healthy volunteers (mean 31 years) were randomised to propofol (n = 30), thiopental (n = 31), dexmedetomidine (n = 10) or placebo (n = 12) at a constant target concentration for about 90 minutes (propofol 0.3, 1.2 or 2.5 µg/ml, thiopental 2, 5 or 7 µg/ml, dexmedetomidine 0.25 or 0.5–0.8 ng/ml). They heard words in a continuous recognition task with repetition after 1, 5 or 10 words (about 6, 15–21 and 33 seconds). Recognition of the words was tested again after about 225 minutes.
  • Grouping: since the effects of the doses overlapped, the authors divided the participants into “high” and “low” performance based on a median split of recognition after 33 seconds under the drug. The 23 who did not respond to voice or firm touch (BIS 72 ± 16) were excluded, and 9 others were excluded for other reasons.
  • High performance (lightly sedated): the words entered long-term memory as well as with placebo (BIS about 94). The loss of these words after 3.5–4 hours was 38.8 ± 23.0 percentage points with propofol, versus 17.2 with thiopental, 22.9 with dexmedetomidine and 11.9 with placebo (propofol versus placebo p = 0.008, and versus thiopental p = 0.037). Recognition of the words from the drug period was 31% with propofol, 39% with thiopental, 34% with dexmedetomidine and 61% with placebo.
  • Low performance (more sedated): they responded to 54% of the words versus 87% in high performance, had 225 ms (18%) longer reaction time and BIS about 89. Recognition after 15–33 seconds was no better than chance, regardless of agent, and the words were remembered very poorly later. The authors interpret this as failure of encoding.
  • Before the drug: recognition of words presented before the drug was equal to placebo, so the effect applies only to material presented while the drug was acting.
  • In brief: those who were lightly sedated took in the words and stored them, but with propofol they had forgotten more of them a few hours later than with the other drugs. Those who were more sedated did not store the words at all, whatever the drug. Words from before the drug were remembered as well as with placebo.
  • The authors' interpretation: sedation prevents anything from being stored in long-term memory at all (failure of encoding), while propofol additionally makes what was actually stored disappear faster afterwards (“drug-induced amnesia”). The mechanism is speculative (interplay between hippocampus and neocortex, interference from new words). Dexmedetomidine had the same profile as thiopental and a smaller loss than propofol. Midazolam was not tested here, and the claim about midazolam rests on earlier studies the authors refer to.
  • The authors' own caveats: the finding for propofol is not conclusive, partly because the high-performance group with propofol had a slightly better baseline (borderline, omnibus test not significant). Recognition after the drug was below 40%, so there may be a floor effect, the lists were built differently, and dexmedetomidine was given to few (4 per group).
  • What it means: these are laboratory data from healthy volunteers at low to moderate doses and without surgical stimulation. They say nothing directly about memory in surgical patients, and the BIS values in the article (89–94 with preserved response, 72 with unresponsiveness) are not the same as in other sources.
Veselis et al. Anesthesiology 2004;101:831–841

Memory loss over time for different agents (Pryor 2010)

  • Design: 61 healthy volunteers (analysed of 67 randomised) received propofol, thiopental, midazolam, dexmedetomidine or placebo, each at two concentrations (propofol 0.45 and 0.90 µg/ml, thiopental 1.5 and 3.0, midazolam 20 and 35 ng/ml, dexmedetomidine 0.20 and 0.40 ng/ml, model-derived). They viewed 375 pictures with repetition after 6, 27 and 63 seconds, and were tested on recognition 15, 45, 105 and 225 minutes after the infusion stopped.
  • Model: memory strength over time was described with a power function, m = λ·t−ψ, where λ is the strength of the initial memory trace and ψ is how fast it decays (R² on average 0.85). The model predicted that the loss became visible 1.7–8 minutes after encoding.
  • What was related to what: λ followed self-reported alertness (r = 0.83, p = 0.005), while ψ followed reaction time (r = 0.95, p < 0.0001) and attenuation of the P2-N2 complex in the EEG at encoding (P2 amplitude r = −0.82, p = 0.007). The correlations are based on group values (nine points) and do not show causation.
  • The profiles: dexmedetomidine lowered the initial trace in step with reduced alertness and barely affected the decay (pure sedation). Propofol gave strong encoding (a paradoxically higher λ at the highest dose) and a marked, dose-dependent faster loss. Midazolam was a mixture: faster loss dominated at low dose and reduced alertness at high dose. Thiopental resembled dexmedetomidine, but the comparison was not significant (the authors point to many comparisons).
  • No retrograde effect: a visual word test, learned just before the drug, showed no difference between the agents and placebo. The difference between 6, 27 and 63 seconds was not affected either.
  • The authors' hypothesis: failing consolidation is due to the drug disrupting synchrony between regions at encoding, which may affect plasticity. They stress that P2-N2 is an indirect and preliminary measure, and that the results only provide a framework for further studies.
  • Limitations: model-derived concentrations without measurement, not entirely equal levels of amnesia between the agents, residual drug at recognition testing, and small groups (12 per agent).
Pryor et al. Anesthesiology 2010;113:313–326

Midazolam and retrograde amnesia (Bulach 2005)

  • Design: 40 adult ASA I–II patients randomised and blinded to midazolam 2, 5 or 10 mg or saline 8 minutes before induction (10 per group). Pictures (posters) and events were shown and tested at fixed time points before and after the dose, and memory was tested again at least 4 hours after the patient left the recovery unit.
  • Retrograde: recognition of posters shown 4, 2 and 1 minute before the dose was equal between groups (9–10 of 10 throughout), and there was no difference either in events such as venous cannulation, transfer to the operating table and sticking out the tongue.
  • Anterograde: after the dose, the midazolam groups remembered less well than control. The poster 4 minutes after the dose was recognised by 8 of 10 in the control group versus 2, 0 and 1 in the midazolam groups, and 8 minutes after by 8 versus 4, 1 and 0 (dose–response p = 0.002). BIS was median 97 in the control group and 71 after 10 mg at 4 minutes.
  • The time point at the dose: only 4 and 3 of 10 remembered mask preoxygenation that started at the same time as the dose after 5 and 10 mg respectively, versus 10 of 10 in the control group. The authors suggest this may indicate a near-immediate retrograde effect, but that it must in that case be very short-lived since memories from the minutes before the dose were intact. One patient in the 10 mg group had a tourniquet inflated to 300 mmHg without remembering it.
  • Conclusion: midazolam 2–10 mg does not give reliable retrograde amnesia, but gives dose-dependent anterograde amnesia, clear at 5 and 10 mg. The authors say that midazolam therefore cannot be used to erase the memory of what has already happened.
  • Limitations: small groups, only explicit visual and event-based memory (no implicit tests and no auditory test, even though awareness often concerns sounds), and all received propofol at induction, which may itself contribute to amnesia close to induction.
  • Relation to Mashour and Pryor 2025: the chapter says there is little support for retrograde amnesia in humans and that some controlled studies show improved memory for material presented just before the dose (retrograde facilitation). Bulach supports the first, but found no facilitation (the difference for the poster at the time of the dose was not significant (p = 0.10) and went in different directions between groups).
  • Control for false memories: no patient “recalled” any of the six control posters shown only after surgery, or the fictitious finger-prick test. The authors take this as a sign that the memory tests did not produce false positives. A few controls still failed to recall everything, which they attribute to inattention in the operating room.
  • BIS and sedation: BIS fell dose-dependently after the dose (p < 0.001). BIS four minutes after the dose correlated with how many events the patient recalled from the time of the dose onwards (r = 0.51–0.56), but not with the event two minutes before (r = 0.02). Patients rated their own sedation higher than the investigators did. The authors think some of the anterograde amnesia may come from the sedation itself, and that propofol just before induction may have contributed.
  • Sample and power: excluded for age over 60 years, weight under 50 or over 100 kg, and no sedative premedication. The authors write themselves that 15 patients per group are needed for 80% power to detect a halving of recall (from 95% to below 50%), that they have only 10, and that a small retrograde effect may have been missed.
  • Funding: Alfred Trust Research Grant 2002. The BIS equipment was from Aspect Medical Systems. The article has no separate declaration of interests.
Bulach, Myles and Russnak. Br J Anaesth 2005;94:300–305

Dreaming and EEG during propofol and desflurane (Leslie 2009)

Randomised, double-blind study (Anesthesiology 2009;111:547–555) with 300 patients aged 18–50 years undergoing non-cardiac surgery with neuromuscular blockers, maintenance with propofol (TCI) or desflurane titrated to BIS 40–55. Patients were interviewed (the Brice questions) as soon as they were orientated. Raw EEG was recorded from induction until after the interview.

  • Dreams equally common: 27% (propofol) and 28% (desflurane) reported dreams. None reported awareness, and no dreams suggested memory of the operation. The dreams were simple (family, friends, work, leisure).
  • When the dreams occur: dreamers had more high-frequency power (30 Hz) and fewer spindles (10.7 Hz) than non-dreamers in the last 5 minutes before the interview, a REM-like pattern. During the operation itself there were no definite differences. The authors conclude that anaesthesia-related dreaming appears to occur just before emergence. The hypothesis that the dreamers were in deep sleep was refuted.
  • Predictors of dreams: dream frequency at home above one per week (OR 3.0), anaesthesia duration up to 100 minutes (OR 2.0) and BIS above 90 at interview (OR 1.9).
  • Propofol versus desflurane in the raw EEG: propofol gave more and faster spindle-like oscillations (peak 11 versus 10 Hz, 8–16 Hz range), desflurane fewer spindles and more delta (delta peak 3 versus 2 Hz). BIS values during maintenance were equal. At eye opening BIS was lower with propofol (75 versus 80) and at interview 85 versus 92, so the relationship between BIS and clinical level of consciousness differs for the two agents. Propofol patients moved more often (31% versus 10% with signs consistent with awareness) and received more fentanyl.
  • What the study says about Mashour and Pryor 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025: it supports that dreaming is a disconnected experience that most often belongs to emergence, and that patients' own timing (“during the anaesthetic”) cannot be taken literally. It says nothing about recall without conscious experience, and therefore cannot settle the disagreement between Mashour and Pryor 2025 and figure 36.1.
  • Caveats: usable raw EEG from only 150 of 300 patients, young patients (18–50 years), the propofol group received more opioid, and whether the findings are due to more dreaming or less amnesia for the dreams is unknown. Funded by ANZCA.
Leslie et al. Anesthesiology 2009;111:547–555

Dreams as a target: EEG-guided emergence with propofol (Sikka 2026)

Prospective quality-improvement study from Stanford (Anesthesiology 2026;145:21–36), 474 patients 2020–2023, no control group. The question was whether a standardised “emergence bundle” can make dreaming under anaesthesia common and safe. The bundle has five elements: (1) verbal priming before induction that one may dream, (2) propofol as the emergence agent, (3) EEG guidance with SedLine towards a “preemergence” state, (4) at least 10 undisturbed (“hands-off”) minutes before emergence, and (5) a modified Brice interview immediately after extubation.

  • The preemergence state in the spectrogram: the infusion is reduced to a minimum at least 10 minutes before planned emergence; the alpha band fades gradually and high-frequency activity (beta) increases, with PSI about 40–70. At signs of premature emergence (PSI above 70 or movement) small propofol boluses of 5–10 mg were given. During surgery itself PSI was 25–50, and just before emergence 80–90 (fig. 2 in the article). EEG is used here not to measure depth but to steer towards a specific brain state.
  • Who read the EEG: a small group of about ten anaesthesiologists and nurse anaesthetists (CRNAs) was trained in the operating room by the physician who developed the protocol, with emphasis on recognising alpha reduction and beta increase in the DSA, and supervised until proficient, typically at least five cases. The team was deliberately kept small for consistency.
  • Results: 452 patients were interviewed; 69% reported dreams. Among the 57 in whom all five elements were delivered, 93% dreamed. 86% of dreams were positive, none very negative. Dreamers rated sleep quality during anaesthesia higher than non-dreamers (9.16 versus 7.65, p < 0.001). In a breast-surgery subset (106 patients) dreaming was unrelated to recovery time, analgesic or antiemetic use in the PACU.
  • Awareness: no patient reported intraoperative awareness. One was uncertain and described people in blue scrubs removing the tumour, without recognising voices or staff; the first definite memory was waking up. This was classified as a surgery-related dream, not awareness.
  • The weakest link: the 10-minute hands-off period was achieved in only 14% of cases. The authors attribute this to operating-room workflow, where calm at emergence “is often not considered a clinical priority”, and call for institutional recognition of emergence quality as a valued clinical outcome. The 93% figure therefore comes from a small, self-selected subset.
  • Caveats: no control group, so the effect of each element cannot be separated; EEG was interpreted retrospectively without real-time documentation of the state's duration; interviewers were clinicians (possible interviewer bias); the PACU analyses were exploratory and underpowered. The editorial in the same issue is Palanca and Sleigh, “Protocolizing Propofol Emergence: Turning ‘Milk of Amnesia’ into Designer Dreams?” (Anesthesiology 2026, PMID 42262384). Doyal, Wanderer and Ende, “Dream Weaving: How Anesthesiologists Can Encourage Dreaming under Anesthesia” (Anesthesiology 2026;145(1):A16), is a one-page infographic based on the Sikka bundle. The same group’s scoping review (Sikka, Hu and Heifets, Br J Anaesth 2026;137:506–524) has its own card below.
  • Read together with Leslie 2009: both find that dreams belong to emergence and that none are awareness; Sikka shows that the proportion who dream can be steered up from Leslie's 27–28% by prolonging and quietening the last phase with propofol and asking immediately. This app is built around exactly that: it is the preemergence pattern in the spectrogram (alpha fading, beta arriving) that staff must be able to see in order to do it.
Sikka, Ngo, Hu, … Heifets. Anesthesiology 2026;145:21–36

Dreaming during anaesthesia: scoping review of 157 studies (Sikka, Hu and Heifets 2026)

Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, pre-registered on OSF. Searches in Medline/PubMed, Embase and PsycINFO up to 26 February 2024: 2,958 hits and 20 from reference lists, 1,721 after removing duplicates, 324 assessed in full text and 157 studies (1921–2024) with 87,866 participants. Of these, 130 were clinical studies in adults (84,945 participants), 11 in children and adolescents (2,301, aged 2 months–17 years) and 16 experimental studies in healthy volunteers (620, but overlapping datasets give only 10 unique samples, n = 356, so the total counts some volunteers more than once). This is a mapping exercise, not a meta-analysis.

  • Definition: only 13 of 141 clinical studies (9.2%) defined “dreaming”. Most build on Brice 1970: an experience (excluding awareness) that the patient recalls and thinks occurred between induction and the first consciousness after anaesthesia. 12 of 16 experimental studies (75%) used a theoretical definition: dreaming as disconnected consciousness, that is internally generated experience without sensory input and without response, as opposed to connected consciousness (awareness of the surroundings). The boundary is not always sharp: dreams containing elements from the operating room may be memories from before anaesthesia or processing of stimuli during it. In two experimental studies, dream-like content and incorporated memories occurred together in more than half of the reports.
  • How many recall: adult clinical studies from 0% (16% of the studies) to 94.6%, and all studies with 65% or more used ketamine (or etoxadrol). Propofol 0–64%, volatile agents (often with nitrous oxide) 0–60% but mostly 3–8%, dexmedetomidine 3–41%. The largest studies were at 3–8%, the largest double-blind RCTs at 3–7%. Children 0–50%, most 5–20%. Experimental studies 0–100%: ketamine 44–100%, dexmedetomidine 35.7–92.5%, propofol 0–77.3%, sevoflurane 11.4–60%, xenon 0–70%. High recall often went together with high awareness (experimentally up to 44.3%, ketamine 25%, dexmedetomidine 22.6%), suggesting lighter sedation. Awareness: among 89 studies reporting it, half reported 0%, and the largest studies 0.1–0.4%.
  • Why the figures differ: the authors think the difference between 3–8% in large clinical studies and often 40–80% in experimental ones “likely” reflects fragile memory and method, not that fewer actually dream: multiple agents, delayed interviews and interference at emergence in clinical settings, against single agents, immediate interviews, controlled emergence and priming through consent in the experiments. They stress themselves that heterogeneity prevents firm causal attribution to individual agents. This is an interpretation, not proof.
  • Content: of 130 adult studies, 90 (69%) reported valence or content. Pleasant dreams predominated, and only nine studies had more unpleasant ones (ether, thiopentone with volatile, ketamine, propofol, volatile). Typical content was everyday life: family, friends, work, holidays, beach. Propofol and dexmedetomidine dreams were mostly static and “not particularly strange” (resembling NREM sleep), while ketamine and sevoflurane dreams were more dynamic. Ketamine gave vivid, surreal, disembodied experiences (flying, colour distortion, altered time and space, death). Nightmares occurred in only five studies, more often with ketamine, and two of them may have been awareness.
  • Predictors of recall (71 adult studies): two were clearly the most consistent: higher home dream recall frequency and preoperative suggestion or priming (for example imagining a favourite place before induction). Interview timing was the most important methodological factor: an immediate interview after emergence gives clearly higher recall than a delayed one. Age, sex, ASA, anxiety: mixed, mostly not significant. Duration of surgery and anaesthesia: no association. Propofol and ketamine tended towards higher recall and volatile agents and dexmedetomidine towards lower in clinical studies, whereas dexmedetomidine gave higher recall in experimental studies. Benzodiazepines gave lower recall in 4 of 11 studies and opioids in 5 of 17. BIS during anaesthesia: mixed (lower BIS gave more recall in 4 studies, no difference in 7); higher BIS at emergence gave more in 2 studies.
  • Outcomes: only 14.6% of the studies examined them. Satisfaction, quality of recovery and postoperative anxiety or depression generally did not differ between dreamers and non-dreamers. The exception: unpleasant dreams gave lower willingness to have the same anaesthetic again (4 studies). Five studies that examined it found no difference in awareness between dreamers and non-dreamers, so dreaming should not be read as a sign of too light anaesthesia. Abuse potential rose in two studies; otherwise too little data. Children: too little data for conclusions.
  • Neural correlates (only 7 studies, 6 experimental): disconnected consciousness (dreaming) versus connected had more slow wave and delta frontomedially, more theta in the right cuneus/precuneus, less beta and gamma temporally and frontally and less information flow from front to back. Versus unconsciousness, dreaming had relatively preserved high-frequency activity and complexity (higher beta/delta, flatter spectral exponent, higher permutation entropy in mid bands). In the TMS-EEG studies (Sarasso 2015, Colombo 2019, Darracq 2018), ketamine with dreams gave high PCI and a wake-like spectral exponent, whereas propofol and xenon without dreams gave low PCI and a steep exponent; since dreaming occurred only with ketamine, agent and dreaming cannot be separated. Leslie 2009 (clinical, propofol): dreaming went with more 30 Hz activity 13–17 and 1–2 minutes before emergence and fewer spindles (10.68 Hz) 1–5 minutes before.
  • Monitoring in the studies: processed EEG (mostly BIS) in 24.6% of the adult studies, SedLine in one, none in the paediatric studies. In the experimental ones EEG was used to analyse brain dynamics, not to monitor depth, and only one used BIS to titrate.
  • The way forward and possible therapeutic use: the authors call for standardised definitions, validated instruments (an expanded Brice interview), an immediate interview within 5–15 minutes, serial awakenings with continuous EEG, and more studies in children, older people and psychiatric patients. They point to possible therapeutic benefit of pleasant, suggestible dreams (a small study found fewer trauma symptoms after dreaming under anaesthesia, Hack 2024) and highlight the Sikka 2026 bundle (93% recall), while calling for ethical guidelines on deliberately influencing subjective states.
  • Caveats and conflicts of interest: everything rests on self-report, so absence of a dream cannot be told apart from failure of encoding, storage or retrieval, and the timing of the dream cannot be established. Only English-language peer-reviewed empirical studies, the search stopped in February 2024, and reviews and editorials were left out. Heifets is an adviser or consultant to Osmind Mental Health, Journey Clinical, Arcadia Medicine, Vida Ventures and Tactogen. The authors state they used ChatGPT 5.3 and Claude to improve readability.
Sikka, Hu and Heifets. Br J Anaesth 2026;137:506–524

Awareness and choice of agent

Vuyk et al. 2025 cites a Cochrane review (Messina 2016). It found that benzodiazepines reduced awareness compared with thiopental, ketamine and placebo, and that ketamine and etomidate reduced wakefulness compared with thiopental. The chapter points out that the evidence is weak, because of risk of bias, very few events and differing definitions of awareness.

Vuyk et al. 2025

Key points

  • Inhibited metabolism gives more effect from the same dose. Many anaesthetic drugs are broken down by CYP enzymes in the liver. Inhibition gives higher concentrations and longer action, induction gives lower. Midazolam, fentanyl, alfentanil and oxycodone (CYP3A4) are most affected by concomitant antifungals, macrolides, HIV drugs or diltiazem.See
  • Propofol, remifentanil and remimazolam depend little on CYP. They are therefore suitable when interactions or liver failure are a concern. Remimazolam may still act longer in liver failure.See
  • Codeine and tramadol depend on genes. CYP2D6 produces the active substance. Ultrarapid metabolisers risk toxicity, poor metabolisers get poor pain relief. Both drugs should be avoided in both groups.Source: CPIC. See
  • Tolerance can lie in both the liver and the brain. Smokers needed more propofol and remifentanil. Remifentanil is not broken down in the liver, so changes in the brain probably also play a part. Chronic alcohol use and red hair are also linked to higher requirements.See
  • Calm and less stimulation may reduce requirements somewhat. Anxiety as a personality trait and loud noise may raise requirements, and music may lower them. But several studies found no association. The effect is small to moderate, and the mechanism has not been shown in humans. (interpretation based on the sources)See
  • Antiseizure drugs pull in different directions. Several drugs together gave a deeper and longer propofol effect without a higher propofol concentration. Enzyme-inducing drugs, on the other hand, raised fentanyl requirements and shortened the action of neuromuscular blockers. Not all antiseizure drugs are GABAergic.See
  • Titrate to effect, not to a standard dose. The spectrogram and the index show the total effect in the brain, whether the cause is the dose, an interaction or organ failure. None of the tolerance factors gives a fixed dose adjustment. (interpretation based on the sources)See and “Why do some patients tolerate more? Smoking, alcohol, cannabis and red hair”

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

Metabolism and CYP: what breaks down what, and what happens when the system is disturbed

Most anaesthetic drugs are broken down in the liver, many by cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP). Another drug, food, recreational drugs, disease or genes can inhibit or increase this breakdown. Inhibition gives a higher concentration and longer effect, induction a lower one.Sources for the table: the prescribing information and two guidelines from CPIC (Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium)

DrugMain routeWhat can change the effect
PropofolUGT1A9 (about 70%), CYP2B6 and CYP2C9 (about 29%), also outside the liverClearance exceeds hepatic blood flow. Pharmacokinetics are not altered by chronic cirrhosis (prescribing information). Gene variants give conflicting findings and are not used for dosing (Budic 2022).
MidazolamCYP3A4Ketoconazole ×5, itraconazole and fluconazole ×2–3, erythromycin ×1.6–2, clarithromycin up to ×2.5, ritonavir-boosted lopinavir ×5.4, grapefruit juice increases the effect. Rifampicin −60%, St John's wort −20–40%.
RemimazolamCarboxylesterases in the liverDoes not inhibit CYP. In hepatic impairment the effect may be stronger and last longer.
Ketamine and esketamineCYP2B6 and CYP3A4, less CYP2C9Clarithromycin ×2.6 exposure, grapefruit juice about ×3 and ticlopidine over ×2 with oral ketamine. St John's wort −58% (Andrade 2017). Longer half-life in moderate hepatic impairment.
DexmedetomidineGlucuronidation and CYP2A6Clearance 74, 64 and 53% of normal in mild, moderate and severe hepatic impairment, so the dose should be reduced.
ClonidineAbout 50% in the liver, 40–60% excreted unchanged in urineThe half-life can rise to 41 hours in severe renal failure.
Thiopental, etomidateLiverThiopental: 10–15% metabolised per hour, half-life 9–11 hours, lower dose in hepatic impairment. Etomidate: half-life roughly doubles in cirrhosis.
Sevoflurane, desfluraneSevoflurane about 5% via CYP2E1, desflurane under 0.02%CYP2E1 can be induced by chronic alcohol use and isoniazid. Barbiturates do not induce sevoflurane metabolism.
Fentanyl, alfentanil, sufentanilCYP3A4Ritonavir reduced fentanyl clearance by about two-thirds. Fluconazole, voriconazole, erythromycin, diltiazem and cimetidine inhibit alfentanil and can cause prolonged respiratory depression. Stopping an inducer (e.g. rifampicin) can make sufentanil concentrations rise.
RemifentanilNon-specific esterases in blood and tissueNot affected by hepatic or renal failure, nor by atypical cholinesterase.
MorphineGlucuronidation to M3G (about 50%) and M6G (5–15%)M6G is active. In renal failure M3G and M6G accumulate.
OxycodoneCYP3A4, less CYP2D6Voriconazole ×3.6 exposure, rifampicin −86%. CYP2D6 inhibition has not been shown to matter clinically.
Codeine, tramadolCYP2D6 makes the active substance (morphine, O-desmethyltramadol)Ultrarapid metabolisers get more active substance and risk toxicity, poor metabolisers get poor analgesia. CPIC recommends avoiding both in both groups. Deaths in children, and advised against under 12 years.
MethadoneMainly CYP2B6, little CYP3A4CPIC 2024: genotyping should not change dosing.
LidocaineLiver, to active metabolites (MEGX, GX)The half-life may double in hepatic failure, with a risk of toxic levels.
  • The main point for EEG monitoring (interpretation based on the sources): the same dose can give more effect over time. This happens when breakdown is inhibited. The spectrogram and the index show the combined effect in the brain, whether the cause is the dose, an interaction or organ failure. So titrate to effect and not only to weight or habit.
  • Little affected: propofol, remifentanil and remimazolam. They depend little on CYP. They are therefore suitable when interactions or hepatic failure are a problem. Remimazolam may still last longer in hepatic failure.
  • Most exposed: midazolam, fentanyl, alfentanil and oxycodone (CYP3A4). This applies with concurrent antifungals, macrolides, HIV drugs or diltiazem. Induction from rifampicin or St John's wort lowers the effect. When the inducer is stopped, levels rise again.
  • Children: the enzyme systems mature after birth. See the card on dexmedetomidine in children.
  • Uncertain: the exact CYP routes for lidocaine, thiopental and clonidine. They are not given in the prescribing information, so they are not in the table.
Prescribing information (eMC, FDA) Budic 2022 Andrade 2017 CPIC: Crews 2021, Robinson 2024

Why do some patients tolerate more? Smoking, alcohol, cannabis and red hair

Tolerance can have two explanations: the drug is broken down faster (pharmacokinetics), or the brain responds less to the same concentration (pharmacodynamics). In smokers both seem to contribute.

  • Smokers needed more propofol and remifentanil. Smokers needed the most propofol for induction (102.8 mg), passive smokers less (84.5 mg) and non-smokers the least (63.2 mg). Remifentanil requirements followed the same pattern. The study is small (90 women) and single-centre, so it is a signal and not proof.Source: Öztürk 2019
  • It is the smoke, not the nicotine, that increases breakdown. Substances in tobacco smoke (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons) induce CYP1A1, CYP1A2 and possibly CYP2E1. Smoking also reduces sedation from benzodiazepines and analgesia from some opioids. Nicotine patches or snus therefore do not give the same enzyme induction (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Zevin and Benowitz 1999
  • The liver does not explain everything. Remifentanil is broken down in the blood, not in the liver, and the smokers still needed more. This points to changes in the brain. Nicotine withdrawal lowers the pain threshold, and smokers who could not smoke needed more analgesia after surgery. This may relate to more nicotinic receptors (α4β2) during withdrawal.Sources: Öztürk 2019, Vega Palma 2023
  • Smokers use more opioids after surgery. Smokers used 13.9 mg morphine equivalents more via PCA than never-smokers, while former smokers did not differ. A meta-analysis found about 34% more in the first 24 hours, but the studies were non-randomised, so certainty is low.Sources: Wang 2023 (1162 patients), Szilagyi 2026
  • Local anaesthesia: smoking could speed up the breakdown of ropivacaine. Ropivacaine is partly broken down by CYP1A2. When CYP1A2 was inhibited (ciprofloxacin), clearance fell by 31%. Smoking induces CYP1A2 and could then have the opposite effect (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Jokinen 2003
  • Sevoflurane: no known difference. No study measures MAC in smokers. Washout after 1 MAC was the same in smokers and non-smokers.Source: Adanir 2010
  • Chronic alcohol raises the propofol requirement. A higher propofol concentration was needed for loss of consciousness (EC50 3.15 versus 2.21 µg/ml), but there was no difference for remifentanil. See the poisoning section in Intensive care.Source: Liang 2011
  • Cannabis: uncertain, possibly higher requirement. The propofol requirement for BIS below 60 was the same, but users needed more propofol for laryngeal mask insertion (314 versus 263 mg). A small retrospective study found more fentanyl, midazolam and propofol, but without control for other factors.Sources: Flisberg 2009, Twardowski 2019
  • Redheads need more desflurane. Red-haired women needed 6.2 vol% versus 5.2 vol% in dark-haired women. Most redheads had mutations in the MC1R gene. The study was very small.Source: Liem 2004 (10 + 10 women)
  • Patients from Asia may need less propofol, not more. Chinese patients in China lost consciousness faster and at a lower estimated concentration than European patients in Austria (1.6 versus 2.4 µg/ml at the effect site), with the same pump, model and propofol from the same production line, without premedication. Both groups lost consciousness at about the same BIS, so the brain appeared to respond in the same way when the patient fell asleep. The difference lay in how much was needed. This may be because the brain is more sensitive, or because the blood concentration was higher than the model calculated. Blood samples and cardiac output were not measured, so this cannot be decided. The authors argue that propofol should in any case be titrated to clinical effect. A model made for simulation-based training estimated the effect-site concentration at loss of consciousness at 1.9 µg/ml in Indians, 2.0 in Black patients, 2.2 in Chinese and 2.8 in Europeans. The aim was to make clinicians aware of the differences, so that sensitive patients are not given too much. Caveats: the values are based on earlier studies with different pumps and protocols, converted with the same pump model (Marsh), and were not measured in blood. The value for Indians comes from a single study of only 18 patients, and the value for Black patients was converted from another study and has no confidence interval. A small Indian study that measured propofol in blood found a lower volume of distribution and clearance than most Western studies. This may suggest that part of the difference is pharmacokinetic. But all patients received morphine before propofol, which the authors think may have lowered cardiac output and thus clearance. Genes and body composition have been proposed as explanations, but none is proven. Findings for single genes, such as UGT1A9 and CYP2B6, are inconsistent across studies. TCI models are largely based on European patients.Sources: Dahaba 2011 (60 patients, ASA I–II, 30–50 years); Lampotang 2016; Puri 2012 (26 patients); Budic et al. 2022 (review)
  • For EEG monitoring (interpretation based on the sources): none of these factors gives a fixed dose adjustment. So titrate to the spectrogram and the clinical response, not to a standard dose.
Öztürk 2019 Zevin and Benowitz 1999 Vega Palma 2023 Wang 2023 Szilagyi 2026 Liem 2004 Flisberg 2009

Antiseizure drugs and anaesthetic drugs: do they enhance or counteract?

Many antiseizure drugs act via the GABA system, and it is natural to expect them to enhance propofol and benzodiazepines. The answer depends on the drug and the mechanism. Interaction in the brain can give more effect from hypnotics, while enzyme induction can raise opioid requirements and shorten the action of neuromuscular blockers.

  • Not all antiseizure drugs are GABAergic. Phenobarbital, primidone, benzodiazepines and stiripentol enhance the GABAA receptor. Vigabatrin and tiagabine increase the amount of GABA. Valproate probably also acts via GABA, but this is debated. Many others work quite differently, for example on sodium channels (phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine), SV2A (levetiracetam) or α2δ (gabapentin, pregabalin).Source: Sills and Rogawski 2020
  • Some drugs speed up breakdown in the liver. Carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital and primidone are the main enzyme inducers. Newer drugs induce less. Valproate, in contrast, is a broad enzyme inhibitor (CYP and UGT). Lacosamide, gabapentin and pregabalin have few interactions.Source: Johannessen and Landmark 2010
  • Opioid requirements rise with the number of antiseizure drugs. In craniotomy, the fentanyl requirement rose from 2.6 µg/kg/h without antiseizure drugs to 7.6 with three drugs.Source: Tempelhoff, Modica and Spitznagel 1990 (61 patients)
  • Neuromuscular blockers act for a shorter time. Recovery after atracurium was faster with carbamazepine, and much faster with two drugs (recovery index 8.0 minutes without, 2.0 with a combination). With phenytoin, rocuronium also wore off faster. Atracurium is mainly not broken down in the liver, so enzyme induction probably does not explain everything (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Tempelhoff 1990 (Anesth Analg), Hernández-Palazón 2001
  • Patients on antiseizure drugs needed less propofol and woke later. During dental treatment in patients with intellectual disability, those taking antiseizure drugs received less propofol (5.7 versus 6.8 mg/kg/h) and woke later (29.5 versus 21.6 minutes). All drugs were pooled, most took several drugs, and the concentration was not measured.Source: Ouchi and Sugiyama 2015
  • The enhancement happens in the brain, not the liver. Valproate alone did not change BIS after propofol. Valproate together with other drugs gave a deeper BIS (25.8 versus 38.9) and a longer time to BIS above 60 (10.9 versus 4.4 minutes), without a higher propofol concentration in the blood. This suggests interaction at the site of action, partly via GABA. The groups were small.Source: Kodama 2020
  • Valproate may lower the propofol requirement in ECT. Patients on valproate needed about 1.1 mg/kg propofol for BIS 60, versus 1.5–1.6 mg/kg without. The study was retrospective, did not involve epilepsy patients, and valproate levels were low.Source: Hızlı Sayar 2014
  • The baseline EEG may be slower. In healthy volunteers, carbamazepine and gabapentin lowered the frequency of the posterior alpha rhythm, most with carbamazepine. Older drugs such as phenytoin, carbamazepine and phenobarbital give more slow and less fast activity. The spectrogram and index before induction may therefore already be affected (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Salinsky 2002, Kim 2015
  • For practice (interpretation based on the sources): the direction is not the same for all drugs. The hypnotic effect may be greater and last longer, especially with several drugs. Opioid requirements may rise and neuromuscular block wear off faster with enzyme-inducing drugs. Look at the baseline EEG before induction, titrate hypnotics to the EEG and clinical response, and monitor neuromuscular block.
Sills and Rogawski 2020 Johannessen and Landmark 2010 Tempelhoff 1990 (two studies) Hernández-Palazón 2001 Ouchi and Sugiyama 2015 Kodama 2020 Hızlı Sayar 2014 Salinsky 2002 Kim 2015

Anxiety, calm and drug requirement: is there evidence that safety lowers the need?

The idea is that an anxious patient has more excitation in the brain and therefore needs more inhibitory drugs, and that calm, safety and little stimulation mean less is needed. The literature supports parts of this, but the findings are mixed, and the mechanism has not been shown in humans.

  • Anxious people may need more propofol. Women with high trait anxiety (anxiety as a personality trait) needed more propofol for both induction and maintenance. Anxiety in the moment had no clear effect in one study, but predicted the propofol requirement in the other. The sevoflurane requirement was related only to pain sensitivity.Sources: Maranets and Kain 1999, Kil 2012
  • But several studies found no relationship with dose. Anxious patients may still have a higher entropy value when they lose consciousness. Anxiety may therefore affect what the monitor shows without changing the dose.Sources: Morley 2008, Kim and Choi 2013
  • Music lowers anxiety in intensive care. Patient-directed music gave lower anxiety and somewhat less sedation than usual care in ventilated patients. But anxiety was not lower than with noise-cancelling headphones.Source: Chlan 2013 (RCT, 373 patients)
  • Music during surgery may give somewhat less propofol. Opioid use was also somewhat lower, but not in the fully blinded studies. The Dutch guideline rates the evidence on drug use as very low.Source: Fu 2020 (meta-analysis)
  • Music does more than remove noise, and noise can raise BIS. Patients needed less propofol with music than with white noise or operating-room noise. Loud noise from the saw (about 80 dB) gave a higher BIS than when the noise was blocked out.Sources: Ayoub 2005, Kang 2008
  • Parental presence does not calm the child more than midazolam. Parental presence did not reduce the child's anxiety. The evidence is very uncertain. Low sensory stimulation, clowns and video games were promising in small studies, but none measured drug requirement.Source: Manyande 2015 (Cochrane)
  • The mechanism has not been shown in humans. In mice, activating the locus coeruleus shortened emergence from isoflurane but did not change induction. No human studies show that increased noradrenergic activity raises the induction dose.Source: Ao 2021
  • Conclusion (interpretation based on the sources): calm and less stimulation can reduce anxiety and, in some studies, the need for sedatives and propofol. That this is due to “more natural inhibition in the brain” is a reasonable hypothesis, but it is not proven. The effect is small to moderate, and the studies diverge.
Maranets and Kain 1999 Kil 2012 Morley 2008 Kim and Choi 2013 Chlan 2013 Fu 2020 Ayoub 2005 Kang 2008 Manyande 2015

The dose is a prediction, the brain gives the answer

Dosing in anaesthesia is based on pharmacological models: dose per kilo, MAC and calculated concentrations. The models describe an average patient. The individual patient can lie far from the model, which is why the brain's response must be observed.Sources: several studies by Sepúlveda and colleagues

  • The pump measures nothing. TCI calculates an expected concentration from age, weight, height, sex and what the pump itself has given. Different models, such as Schnider and Eleveld, give different numbers for the same patient and dose.Source: Obert 2024
  • Same brain, different numbers on the pump. The patients lost consciousness after almost the same amount of propofol (1.67 mg/kg with slow and 1.91 mg/kg with fast induction). Yet the pump showed almost twice the concentration with fast induction (4.6 vs 2.6 µg/ml). The reason is that the effect-site concentration is not measured, only calculated. The authors' explanation is that the models describe the first minutes after a fast dose poorly. With slow induction, blood and brain have time to keep pace, and the number becomes more reliable. Of four models, only Eleveld gave the same number at both speeds.Sources: Sepúlveda 2020 and 2021
  • The number at loss of consciousness is not “the patient's dose”. It is tempting to use the concentration the pump showed when the patient fell asleep as the target from then on. But after a fast induction that number is often too high, for the reason above. When the number was used as the target for 20 minutes, the Schnider model gave an overdose: BIS kept falling for 11 minutes, deeper than intended. With the Marsh model the number was so low that the pump stopped for almost four minutes, and all patients woke up. In volunteers, too, the number at loss of consciousness differed after bolus and infusion and between models, even though the index was the same. Effect-site TCI therefore cannot predict the effect in the individual. It is useful for keeping the state stable once the right level has been found, and that level has to be found with the EEG and clinical response.Sources: Coppens 2010, Sepúlveda 2010
