  • General EEG slowing does not identify delirium. It was burst suppression, rhythmic or periodic patterns and seizures that distinguished the delirious, not dominant frequency or amplitude.See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Sedation is not sleep

Sedation is not sleep, and sleep in intensive care is disrupted

General anaesthesia is, in fact, a reversible drug-induced coma. The word “sleep” is used to avoid worrying patients. The difference is also visible on the EEG, and intensive care patients get little true sleep.Source: Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010

  • The EEG separates sedation from sleep. Burst suppression and isoelectric EEG never occur in normal sleep. GABAergic alpha lies in the same frequency range as sleep spindles but lacks the spindles’ shape. Dexmedetomidine produces spindles and slow waves resembling N2, but K-complexes have not been described. The patterns look alike, but they differ.Sources: Akeju and Brown 2017, Eikermann et al. 2025
  • The drugs alter sleep architecture. Propofol suppresses slow-wave sleep. Benzodiazepines reduce both slow-wave sleep and REM. Opioids suppress both, more so at higher doses. In long-term ventilated patients, propofol sedation abolishes REM.Sources: Telias and Wilcox 2019, Kondili 2012
  • ICU sleep is fragmented. During sedation and mechanical ventilation, deep NREM, REM and circadian rhythm are severely reduced or abolished, and about half of sleep occurs during the day. In up to 70 % of sedated or ventilated patients the EEG does not fit standard sleep criteria, but the figure comes from a single study. Even in non-sedated intensive care patients, REM was completely absent in half.Sources: Eikermann et al. 2025, Marchasson 2024
  • The EEG can show whether it is sedation or sleep. A sedation EEG with alpha–delta or burst suppression is not sleep, even if the patient lies still with eyes closed. The spectrogram can show whether the patient is in a drug-induced state or in sleep with spindles and cyclic alternation. Only polysomnography determines sleep stage precisely.Source: Eikermann et al. 2025

The studies in detail:

Brown 2010 Akeju and Brown 2017 Telias and Wilcox 2019 Eikermann et al. 2025 Kondili 2012

Lost sleep, REM and delirium: associations, not proof

Lost sleep is linked to poorer brain function and a worse course. Almost all the findings, however, come from mice, healthy volunteers or observational studies.

  • The brain needs sleep. In mice the interstitial space increased by about 60 % in both natural sleep and anaesthesia, and β-amyloid was cleared faster. In healthy adults, β-amyloid increased by about 5 % after a night without sleep. At 6 hours in bed or less, cognitive impairment built up gradually, without participants noticing how impaired they were.Sources: Xie 2013, Shokri-Kojori 2018, Van Dongen 2003
  • Little REM is linked to a worse course and delirium. Non-sedated intensive care patients without REM (66 of 131) more often had a poor outcome (24 % versus 9 %). Severe REM reduction is also linked to delirium. GABA agonists are linked to deeper sedation, less REM and more neurocognitive disorders, but this comes from a retrospective cohort.Sources: Marchasson 2024, Trompeo 2011, Azimaraghi 2022
  • The direction is unclear. Sleep loss is regarded as a potentially modifiable risk factor for delirium. But delirium also disturbs sleep, and they may share pathophysiology. Sleep-promoting agents can themselves increase the risk of delirium.Sources: Telias and Wilcox 2019, Eikermann et al. 2025
  • Caveats. The finding on waste clearance in the brain comes from mice, and it has not been shown that sedation has the same effect in intensive care patients. The REM study is small, single-centre and of non-sedated patients, and shows an association, not a cause.Sources: Xie 2013, Marchasson 2024

The studies in detail:

Xie 2013 Shokri-Kojori 2018 Van Dongen 2003 Marchasson 2024 Trompeo 2011 Azimaraghi 2022

How light should sedation be?

The goal of sedation in intensive care is safe ventilator treatment with as little drug as possible. Light sedation is supported, but no sedation has not been shown to be better.Sources: PADIS 2018, Rasulo 2023

  • Light sedation is preferred over deep. The guideline suggests light rather than deep sedation (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). Prolonged deep sedation (RASS ≤ −3) is linked to longer ICU and hospital stays, and to delirium.Sources: PADIS (Devlin 2018), Eikermann et al. 2025
  • No sedation has both benefits and drawbacks. In a small single-unit study (140 patients), no sedation gave more ventilator-free days, but more delirium (20 % versus 7 %) and more often a need for extra staffing (20 % versus 5 %). In a larger study (700 patients), there was no significant difference in 90-day mortality. There, 27 % of the no-sedation group still received sedation within 24 hours, most often because of agitation.Sources: Strøm 2010, NONSEDA (Olsen 2020)
  • α2 agonists are no shortcut. Neither dexmedetomidine nor clonidine gave faster extubation than propofol. Agitation and severe bradycardia were more frequent.Source: A2B (Walsh 2025)
  • Staffing matters. The no-sedation study was done in a unit with 1:1 nursing, and NONSEDA did not measure nurses’ workload. Reflection from the author of the app: the patient was sometimes sedated because he could not be managed awake. Interpretation based on the sources: the goal is as light as is safe and manageable with the staffing the unit has, and the EEG can show whether the patient is sedated deeper than necessary.Sources: Strøm 2010, NONSEDA

The studies in detail:

Devlin 2018 Strøm 2010 NONSEDA (Olsen 2020) Walsh 2025 Eikermann et al. 2025

Agitation, delirium and asynchrony: what the EEG can and cannot tell

When the patient is agitated or delirious, it is tempting to increase the hypnotic. The EEG can show whether the patient is already deeply sedated, but cannot make the diagnosis.

  • General slowing does not identify delirium. In ventilated patients with new-onset altered consciousness, it was burst suppression, rhythmic or periodic patterns and seizures that distinguished the delirious from the others. Dominant frequency and amplitude did not. The study was small (91 patients), and the EEG was mostly recorded while delirium was already present.Source: Eskioglou 2021
  • Hypnotics prevent movement poorly. Midazolam alone cannot abolish movement in response to painful stimuli. Propofol alone must reach 15–16 µg/ml to prevent movement at incision, whereas burst suppression occurs at about 5 µg/ml. Pain should be treated before a sedative is considered.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, PADIS (Devlin 2018)
  • Deep sedation can increase asynchrony. Ineffective triggering rose from 7.6 % under light to 21.8 % under deep propofol sedation, in a small study (14 patients). In reverse triggering, increasing sedation is not suggested.Sources: Vaschetto 2014, Saavedra 2022
  • Interpretation based on the sources. If the EEG shows that the patient is already deeply sedated, movement and fighting the ventilator are a sign that something other than hypnosis needs treating: pain, discomfort, ventilation or surroundings.

The studies in detail:

Eskioglou 2021 Hendrickx 2008 Devlin 2018 Vaschetto 2014 Saavedra 2022

How light should sedation be? NONSEDA, Strøm and workload

The goal of sedation in intensive care is safe ventilator treatment with as little drug as possible. Light rather than deep sedation is suggested (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). Two randomised trials have examined how far down one can go.Sources: PADIS 2018, Rasulo 2023

  • No sedation gave more ventilator-free days, but more delirium and more need for staff. The trial randomised 140 patients in one unit in Denmark. No sedation gave more ventilator-free days (13.8 versus 9.6; difference 4.2 days, 95 % CI 0.3–8.1) and a shorter intensive care stay. Delirium was more frequent without sedation (20 % versus 7 %), and 20 % versus 5 % needed extra staffing. Caveats: the unit had 1:1 nursing and an intensivist present at all times, only about a third of those assessed were randomised, the study was not blinded, and 18 % in the no-sedation group still received continuous sedation.Source: Strøm 2010 (Lancet 375:475–480)
  • No sedation gave no significant difference in mortality. The trial had 700 patients in 8 units in Denmark, Norway and Sweden. 90-day mortality was 42.4 % without sedation and 37.0 % with light sedation (difference 5.4 percentage points, 95 % CI −2.2 to 12.2; p = 0.65). 27 % of the no-sedation group received sedation within 24 hours, most often because of agitation. Reintubation after accidental extubation was more frequent without sedation (8.9 % versus 4 %). Days free of coma or delirium and days in intensive care were similar.Source: NONSEDA (Olsen et al., N Engl J Med 2020)
  • NONSEDA has important caveats. The groups differed by only about one RASS point, and the study was not blinded. It did not measure nurses' workload or psychological after-effects. The result may not apply to units without 1:1 nursing.
  • α2 agonists did not give faster extubation. Dexmedetomidine and clonidine gave neither faster extubation than propofol nor less restlessness. Agitation was more frequent (see “Movement and fighting the ventilator”).Source: A2B (Walsh 2025)
  • Reflection from the author of the app (experience from cardiac postoperative care): the doctors wanted the patients as light as possible, preferably awake. For the nurses it was sometimes difficult and unpredictable, and the patient was sedated because he could not be managed awake. This fits with agitation being the most common reason for sedation in NONSEDA, and with no sedation requiring more staff in Strøm.
  • Interpretation based on the sources: light sedation is supported, but no sedation has not been shown to be better. The goal is as light as is safe for the patient and possible to manage with the staffing the unit has. The EEG can show whether the patient is sedated deeper than necessary (alpha–delta, burst suppression), but is not in itself an argument for no sedation.
Strøm et al. Lancet 2010;375:475–480 Olsen et al. N Engl J Med 2020 (NONSEDA) Devlin 2018 (PADIS) Walsh 2025 (A2B)

Movement and fighting the ventilator: less stress before more hypnotic

Suggestion from the author of the app: when an intensive care patient moves or fights the ventilator, one should look for the cause and reduce stress before increasing the hypnotic dose. These are the individual measures:

  • Hypnotics do not prevent movement well. Midazolam alone cannot abolish movement in response to painful stimuli. Propofol alone must reach 15–16 µg/ml before movement at incision is prevented, whereas burst suppression occurs at about 5 µg/ml. Immobility arises mainly in the spinal cord (see the Components tab). Increasing the hypnotic until the patient lies still can therefore give very deep hypnosis.Sources: Hendrickx 2008, Vuyk et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025
  • Treat pain first. Pain should be treated before a sedative is considered (good practice statement). Pain and sedation should be managed step by step, guided by assessment and a protocol (conditional recommendation, moderate evidence).Source: PADIS 2018
  • Less light and noise. Strategies that reduce noise and light are suggested to improve sleep (conditional, low evidence).Source: PADIS 2018
  • Ventilator settings. Assist-control ventilation at night is suggested rather than pressure support to improve sleep (conditional, low evidence). The guideline makes no recommendation on adaptive modes. Whether fighting the ventilator is best solved with other settings is not covered in the sources here.Source: PADIS 2018
  • Check for a full bladder. Acute urinary retention has been described as a cause of delirium in older people (“cystocerebral syndrome”). The proposed mechanism is increased adrenergic activity when the bladder cannot be emptied. The evidence is weak, but it is a simple thing to check.Source: Ble 2001 (case report and literature review)
  • α2 agonists are not the answer to agitation in themselves. In 1404 ventilated patients in 41 UK intensive care units, neither dexmedetomidine nor clonidine gave faster extubation than propofol. Agitation was more frequent with dexmedetomidine (RR 1.54) and clonidine (RR 1.55), as was severe bradycardia (RR 1.62 and 1.58).Source: A2B (Walsh 2025)
  • Interpretation based on the sources: if the EEG shows that the patient is already deeply sedated, movement and fighting the ventilator are a sign that something other than hypnosis needs treating: pain, discomfort, ventilation or surroundings.
Suggestion from the author of the app Devlin 2018 (PADIS), Hendrickx 2008, Vuyk et al. 2025; Sleigh et al. 2025, Ble 2001, Walsh 2025 (A2B)

What can be done to help the patient cooperate with the ventilator?

When patient and ventilator are out of step, it is called asynchrony: a mismatch between what the patient demands and what the ventilator delivers. Asynchrony is associated with worse outcomes. The first step is to identify the type, because the measures differ.Source: Saavedra 2022

  • The patient tries but the ventilator does not respond (ineffective triggering): possible causes are an insensitive trigger setting, long inspiratory time, weak drive, inadequate PEEP and auto-PEEP. Measures are adjusting the trigger, shortening inspiratory time, reducing pressure support and titrating PEEP.
  • Air hunger (insufficient flow): often with low flow or low tidal volume, or high drive from agitation, pain or fever. Measures are more flow or tidal volume, shorter rise time, or switching to pressure support.
  • Double triggering (two breaths stacked): with low tidal volume, insufficient flow, high drive or short inspiratory time. Measures are larger tidal volume, more flow or longer inspiratory time, and optimal analgesia and sedation. Neuromuscular blockade can be considered when strict lung-protective ventilation is needed.
  • Premature or late cycling: the ventilator's inspiratory time does not match the patient's own. The measure is to match the mechanical inspiratory time to the patient's.
  • Reverse triggering: the patient's diaphragm contracts in response to a ventilator breath. Increasing sedation is not suggested as treatment. A lower respiratory rate or a somewhat higher tidal volume has helped, and neuromuscular blockade gave only temporary improvement.
  • Deep sedation can increase asynchrony. In a small study (14 patients) the proportion of ineffective triggering during pressure support rose from 7.6 % with light propofol sedation to 21.8 % with deep sedation (about 2.5 µg/ml). With NAVA, where the ventilator is driven by the electrical activity of the diaphragm, it was 0 % regardless of depth.Source: Vaschetto 2014
  • Spontaneous modes can help. Patients who do not need deep sedation may benefit from a spontaneous mode.Source: Saavedra 2022
  • Interpretation based on the sources, step by step: (1) look at the pressure and flow curves and identify the type of asynchrony; (2) adjust the ventilator for that type; (3) treat what increases the drive: pain, fever, agitation, discomfort and surroundings (see the card above); (4) review the depth of sedation, and use the EEG to see whether the patient is already deeply sedated. More hypnotic can make asynchrony worse.
Saavedra 2022, Vaschetto 2014
The studies in detail: sedation and sleep, sleep medicine (Eikermann et al. 2025), sleep and the brain, REM sleep, NONSEDA and Strøm, EEG in delirium (6 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Propofol and midazolam do not produce physiological sleep: sleep deprivation as part of ICU delirium

  • The claim: Brown, Lydic and Schiff (NEJM 2010) write that general anaesthesia “is, in fact, a reversible drug-induced coma”, and that anaesthesiologists call it “sleep” to avoid disquieting patients, but unfortunately also in technical descriptions. At surgical depth anaesthesia can functionally approximate brain-stem death (unconscious, depressed brain-stem reflexes, no response to nociception, no respiratory drive), and emergence follows the same steps as recovery from coma (table 1 in the article). Sleep is actively generated by nuclei in the hypothalamus, brain stem and basal forebrain, cycles between NREM and REM every 90–120 minutes, and serves cardiovascular, immune and cognitive function. Brown has said the same publicly: patients are told they will “go to sleep”, but that is not the state they are in, and he has used the Michael Jackson case as an example (NPR interview 2011).
  • How the EEG separates sleep from anaesthesia (Akeju and Brown 2017): (1) Slow waves occur in both, but in sleep they are synchronous with brief pauses in cortical firing, under propofol asynchronous with prolonged pauses, and with more cortical sources. (2) Alpha is not a feature of NREM sleep; GABAergic alpha is frontal, high-amplitude and coherent, lies in the same frequency range as sleep spindles (12–16 Hz), but lacks the spindles' transient envelope and refractory period of several seconds, and occurs only together with slow waves. (3) Burst suppression and isoelectric EEG never occur in normal sleep; they belong to anoxic brain injury, hypothermia and Ohtahara syndrome. (4) Gamma in REM is not the same as ketamine's narrow-band 30–45 Hz “gamma burst”. (5) Sedation with GABAergic agents produces beta activity, whereas NREM sleep reduces beta; the common sleep medications (zolpidem, benzodiazepines) produce the same beta and similar cognitive side effects. (6) Dexmedetomidine produces spindles and slow waves resembling N2, but K-complexes have not been described. Their conclusion: neither anaesthetics nor sleep medications produce physiological sleep, they are unlikely to compensate for sleep need, and the oscillations they produce probably contribute to drug-induced brain dysfunction. The authors declare no competing interests.
  • ICU delirium and paradoxical excitation: Brown 2010 proposes that delirium with benzodiazepine sedation in the ICU may share a circuit mechanism with the paradoxical excitation seen at low doses of nearly every anaesthetic (GABA-mediated disinhibition in striatothalamic pathways), in line with zolpidem “waking” some patients in a minimally conscious state. This is a hypothesis in the article, not a finding.
  • What sedatives do to sleep architecture (Telias and Wilcox 2019, review): propofol is a potent suppressor of slow-wave sleep (SWS) and produces burst suppression at high doses; benzodiazepines shorten sleep latency but reduce both SWS and REM; opioids suppress SWS and REM dose-dependently. In 21 ventilated patients on continuous intravenous sedation, Gehlbach 2012 found pronounced temporal disorganisation of circadian rhythm and sleep–wake regulation, with few normal sleep EEG findings. Sedation frequently produces “atypical” EEG patterns not seen in normal sleep.
  • Sleep loss and delirium: sleep deprivation is regarded as a potentially modifiable risk factor for delirium, but the direction is unclear: delirium also disturbs sleep, and they may share pathophysiology. Trompeo 2011 found that severe REM reduction (below 6% of total sleep time) was associated with delirium in ICU patients, without causation being shown. Dexmedetomidine resembles natural sleep more than the GABA agonists do (spindles and slow waves, see the Agents tab); small pilot studies showed better sleep efficiency, and low-dose nocturnal dexmedetomidine reduced delirium without improving self-reported sleep quality.
  • What EEG can contribute: a sedation EEG with alpha-delta or burst suppression is not sleep, even if the patient lies still with eyes closed. It is an argument for measuring rather than assuming: the spectrogram shows whether the patient is in a drug-induced state or in sleep with spindles and cyclic alternation. Drouot scoring of “pathological wakefulness” and “atypical sleep” is validated only in non-sedated patients.
  • The Michael Jackson case, what is documented: Jackson received propofol at home for insomnia and died in 2009; his physician Conrad Murray was convicted of involuntary manslaughter in 2011. Expert witnesses at the trial included the anaesthesiologists Steven Shafer (for the prosecution) and Paul White (for the defence) and the sleep specialist Nader Kamangar, who testified that propofol has no medical benefit for insomnia. Emery Brown was not a witness in the case but has used it in public communication. Whether chronic propofol “sleep” made Jackson sleep-deprived is a hypothesis raised publicly, not a forensic finding.
  • Terminology: the sources in this app use “unconsciousness”, “hypnosis” and “sedation”, not “sleep”. Telling patients and relatives that they will “sleep” is established practice, but it is worth knowing that it is wrong, and that “sedation for days” does not meet the need for sleep.
Brown, Lydic and Schiff. N Engl J Med 2010;363:2638–2650 · Akeju and Brown. Curr Opin Neurobiol 2017;44:178–185 · Telias and Wilcox. Crit Care 2019;23:82 · Gehlbach 2012 and Trompeo 2011 (cited by Telias) · NPR Fresh Air 2011 · Medscape and CNN, trial 2011

What the textbook chapter on sleep medicine adds (Eikermann et al. 2025, Eikermann, Fassbender and Azimaraghi)

  • Sleep onset is sharp, induction is gradual: physiological sleep begins as a sharp alpha–theta transition in the EEG, without intermediate stages, and the same applies to the NREM→REM switch (pontine “flip-flop” switches). Anaesthetic induction, by contrast, is a continuous decline from awake through reduced responsiveness to unresponsive. Sleep has spontaneous onset and termination, is readily reversed by noxious stimuli and is homeostatically regulated; anaesthesia lacks the stage structure, and arousal from drug-induced unconsciousness requires some drug elimination. The chapter states that EEG patterns during sleep and anaesthesia differ despite similarities between slow-wave sleep and anaesthesia, citing Brown 2010.
  • The stages as the chapter defines them: N1 is the alpha→theta transition, N2 has spindles and K-complexes, N3 is slow-wave sleep (delta), REM is low-amplitude mixed activity with atonia and eye movements. Benzodiazepines, opioids and antidepressants suppress REM; the elderly have less slow-wave sleep. Polysomnography (EEG, EOG, chin EMG) is the only method that determines sleep stage precisely; actigraphy and questionnaires do not.
  • The “shared circuit” hypothesis, and why it does not hold for anaesthesia: many sedatives (dexmedetomidine, ethanol, isoflurane) activate sleep-promoting VLPO neurons, and loss of VLPO neurons attenuates the sedative response to dexmedetomidine, suggesting a causal role for sedation. But animals with complete VLPO lesions can still be anaesthetised (transient resistance to volatile agents, later increased sensitivity owing to increased homeostatic sleep drive), and direct inhibition of the TMN produces sedation, not anaesthesia. The chapter's conclusion (fig. 9.12): anaesthetics activate VLPO/MnPO and induce arousable unconsciousness (sedation) at low doses, but general anaesthesia cannot be achieved via arousal-inhibiting circuits alone; at anaesthetic doses, circuits downstream (including the neocortex) are modulated simultaneously so that the brain's information processing is disrupted across spatial and temporal scales. Thalamocortical networks remain active during sleep, unlike during anaesthesia.
  • Postoperative sleep: REM falls substantially on the first night after surgery and anaesthesia, with REM rebound (more and more intense REM) on nights 2–4; disturbances can last up to 6 months depending on the extent of surgery. Surgery alone (without general anaesthesia) reduces REM; pain, inflammation, immobility and anxiety contribute. In long-term ventilated patients propofol sedation abolishes REM and diminishes sleep quality (Kondili 2012), whereas low-dose propofol permits REM. Ketamine is little studied, probably with mild REM effects. Circadian effects of anaesthetics are unresolved; 3 hours of anaesthesia did not alter the body-temperature rhythm in humans.
  • Sleep in the ICU: sleep fragmentation occurs consistently during sedation and mechanical ventilation; deep NREM, REM and circadian rhythms are severely reduced or abolished, and about half of sleep occurs during the daytime. In up to 70% of sedated or ventilated patients the EEG is “atypical” and does not fit standard criteria for sleep and wakefulness; alternative ICU scoring systems (Watson 2013) have been proposed but not validated. Frontal portable EEG monitors with electrode placements approximating the AASM recommendation can be used. Sound above 77 dB increased arousals in stable ventilated patients (Elbaz 2017), with alarms the largest source; dim light around the clock hinders photoentrainment. Earplugs and eye masks consistently improve sleep quality.
  • Sedation depth, REM and delirium: prolonged deep sedation (RASS ≤ −3) is associated with longer ICU and hospital stays and delirium; GABA agonists (propofol, benzodiazepines) may increase sedation depth, reduce REM and thereby increase neurocognitive disorders (Azimaraghi 2022, retrospective cohort from the same author group). Opioids reduce REM and worsen sleep apnoea; unrecognised pain leads to excessive sedative use. Melatonin has produced conflicting results; the orexin antagonist suvorexant is promising but not studied in the critically ill. Sleep deprivation impairs immune function, glucose tolerance, produces a catabolic stress response, respiratory muscle fatigue, impaired attention and working memory and increased vulnerability to delirium, but sleep-promoting agents can themselves increase delirium risk.
  • Narcolepsy: these patients have increased sensitivity to anaesthetics with delayed emergence, postoperative hypersomnia and apnoeic episodes; the chapter recommends monitoring of anaesthetic depth in this group, without specifying the method.
  • Caveats: the chapter is a textbook review; many of the mechanistic findings are animal studies (VLPO lesions in rats and mice), and the 70% atypical-EEG figure comes from a single study. Conflicts of interest are not stated in the chapter text available to us.
Eikermann et al. 2025 (Miller's Anesthesia, 10th ed.) · the chapter's references: Brown 2010, Akeju and Brown 2017, Moore 2012, Kondili 2012, Watson 2013, Elbaz 2017, Azimaraghi 2022

Why sleep matters for the brain: waste clearance, amyloid and cognition

Three studies and the textbook chapter on sleep medicine show why lost sleep is more than tiredness. The findings are from mice and from small experiments in healthy people, not from sedated intensive care patients.

  • Waste clearance (Xie 2013, Science 342:373–377): in mice the interstitial space increased by about 60 % in both natural sleep and anaesthesia. This gave faster exchange between cerebrospinal fluid and interstitial fluid and faster clearance of β-amyloid.
  • Amyloid in humans (Shokri-Kojori 2018, PNAS): 20 healthy adults (22–72 years) had PET after a night of sleep and after a night without sleep (about 31 hours awake). β-amyloid increased by about 5 %, including in the thalamus and hippocampus, and a larger increase was associated with worse mood.
  • Cognition (Van Dongen 2003, Sleep 26:117–126): 48 healthy people (21–38 years) spent 4, 6 or 8 hours in bed for 14 days. At 6 hours or less, cognitive impairment accumulated in a dose-dependent way, equivalent to up to 2 nights without any sleep. Self-reported sleepiness rose at first and then levelled off, so participants were largely unaware of how impaired they were.
  • Health and mortality (Eikermann et al. 2025): sleep restriction is an independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease, metabolic disease and all-cause mortality, and adults are advised to get at least 7 hours. Sleep deprivation delays the antibody response to influenza vaccine, impairs glucose tolerance and causes insulin resistance in healthy young people, and produces a catabolic state with increased oxygen consumption, CO2 production and catecholamines.
  • Caveats: Xie is an animal study, and anaesthesia also increased the interstitial space in the mice. That sedation in intensive care patients has the same effect has not been shown. Shokri-Kojori and Van Dongen are small studies in healthy people. The relationship between sleep loss and delirium may run in both directions.
Xie 2013 Shokri-Kojori 2018 Van Dongen 2003 Eikermann et al. 2025

Sleep in intensive care: outcomes were worse without REM sleep (Marchasson 2024)

Marchasson et al. (Crit Care 2024;28:331, doi 10.1186/s13054-024-05118-4), “Impact of sleep disturbances on outcomes in intensive care units”. A post-hoc analysis of three observational studies of 131 conscious patients without continuous sedation who had full polysomnography at different times during the intensive care stay: 34 with acute respiratory failure, 45 on mechanical ventilation with weaning difficulties and 52 immediately after extubation.

  • Deep sleep: preserved in acute respiratory failure, but markedly reduced under mechanical ventilation and after extubation (p < 0.01).
  • Atypical sleep: more frequent under mechanical ventilation than in patients breathing spontaneously (p < 0.01).
  • REM sleep: uncommon at all time points and completely absent in 66 of 131 (50 %), and in 63 % after extubation.
  • Outcome: a poor outcome (intubation, prolonged weaning or reintubation) occurred in 22 of 131 (17 %). Patients without REM sleep more often had a poor outcome than those with preserved REM: 24 % versus 9 % (p = 0.03). ICU mortality did not differ significantly (12 % versus 3 %, p = 0.11).
  • Caveats: an association, not a cause. A small single-centre study with single recordings. The patients were not sedated, so the findings cannot be transferred directly to a sedated intensive care patient. The study does not show what makes REM sleep disappear.
Marchasson et al. Crit Care 2024;28:331

EEG in ventilated patients with new-onset altered consciousness and delirium (Eskioglou 2021)

Pre-planned analysis from the CERTA study (Acta Neurol Scand 2021;144:296–302): 91 non-neurological intensive care patients in Lausanne (median 66 years, sepsis most common) who had an EEG because of new-onset altered consciousness, median 5 days after admission. 64% were sedated during the EEG (propofol and/or midazolam). The EEG was interpreted according to the 2012 ACNS nomenclature, blinded to delirium. 42 (46%) developed delirium, half diagnosed with CAM-ICU and the rest from the chart and antipsychotic use.

  • Burst suppression only in the delirious: 10% versus 0% (p = 0.02). Of the four, two were unsedated and two received propofol 2.2–2.5 mg/kg/h; all had sepsis, two died.
  • Rhythmic or periodic patterns (the ictal-interictal continuum) in 43% versus 22% (p = 0.03), and seizures or status epilepticus in 7% versus 0% (p = 0.05).
  • At least one of the three findings in 32 of 91 (35%) gave a higher delirium rate (42 versus 15%, p = 0.006).
  • What did not discriminate: dominant frequency (theta in about 70% in both groups), amplitude, reactivity, triphasic waves (33 versus 27%), NREM sleep elements and sedative doses during the first 5 days. General EEG slowing, which is often linked to delirium, therefore did not discriminate here, because it is common in intensive care patients regardless of cause.
  • ACNS definitions used: continuous (suppression below 10%), discontinuous (10–49%), burst suppression (≥ 50%) and suppressed (below 10 µV).
  • Caveats: small sample, selected population without acute brain injury, EEG mostly recorded while delirium was already present (81 of 91), CAM-ICU missing in half, borderline significance for seizures, no correction for multiple comparisons. Funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation.
Eskioglou et al. Acta Neurol Scand 2021;144:296–302

Key points

  • EEG during poisoning says most about the drug and little about prognosis. In poisoning, burst suppression is not in itself a sign of brain injury. Four patients with alpha or beta coma after poisoning without hypoxia all recovered. Assessment of prognosis and brain death must wait until the drugs have cleared (interpretation based on the sources).See “EEG in toxic coma: patterns that can mislead”
  • Poisoning can mimic brain death. In baclofen poisoning, pupillary reflexes were absent in all nine described cases, and the EEG showed burst suppression. Yet the patient recovered fully. A review found 56 such cases involving 19 different substances.See “EEG in toxic coma: patterns that can mislead”
  • Tolerance and synergy make habitual dosing unreliable. With chronic alcohol use, more propofol is needed for loss of consciousness: 3.15 versus 2.21 µg/ml at the effect site. Opioids combined with benzodiazepines cause more respiratory depression. The spectrogram can show where the patient actually is (interpretation based on the sources).See “Alcohol: tolerance, induction and withdrawal”, “Opioids, benzodiazepines and gabapentinoids: tolerance and synergy”
  • GHB causes abrupt coma and abrupt awakening. The half-life is about 20–40 minutes, and patients often wake suddenly. There are no EEG data from GHB poisoning in humans. When used for sedation, GHB produced slow activity, and about one in three had burst suppression.See “GHB: sudden coma, sudden awakening and dangerous withdrawal”
  • Withdrawal can be severe and should be anticipated. GHB withdrawal starts 1–6 hours after the last dose, often fulminant, and lasts 3–21 days. Abrupt discontinuation of benzodiazepines after prolonged sedation can cause withdrawal with seizures. Patients on methadone or buprenorphine should be allowed to continue it in intensive care.See “GHB: sudden coma, sudden awakening and dangerous withdrawal”, “Opioids, benzodiazepines and gabapentinoids: tolerance and synergy”

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

Poisoning and recreational drugs in intensive care: synergy, tolerance and EEG

Poisoned patients often have several substances in the body at once. Many of them act on the same receptors as the sedatives. This can give a stronger effect (synergy), a weaker effect (tolerance) or withdrawal when the substance wears off. The cards below are based on peer-reviewed literature. Where data are lacking, it says so.

GHB: sudden coma, sudden awakening and dangerous withdrawal
Andresen 2008 Liakoni 2016 Aronsen 2020 Entholzner 1995 Karila 2024
  • How GHB works is unclear. GHB activates GABAB receptors at high concentrations and a separate GHB receptor at low ones.Source: Andresen 2008
  • The patient arrives in deep coma and wakes suddenly. The picture ranges from alcohol-like intoxication to coma, bradycardia and respiratory depression. The pupils are typically not small, unlike with opioids. The half-life is about 20–40 minutes.Source: Andresen 2008
  • In Oslo most had reduced consciousness, but only one was intubated. Of 329 cases at the Oslo emergency clinic 2013–15, 69% had GCS below 15 and 14% GCS 7 or lower. 29% had also taken alcohol. 9% were given naloxone, and 48% were sent on to hospital.Source: Aronsen 2020
  • Many also take alcohol, but it made no clear difference to coma. In a Swiss series (78 cases), 65% had also taken alcohol or other drugs. With alcohol, coma was somewhat more frequent and lasted somewhat longer, but the differences were not significant. Median time to awakening was 90 minutes, and in 32% it came suddenly.Source: Liakoni 2016
  • There are no human EEG data from GHB poisoning. Used for sedation, GHB (50 mg/kg) gave slow activity (delta–theta or pure delta) and less alpha and beta within 10 minutes. About one patient in three had burst suppression. No seizure activity was seen. Deep GHB coma can therefore probably give a very slow EEG and burst suppression that disappears when the drug is gone (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Entholzner 1995
  • GHB withdrawal comes quickly and can be severe. It starts 1–6 hours after the last dose, often with a fulminant course, and lasts 3–21 days, about 9 on average. High-dose benzodiazepines are first choice. If there is no response after 24 hours, phenobarbital in the ICU is proposed. Propofol and pentobarbital are also mentioned. There are no RCTs.Source: Karila 2024
  • Dexmedetomidine in GHB withdrawal is described in only one case report. It was given as an adjunct in benzodiazepine-resistant delirium, and the patient did not need ventilation. Bradycardia and hypotension limited the dose.Source: Tay 2016

Micro level: receptors and neurons

  • The brain makes GHB itself. It is formed from GABA via succinic semialdehyde. In the rare inherited disease SSADH deficiency, the enzyme that converts succinic semialdehyde further is missing, and GHB accumulates.Source: Lee 2022
  • The effects go via GABAB. GABAB is a G-protein-coupled receptor, not an ion channel like GABAA, and the inhibition is slower. In mice lacking GABAB1, GHB no longer reduced activity or body temperature or induced delta waves on the EEG. The GHB binding sites were still present, so they are something other than GABAB.Source: Kaupmann 2003
  • GHB and baclofen both act on GABAB, but on different neurons. In the VTA (ventral tegmental area), GABAB opens potassium channels (GIRK) much more easily in the inhibitory GABA neurons than in the dopamine neurons. Baclofen inhibited both cell types, GHB only the GABA neurons. The dopamine neurons are then released from inhibition. This is a likely explanation for why GHB can be rewarding and addictive, unlike baclofen.Source: Cruz 2004
  • The high-affinity binding site is probably the enzyme CaMKIIα. It appears to be the hub domain of the enzyme. What the binding does is not clear, and it has not been shown to contribute to sedation. Certain GABAA variants have also been proposed as binding sites.Sources: Leurs 2021, Bay 2014
  • The delta waves from GHB require GABAB. They disappeared in mice without GABAB. In narcolepsy, sodium oxybate gave more deep sleep and more delta power. It could not be decided whether this was true sleep or a drug effect resembling anaesthesia.Sources: Kaupmann 2003, Black 2010
  • Benzodiazepines may fall short in GHB withdrawal (interpretation based on the sources). Benzodiazepines enhance GABAA, while the main effects of GHB go via GABAB. How the receptors change with tolerance has only been proposed, not shown in primary studies.Sources: Kaupmann 2003, Bay 2014, Brunt 2014
Alcohol: tolerance, induction and withdrawal
Liang 2011 Ultane prescribing information Rayner 2012 Umar 2023
  • Chronic alcohol use raises the propofol requirement. In 30 men with chronic alcohol use, the effect-site EC50 was 3.15 µg/ml, versus 2.21 µg/ml in controls. EC50 is the concentration that gave loss of consciousness in half. For remifentanil there was no difference.Source: Liang 2011
  • The tolerance probably lies mostly in the brain, not in breakdown. Chronic alcohol use can induce CYP2E1, which breaks down sevoflurane. For most anaesthetics, however, the tolerance is probably more related to adaptation in the brain than to faster breakdown (interpretation, not examined in the sources).Source: Ultane prescribing information
  • How much acute intoxication lowers the anaesthetic requirement has not been quantified. No studies on this were found.
  • Dexmedetomidine can spare benzodiazepines in alcohol withdrawal, but should not be used alone. In 20 patients with benzodiazepine-resistant withdrawal, benzodiazepine use fell by 61.5% in the first 24 hours. Heart rate fell by about 23 beats/min, and one patient had two 9-second pauses without a heartbeat. Dexmedetomidine may not prevent withdrawal seizures.Source: Rayner 2012
  • Phenobarbital shortened hospital stay. A meta-analysis found a 2.6-day shorter hospital stay, but no clear difference in ICU stay or intubation.Source: Umar 2023
Opioids, benzodiazepines and gabapentinoids: tolerance and synergy
Smith 2022 Midazolam SmPC FDA 2016 Sun 2017 Gomes 2017
  • Patients on methadone or buprenorphine should be allowed to continue it in intensive care. It is given in addition to analgesia, and the patient should be assessed for withdrawal.Source: Smith 2022
  • Long-term benzodiazepine sedation can cause tolerance and withdrawal. Tolerance may mean the dose has to be increased. Abrupt discontinuation after ICU sedation can cause withdrawal with convulsions. The risk of dependence is higher with a history of alcohol or drug abuse.Source: Midazolam SmPC
  • Opioids and benzodiazepines together give more respiratory depression. In 2016 the FDA added its strongest warning to both. In patients with an opioid prescription, overdose was 2.42% per year with a concurrent benzodiazepine, versus 1.16% without (adjusted OR 2.14).Sources: FDA 2016, Sun 2017
  • Gabapentin together with opioids is associated with more opioid-related deaths. The adjusted OR was 1.49. The interaction between hypnotics and opioids is described in the cards on Hendrickx 2008.Source: Gomes 2017
  • The spectrogram can show where the patient actually is (interpretation based on the sources). Tolerance means that the same dose gives less effect in the brain, and synergy that it gives more. Both make dosing by habit uncertain.
EEG in toxic coma: patterns that can mislead
Rayi (StatPearls) 2025 Carroll and Mastaglia 1979 Sutter and Kaplan 2012 Shanker 2021 Farhat 2020 Murphy 2021
  • Benzodiazepines and barbiturates can give lots of beta. The EEG may then show abundant fast beta activity.Source: Rayi 2025
  • Alpha and beta coma after poisoning can have a good prognosis. Four patients with poisoning without hypoxia had alpha or beta coma, and all recovered. Beta and triphasic patterns may suggest a good prognosis, but this depends on the cause. See also the shared case of alpha coma in a child with benzodiazepine poisoning above.Sources: Carroll and Mastaglia 1979, Sutter and Kaplan 2012
  • Triphasic waves can be caused by drugs. They are also seen in drug-induced encephalopathy, not only in hepatic or renal failure.Source: Rayi 2025
  • In poisoning, burst suppression is not in itself a sign of brain injury. High doses of sevoflurane, barbiturates, propofol and etomidate give burst suppression.Source: Shanker 2021
  • Poisoning can mimic brain death. In baclofen poisoning the pupillary reflexes were absent in all nine reported cases, and the EEG showed burst suppression. The patient nevertheless recovered fully. A review found 56 such cases involving 19 different substances, most often snake envenomation, baclofen, tricyclic antidepressants and bupropion.Sources: Farhat 2020, Murphy 2021
  • In practice, the EEG says most about the drug and little about prognosis (interpretation based on the sources). This applies especially without hypoxia. Assessment of prognosis and brain death must wait until the substances have left the body.

Key points

  • aEEG is a heavily simplified EEG for newborns. The signal from two or four electrodes is filtered, rectified and compressed in time. Many hours then fit on the screen as a band. The upper and lower margins show the highest and lowest voltage. (see “What aEEG is, and how the trace is made”)
  • Read the pattern, not just the voltage. The background is classified as continuous normal, discontinuous normal, burst suppression, low voltage and flat trace. Voltage limits alone can mislead, for example when the ECG or baseline drift lifts the lower margin. (see “The background: pattern and voltage”)
  • aEEG is good for trends and prognosis, but weak for seizures. aEEG identified neonates with seizures with a sensitivity of 71 % and specificity of 84 %, with low certainty. Short seizures and seizures far from the electrodes are missed, and artefacts can look like seizures. Full EEG is the reference. (see “Seizures: aEEG raises suspicion, full EEG gives the answer”)
  • Cooling changes the time frame for prognosis. With cooling, an abnormal aEEG in the first 6 hours means less. Infants with a good outcome had a normal background within 24 hours without cooling and within 48 hours with cooling. (see “Prognosis after oxygen deprivation at birth, with and without cooling (Thoresen 2010)”)
  • Drugs and artefacts can change the trace. Phenobarbital, morphine and midazolam depress the aEEG. The ECG, movement and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation can lift the lower margin or mimic seizures. The raw EEG alongside the band is the most important safeguard. (see “Drugs and artefacts”)
  • Sleep–wake cycling is a good sign. Infants who never developed cycling almost always had a poor outcome. (see “Prognosis after oxygen deprivation at birth, with and without cooling (Thoresen 2010)”)

The theme cards below explain the context, with the sources under each point.

What aEEG is, and how the trace is made

aEEG (amplitude-integrated EEG) is widely used in neonatal intensive care because the staff can apply the electrodes and read the trace at the bedside. It shows how the brain's electrical activity changes over hours and days, but says little about the details.

  • aEEG turns the raw EEG into a band. The raw EEG from two or four electrodes is filtered, rectified and compressed in time. The upper and lower margins of the band correspond to the highest and lowest voltage in the raw EEG. The vertical axis is linear from 0 to 10 µV and logarithmic from 10 to 100 µV. This enhances low signals and attenuates high ones. The trace is usually written at 6 cm per hour.Sources: Cochrane 2025, Tao and Mathur 2010
  • The electrodes sit close to the watershed areas. Either one pair over both parietal lobes (P3–P4) or two channels, one on each side (C3–P3 and C4–P4). The watershed areas are often affected by oxygen deprivation at birth, and these positions are less prone to artefacts. Two channels were better than one, especially with injury on one side.Sources: Cochrane 2025, Tao and Mathur 2010
  • The raw EEG alongside the band helps. Newer devices show the raw EEG together with the band. This makes it easier to tell seizures from artefacts.Sources: Cochrane 2025, Tao and Mathur 2010
  • Simplification has a price. With few electrodes and compressed time, short seizures, especially those under 30 seconds, and seizures far from the electrodes are easily missed. Seizure duration is often underestimated.Source: Cochrane 2025
Cochrane 2025 Tao and Mathur 2010 Thoresen 2010

The background: pattern and voltage

The background can be assessed in two ways: by its pattern or by the voltage of the upper and lower margins. The two can be used together.Source: Thoresen 2010

  • The pattern separates normal from abnormal. Continuous normal voltage (CNV) and discontinuous normal voltage (DNV) are regarded as normal. CNV has no periods of low amplitude, whereas DNV has short quiet periods. Burst suppression (BS), low voltage (LV) and flat trace (FT) are regarded as abnormal. Burst suppression means virtually absent activity (below 2 µV) between bursts above 25 µV.Source: Thoresen 2010
  • Voltage divides the background into three groups. Normal: lower margin above 5 µV and upper above 10 µV. Moderately abnormal: lower margin below 5 µV and upper above 10 µV. Severely abnormal: both lower. Abnormal voltage was an entry criterion in the cooling trials CoolCap and TOBY.Source: al Naqeeb 1999, as given in Thoresen 2010
  • Voltage can mislead. The ECG and other continuous artefacts can lift the lower margin. Baseline drift can lift the lower margin above 5 µV. Burst suppression may then be read as normal voltage, and an infant who should have been cooled may be missed. Conversely, DNV may end up as moderately abnormal because the quiet periods pull the lower margin down.
  • Hellström-Westas' classification has its own limits. Continuous: upper margin above 10 µV and lower above 5 µV. Discontinuous: upper margin above 10 µV and lower below 5 µV. Low voltage: upper margin below 10 µV and lower below 5 µV. Flat trace: both margins below 5 µV. Burst suppression is divided into more and fewer than 100 bursts per hour.Source: Hellström-Westas, as given in Tao and Mathur 2010
  • Always look for the pattern, even when using the voltage limits. The voltage method is easiest for the inexperienced. The pattern method together with the raw EEG performed best. In one study without raw EEG, readers agreed more with the voltage method, but agreement with full EEG was only fair for both methods.Sources: Thoresen 2010, Tao and Mathur 2010
  • Sleep–wake cycling shows as a band that changes width. The variations are regular. A narrow band means wakefulness or active sleep, a wide band means quiet sleep.Source: Tao and Mathur 2010
  • During cooling, drugs act for longer. Anticonvulsant and sedative drugs have a longer half-life during cooling. They may depress the aEEG and delay a normal background and sleep–wake cycling.Source: Thoresen 2010 (discussion)
Thoresen 2010 Tao and Mathur 2010

Prognosis after oxygen deprivation at birth, with and without cooling (Thoresen 2010)

74 term infants with asphyxia, 31 without and 43 with cooling, were followed with aEEG for up to 72 hours and had a developmental test at 18 months.Source: Thoresen, Hellström-Westas, Liu and de Vries, Pediatrics 2010;126:e131–e139

  • An abnormal aEEG in the first 6 hours means less when the infant is cooled. An abnormal pattern (BS, LV or FT) at 3–6 hours predicted a poor outcome with a positive predictive value of 84 % without cooling, but only 59 % with cooling. A normal pattern predicted a good outcome in all 15 cooled infants. Moderately abnormal voltage did not predict outcome.
  • Time to a normal background was the best predictor. All infants with a good outcome had a normal background within 24 hours without cooling and within 48 hours with cooling. All who never regained a normal background had a poor outcome, and 72 % of them died.
  • Without sleep–wake cycling, the outcome was almost always poor. 29 of 33 infants who never developed cycling had a poor outcome. In infants with a good outcome, cycling appeared after a median of 24 hours without and 36 hours with cooling.
  • Before cooling became routine, 6–12 hours after birth was the most valuable time window. Sensitivity was then 91–100 % and the positive predictive value about 85 %. Among infants with a severely abnormal trace at 6 hours that normalised within 24 hours, 61 % had mild or no disability.Source: van Rooij, as given in Tao and Mathur 2010
  • Using aEEG to select infants for cooling is disputed. CoolCap and TOBY used an abnormal aEEG as an entry criterion, whereas two other large cooling trials did not. In one group, a normal or mildly abnormal aEEG had a low negative predictive value, probably because ECG artefact lifted the lower margin. They stopped using aEEG to select infants.Source: Sarkar and colleagues, as given in Tao and Mathur 2010
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): in an infant who is being cooled, a poor aEEG in the first hours should not be read as a verdict. It is the course over the first 48 hours that counts.
  • Caveat: the sample is small. 74 infants from the neonatal units in Bristol between 1998 and 2008, recorded with a single channel (P3–P4). The infants took part in randomised cooling trials. The study was funded in part by the manufacturer of the aEEG device used.
Thoresen et al. Pediatrics 2010 Tao and Mathur 2010

Preterm infants

In preterm infants aEEG is still a field of research, but the patterns change predictably with maturation.Source for the whole card: Tao and Mathur 2010

  • The more immature the infant, the more discontinuous the trace. The background has more bursts and longer periods of low voltage. The proportion of continuous activity increases with gestational age and with age after birth.
  • Cycling can be seen early. Cyclical variations have been seen as early as a mean gestational age of 28 weeks. A cycle was defined as regular variations lasting at least 20 minutes.
  • Brain haemorrhage worsens the trace. Preterm infants under 30 weeks with intraventricular haemorrhage had a more discontinuous trace, more seizures and less cycling, more so the larger the bleed. With progressive ventricular dilatation, the changes appeared before clinical signs of raised pressure. In most, they improved after drainage.
  • Many bursts and early cycling are good signs. More bursts per hour and earlier cycling are associated with better outcomes. Fewer than 130 bursts per hour are associated with poorer outcomes.
Tao and Mathur 2010

Drugs and artefacts

  • Drugs depress the trace, usually transiently. This applies to anticonvulsants and opioids. Phenobarbital gives lower voltage and longer pauses between bursts. Morphine and midazolam act similarly, and the changes were reversed with naloxone. Surfactant also gave less activity and fewer bursts. Three or more anticonvulsants delayed sleep–wake cycling. During cooling the drugs last longer.Sources: Tao and Mathur 2010, Thoresen 2010
  • Artefacts are common. In published studies, artefacts made up 12–60 % of recordings, even with the raw EEG available. The ECG, movement, high-frequency oscillatory ventilation and electrode placement affect the trace.
  • ECG artefact can make a depressed trace look better. When the background is severely depressed, ECG artefact can lift the lower margin. A lower margin above 5 µV may then look more reassuring than it is.
  • Some things look like seizures without being seizures. High-frequency oscillatory ventilation and muscle activity on both sides can produce waves that resemble seizures. Comparison with the raw EEG is essential.
  • Interpretation based on the sources: these are the same sources of error as with frontal EEG in adults, and the same answer applies: read the raw EEG, not just the trend.
  • Frontal anaesthesia monitors are not an alternative to aEEG. The knowledge about aEEG, with its voltage limits, timings and accuracy, applies to aEEG with electrodes over central and parietal areas near the watershed zones. No peer-reviewed studies have been found in which frontal monitors of anaesthetic depth were tested for background, seizures or prognosis in neonatal intensive care. Frontal EEG cannot rule out seizures. For anaesthesia in small children, by contrast, frontal EEG has been studied (see Spectrogram → Newborns and preterm).Source: Gimson and Smith 2021
Tao and Mathur 2010 Thoresen 2010

Seizures: aEEG raises suspicion, full EEG gives the answer

Full EEG is the reference for seizures in newborns. A Cochrane review compared aEEG with full EEG in 16 studies with 562 neonates.Source: Rakshasbhuvankar and colleagues, Cochrane 2025

  • Most neonatal seizures cannot be seen. 65–80 % of seizures have no visible signs, and many events that look like seizures are not. Clinical observation alone therefore gives both too few and too many diagnoses.
  • aEEG misses some infants with seizures, and the certainty is low. Sensitivity was 71 % and specificity 84 %. The figures were lower in the three studies with the lowest risk of bias. When aEEG was interpreted at the bedside in real time, sensitivity was 0 and 57 % in the two studies that did so.
  • A seizure shows as a brief rise of the lower margin. Often the upper margin rises too. The raw EEG then shows repetitive discharges that evolve and last at least 10 seconds.
  • Raw EEG and experience decide how many seizures are found. Short seizures, seizures far from the electrodes, low voltage and an inexperienced reader cause seizures to be missed. For individual seizures, sensitivity was 76 % with raw EEG versus 39 % without. Without the raw EEG, neonatologists detected only 12–38 % of individual seizures. With two channels and the raw EEG, sensitivity and specificity approached 80 %. A seizure algorithm detected 73 % of seizures over 30 seconds and 87 % of seizures over 60 seconds.Sources: Cochrane 2025 (earlier review), Tao and Mathur 2010
  • Seizures are divided into three groups. Single seizures, repetitive seizures and status epilepticus, in which seizure activity lasts more than 30 minutes.Source: Hellström-Westas, as given in Tao and Mathur 2010
  • False seizures are most common with bedside reading and among the inexperienced. The causes are muscle movement, patting, hiccups and poor electrode contact.
  • The conclusion: aEEG should not be the main method for treating neonatal seizures. It risks both too little and too much anticonvulsant treatment. Full EEG is recommended for 24 hours in high-risk neonates, but is not available everywhere. aEEG probably adds to clinical observation alone.

The same principle as in adults: a simplified monitor raises suspicion, full EEG and a neurologist give the answer. See also and .

Cochrane 2025 Tao and Mathur 2010

Key points

  • The spectrogram can mirror systemic perfusion. In septic shock, the EEG showed slow theta, delta and suppression that persisted after propofol was stopped. Alpha and beta returned with haemodynamic improvement. Septic encephalopathy also slows the EEG, however, so the cause cannot be separated in a single case.See
  • One-sided suppression is not sedation. Sedation acts on both hemispheres, so marked one-sided suppression argues against sedation alone being the explanation. New asymmetry should first be checked for technical causes. It should then lead to clinical assessment and imaging, not just an adjustment of sedation (interpretation based on the sources).See “Clinical example: one-sided suppression in an ECMO patient revealed a blood clot (shared case)”
  • Reactivity can be seen in everyday care. In a comatose patient with only delta, power increased from theta into beta when relatives were present. Test reactivity deliberately, note the time and repeat over days. Increased beta can also be EMG, so check the raw EEG and the EMG indicator (interpretation based on the sources).See “Clinical example: comatose patient with only delta responds when relatives visit (shared case)”
  • Alpha coma can be poisoning. In an unconscious child, the EEG showed a strong band around 10–12 Hz, and the cause was a benzodiazepine overdose. Such a picture may raise suspicion of a GABAergic drug, but the diagnosis is made clinically and with tests, not from the EEG alone (interpretation based on the sources).See
  • The examples illustrate, they do not prove. The shared cases are unpublished, not peer reviewed and described from screenshots. A frontal monitor covers only a small part of the cortex.See “Clinical example: one-sided suppression in an ECMO patient revealed a blood clot (shared case)”, “Clinical example: alpha coma in an unconscious child turned out to be benzodiazepine poisoning (shared case)”

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

Clinical example: the spectrogram as a mirror of systemic perfusion in septic shock (Fischer 2026)

Case report from Clínica Universidad de los Andes, Chile. A 70-year-old man without comorbidity, septic shock with multi-organ failure after bowel perforation, APACHE II 29, SOFA 11, three vasoactive agents, high-volume haemofiltration. The unit uses frontal 4-channel pEEG with spectrogram routinely in all patients with continuous sedation or GCS below 8.

  • Early phase (skin hypoperfusion, high lactate): slow theta background (3.5–7 Hz), continuous diffuse delta and periods of suppression. Propofol was stopped because the theta background persisted. Deep sedation, theta and suppression episodes nevertheless continued without sedation.
  • After haemodynamic improvement (adrenaline discontinued, milrinone started, lower vasopressor doses, better skin perfusion and organ function): alpha (8–13 Hz) and beta emerged, the suppression periods disappeared, and consciousness improved to SAS 3/RASS −2. Discharged home, Rankin 2 after six months.
  • The authors link the pattern to reduced cerebral perfusion. Low systemic perfusion coincided with burst suppression and slow waves, even without known vascular disease. On improvement the fast waves returned. This fits the cerebral blood flow thresholds: alpha and beta fall at 25–35 ml/100 g/min, and delta and theta increase below 17–18. Seizures (standard EEG), structural injury (CT), hypothermia and metabolic causes were excluded.
  • Caveats: one patient and no direct measurement of cerebral blood flow. Sepsis encephalopathy in itself gives a slow EEG independent of perfusion, so the cause cannot be separated. The same phenomenon is described in the Perfusion tab.Source: Guay 2025
Fischer et al. Rev Chil Anest 2026;55:234–238

Clinical example: unilateral suppression in an ECMO patient revealed a blood clot (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is described from one screenshot of the spectrogram over about 17 minutes and information from the person who shared it. The screenshot is not reproduced in the app.

  • The patient: an ICU patient with COVID-19 on ECMO, sedated.
  • What the spectrogram showed: a clear difference between the hemispheres. In the upper panel activity was almost absent, interrupted only by short, scattered bursts, a picture resembling burst suppression. In the lower panel there was continuous activity with power in delta and even, low power up towards 30 Hz.
  • The course: according to the person who shared the case, there was a blood clot in the brain. It showed up nowhere other than in the EEG, and the patient was sent for intervention and recovered.
  • Unilateral suppression does not fit with sedation alone. In a sedated patient the neurological examination is severely limited, and a stroke can be missed. Sedation acts on both hemispheres, so marked unilateral suppression argues against sedation alone being the explanation. Ischaemia causes loss of activity and asymmetry. A similar asymmetry has been seen with carotid stenosis and low blood pressure.Sources: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016, Sheorajpanday 2009, Nycz 2022
  • What to do (interpretation based on the sources): new or increasing asymmetry should first be checked for technical causes such as electrode contact and impedance. If the signal is good, it should prompt clinical assessment and imaging, not just adjustment of sedation.
  • Caveats: one case, described from one screenshot. It is not known which side and which vessel were affected, or which drugs and doses the patient received. A frontal monitor covers only a small part of the cortex and can miss infarcts elsewhere.
Shared clinical example van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016, Sheorajpanday 2009, Nycz 2022

Clinical example: comatose patient with only delta reacts when relatives visit (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is described from two screenshots of the spectrogram and information from the person who shared it. The screenshots are not reproduced in the app.

  • The patient: a comatose ICU patient without sedation, with an EEG that for long periods showed only delta.
  • Without visitors: in one picture (about 20 minutes) the power in both hemispheres lay below about 4 Hz, with very little activity above. The picture was stable without changes.
  • With relatives present: in the other picture, power from theta up into beta, about 15–30 Hz, increased in both hemispheres in periods, while delta persisted.
  • Preserved reactivity is a good sign, and it may return late. EEG reactivity means that frequency or amplitude changes when the patient is stimulated. Reactivity distinguishes between coma states better than the pattern itself. Preserved reactivity indicates a good outcome after anoxic brain injury. In three patients who eventually became independent after prolonged coma following cardiac arrest, reactivity returned after 3, 8 and 73 days. This case shows that relatives' voices and touch can produce a reaction visible on a frontal monitor.Sources: Sutter and Kaplan 2012, Ko and Engelhard 2025, Forgacs 2020
  • What can be done (interpretation based on the sources): test reactivity deliberately, with speech, touch and possibly a noxious stimulus. Note the time so the change can be found in the spectrogram. Repeat the test over days, since reactivity may return late.
  • Caveats: increased beta can also come from muscle activity (EMG), movement or other artefacts, so the raw EEG and the EMG indicator should be checked. Formal assessment of reactivity is done with standardised stimuli and a full EEG. One case, and the patient's outcome is not known.
Shared clinical example Sutter and Kaplan 2012, Ko and Engelhard 2025, Forgacs 2020

Clinical example: alpha coma in an unconscious child turned out to be benzodiazepine poisoning (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is described from one screenshot and information from the person who shared it. The screenshot is not reproduced in the app.

  • The patient: an unconscious 3-year-old child. At first it was unclear what had happened.
  • What the EEG showed: a strong, continuous band around 10–12 Hz in both hemispheres, together with delta, and little activity above about 20 Hz. The pattern was symmetrical and stable over about 20 minutes. The raw EEG showed regular, high-amplitude waves in the alpha range. The index was 34.
  • The explanation: it turned out to be a benzodiazepine overdose.
  • The same alpha pattern can mean very different things depending on the cause. Alpha coma is alpha activity (8–13 Hz) in a patient who cannot be roused. Alpha is mostly seen frontally. In poisoning, for example with barbiturates, benzodiazepines and anaesthetics, alpha is more diffuse, reactivity is usually preserved and up to 90% recover. With brainstem lesions, alpha is posterior and often varies with external stimuli, but the prognosis is poor. After cardiac arrest (hypoxic-ischaemic injury), alpha is also more diffuse, but reactivity is usually absent and the outcome is mostly poor. So it is the cause and the reactivity, not the location, that distinguish poisoning from cardiac arrest.Source: Sutter and Kaplan 2012
  • Why it is instructive (interpretation based on the sources): the pattern resembles alpha–delta under anaesthesia with propofol or sevoflurane. Benzodiazepines also act on the GABAA receptor (see the Drugs tab), and children generally have stronger alpha under GABAergic anaesthesia than adults. In an unconscious patient of unknown cause, such a picture may therefore raise suspicion of a GABAergic drug. The diagnosis is nevertheless made clinically and with tests, not from the EEG alone.Sources: Lee 2017, Akeju 2015
  • Caveats: one case, described from one screenshot. The source on alpha coma mainly discusses adults. It is not known which benzodiazepine or dose, whether reactivity was tested, or how the child fared.
Shared clinical example Sutter and Kaplan 2012, Lee 2017, Akeju 2015

Fundamentals: what EEG is and how it is measured

Basics: what EEG is, how it is measured and what it cannot tell you. This tab is for readers new to EEG, and the other tabs build on it. The main message is that EEG is the only routine measure of the target organ itself, that a TCI pump shows a prediction rather than a measurement, and that the index number must always be read together with the raw EEG and spectrogram.

Key points

  • EEG measures the target organ itself. The signal arises from summed postsynaptic potentials in cortical pyramidal cells and shows cortical function in real time, not structure. During anaesthesia it is the only routine measure of the target organ.See
  • A frequency band is a description, not a mechanism. Frontal alpha under propofol has a different origin from posterior alpha in an awake person with closed eyes, even though both are 8–13 Hz. A frontal monitor does not see the posterior alpha.See
  • What looks like gamma is often muscle. Gamma is attenuated by skull and skin and overlaps with muscle activity. In a patient without neuromuscular blockade, “gamma” on a frontal monitor is therefore often EMG from the forehead and eye muscles.See
  • Frontal monitors have a limited view. They use only the front part of the 10–20 system. That is enough for frontal alpha and slow activity, but not for localising seizures or seeing posterior alpha. Only sensors with electrodes over both sides can show asymmetry.See
  • The pattern tells you more than the number. Sustained alpha spindles around 10 Hz coupled to slow delta suggest adequate hypnosis under propofol and volatile agents. This does not apply to ketamine or nitrous oxide, and older patients produce weaker alpha. Burst suppression and sustained suppression are the clearest, though non-specific, signs of too much.See “An ‘imperfect but useful mirror’: an introduction to EEG monitoring (Hight 2020)”

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

What EEG is

  • EEG is the sum of many small potentials in the cortex. It consists of voltage differences in microvolts between electrodes on the scalp. They are created by summed postsynaptic potentials in large populations of cortical pyramidal cells lying in parallel. Action potentials contribute little. The signal from deep structures weakens with the square of the distance, and skull and skin attenuate the fast frequencies in particular.
  • The first human EEG came in 1929. Caton recorded spontaneous potentials from the animal brain in 1875. Hans Berger in Jena later made single-channel recordings in humans, first in patients with skull defects, and published the first human EEG in 1929. He described alpha and beta waves, alpha blocking on visual stimulation, and the difference between adults and infants. Adrian and Matthews confirmed the findings in 1934 and gave Berger the credit.
  • EEG shows how the cortex is working, not what the patient is thinking. EEG describes cortical function in real time, not structure. During anaesthesia it is the only routine measure of the target organ itself; all other monitors measure circulation, respiration or drug concentration.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 4

A weak signal: electrodes, impedance and noise

  • EEG is much weaker than the ECG. EEG on the scalp is about 1–100 µV, while the ECG on the skin is about 1–2 mV. EEG is therefore ten to several hundred times weaker.Source: Brown and Gupta 2008
  • This is why noise easily becomes larger than the brain signal. Muscles, eye movements, the mains supply (50 Hz), diathermy and poor electrode contact produce signals that can drown out the EEG.Source: Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • Impedance is the resistance between skin and electrode. High impedance, and especially unequal impedance between the electrodes, makes the EEG more susceptible to noise from the mains. The skin is prepared to obtain low and equal impedance.Sources: Ferree 2001; Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • An impedance alarm means poor contact, not a change in the brain. A loose electrode or a broken cable gives noise, an impedance alarm or many artefacts. A truly flat EEG has normal impedance in all channels.Sources: Guay 2025; Ching 2012
  • Check the scale, as you would on an ECG. The gain (µV/mm) and the colour scale determine how strong the EEG looks. Check the settings at the start of every anaesthetic.Source: Hight 2020

The frequency bands

  • A band is a description, not a mechanism. The same frequency can have different origins. Frontal alpha under propofol (thalamocortical, see the Spectrogram tab) is not the same as posterior alpha in an awake person with eyes closed, even though both are 8–13 Hz.
  • Posterior alpha weakens when the eyes open, and also shows how activated the brain is. In an awake person resting with closed eyes, alpha is strongest at the back of the head. This is called the posterior dominant rhythm. When the eyes open, alpha becomes weaker. This was described in the very first EEG recordings of humans and is still used to test whether the EEG reacts. The reason is not only visual input: alpha falls evenly across the whole head, not only at the back, and at the same time skin conductance rises, which is a measure of how activated the body is. The other frequency bands change more in specific areas, which is interpreted as processing of what is seen. In short: at rest much alpha, with increased activation less alpha.Source: Barry 2007 (28 students)
  • Alpha may be active inhibition. A widely used explanation is that alpha marks areas that are inhibited because they are not needed at the moment, so that information is routed to the areas in use (“gating by inhibition”). With eyes closed the visual cortex has little to do and shows much alpha; when it is engaged, alpha falls. This is a well-supported hypothesis, not definitively proven.Source: Jensen and Mazaheri 2010
  • What it means for anaesthesia and intensive care (interpretation based on the sources): a frontal monitor does not see posterior alpha, but often sees alpha coma. At loss of consciousness under propofol the posterior alpha disappears and a frontal alpha with a different origin appears (see the Components tab). So a frontal monitor does not see the normal alpha of an awake person with closed eyes. Alpha coma is something else: the alpha is mostly seen frontally, unlike the posterior distribution of healthy subjects. The distribution nevertheless depends on the cause: more diffuse alpha in poisoning and hypoxic-ischaemic injury, posterior alpha with brainstem lesions, and incomplete forms may also have a more posterior alpha. A frontal monitor can therefore often see alpha coma, but not every form. In intensive care, reactivity is the key: alpha that changes with stimulation suggests preserved function, while alpha that does not react may be alpha coma (see the Intensive care tab). Reactivity is formally assessed with standardised stimuli and full EEG. On a frontal monitor a change with stimulation can be seen in the spectrogram, but increased fast activity may also be EMG, so the raw EEG and the EMG indicator must be checked (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Purdon 2013; Sutter and Kaplan 2012; Degano 2025; Amoranto and Fernandez 2024
  • The EEG signal is so small that noise easily outgrows it. EEG is measured in microvolts (µV), millionths of a volt. Interference from muscles, eye movements, the mains (50 Hz), diathermy or poor electrode contact easily becomes larger than the brain signal itself. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) decides what can be interpreted. Low and equal impedance and good skin preparation therefore matter a great deal (see the card “Electrodes” below). Amplitude also falls with age.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti ch. 4; Purdon 2015; Obert 2024
  • An image: the rowing wave in the stands. Think of the rowing wave Norwegian supporters made during the 2026 football World Cup, which went viral around the world: thousands sit down on the benches and row in the same calm rhythm while shouting “Ro!” (“Row!”), and the whole stand moves as one large, slow wave. That is what slow waves in the EEG are like: large networks of neurons work in synchrony, and the deflection becomes large. Fast waves resemble the rest of the stadium: some clap, some shout, some take flash photos, but not in time. The result is many small movements that do not add up, and the deflection is small. Fast activity with large amplitude does not fit the picture, and usually comes from muscle, not from the brain (see the points below).
  • Slow waves have high amplitude, fast waves low (1/f). EEG power falls steadily with frequency (see “Aperiodic EEG activity”). Amplitude depends on how many neurons are active in synchrony, and the larger the network involved, the lower the frequency. The reason lies in the brain’s physical architecture: most connections between neurons are local, and signals take time to travel through axons and synapses. Fast rhythms therefore stay within a small area, whereas slow rhythms can recruit very large, synchronous networks. Sustained fast activity with high amplitude therefore does not come from the cortex, but from muscle (EMG) or other artefacts (interpretation based on the sources). This makes strong EMG easy to see in the raw EEG.Sources: Avella Gonzalez 2014; Lea-Carnall 2016; Buzsáki and Draguhn 2004
  • What looks like beta and gamma on a frontal monitor is often muscle. Gamma from the brain has very low amplitude and is largely filtered out by skull and skin. Muscle activity lies in the same frequency range (about 20–300 Hz), but can reach about 100 µV in EEG, whereas high-frequency brain activity may be below 1 µV, several orders of magnitude smaller. Strong EMG is therefore easy to see in the raw EEG as fast activity with high amplitude. The difficulty is weak, sustained muscle tension, which can pass visual screening. In volunteers who were paralysed, even “clean” resting EEG turned out to be heavily contaminated by muscle activity above about 20 Hz: without paralysis, power was about 5 times higher at 40 Hz and about 10 times higher at 80 Hz. In a patient without neuromuscular blockers, beta and gamma in the spectrogram are therefore often EMG from the forehead and temples, even when the raw EEG looks calm. Frontal EMG, blinking and eye movements, together with low amplitude and fast activity, are precisely what characterise an awake EEG.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti ch. 4 (30–80 Hz is “typically filtered out by the skull and not visible on conventional surface EEG”); Muthukumaraswamy 2013
  • Without EMG, the index can read “asleep” in an awake patient. Awake volunteers given neuromuscular blockers were fully awake and calculated correctly. Even so, BIS fell to 44–47, and Entropy and qCON fell below 60 in most trials. These indices thus need muscle activity (EMG) to generate correct values in an awake person, and may therefore be unreliable for detecting awareness when the patient has received neuromuscular blockers. The raw EEG still looked awake, with low amplitude and fast activity, just without EMG and eye movements. So it is the index that becomes misleading, not the EEG (see Schuller 2015 and Hight 2017 in the Spectrogram tab).Sources: Schuller 2015 (BIS); Schuller 2023 (Entropy, 17 of 19 trials); Schuller 2025 (qCON, 15 of 19 trials)
  • Ketamine can produce real low gamma, but on the monitor it may still be EMG. Low gamma (25–40 Hz) under ketamine has been demonstrated with surface EEG in research studies. On a clinical monitor without neuromuscular blockers, part of what is shown as gamma may still be weak EMG, because weak muscle activity is not always visible in the raw EEG (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Purdon 2015; Vlisides 2017
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 4 and 5

Electrodes, the 10–20 system and frontal monitors

  • The 10–20 system gives the electrodes fixed positions. Electrodes are placed at 10% and 20% of the distances nasion–inion and between the preauricular points. The letters denote region (Fp frontopolar, F frontal, C central, T temporal, P parietal, O occipital), odd numbers left, even numbers right, z the midline. The standard set-up has 21 positions; the IFCN now recommends 25 with an inferior temporal row. Note that F7 and F8 actually lie over the anterior temporal lobe.
