  • Impedance should be low and balanced. Modern equipment accepts up to 10 kΩ as long as the electrodes are balanced; below 100 Ω suggests a salt bridge or a fault. The skin is prepared to lower the impedance.
  • Too high a high-pass filter can hide the slow activity that anaesthesia produces. The differential amplifier measures the difference between two inputs (active and reference) against ground. Before digitisation an anti-aliasing filter is used (Nyquist: the sampling frequency must be at least twice the highest frequency, recommended at least 256 Hz). For display, a low-pass filter (commonly 70 Hz), a high-pass filter (0.5–1 Hz) and a notch filter (50 Hz in Europe) are used.
  • Bipolar and referential montages complement each other. A bipolar montage shows the difference between two neighbouring electrodes. A referential montage shows each electrode against a common reference (ear, Cz or average). Both should be used, because they give complementary information; neither of them is “old-fashioned”. The Laplacian montage uses a weighted average of the neighbouring electrodes as a local reference.
  • Frontal anaesthesia monitors see only the front of the head. All use only the anterior part of the 10–20 system. The sensors vary: some have four channels over both sides (F7, Fp1, Fp2, F8), others have electrodes over one side of the forehead or one to two channels. Only sensors with electrodes over both sides can show asymmetry. Common to all: they are sufficient for frontal alpha and slow activity under GABAergic agents, but not for lateralisation further back, seizure localisation or posterior alpha, and a unilateral sensor cannot tell the sides apart (see Nycz 2022 in the Perfusion tab). That is why the ICU literature distinguishes between questions that can be answered with a simplified montage and questions that require full 10–20.Sources: Mehler 2024 (four-channel montage); Rasulo 2023; Taccone 2026
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 4; Mehler 2024 (four-channel montage)

Aperiodic EEG activity (“1/f”): the background is signal, not noise

New research, not yet clinical practice. The card is included because it helps explain why the same change on the monitor can have different causes. No monitor shows this today.

What it is: the spectrogram splits the EEG into frequencies. You then see two things at once:

  • The rhythms: clear bands at particular frequencies, for example alpha around 10 Hz under propofol. This is called the periodic part.
  • The background: an even “foundation” that is always there, even when there is no rhythm. It is strongest at the slow frequencies and becomes weaker the faster the frequency. This is called the aperiodic part (without a fixed rhythm), or “1/f”, because power falls roughly as 1 divided by the frequency.
  • The slope: how quickly the background falls from slow to fast frequencies. A steep slope means much slow and little fast activity. A flat slope means relatively more fast activity.

Why it is useful to know: when the power in a frequency band changes, it may be because the rhythm changes, because the background changes, or both. The monitor does not distinguish between them. One example is weak alpha in older patients: some of it is a weaker alpha rhythm, and some is a lower background. The figure shows the principle.Sources: Tröndle 2023; Leroy 2023

What research has shown so far:

  • The slope separates wakefulness from both anaesthesia and sleep, including REM sleep. In one of the early human studies (2020), the background between 30 and 45 Hz became steeper under propofol, both in scalp EEG and with electrodes inside the brain (470 of 485 depth electrodes, 96.9%). It also separated wakefulness from deep sleep and from REM sleep, which otherwise resembles wakefulness in the EEG. The slope correctly classified awake versus propofol anaesthesia in approx. 77% of cases, compared with approx. 52% for slow waves. Caveats: small groups (9 and 12 patients under anaesthesia), and all received midazolam premedication, which the authors suggest may have increased slow waves already before induction. The anaesthesia data are from Oslo University Hospital. The study did not test use in clinical monitoring. Frontal EEG at 30–45 Hz can also contain muscle activity (EMG), so the slope can hardly be read directly from an anaesthesia monitor (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Lendner 2020
  • Anaesthesia makes the background steeper. In one study the slope separated awake from anaesthetised patients very well.Source: Widmann 2025
  • Age makes it flatter. At rest, older people have a lower and flatter background than young people. Under propofol, much of the difference between young and old lay in the background, not in the rhythms.Sources: Tröndle 2023; Leroy 2023
  • Alpha frequency falls with age, but whether alpha also becomes weaker is unresolved. That alpha frequency falls with age is well documented in large studies. Lower alpha frequency predicted greater cognitive decline over ten years, particularly when alpha frequency and background did not match. A large atlas shows that alpha frequency rises in childhood, stays high through young and middle adulthood and falls later, but it is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed. All these studies find that the background becomes flatter with age. Whether the alpha rhythm itself becomes weaker is disputed: three studies found weaker alpha even after subtracting the background (in one of them mostly posteriorly, while beta was stronger over sensorimotor areas in older adults), whereas one large study found no age difference in alpha power when controlling for the background. The studies concern resting EEG in awake people, not alpha under anaesthesia.Sources: Cesnaite 2023 (1703 people, mean age 70); Finley 2024 (235 people); Bonyadian 2026 (2172 people, aged 5 to 89, preprint); Donoghue 2020; Tröndle 2023; Park 2025 (54 people)
  • The agents may perhaps be distinguished. The slope differed between sevoflurane and propofol.Source: Dragovic 2025, discussed in Connor 2026
  • Caveats: few and small studies, the numbers depend on the analysis method, and values from different studies cannot be compared directly.

How is it calculated? From Fourier to FOOOF

  1. Fourier gives the spectrum. The raw EEG is divided into short windows, and the Fourier transform breaks each window down into sine waves of different frequency. The result is a power spectrum: how much power there is at each frequency. This is the same as what lies behind the spectrogram. Fourier does not distinguish rhythm from background: all power at 10 Hz is counted as “alpha”, whether it comes from an alpha rhythm or from the background.
  2. FOOOF separates rhythm from background. FOOOF stands for “fitting oscillations and one over f”. The method takes the spectrum from step 1 and does four things:
    • first draws a line through the background, ignoring the peaks;
    • subtracts the line, so that only the peaks remain;
    • finds the peaks one by one as bell-shaped curves, as long as they rise above the noise level;
    • redraws the background line without the peaks, so that it becomes more precise.
    Source: Donoghue 2020
  3. What you get. For the background: the level (offset), the slope (the exponent) and possibly a “knee” where the line bends. For each rhythm: the frequency of the peak, how high it rises above the background, and how wide it is.
  4. Without FOOOF the age difference in alpha is exaggerated. The same fall in “alpha power” may be due to the rhythm becoming weaker, the peak shifting (for example from 10 to 8 Hz), or the background changing. A frequency band can also show power without a real rhythm being there. FOOOF separates these. An example from resting EEG: older adults (60–70 years, n = 14) had a lower alpha frequency than young adults (20–30 years, n = 16) (9.6 versus 10.7 Hz), weaker alpha above the background and a flatter background (exponent 0.75 versus 1.43). The age difference in alpha is exaggerated when rhythm and background are not separated, partly because more of the older adults’ alpha lies below 8 Hz, outside the usual alpha band. The result still depends on the settings, for example whether a knee is included or not.Source: Donoghue 2020

More on Fourier and the spectrogram:

The studies in detail (numbers and method)
  • The exponent follows hypnosis. Frontal EEG in 62 awake subjects and 125 during maintenance with propofol, sevoflurane or desflurane was decomposed with the FOOOF algorithm. α was 1.61 awake versus 2.60 under anaesthesia (AUC 0.98). When the usual spectral parameters (beta ratio, SEF95, spectral entropy, alpha/delta ratio) were computed on the aperiodic model alone instead of the whole spectrum, the ability to separate awake from anaesthetised rose from AUC 0.71–0.95 to 0.98 for all four, on a par with permutation and approximate entropy. The interpretation is that the aperiodic part reflects the hypnotic component, while the periodic oscillations, especially alpha, disturb the indices and rather say something about the quality of the anaesthesia (nociception, frailty) than about the level of consciousness. Simulations link α to the balance between synaptic excitation and inhibition.Sources: Widmann 2025 (BJA); Gao 2017 (simulations)
  • Much of the age difference at loss of consciousness lies in the background. 9 young (18–30 years) and 14 older (over 70 years) subjects were followed during manual propofol induction with 21 electrodes. Loss of consciousness produced an increased exponent and offset in both groups, the alpha peak shifted from about 10 to 11 Hz, and the adjusted alpha power above the background increased. The older subjects received half the propofol dose (1.8 versus 3.4 mg/kg), but 4 of 14 developed burst suppression versus 2 of 9 young. The young showed a “travelling” burst of power from gamma via beta to alpha around loss of consciousness (as in Purdon 2013), and in 8 of 9 young the exponent fell just before loss of consciousness, consistent with paradoxical excitation. When the background was subtracted, older and young looked far more alike. Exploratory pilot without correction for multiple testing.Source: Leroy 2023
  • Separating out the background changes the interpretation. All of today's indices compute on the whole spectrum and treat all agents alike. In one example the spectrogram does not reveal the agent, while the log-log slope does: β 2.70 in the example, close to what has been found for sevoflurane (2.71) versus propofol (2.45). Furthermore, when the aperiodic part is subtracted, alpha and beta rise before loss of consciousness, while delta rises abruptly at loss of consciousness.Sources: Connor 2026 (editorial); Dragovic 2025; Brake 2024
  • This fits with other findings on age and alpha. Lower power in older patients has been described before; much of that may be the background, not the rhythms. Alpha as a “quality marker” fits with findings on nociception, delirium and low alpha with a propensity for burst suppression. No commercial monitor displays the exponent today; this is research, not a clinical tool.Sources: Kratzer 2020 and Purdon 2015 (BJA, lower power); Leroy 2023 (background); García 2021 (nociception); Gutiérrez 2019 (delirium); Shao 2020 (burst suppression)
  • Conventional analysis overestimates the age difference in alpha. Eyes-closed resting EEG in healthy young and older adults, 533 people pooled across three samples. Total alpha power was lower in older adults, but the offset and slope of the background were also lower (a flatter line). Because the whole spectrum shifts, conventional analysis of total alpha power overestimates the age difference. When the background was removed, adjusted alpha power was still lower in older adults. This is resting EEG without anaesthesia.Source: Tröndle 2023 (registered report, Cortex)
  • The direction is not the same (interpretation based on the sources): at rest the background becomes flatter with age, whereas anaesthesia makes it steeper. Lower total alpha in an older patient may therefore reflect both less rhythmic alpha and a lower background, and the numbers on the monitor do not separate them.Sources: Tröndle 2023; Widmann 2025
  • Caveats: Widmann is a signal-analytic study without control for doses or age. The FOOOF settings (with or without a “knee” around 20 Hz) affect the numbers, so exponent values from different studies cannot be compared directly. Conflicts of interest: Kreuzer, García, Kratzer and Schneider hold patents on intraoperative EEG analysis, García is co-founder of Lantern Laboratories, Kreuzer has received funds from Masimo, Narcotrend, Medtronic and Fresenius for EEG teaching; Koch (Leroy 2023) holds patents sold to Medtronic. Connor reports none of relevance.

Typical tendencies, not diagnostic criteria

Younger, more robust brainOlder or more vulnerable brain
Total EEG power under anaesthesiaHigherLower (Purdon 2015, Kratzer 2020)
Frontal alpha under propofol and volatile agentsClearWeaker or absent; low alpha is linked to a greater tendency to burst suppression (Shao 2020)
Aperiodic backgroundReferenceAt rest lower and flatter (Tröndle 2023); under propofol much of the age difference lies in the background (Leroy 2023)
Burst suppressionLess frequentMore frequent, even at lower doses: 4 of 14 older patients on half the dose versus 2 of 9 young (Leroy 2023)

Age, drug, dose, haemodynamics, artefacts and suppression all affect the EEG. Low alpha or a changed slope alone shows neither excessively deep anaesthesia nor a vulnerable brain. EEG-based “frailty scores” mostly measured age.Source: Ostertag 2025 (see the Spectrogram tab)

Widmann 2025, Leroy 2023, Connor 2026, Tröndle 2023

An “imperfect but useful mirror”: an introduction to EEG monitoring (Hight 2020)

Course and review article (Continuing Professional Development) in Can J Anesth 2020 by Hight, Kaiser, Sleigh and Avidan. It deals with raw EEG and the spectrogram, explicitly not with the proprietary indices. Much of the content is covered in more detail in the Spectrogram tab; here is what it adds.

  • EEG can be displayed in three ways. Raw EEG (amplitude over time), power spectrum (power per frequency) and spectrogram/DSA (power per frequency over time). The frequency bands are arbitrarily defined and do not reflect the biology of the brain, and Fourier analysis in bands can lose information (for example phase-amplitude coupling between delta and alpha).
  • Sustained alpha spindles suggest adequate hypnosis. The pattern is alpha spindles around 10 Hz, phase-amplitude coupled with slow delta around 1 Hz, under propofol and volatile agents. Exceptions: ketamine and nitrous oxide do not produce the pattern, and older patients and patients with neurodegenerative disease produce weaker alpha.
  • Faster and intermittent spindles suggest too little. As the dose falls, the spindle frequency increases before the spindles become intermittent and disappear. There is a risk of underdosing during “Mind the Gap” (transport without end-tidal measurement) and with propofol plus neuromuscular blockers.
  • Burst suppression and sustained suppression suggest too much. They are the clearest, but non-specific, signs. MAC is defined by movement (spinal cord), not cortex, so an EEG-based MAC could say more about the effect on the brain. An association between suppression time and delirium has been shown, but “it is not yet clear whether prolonged EEG suppression is harmful”.
  • With delta arousal, consider analgesia rather than reducing the anaesthetic agent. Nociceptive responses are beta arousal, delta arousal (first reported in the early 1990s, “rarely heeded since”) and alpha dropout. Delta arousal may be a sign of endogenous antinociception.
  • A lower concentration is needed to wake up than to lose consciousness (neural inertia). This has been shown in fruit flies, mice and humans, and is more pronounced when the arousal systems are weakened (age, narcolepsy, droperidol, clonidine, antimuscarinic agents). So be cautious about lowering the concentration below the one that produced unconsciousness in reliance on an “anaesthesia pattern”: once consciousness returns, a large dose increase may be required. MACawake is probably lower than the MAC for loss of consciousness.
  • A frontal “deep” pattern does not exclude connected consciousness. The isolated forearm shows this (no reports during burst suppression), and the reason is unresolved. Perhaps the forehead is the wrong place (posterior “hot zone”), or consciousness depends on connectivity between regions (frontoparietal, also for ketamine). Avidan is a co-author here and lead author of the “black swans” commentary in the Components tab.
  • EEG was proposed for anaesthesia as early as 1937. Gibbs, Gibbs and Lennox then recommended that anaesthesiologists should use EEG routinely. The idea is thus almost 90 years old, not a new trend. Even so, EEG has not become a fixed standard the way pulse oximetry and capnography did (see ).
  • Conflicts of interest: none declared. The article was funded by the Bangerter-Rhyner Foundation and Inselspital.
Hight, Kaiser, Sleigh, Avidan. Can J Anesth 2020

Key points

  • The number is used, the curves rarely. Almost everyone uses the index value. Only a small minority use the raw EEG, spectrogram and suppression ratio. Only 27 % said they could recognise burst suppression, and 86 % wanted more knowledge.Source: Aasheim 2024 (see “How the monitors are used in Norwegian practice”)
  • The sickest are monitored least and lie deepest. At OUS only 21 % of patients receiving muscle relaxants had BIS. At least 5 minutes below BIS 30 occurred in about 26 % in ASA 1 and 50 % in ASA 4. The study is observational and does not show cause.Source: Aasheim 2026 (see “How the monitors are used in Norwegian practice”)
  • The same number means different things on different monitors. The recommended range is PSI 25–50 and BIS 40–60 (45–60 in Schneider 2004). When BIS was within its range, only 40 % of PSI values were within theirs. So always state which monitor the number comes from.Sources: Schneider 2004, Lewis 2019 (see “Same number, different scale: the indices cannot be compared directly”)
  • If the index is unexpected or changes abruptly, work through the sources of error. Ketamine can raise the index. Dexmedetomidine, neuromuscular blockers, ephedrine and magnesium can shift it regardless of hypnotic depth. Rule out dosing errors first, and look at the raw EEG and spectrogram before changing the dose.Sources: Pinheiro 2026, Takizawa 2006, Altıparmak 2018 (see “When the index surprises: the sources of error”)
  • Only muscle relaxation must be measured. The Norwegian standard 2024 requires neuromuscular monitoring. Consciousness is to be assessed with clinical signs, but these have been shown to be unreliable under neuromuscular block. Monitoring of anaesthesia depth “must be individually considered”. The British guideline states that processed EEG should be used with TIVA and neuromuscular blockade, and that the index value alone should not be relied upon.Sources: Leonardsen 2024, Klein 2021 (see “What the standards require”)
  • The same evidence standard for every monitor. A common argument against EEG is that large studies have not shown better outcomes. Neither has pulse oximetry: it detected more episodes of low SpO₂, but did not reduce complications or mortality. Pulse oximetry and capnography nevertheless became standard because they show something we would otherwise not see, and give early warning of deterioration. That does not mean EEG is proven useful, but that EEG should be judged by the same standard as the other monitors.Sources: Pedersen 2014, Aitkenhead ch. 18 (see “The demand for proof: pulse oximetry and capnography became standard without outcome studies”)

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Same number, different scale: the indices cannot be compared directly

A number such as “index 25” or “index 40” means nothing until you know which monitor it comes from. The monitors calculate differently and have different scales and different recommended ranges.

  • Each monitor has its own recommended range. During general anaesthesia the range for PSI is 25–50. For BIS it is 45–60 in one study, and 40–60 in the studies in the Cochrane review. For qCON, 40–60 is proposed, but only on the basis of a small observational study. The same number, for example 30, can therefore be within the range on one scale and below it on another.Sources: Schneider 2004, Lewis 2019 (Cochrane), Pantalacci 2023
  • The monitors agree poorly. BIS and PSI measured simultaneously in 57 patients correlated only moderately (r = 0.67). When BIS was within its range, only 40 % of PSI values were within theirs. When PSI was within its range, only 50 % of BIS values were within theirs. The indices are intended by their manufacturers to measure the same thing, but do not give the same answer.Source: Schneider 2004
  • For practice (interpretation based on the sources): always state which monitor the number comes from. This applies in the record, in teaching and when studies are compared. “Low index” is meaningful only against the recommended range for that monitor. If a unit changes monitor, familiar limits cannot be transferred.
  • Nor do the raw EEG and spectrogram look the same on every monitor. The number and placement of electrodes, filter settings, the way the spectrogram is calculated (for example ordinary Fourier analysis or multitaper, which gives less noise) and the scales for amplitude and colour vary. The same EEG can therefore look different on two monitors. The patterns, such as alpha–delta or burst suppression, can still be recognised when you know how the display is set up (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Lobo and Lamperti ch. 4, Prerau 2017. See
Schneider 2004 Lewis 2019 (Cochrane) Pantalacci 2023

How the monitors are used in Norwegian practice

Two Norwegian studies show how EEG monitors are actually used: a survey of anaesthesia staff at Norwegian hospitals, and BIS data from the electronic chart in 97,733 patients at Oslo University Hospital. The monitors are widely used, but not always in the way or where one might expect.Sources: Aasheim 2024 (the survey), Aasheim 2026 (the OUS data)

  • The number is used, the curves rarely. The index value is used by almost everyone (99 % of the anaesthetists, 98 % of the nurses). Raw EEG, spectrogram and suppression ratio are used by between 7 and 18 %. Only 27 % said they could recognise burst suppression (67 % of the anaesthetists, 18 % of the nurses). Even so, over 60 % felt they had sufficient knowledge, and 86 % wanted more.Source: Aasheim 2024
  • More fear of awareness than of too deep anaesthesia. 90 % increased the dose at a high index, but only 55 % reduced it at a low one. The authors interpret this as a stronger fear of awareness than of too deep anaesthesia.Source: Aasheim 2024
  • The monitor is used least in the sickest. At OUS, 27 % had continuous BIS: 33 % with TIVA, 7 % with volatile anaesthesia and only 21 % of those who received muscle relaxants. The proportion fell with ASA class. The typical BIS patient was ASA 1–2 on TIVA without relaxants. In the survey, by contrast, 68 % reported using the monitor mainly with neuromuscular blockade. Self-reported use and recorded data thus point in different directions, but the samples differ (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Aasheim 2026, Aasheim 2024
  • The old and sick were deepest. BIS fell with age and ASA class, and women were 2.4 units lower than men. The differences in means are small. What is clinically interesting is the tails: at least 5 minutes below BIS 30 occurred in about 26 % of ASA 1 and 50 % of ASA 4. The authors ask whether Schnider TCI is sufficiently individualised for vulnerable patients.Source: Aasheim 2026
  • Caveats. The survey is voluntary and self-reported, without a reliable response rate. The cohort study is observational, had only the index (not raw EEG or suppression ratio) and lacked dosing data. The findings should not be interpreted as cause and effect.Sources: Aasheim 2024, Aasheim 2026

The studies in detail:

Aasheim 2024 Aasheim 2026

When the index surprises: the sources of error

The index alone cannot be trusted. If it is unexpectedly high or low without an obvious reason, the sources of error should be gone through systematically with the ANESTHESIA mnemonic. The first step is to rule out dosing errors.Source: Pinheiro 2026 (narrative review)

  • Drugs can shift the number regardless of depth. Ketamine gives more beta/gamma and raises the index even as anaesthesia deepens. Dexmedetomidine and clonidine lower it, also at moderate sedation. Neuromuscular blockers lower the index because EMG disappears, also in awake patients. Sugammadex and neostigmine raise it. When the block is reversed, muscle activity in the forehead returns (EMG), but in one study beta also increased and delta fell without EMG explaining it. Whether the rise is artefact, genuinely lighter anaesthesia or signals from the muscles to the brain is unresolved. The rise was small (BIS about 44 to 50), and no one woke up. On nitrous oxide the sources disagree: Pinheiro holds that usual adjunct doses change the index little, whereas Purdon lists nitrous oxide with ketamine as the agents that most often make clinicians doubt the index.Sources: Pinheiro 2026, Purdon 2015; Kim 2023; Rubio-Baines 2023
  • An abrupt change is not necessarily a change in depth. Ephedrine raised BIS under propofol (8 of 20 above 60) without a change in propofol concentration, whereas phenylephrine did not. Magnesium gave a lower BIS throughout caesarean section in an RCT. Spinal lidocaine sedated healthy volunteers, but BIS did not differ between groups in the blinded part. So look at the raw EEG and spectrogram before changing the hypnotic dose.Sources: Takizawa 2006, Altıparmak 2018, Pollock 2000
  • The index lags behind. The BIS value appears 20–30 seconds after the EEG it is calculated from. During rapid changes, such as at induction, the raw EEG and spectrogram therefore show the change before the number (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)
  • Equipment and patient can also cause errors. Diathermy, facial nerve stimulators (even in standby), forced-air warming near the head and arterial pulsation can produce artefacts, and SQI may remain high. Genetically low-amplitude EEG in 5–10 %, hypothermia, ischaemia, seizures and neurological disease can also give unexpected values. So note the baseline index and DSA before induction.Source: Pinheiro 2026
  • The monitor itself plays a part. Different monitors, also from the same manufacturer, give different values at the same depth. This fits with BIS and PSI measured simultaneously correlating only moderately.Sources: Pinheiro 2026, Schneider 2004
  • Caveats. The review has no systematic search or quality assessment, and many claims rest on case reports. Not every unexpected value is an artefact.Source: Pinheiro 2026

The studies in detail:

Pinheiro 2026 Purdon 2015 Takizawa 2006 Altıparmak 2018 Pollock 2000 Schneider 2004

The index rises after sugammadex: was the patient too light?

  • The index often rises a little when the block is reversed. BIS rose from about 44 to 50 and PSI from 32 to 36 under stable sevoflurane. Some patients moved or coughed, but all were unresponsive and no one remembered anything.Source: Kim 2023 (46 patients)
  • The EEG itself also changes. Beta and spectral edge frequency rose and delta fell, and this was not explained by muscle activity. The pattern resembled lighter anaesthesia, but no one woke up.Source: Rubio-Baines 2023 (25 patients)
  • One possible explanation is signals from the muscles to the brain. When the block is reversed, the muscles are stretched and working again, and their sense organs send signals upwards. This may give the brain a small arousal signal. It has been proposed but not tested. EMG artefact and redistribution of drugs are other suggestions.Sources: Kim 2023; Rubio-Baines 2023
  • A rise after sugammadex is not in itself a sign that the patient was too light. Look at what had been given, how the raw EEG and spectrogram looked before reversal, and whether the rise came together with EMG and movement. (interpretation based on the sources)See also “Movement is mostly about spinal cord and analgesia”
  • But a paralysed patient can be conscious without being able to show it. With the isolated forearm technique, about one in three responded to command during anaesthesia, but very few remembered it. Follow up patients you are unsure about with questions about recall.Sources: Sleigh et al. 2025; Linassi 2018

What the standards require

The standards say different things about EEG monitoring, but share one feature: responsibility for interpretation lies with the person at the patient’s side.

  • Norway: the components are treated differently. General anaesthesia consists of several components: unconsciousness, amnesia, suppression of the response to pain (nociception) and immobility. They must be assessed separately. The Norwegian standard 2024 treats them differently (points below).Source: Leonardsen 2024. See
  • Muscle relaxation must be measured. Neuromuscular monitoring is a minimum requirement with non-depolarising blockers.
  • Consciousness is to be assessed clinically. “Clinical assessment of level of consciousness, respiration and circulation” is a minimum requirement in sedation. The requirements for regional and general anaesthesia come in addition, so this applies there too.
  • Anaesthesia depth is considered individually. “Monitoring of anaesthesia depth (e.g., BIS and EEG) must be individually considered”. The standard does not define anaesthesia depth, and separates it from consciousness without explaining the difference.
  • Analgesia (nociception) has no requirement of its own. The standard has no separate monitoring requirement for nociception.
  • The paradox (interpretation based on the sources): the only component that must be measured objectively is muscle relaxation. That is precisely the one that removes the patient’s ability to show that they are awake. Consciousness is to be assessed with clinical signs, but these signs have been shown to be unreliable, particularly when the patient is paralysed (see the points below).
  • Reflection from the author of the app: EEG ought to be listed under the assessment of consciousness, not under an undefined concept such as “anaesthesia depth”. EEG measures the brain, the organ where consciousness resides. At the same time, EEG cannot rule out consciousness either: connected consciousness has been demonstrated in patients with frontal alpha–delta and BIS 37–44. EEG improves the assessment, but does not make it certain.Source: Gaskell 2017 (see the Components tab)
  • Which clinical signs show consciousness? In sedation, one looks at whether the patient responds to speech or touch, and whether protective reflexes such as coughing are preserved. Under general anaesthesia, movement and autonomic signs have traditionally been used. The points below show how unreliable these signs are.Source: Leonardsen 2024
  • Movement disappears with neuromuscular block. It is then no longer a warning.
  • Heart rate and blood pressure are unreliable. Surgery and other drugs also affect them. In published awareness cases only 20% had tachycardia and 18% hypertension. In US closed claims the figures were 7% and 15%.Sources: NAP5 ch. 19, Ghoneim 2009, Domino 1999
  • Lacrimation is just as unreliable. Lacrimation is named explicitly, together with heart rate and blood pressure, as an unreliable sign of consciousness, for the same reason.Source: NAP5 ch. 19
  • Sweating is not reliable enough either. Sweating is counted, together with heart rate, blood pressure and pupils, among signs that are not reliable enough to prevent awareness, particularly with autonomic neuropathy. The sources here do not quantify sweating on its own.Source: Aitkenhead ch. 18
  • The pupils say more about nociception and opioids than about consciousness. Opioids cause small pupils (miosis). Pupillary dilation in response to a noxious stimulus is a brainstem reflex that measures nociception, and is unaffected by neuromuscular blockers. It is blunted by opioids but not by volatile agents. Under propofol TIVA, patients could have a brisk pupillary reflex without moving.Source: Packiasabapathy 2021
  • Overall: under general anaesthesia with neuromuscular block the clinical signs of consciousness are few and uncertain. This is where EEG can provide information that is otherwise missing (interpretation based on the sources).
  • United Kingdom: processed EEG should be used with TIVA and neuromuscular blockade. This applies from before induction until full recovery from the block. It should be considered with inhalational anaesthesia and in high-risk patients. The rationale is NAP5: most awareness cases occurred with a neuromuscular blocker, and almost two-thirds before the start or after the end of surgery. The index value alone should not be relied upon, and a basic understanding of the raw EEG and spectrogram is needed. The guideline is thus more binding than the Norwegian standard.Source: Klein 2021
  • Practice lags behind the British recommendation. Only 49 % in the Norwegian survey had guidelines for use, and at OUS 21 % of patients receiving muscle relaxants had BIS. Measured against the British recommendation, there is a gap (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Aasheim 2024, Aasheim 2026
  • The aims of anaesthesia also concern the brain. In a Delphi consensus, 23 experts defined what anaesthesia should achieve. The aims include, among others, an adequate level of anaesthesia without oversedation, protecting cognitive function, avoiding postoperative delirium and preserving organ function, including the brain. The document does not mention EEG. But these aims concern the brain, and EEG is the only routine monitor that measures the brain directly (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Berger-Estilita 2026
  • Few experts see awareness as a barrier to TIVA. Only 20.6–21.5% agreed that the risk of awareness is a barrier to using TIVA. Lack of TCI pumps and processed EEG was mentioned as a practical barrier, but that statement did not reach consensus.Source: Uitenbosch 2022 (international Delphi consensus on TIVA)
  • Not built on outcome studies. The requirement for processed EEG rests on the same logic as for other monitors: early warning of errors and deterioration, not randomised outcome studies.Source: Klein 2021

The studies in detail:

Leonardsen 2024 Klein 2021 Berger-Estilita 2026 Uitenbosch 2022 Aasheim 2024 Aasheim 2026

Artefacts and interpretation: where to find it

Eye movements, EMG, electrode movement, 50 Hz and ECG are described in the card “Artefacts and sources of error in EEG” in the Spectrogram tab. Reactivity and coma patterns are described in the Intensive care tab. Normal sleep phenomena (vertex waves, spindles, K-complexes) can resemble anaesthesia patterns. Sleep spindles at 12–14 Hz during N2 have the same thalamocortical origin as frontal alpha under propofol, but not the same frequency or duration.Source for reactivity and coma patterns: Sutter and Kaplan 2012

The demand for proof: pulse oximetry and capnography became standard without outcome studies

A common argument against EEG monitoring is that large randomised trials have not shown better outcomes. But the established monitors have no such proof either.

  • No one has compared anaesthesia with and without monitoring. Now that standards are mandatory, «it will be impossible to prove that monitors make a difference». The rationale is instead that monitoring detects errors and deterioration early. In one study, modern monitoring standards halved the number of cardiac arrests, mainly because fewer had respiratory causes. In the Australian Incident Monitoring Study, 52 % of incidents were first detected by a monitor, and in more than half of these it was the pulse oximeter or capnograph.Source: Aitkenhead ch. 18
  • Pulse oximetry found more problems, but did not improve outcomes. Continuous pulse oximetry gave fewer episodes of SpO₂ below 90 % (235 participants) and more changes in treatment. There was nevertheless no reduction in cardiac, respiratory, neurological or infectious complications, and no difference in in-hospital mortality (20,802 and 22,021 participants). Pulse oximetry is nevertheless a minimum standard.Sources: Pedersen 2014 (Cochrane), Norwegian standard 2024, Klein 2021
  • The standards justify monitoring by early warning. Monitoring reduces the risk of incidents by detecting the consequences of errors and giving early warning of deterioration. The requirement for processed EEG during TIVA with neuromuscular blockade rests on the same logic and on NAP5, not on randomised outcome studies (see “What the standards require”).Source: Klein 2021
  • The EEG trials give mixed answers. ENGAGES and ENGAGES-Canada reduced burst suppression without reducing delirium, whereas Balanced found less delirium. Several authors point out that the trials measured indices, not the raw EEG.Sources: Burst suppression tab, Gruenbaum 2026
  • Reflection from the author of the app: we have never demanded as much of any other monitor before adopting it. Pulse oximetry and capnography became standard because they show something we cannot otherwise see, not because they were proven to save lives. The EEG is the only monitor that measures the target organ of general anaesthesia.
  • From surviving anaesthesia to preserving organ function. When the EEG is read as a picture of cortical integrity rather than a number for anaesthetic depth, anaesthesia becomes a matter of organ protection and not only of immobility. This is just as perfusion is titrated to protect the heart. EEG in the critically ill may usher in «a new era for brain health». Mortality has fallen sharply, even though patients have become sicker. Anaesthesia-related mortality fell from 357 per million before the 1970s to 34 per million in the 1990s and 2000s, and total perioperative mortality from about 10,600 to about 1,200 per million (meta-analysis of more than 21 million anaesthetics). No comparable pooled figures exist for the period before 1950. Reflection from the author of the app: the goal is no longer just to survive the anaesthetic. It is to preserve all organ functions throughout the whole course of care, including the brain's.Sources: Gruenbaum 2026, Guay 2025, Bainbridge 2012
Aitkenhead ch. 18 (2007) Pedersen et al. Cochrane 2014 Klein et al. 2021
The studies in detail: Norwegian use (Aasheim 2024 and 2026), sources of error (Pinheiro 2026), standards and consensus (4 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

How EEG monitors are used in Norway (Aasheim 2024)

Cross-sectional survey with a web form sent to anaesthesia staff at all 54 Norwegian hospitals from autumn 2020 to June 2021 (Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2024;68:781–787), based on an Australian questionnaire (Ben-Menachem). 391 responded: 324 nurse anaesthetists and 67 anaesthetists, out of an estimated 1,800 and 1,500 in the country. More than half had over ten years of experience.

  • Access and use: 76% reported that a monitor was present in over 80% of operating rooms. 62% used it on more than half of their patients, 4% never. 49% had guidelines for use, 31% did not, 19% did not know. Used most often with neuromuscular blockade (68%), TIVA (43%) and obesity (29%); 22% “always when available”. 49% never used a monitor in children.
  • What is used: the index value in 99% of the anaesthetists and 98% of the nurses (BIS is the most widely used monitor, entropy exists at some hospitals). Raw EEG in 15% and 10%, spectrogram in 18% and 7%, suppression ratio in 18% and 9%, SEF95 in 1% and 3%. Heart rate (100%) and blood pressure (96%) were the dominant clinical signs, and 58% considered clinical signs more reliable than BIS.
  • Burst suppression: 27% reported that they could recognise the pattern (67% of the anaesthetists, 18% of the nurses, p < 0.0001), and 39% knew that it means too deep anaesthesia. At the same time, over 60% in both groups felt they had sufficient knowledge, and 86% wanted more.
  • Asymmetric dosing: 90% increased the dose at high index values, 55% reduced it at low values. Respondents were neutral to the statement that an index below 40 is associated with complications, and rated the monitor as more useful against awareness (76% agreed) than for reducing dose and emergence time. The authors interpret this as a stronger fear of awareness than of too deep anaesthesia.
  • Conclusion: widespread use, but the information beyond the index number (raw EEG, spectrogram, suppression) is little used, and the ability to recognise burst suppression is low. The authors call for training and more standardised guidelines. That is the background for this app.
  • Caveats: voluntary, anonymous web survey without a response rate that can be calculated reliably (about 18% of the nurses and 4% of the anaesthetists in the country), possible bias towards those who use the monitor a lot or are strongly opposed, no demographics (urban versus rural), self-reported knowledge. No conflicts of interest, no external funding. The discussion refers to BIS-guided anaesthesia reducing POCD at three months in older patients (ref. 19); see the Intensive care and Spectrogram tabs for the more divergent RCT evidence (ENGAGES, Evered 2021).
Aasheim, Rosseland, Leonardsen, Romundstad. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2024;68:781–787

Who gets the lowest BIS in Norwegian practice: age, sex and ASA (Aasheim 2026)

Observational cohort study from the four hospitals of Oslo University Hospital, 2017–2020 (Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2026;70:e70281). BIS values were extracted automatically from the electronic chart (MetaVision) and analysed with a linear mixed model with time, age, ASA and sex as covariates and patient as a random effect. Standard TIVA at the hospitals was Schnider TCI for propofol and Minto for remifentanil; 82% of BIS patients received TIVA.

  • Who was monitored: 97,733 patients received general anaesthesia, 26,650 (27%) had continuous BIS. BIS was used in 33% of TIVA patients versus 7% with volatile anaesthesia, and in only 21% of the 55,965 who received muscle relaxants. The proportion monitored fell with ASA class (ASA 1 TIVA 34%, ASA 4 TIVA 22%, ASA 4 volatile 4%). The typical BIS patient was ASA 1–2 on TIVA without relaxants, that is, not the patients at greatest risk of awareness and delirium. The authors call this unexpected and a patient-safety concern.
  • Who was deepest: in the adjusted model (table 3) men had BIS values 2.4 units higher than women (95% CI 2.3–2.8), each year of age lowered BIS by 0.05 (−0.055 to −0.045), and ASA 2, 3 and 4 were 0.2, 0.56 and 0.86 lower than ASA 1 respectively. Mean BIS rose with time into surgery (about 39 at the start), most clearly in ASA 1 (to nearly 48 after 300 min), whereas ASA 4 fell to around 30–35 (fig. 4). The differences are statistically secure because of the sample size but small in absolute terms; what is clinically interesting is the tails.
  • Burst-suppression level (BIS below 30): the proportion with a mean BIS below 30 for the whole procedure rose with ASA class, roughly 10% in ASA 1–2, 15% in ASA 3 and 22% in ASA 4 (fig. 5, read from the figure). At least 5 minutes below 30 occurred in about 26% of ASA 1 and 50% of ASA 4 (fig. 6). Mean BIS above 65 was rare (1–2%) and evenly distributed across sex and ASA. The authors cite Bruhn 2000: BIS below 30 corresponds to increasing suppression.
  • The authors' interpretation: lower BIS in the old and sick with standard Schnider TCI may mean that the model, or the way it is applied, is not sufficiently individualised for vulnerable patients; they cite Obert 2024 on slow induction (Spectrogram tab). Lower BIS in women may reflect clinicians perceiving female sex as a risk factor for awareness and dosing higher, or the Schnider model's fixed central volume (V1) not accounting for body composition, unlike Eleveld. They stress themselves that the associations should not be interpreted causally.
  • What is missing: only the BIS index was available, not raw EEG, suppression ratio or SEF, so artefacts and actual suppression could not be confirmed. No dosing data, no delirium data, BIS used selectively (not randomly), no pre-registration, and mean BIS hides within-procedure variation. The authors call for studies combining BIS with raw EEG, spectrogram and suppression measures, and measuring delirium in the frail.
  • The editorial comment in the journal points to what remains unresolved: whether deeper anaesthesia in the old and sick should be met with lower doses, or with better brain perfusion (see the Perfusion tab on autoregulation and alpha dropout).
  • Conflicts of interest: the authors declare no conflicts of interest and no funding. The study was approved by the data protection officer at OUS; the regional ethics committee judged that ethical approval was not required.
Aasheim, Rosseland, Ponzi, Kristiansen, Romundstad. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2026;70:e70281

Artefacts and pitfalls in processed EEG: the ANESTHESIA mnemonic (Pinheiro 2026)

Narrative review (Cureus 2026, PubMed to August 2025, selection at the authors' discretion). The point: the index alone cannot be trusted, and when it is unexpectedly high or low without an obvious reason, the sources of error should be gone through systematically. The authors group them in four.

  • Pharmacological: ketamine gives more beta/gamma and less delta and raises the index despite deeper anaesthesia. Dexmedetomidine and clonidine give spindles and slow waves and lower the index, also at moderate sedation. Nitrous oxide (an NMDA antagonist, like ketamine) changes the index little according to Pinheiro when given in usual adjunct doses on top of GABAergic anaesthesia, but Purdon 2015 (Part I) lists nitrous oxide with ketamine as the two agents that most often make clinicians doubt the index: both produce beta/gamma that tends to raise the index at clinically accepted doses, and on switching to above 70% nitrous oxide a transient, profound slow-delta pattern appears after 2–4 minutes before beta/gamma takes over. Abrupt withdrawal can lower the index paradoxically (“withdrawal-suppression”); rapid washout of isoflurane/sevoflurane can give a paradoxical low-voltage EEG with a falsely low index and burst suppression. Neuromuscular blockers lower the index by removing EMG, also in awake patients; sugammadex and neostigmine raise it, mostly via EMG, and sugammadex can produce an arousal effect under propofol. Opioids in analgesic doses change the index little, high doses can lower it. Neuraxial block, vasopressors, methylene blue and magnesium can also shift the index (next point).
  • Blocks, vasopressors, methylene blue and magnesium, explained: the common denominator is that the index measures how active the cortex is, and anything that increases or dampens activation shifts the number.
    • Neuraxial block: the block shuts off much of the sensory input from the body, so the arousal system in the brainstem receives fewer signals. In a randomised, blinded study, healthy volunteers were measurably sedated by spinal lidocaine, and the authors attribute the early sedation to reduced afferent input. BIS nevertheless did not differ between groups in the blinded part, so the sedation itself is better documented than the effect on the index (Pollock 2000).
    • Vasopressors: under propofol anaesthesia, ephedrine raised BIS (8 of 20 went above 60), while phenylephrine did not. Propofol concentration and cardiac output were unchanged, so the rise was not due to less propofol but probably to an effect on the brain (Takizawa 2006). That phenylephrine differs may relate to it acting almost only on alpha-1 receptors in the vessels, while ephedrine, adrenaline and isoprenaline also act on beta receptors and ephedrine is a central stimulant (interpretation based on the sources). For isoprenaline there is one case report.
    • Methylene blue: one case report describes a marked fall in BIS after methylene blue for methaemoglobinaemia (cited by Duarte and Saraiva 2009). The mechanism is not clear.
    • Magnesium: in a double-blind RCT of 100 women having caesarean section under general anaesthesia (sevoflurane), magnesium 30 mg/kg followed by 10 mg/kg/h gave a lower BIS throughout surgery, with no difference in fentanyl use or haemodynamics, and less pain afterwards. The authors call the mechanism unclear and point to NMDA and calcium channels (Altıparmak 2018). Magnesium crosses the blood–brain barrier poorly, so the effect may equally be due to less nociceptive activation.
    • In practice: when the index changes abruptly after a vasopressor, magnesium or a block, it does not automatically mean that hypnotic depth has changed. Look at the raw EEG and the spectrogram before changing the hypnotic dose.
  • Electromagnetic and mechanical: high impedance (temperature, humidity, poor skin preparation), pacemakers and other implants, diathermy, EMG tubes, facial nerve stimulators (even in standby, because of impedance testing), navigation equipment near the head, forced-air warming blankets near the head, endoscopic shavers, Doppler, pulsatile cardiopulmonary bypass and arterial pulsation (images 15 and 2 in the image quiz). SQI may remain high during such artefacts. ECG can dominate a low-voltage EEG.
  • Pathophysiological: age (the indices were built on adults; infants under 1 year and older patients deviate, see the Spectrogram tab), nociception (beta arousal, delta arousal, alpha dropout after García 2021), genetically low-voltage EEG in 5–10% of the population (check the baseline before induction), ischaemia, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, seizures and the post-ictal phase (a slow pattern that may persist after consciousness has returned), haemodynamics and positioning (forehead oedema in prolonged Trendelenburg), space-occupying lesions (side-to-side difference, a pseudomeningocele can mimic ictal activity), neurological disease (Alzheimer, vascular dementia, cerebral palsy give a lower index).
  • Model-dependent: different monitors, also from the same manufacturer, give different values at the same depth because of different algorithms and artefact filters; each new model has its learning curve.
  • ANESTHESIA (the mnemonic): Anaesthetic agents and other drugs (end-tidal/age-adjusted MAC, pump, TCI target, extravasation, backflow, occlusion); Neuromuscular blockade and reversal, neurological disease; Equipment (SQI, electrodes, sweat); Stimulus (nociception, nociception monitor, EEG patterns); Temperature, metabolism, tumour; Haemodynamics and positioning; Electromagnetic and mechanical interference; Seizure (pro- and anticonvulsants); Ischaemia and injury (NIRS if available); Age (infants, older patients). First: exclude dosing errors before other sources. Before induction: note the baseline index and DSA. If the artefact cannot be removed, it should at least be taken into account when the dose is adjusted.
  • Caveats: narrative review without systematic search or quality assessment; many claims rest on case reports. The authors stress that not every unexpected value is an artefact. One author reports speaker fees from MSD, unrelated to the work.
Pinheiro et al. Cureus 2026;18:e103656

What standards and consensus documents say about EEG monitoring

  • Norwegian standard for the safe practice of anaesthesia, 2024 revision (Leonardsen 2024): minimum monitoring in general anaesthesia is pulse oximetry, clinical assessment of level of consciousness, respiration and circulation, ECG, blood pressure, oxygen alarm, capnography, disconnection alarm, multigas analysis with volatile agents and neuromuscular monitoring with non-depolarising blockers. “Monitoring of anaesthesia depth (e.g., BIS and EEG) must be individually considered.” The anaesthetic record must document monitoring equipment, with BIS given as an example. Adopted by the Norwegian Association of Anaesthesiologists and the Norwegian Association of Nurse Anaesthetists, in force from 1 March 2024; the authors declare no conflicts of interest.
  • Association of Anaesthetists 2021 (Klein 2021): processed EEG “should be used” when TIVA is given with a neuromuscular blocker, from before induction until full recovery from the block is confirmed, and “should be considered” with inhalational anaesthesia and in high-risk patients. The rationale is NAP5: most definite or probable awareness cases occurred with a neuromuscular blocker, and almost two-thirds before the start or after the end of surgery, where end-tidal gas monitoring does not help. With volatile anaesthesia an alarm at end-tidal below 0.7 age-adjusted MAC is recommended. And, quoted in substance: anaesthetists should not rely solely on the index value, but develop a basic understanding of the raw EEG, power spectrum, spectrogram and relative band powers. With manual charts pEEG should be recorded at least every 5 minutes. The first author reports educational grants/honoraria from, among others, Masimo (spelled “Massimo” in the article).
  • Definition and aims of anaesthesia, Delphi consensus (Berger-Estilita 2026): 23 experts, three rounds, 80% agreement as threshold, 49 aims in seven domains. Relevant aims: “a sufficient level of sedation/anaesthesia and avoid oversedation” (INT7), “protect cognitive functions and avoid postoperative delirium” (PRE5, DIS4, DIS5), “avoid long-term cognition disturbances” (LTO6), and “preserving or enhancing organ function, inclusive of brain and cognitive function” in the definition itself. The document does not mention EEG, but the aims are those EEG monitoring targets. Patient experiences (PREMs) were not included as aims. Several authors report honoraria or travel support from Medtronic and other suppliers.
  • Multinational Delphi consensus on TIVA (Uitenbosch 2022): 29 panellists, 79% European, 12 statements, strong consensus at ≥ 75%. Only four reached consensus: TIVA is useful in paediatric anaesthesia, reduces PONV, is better for the environment, and physiological effects (airway, haemodynamics) guide the choice. “The risk of awareness is an obstacle to TIVA” received only 20.6–21.5% agreement. Access to TCI pumps and pEEG was mentioned as a practical barrier, but the statement on practical obstacles did not reach consensus (34.4 → 64.3%). Evidence for less emergence agitation in children reached 74.1%, just below the threshold.
  • Norwegian practice: Aasheim 2024 (Fundamentals tab) shows what Norwegian departments actually do. Taken together: the British guideline is more binding than the Norwegian standard, and both place the responsibility for interpretation with the person at the patient's side.
Leonardsen et al. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2024;68:567–574 · Klein et al. Anaesthesia 2021;76:1212–1223 · Berger-Estilita et al. Anaesth Crit Care Pain Med 2026;45:101614 · Uitenbosch et al. J Clin Med 2022;11:3486

Key points

  • TCI is a prediction, not a measurement. The pump calculates an expected concentration from age, weight, height, sex and what it has delivered. Nothing is measured. Schnider and Eleveld give different numbers for the same patient and dose.See
  • The number on the pump says as much about speed and model as about the patient. The patients fell asleep after about the same amount of propofol, whether it was given fast or slowly. Even so, the pump showed almost twice the concentration with fast induction (4.6 versus 2.6 µg/ml). Only Eleveld showed the same number with fast and slow induction, yet the brain behaved quite differently in the two groups. In older patients, Eleveld more often gave excessive depth than Schnider in one study.See
  • The effect-site number is built on simplifications. It is calculated from an assumption about how quickly the drug reaches the brain. That assumption comes from rapid bolus doses, is not adjusted for age in the propofol models used clinically, and assumes that the patient falls asleep and wakes up at the same concentration. None of these holds fully.See
  • Do not use the induction number for the rest of the operation. The effect keeps increasing after the number is reached. In one study the index kept falling for 11 minutes to a deeper level than intended. Adjust the dose according to EEG or the index.See
  • Fast and slow induction are two different routes. With fast induction, the pupillary and corneal reflexes were already gone as the patient stopped responding, and the three oldest developed burst suppression. With slow induction, the reflexes were preserved and alpha appeared in the EEG before the patient stopped responding. Slow induction may be gentler, particularly for older patients, but it has not yet been tested in a clinical trial.See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

TCI is a prediction, not a measurement

  • The pump measures nothing. It knows age, weight, height and sex, and what it has itself delivered. From that, a population model calculates an expected plasma and effect-site concentration.
  • Different models give different numbers for the same patient. The Schnider model is based on healthy volunteers, only nine of them over 65 years. The Eleveld model is built on a broader population and gives a lower calculated effect-site concentration than Schnider for the same patient and dose. The patient is the same; the prediction is not.Sources: Schnider 1999, Eleveld 2014, Obert 2024
  • EEG shows how this particular brain responds. The models are uncertain during induction because the phase is dynamic. With age and disease, the patient also deviates from the population. Slow, spectrogram-guided induction is one attempt to let the response, not the model, determine the dose.Sources: Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025 and Obert 2024 (see the Spectrogram tab)
  • The effect-site concentration is also a model quantity. It is based on ke0 and is not measured.Source: Proekt and Kelz 2021 on hysteresis (see the Spectrogram tab)
Schnider 1999, Eleveld 2014, Obert 2024

Same patient, different numbers: model and speed

The number the pump shows as the patient loses consciousness (calculated effect-site concentration, Ce) depends both on how fast propofol is given and on which model does the calculation.Sources: three studies from the Sepúlveda group and one from Ghent (Sepúlveda 2010, Sepúlveda 2020, Sepúlveda 2021, Coppens 2010)

  • Slow induction gives lower numbers on the pump. The patients stopped responding at a calculated 2.6 µg/ml with slow induction, versus 4.6 µg/ml with fast induction. The dose was about the same (1.67 versus 1.91 mg/kg). The same pattern has been seen in healthy volunteers and is described clinically: around 5 µg/ml with fast and around 2.5 with stepwise slow induction.Sources: Sepúlveda 2020, Sepúlveda 2010, Sepúlveda and Demaría 2019
  • The models disagree. For the same patients, Schnider gave twice the number with fast as with slow induction (6.6 versus 3.2 µg/ml). Eleveld gave almost the same (3.1 versus 3.2) and was the only one of four models not affected by speed. Original Marsh went in the opposite direction. At the same endpoint, Ce ranged from 1.96 (Marsh) to 5.54 µg/ml (Schnider).Sources: Sepúlveda 2021, Sepúlveda 2010, Coppens 2010
  • The same number does not mean the same brain. All the patients stopped responding, and Eleveld showed roughly the same concentration in both groups. Yet the brainstem reflexes were gone and alpha appeared later with fast induction. With slow induction, the reflexes were preserved and alpha appeared early. The same calculated concentration can therefore correspond to different brain states depending on how the patient got there, and only the EEG shows the difference (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Sepúlveda 2021, Sepúlveda 2020, Obert 2020
  • Eleveld may give excessive depth in older patients. In women aged 65 and over, guided by BIS, Eleveld more often gave excessive depth than Schnider (63.2% versus 27.3%) and more often burst suppression (31.6% versus 4.5%). The authors recommend particular attention when the model is used in older patients. Caveat: observational study of 78 women undergoing breast surgery, not randomised, and the concentrations are calculated, not measured.Source: Linassi 2023
  • Fast administration gives a brief, high peak in the blood. 50 patients (30–76 years) received the same dose, 1.2 mg/kg, given at five different rates from 10 to 160 mg/kg/h. At the fastest rate, measured arterial concentration reached about 20–37 µg/ml within the first minute, versus only 3–5 µg/ml at the slowest. After about two minutes it fell again to around 2–5 µg/ml (read from Figure 2 of the article). Slow administration thus gives a low, steady rise. Three findings are useful:
    • TCI models assume that propofol mixes in the blood instantly. That is not true, so they miss the concentration in the first minutes. This is also when variability between patients is greatest.
    • The rate changed how the blood concentration developed, and in older patients it took longer before propofol reached the artery.
    • The rate did not change how fast propofol moved from the blood to the brain (ke0), measured with BIS. The authors warn against extrapolating this to fast manual bolus doses.
    This does not contradict Sepúlveda. Masui measured only BIS, whereas Sepúlveda and Obert measured reflexes and EEG patterns and found that the brain reached unconsciousness in different ways (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Masui 2009
  • Eleveld is made for all ages, but shares the basic assumptions of other models. The model is built on pooled data from 30 earlier studies, with 1033 people from premature neonates to 88 years. The concentration giving half effect on BIS falls with age: from about 3.4 µg/ml at 20 years to about 2.3 µg/ml at 80 years. The aim was one model for all ages and body sizes, not to outperform the other models. Because the effect is modelled against BIS, the expected and measured index can be compared. This shows whether the patient is sensitive, normal or resistant to propofol. But like Schnider and Marsh, Eleveld is a conventional three-compartment model that assumes the drug mixes in the blood instantly. The studies also took blood samples at different times and sites (arterial or venous), which causes differences between models. Eleveld therefore does not describe the brief peak that Masui measured either (interpretation based on the sources). Struys is a co-author of both the model and the review.Sources: Eleveld 2018, as described in Vandemoortele 2022
  • The index did not follow the number on the pump. CSI was the same at loss of consciousness after bolus and infusion (70 versus 71). PSI was higher with fast than with slow induction (87 versus 67), that is, a higher index in the group that had received the most.Sources: Sepúlveda 2010, Sepúlveda 2021
  • The model rests on assumptions that do not hold during induction. ke0 in Schnider and modified Marsh is derived from time to peak effect after a rapid bolus, and the models describe the early distribution after a bolus poorly. ke0 also assumes a linear relationship between concentration and effect, and is not age-adjusted in the propofol models in clinical use. In addition, patients lose and regain response at different concentrations. That does not fit a single concentration–effect curve.Sources: Sepúlveda 2021, Sepúlveda 2010, Sepúlveda and Demaría 2019
  • Caveats. The studies are small (16 patients or volunteers) and have no plasma measurements. The 2019 review is narrative and rests partly on unpublished data.

The studies in detail:

Sepúlveda 2020 Sepúlveda 2021 Sepúlveda 2010 Coppens 2010 Sepúlveda and Demaría 2019

The number at loss of consciousness is not a maintenance target

It is tempting to let the pump hold the number it showed as the patient fell asleep for the rest of the anaesthetic. This does not work.Sources: Coppens 2010, Sepúlveda 2010, Sepúlveda 2020

  • The effect continues after the number is reached. 60 patients received propofol until they stopped responding to their name. The pump then held the Ce from that moment for 20 minutes. With both Schnider variants, BIS kept falling for 11 minutes, to a deeper level than intended. With Marsh, all patients woke up, because the pump stood still for 233 seconds.Source: Coppens 2010
  • The number after a bolus leads to overdosing. Ce at loss of consciousness after an induction dose should not be used as a reference for maintenance, because it would lead to overdosing.Sources: Sepúlveda 2010, Sepúlveda 2020
  • The model is good at keeping the state stable, not at predicting the effect. The strength of effect-site TCI is not to predict the effect in the individual, but to keep the state stable once a clinical endpoint has been reached. Surrogate measures such as BIS are needed to see when steady state is reached.Source: Coppens 2010
  • EEG or an index is needed to find the patient’s own level. The number depends on model and speed, and the same number gives a different effect over time. One example: after slow induction with Schnider, Ce is reduced by 15% below the level at loss of response.Source: Mehler 2024

The studies in detail:

Coppens 2010 Sepúlveda 2010 Sepúlveda 2020 Mehler 2024

Two routes to unconsciousness: fast and slow induction

With fast and slow induction the patients reach the same endpoint, but the brain gets there in different ways. This was shown by one randomised study in ASA 1 patients, published in two parts. It compared fast induction (equivalent to a bolus) with slow infusion until loss of response.Sources: Sepúlveda 2020, Obert 2020 (Santiago)

  • Fast induction works bottom-up, slow induction top-down. As the response disappeared, pupillary and corneal reflexes were absent in all 8 in the fast group and preserved in all 8 in the slow group. The authors interpret fast induction as “bottom-up” (brainstem inhibition) and slow as “top-down” (loss of cortical integration).Source: Sepúlveda 2020
  • With slow induction, alpha appears before the patient stops responding. With fast induction, frontal alpha only appeared several minutes afterwards. With slow induction, the pattern regarded as “adequate anaesthesia” was already present before loss of response to verbal command. The authors write that “anyone can become a black swan with slow induction”.Source: Obert 2020
  • The indices follow different courses. The beta ratio fell steeply before loss of response to pain with fast induction, but was low long before with slow induction. Relative alpha and the alpha/delta ratio tracked loss of response to verbal command best.Source: Obert 2020
  • Burst suppression occurred only with fast induction. Three of nine in the fast group developed it, the oldest (57, 57 and 61 years). None in the slow group did. Larger materials show the same. The authors propose slow induction as safer, especially in older patients, but say themselves that this must be tested in a clinical trial.Sources: Sepúlveda 2020, Obert 2024, Ostertag 2025
  • Caveats. 16 patients (Obert 2020 reports 18 included), only healthy subjects under 65, only frontal EEG, and consciousness measured as response, not as experience.

The studies in detail:

Sepúlveda 2020 Obert 2020 Obert 2024 Ostertag 2025

The cards on burst suppression are collected in the tab.

The studies in detail: fast versus slow induction, Ce as a maintenance target, the effect-site model (3 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Fast versus slow induction: two routes to unconsciousness (Sepúlveda 2020, Obert 2020)

One randomised study from Clínica Alemana in Santiago (NCT03140982), published in two parts: the clinical and neurological part in Anaesthesia 2020;75:196–201 and the EEG analysis in Sci Rep 2020;10:19444. ASA 1 patients aged 18–65 for hip arthroscopy received either propofol TCI to an effect site of 5.4 µg/ml (Marsh, ke0 1.21, “fast”, equivalent to a bolus) or 10 mg/kg/h until loss of response (“slow”). A neurologist blinded to group tested the FOUR score every 30 seconds. Frontal four-channel EEG (SedLine).

  • Time and concentration: loss of consciousness after a median of 10.5 minutes (slow) versus 1.4 (fast). Calculated effect-site concentration at loss of response 2.6 versus 4.6 µg/ml, cumulative dose 1.67 versus 1.91 mg/kg. Same endpoint, almost double the model concentration.
  • Brainstem reflexes: preserved (pupillary and corneal reflexes) in all 8 in the slow group, absent in all 8 in the fast group at the moment the response disappeared (p = 0.010). The authors interpret fast induction as “bottom-up” (brainstem inhibition) and slow as “top-down” (loss of cortical integration), with reference to Mashour and Hudetz 2017 (see the Components tab).
  • Alpha before or after: with slow induction, frontal alpha power rose before loss of response; with fast induction, alpha only appeared several minutes afterwards. Obert 2020 shows that with slow induction, loss of response to verbal command (LOvR) could be distinguished from loss of response to pain (LOpR, 0–210 seconds later), and that the alpha and delta pattern regarded as “adequate anaesthesia” was already present before LOvR. The authors write that “anyone can become a black swan with slow induction” (cf. Gaskell 2017 and Mashour and Avidan 2017 in the Components tab).
  • Beta ratio and indices: the beta ratio (BIS surrogate) fell steeply before LOpR with fast induction, but was already low long before with slow induction, so the index follows different courses depending on speed. Relative beta remained high for minutes after LOpR with slow induction, that is, a prolonged “paradoxical excitation”. Relative alpha and the alpha/delta ratio tracked the transition to LOvR best, the beta/alpha ratio tracked LOpR best.
  • Burst suppression only with fast induction: three of nine in the fast group (57, 57 and 61 years, the oldest) developed burst suppression during induction and were excluded from the EEG analysis. None in the slow group. Obert 2024 and Ostertag 2025 found the same in larger materials.
  • Clinical message from the authors: the effect-site concentration at loss of response after a bolus (Marsh, ke0 1.21) cannot be used as a maintenance target, because it would lead to overdosing. Slow induction is proposed as safer, especially in older patients, but the authors themselves say this must be tested in a clinical trial.
  • Same patients, four models (Sepúlveda 2021, Rev Esp Anestesiol Reanim): an additional analysis of the same 16 patients calculated the effect-site concentration at loss of consciousness with four models. Slow versus fast induction: original Marsh (ke0 0.2) 2.15 versus 1.8 µg/ml; modified Marsh 2.7 versus 4.6; Schnider 3.2 versus 6.6; Eleveld 3.2 versus 3.1. Only Eleveld gave the same number regardless of speed. PSI at loss of consciousness was 67 (slow) versus 87 (fast), that is, a higher index in the group that had received the most. The authors call the numbers “contradictory” and point out that ke0 in Schnider and modified Marsh is derived from time to peak effect after a rapid bolus, while Schnider's own Emax model gives an EC50 of 2.35 µg/ml for loss of consciousness with slow infusion.
  • Caveats: 16 patients (8 + 8) in Sepúlveda 2020 and 2021, while Obert 2020 reports 18 included (see discrepancies). Only healthy subjects under 65, only frontal EEG, Marsh model (not Schnider or Eleveld), and consciousness measured as response (FOUR score), not as experience. No conflicts of interest in Sepúlveda 2020; none in Obert 2020.
Sepúlveda et al. Anaesthesia 2020;75:196–201; Obert et al. Sci Rep 2020;10:19444; Sepúlveda et al. Rev Esp Anestesiol Reanim 2021;68:245–251

Why Ce at loss of consciousness after a bolus cannot be used as a maintenance target (Sepúlveda 2010, Coppens 2010)

Two studies from 2010 that form the basis for most of the criticism above.

  • Sepúlveda 2010 (Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2010;54:447–452): 16 healthy volunteers aged 21–45 received, in randomised order, both a bolus of 1.8 mg/kg (1,200 ml/h) and an infusion of 12 mg/kg/h, with the Cerebral State Index as monitor. Loss of consciousness after 0.97 minutes (bolus) versus 6.8 minutes (infusion). Calculated Ce at loss of consciousness, bolus versus infusion: Schnider (ke0 0.45) 4.40 versus 2.81 µg/ml; modified Marsh (ke0 1.21) 3.55 versus 2.50; original Marsh (ke0 0.26) 1.28 versus 1.72. CSI at loss of consciousness was the same (70 versus 71). Conclusion: “Ce predicted at loss of consciousness after a TCI induction dose should not be used as a reference value for titrating hypnosis during maintenance.” The authors believe the error lies in the “front-end” kinetics: the models describe the early distribution after a bolus poorly. No plasma measurements. No conflicts of interest, departmentally funded.
  • Coppens 2010 (Br J Anaesth 2010;104:452–458, Ghent, with Schnider as co-author): 60 patients received propofol at 300 ml/h until they stopped responding to their name, and the calculated Ce at that moment was set as the effect-site target for 20 minutes with one of three models. Ce at loss of response was 1.96 (Marsh, ke0 0.26), 5.54 (Schnider, fixed ke0 0.456) and 5.08 µg/ml (Schnider, ke0 adjusted to time to peak effect 1.6 min). With Marsh, all patients woke up (after an average of 401 seconds, because the pump stood still for 233 seconds); with the two Schnider variants, BIS kept falling for 11 minutes to a deeper level than intended, and one patient woke up. Conclusion: targeting Ce at loss of consciousness does not give an immediately constant effect with any of the models, and surrogate measures such as BIS are needed to see when steady state is reached. The authors write that the strength of effect-site TCI is not to predict the effect in the individual, but to keep the state stable once a clinical endpoint has been reached.
  • What the two show together: the number the pump displays at loss of consciousness depends on model and speed, and the same number gives a different effect over time. That is why EEG (or an index) is necessary to find the patient's own level, and why the Sepúlveda group proposes slow induction, in which Ce and effect have time to follow each other. Mehler 2024 (Spectrogram tab) draws the consequence and reduces Ce by 15% below the level at loss of response when Schnider is used after slow induction.
Sepúlveda et al. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2010;54:447–452; Coppens et al. Br J Anaesth 2010;104:452–458

A critical look at the effect-site model for propofol (Sepúlveda and Demaría 2019)

Review article in Rev Esp Anestesiol Reanim 2019;66:425–433.

  • The questions the article raises: do the EEG indices represent the effect? Are the indices used to build the models comparable, and what is the real response time of the monitors? Is ke0 affected by infusion rate and by age? Are induction and emergence mirror images, as the Emax models assume?
  • ke0: a first-order transfer constant in a linear, proportional model, tied to one specific PK model. The models are useful as a titration reference, but incomplete for induction, changes of plan and emergence, because they assume a linear relationship between plasma concentration and effect.
  • Clinical observation: fast induction towards an arbitrary EC95 requires a Ce of around 5 µg/ml (equivalent to about a 2 mg/kg bolus), while stepwise slow induction gives loss of consciousness at around 2.5 µg/ml.
  • Age and ke0: for remifentanil, equilibration is about three times slower in older patients (Minto), and similar is seen for fentanyl, cisatracurium and sevoflurane, but ke0 is not age-adjusted in the propofol models in clinical use.
  • Neural inertia: different concentrations for losing and regaining response (Friedman 2010, fruit flies and rats) do not fit a single concentration–effect curve. See Proekt and Kelz 2021 and Warnaby 2017 in the Spectrogram tab.
  • Caveats: narrative review; some of the arguments rest on unpublished data (EuroSIVA 2009). No conflicts of interest declared.
Sepúlveda and Demaría. Rev Esp Anestesiol Reanim 2019;66:425–433

Key points

  • Emergence is not induction in reverse: Consciousness is lost at a higher concentration than the one at which it returns (hysteresis), induction is gradual while emergence is abrupt, and several circuits govern only one of the two transitions. Hysteresis in humans remains debated, however. (see “Emergence is not induction in reverse”)
  • Emergence is an active process: Dopamine from the VTA, noradrenaline, orexin and acetylcholine can hasten emergence in animal studies, often without altering induction. No nucleus acts alone; the network decides. (see “The brain has its own arousal pathways”)
  • Deep structures wake before the functions: The brainstem and thalamus are active as consciousness returns, whereas cognitive functions return stepwise over the following hours. The findings measure different phases and do not contradict each other. (see “What wakes first”)
  • Awake is not the same as conscious: Dopaminergic arousal reversed most agents, but not ketamine, and a drug that changed the EEG did not wake the animals. This fits with the arousal pathways acting on level, whereas ketamine disrupts content. (see “Awake is not the same as conscious”)
  • Clinically today: Emergence is still driven mainly by elimination of the agent. A low dose or “alpha without theta” does not guarantee rapid emergence, and no dopaminergic method is established in humans. (see “What it means clinically today”)

The theme cards below tell the story, with the sources under each point. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Emergence is not induction in reverse

For a long time, emergence was seen as a passive process: the agent disappears, the concentration falls below a critical value, and the brain goes back the same way. Three findings fit poorly with that picture.Source: Kelz 2019

  • Consciousness is lost at a higher concentration than the one at which it returns. This is called anaesthetic hysteresis. It is explained by neural inertia: the brain resists changing state, in both directions. In healthy volunteers given propofol TCI, pharmacokinetics alone did not explain this loop. One review considers hysteresis a general property of the nervous system.Sources: Friedman 2010, Huang 2021, Kelz 2019
  • Induction is gradual, emergence is abrupt. During induction the whole brain changed gradually. Emergence came as an abrupt jump in connectivity between thalamus, brainstem and cortex. The authors call it a “reboot” of consciousness.Source: Huang 2021
  • Some circuits govern only one of the transitions. Inhibiting orexin delayed emergence without altering induction. Several nuclei govern only emergence, while others (PnO) govern only induction.
