Other circuits take part in both: inhibiting the PPT in the brainstem gave both faster induction and slower emergence in mice.Sources: Kelz 2008 (discussed in Kelz 2019), Zhang and Wei 2025, Li 2024
  • Hysteresis in humans is not settled. Several studies found hysteresis, whereas two studies did not find it for propofol. The concentrations are model-calculated, not measured.Sources: found hysteresis: Ferreira 2020, Nir 2019, Sepúlveda 2019, Huang 2021. Did not find hysteresis: Kuizenga 2018, Warnaby 2017

The studies in detail:

Friedman 2010 Huang 2021 Kelz 2019 Zhang and Wei 2025 Li 2024

The brain has its own arousal pathways, and they act as a network

If emergence were merely the absence of agent, it could not be hastened without removing the agent. In animal studies it can: animals can be woken while the gas is still running. Emergence appears to be actively driven by arousal systems in the brainstem and hypothalamus.Source: Solt 2011

  • Dopamine from the VTA can wake animals during ongoing anaesthesia. Methylphenidate, dextroamphetamine and electrical stimulation of the VTA woke rats while the agent was still being given. Stimulation of the substantia nigra, which also contains dopamine neurons, did not work, and D1 blockade abolished the effect of dextroamphetamine. The effect applied to sevoflurane, isoflurane, propofol, dexmedetomidine and fentanyl, but not ketamine. Which receptors carried it varied with the agent.Sources: Solt 2011, Solt 2014, Kenny 2015, Kato 2021, Vincent 2024
  • Noradrenaline primes the brain for emergence but does not keep it awake on its own. Mice without noradrenaline woke much later, and noradrenaline in the central thalamus hastened emergence from propofol. But atomoxetine, which raises noradrenaline, woke none of the rats.Sources: Kelz 2019, Kenny 2015
  • Orexin, acetylcholine and adenosine also affect emergence. Orexin affects emergence, not induction, and plasma orexin-A rises during emergence in patients. Cholinergic stimulation in the central thalamus and prefrontal cortex woke animals under gas, but physostigmine has not had a consistent effect in humans. Caffeine hastened emergence in rats and in healthy volunteers.Sources: Zhang and Wei 2025, Kelz 2019
  • No nucleus acts alone; the network decides. The PPT in the brainstem could wake mice under sevoflurane, but its activity only returned as the mice woke. The PPT is therefore “one node among many”. In animal experiments, stimulation of the thalamus, parabrachial nucleus, VTA, locus coeruleus, basal forebrain or prefrontal cortex has also reversed anaesthesia.Sources: Li 2024, McKinstry-Wu and Kelz 2024 (editorial), Mashour 2022

The studies in detail:

Solt 2011 Solt 2014 Kenny 2015 Kato 2021 Vincent 2024 Kelz 2019 Zhang and Wei 2025 Li 2024 McKinstry-Wu and Kelz 2024 Mashour 2022

What wakes first: deep structures, then the functions

The studies asking what returns first seem to point in different directions, but they measure different phases of emergence.

  • Deep structures start as consciousness returns. The brainstem, thalamus, hypothalamus and anterior cingulate were active (PET) at return of consciousness, after both dexmedetomidine and propofol. Connectivity between thalamus, brainstem and cortex jumped. Reawakening probably proceeds from caudal to rostral structures.Sources: Långsjö 2012, Huang 2021, Mashour 2022
  • Cognitive functions return stepwise in the hours afterwards. In 60 healthy adults, abstract problem solving (prefrontal function) returned first, reaction time and attention later. After about 3 hours they were on a par with awake controls.Source: Mashour 2021
  • The findings do not contradict each other (interpretation based on the sources). One study measures the moment consciousness returns, and there deep structures start first. The other measures how cognitive functions return after the person is already awake. “Prefrontal first” thus refers to the order among cognitive functions, not to which part of the brain wakes first.Sources: Långsjö 2012, Mashour 2021
  • Frontal EEG may not see the start. Frontal EEG measures the cortex. The authors speculate that monitors measuring the cortex may miss that consciousness starts in deeper structures.Source: Långsjö 2012

The studies in detail:

Långsjö 2012 Huang 2021 Mashour 2022 Mashour 2021

Awake is not the same as conscious: level and content

Wakefulness (arousal) and consciousness (awareness) are different things: response is not the same as consciousness, and lack of response is not the same as unconsciousness. This distinction helps in understanding what the arousal experiments actually show.Sources: Mashour 2022, Sanders 2012

  • Level and content may be governed by different networks (hypothesis). On this view, the level of consciousness is governed bottom-up from the brainstem, hypothalamus and thalamus, whereas content is governed top-down in cortical and thalamocortical networks. Dexmedetomidine acts mainly on level. Ketamine activates arousal-promoting nuclei but disrupts content.Source: Mashour and Hudetz 2017
  • The rat experiments measure level, not content. The endpoint is whether the animal regains the righting reflex, that is, whether it is awake enough to turn over. That is a measure of level (arousal), and it says little about the content of experience (interpretation based on the sources).Source: the rat experiments of Solt and colleagues
  • Ketamine could not be reversed. VTA stimulation and d-amphetamine woke rats from dexmedetomidine, sevoflurane and fentanyl, but not from ketamine. Interpretation based on the sources: this fits with ketamine acting not by lowering level but by disrupting content, so turning up the arousal system does not help. This has not been tested directly.Sources: Kato 2021, Vincent 2024
  • An EEG that looks more awake is not an awake animal. Atomoxetine shifted the EEG towards theta without waking the animals.Source: Kenny 2015

The studies in detail:

Mashour 2022 Sanders 2012 Mashour and Hudetz 2017 Kato 2021 Vincent 2024 Kenny 2015

What it means clinically today

The research changes how emergence is understood, but little of it is clinical practice yet.

  • Elimination is still the main route. Emergence is still driven mainly by elimination of the agent. Possible interventions fall into three groups: altering pharmacokinetics, acting directly at the binding site, or using the brain’s own arousal pathways. No dopaminergic method is established in humans, methylphenidate is not approved for this, and amphetamines cause a rise in blood pressure and tachycardia.Source: Vincent 2025
  • A low dose is no guarantee. Because the inertia lies in the network and not only in the concentration, neither a low dose nor “alpha without theta” guarantees rapid emergence.
  • Hysteresis can be seen in the EEG. After burst suppression, the EEG does not return to its baseline pattern at the same calculated concentration. Emergence from sevoflurane often passes through a delta-dominated stage. The course, not only the dose, may matter for delirium.Sources: Sepúlveda 2026, Hesse 2019, Miyasaka 2025
  • Physostigmine does not reliably reverse anaesthesia. It has been called standard treatment for emergence delirium, but as a means of reversing anaesthesia its effect has not been consistent. Centrally anticholinergic drugs are advised against in older patients perioperatively.Sources: Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010, Kelz 2019, Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025
  • Sleep, disease and sex may affect emergence. Sleep deprivation lowered the dose needed for unconsciousness in rats, and some patients with narcolepsy wake later. Female rats woke later than male rats after dexmedetomidine. Transfer to humans is unknown.Sources: Kelz 2019, Kato 2021

The studies in detail:

Vincent 2025 Sepúlveda 2026 Hesse 2019 Miyasaka 2025 Brown 2010 Kelz 2019 Kato 2021
The studies in detail: hysteresis, the neurotransmitters, dopamine and the VTA, the PPT (four cards)

Summaries of each article, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Emergence is not induction in reverse: hysteresis, neural inertia and “reboot”

Traditionally, emergence has been seen as induction in reverse: the agent disappears, and the brain returns along the same path. Several lines of evidence say that this is not correct. The phenomenon is called anaesthetic hysteresis (loss of consciousness requires a higher concentration than the one that keeps the patient unconscious during emergence) and is explained by neural inertia: the brain resists changing state in both directions.Source: Friedman 2010

  • In humans, consciousness returns with an abrupt jump, a “reboot”. 26 healthy volunteers (18 analysed) received propofol TCI (Marsh), stepped up by 0.4 µg/ml every 5 minutes to loss of response, then free emergence. Loss of response occurred at a higher calculated effect-site concentration than return of response (p < 0.0001), a hysteresis loop. Induction was gradual: the time scale of neural processing (autocorrelation) increased across the whole brain and connectivity fell. Emergence was abrupt: the cortical time scale normalised suddenly, and connectivity between thalamus, pallidum, brainstem and cortex jumped. The authors themselves use the word reboot: “a rapid increase in the speed of cortical processing and subcortico-cortical interactions may be a mechanism that reboots consciousness”. Pharmacokinetics alone did not explain the asymmetry. Limitation: the concentration is model-calculated, not measured, and only propofol.Source: Huang 2021, Neuroimage (fMRI)
  • Many nuclei govern only emergence, not induction. This applies to orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus: removal of orexin delayed emergence without altering the EC50 for loss of righting. The same applies to serotonergic neurons in the dorsal raphe, dopaminergic neurons in the VTA, orexinergic terminals in the basal forebrain and locus coeruleus, PVT, lateral habenula and prefrontal cortex. Other nuclei (PnO) control only induction. In patients, plasma orexin-A rises during emergence, not during induction. Caveats: almost exclusively male mice and rats, mostly isoflurane, and only 3 of the studies report EC50; the patterns vary between agents.Sources: Zhang and Wei 2025 (review of animal studies), Kelz 2008
  • Emergence can be actively induced. In rats, methylphenidate (dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor) halved the time to emergence (median 280 to 91 s) and restored righting in 11 of 12 animals during ongoing isoflurane. The EEG shifted from delta to theta within 30 seconds, and ventilation increased. Droperidol (D2/α1 antagonist) blocked everything. Emergence is thus an active arousal process from the brainstem and hypothalamus, not merely the absence of agent. Methylphenidate is not approved for this in humans.Source: Solt 2011, Anesthesiology
  • Wakefulness and consciousness are different things. Response is not the same as consciousness, and lack of response is not the same as unconsciousness (“unresponsiveness ≠ unconsciousness”). In animal experiments, stimulation of the thalamus, parabrachial nucleus, VTA, locus coeruleus, basal forebrain or prefrontal cortex reverses anaesthesia, and recovery probably proceeds from caudal to rostral structures. Conflict of interest: Mashour is a consultant for TRYP Therapeutics.Sources: Mashour 2022, Anesth Analg; Sanders 2012
  • Clinically, hysteresis can be seen in the EEG, and a low dose does not guarantee rapid emergence. That the EEG does not return to the baseline pattern at the same calculated concentration after burst suppression is hysteresis seen in the EEG. Emergence from sevoflurane often passes through a delta-dominated stage, and the course, not just the dose, may matter for delirium. “Alpha without theta” or a low dose does not guarantee rapid emergence, because the inertia resides in the network, not only in the concentration. Hysteresis in humans is nevertheless debated: some studies did not find it for propofol, others did.Sources: Sepúlveda 2026 (Burst suppression tab), Hesse 2019, Miyasaka 2025. Did not find hysteresis: Kuizenga 2018, Warnaby 2017. Found hysteresis: Ferreira 2020, Nir 2019, Sepúlveda 2019, Huang 2021
Huang 2021, Zhang and Wei 2025, Solt 2011, Mashour 2022

How the brain wakes up: the neurotransmitters behind emergence (Kelz 2019)

Narrative review. Emergence was long seen as a passive process occurring when concentration falls below a critical value. Here it is described as an active, controllable process that can be driven by mechanisms distinct from induction. Much rests on animal studies, but only signalling systems for which there are also human data are included.Source: Kelz, García, Mashour and Solt, Anesth Analg 2019;128:726–736

  • Emergence is not induction in reverse, for two reasons. Some neuronal groups for sleep and wakefulness take part differently in the two transitions. And there is hysteresis: the concentration at which consciousness is lost is higher than that at which it returns. This has traditionally been explained by pharmacokinetics, but the authors argue newer data suggest hysteresis is a general property of the nervous system.
  • Acetylcholine can wake, but physostigmine does not work consistently in humans. Propofol and volatile agents lower cortical acetylcholine, ketamine and nitrous oxide raise it. A nicotinic agonist in the central thalamus reversed sevoflurane and desflurane during ongoing administration, whereas a nicotinic antagonist did not change induction. A cholinergic agonist (carbachol) in prefrontal cortex produced full arousal in rats at about 1 MAC sevoflurane, but not in parietal cortex. Physostigmine has reversed sevoflurane and propofol in humans, but not consistently. Low-dose ketamine during isoflurane produced burst suppression but faster emergence (about 45 %), called «paradoxical emergence».
  • Physostigmine is used for agitation on emergence. It has been called «a standard treatment for emergence delirium». Physostigmine crosses the blood–brain barrier and increases cholinergic activity in the cortex. Atropine, scopolamine, first-generation antihistamines and phenothiazine antiemetics are advised against in older patients perioperatively because of central anticholinergic effects. Reflection from the author of the app: on a cardiac intensive care unit many years ago, physostigmine was given when patients woke agitated after cardiac surgery. The indication was agitation; whether central anticholinergic syndrome was suspected, for example after atropine, is not known.Sources: Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010; Mahanna Gabrielli et al. 2025
  • Norepinephrine primes the brain for emergence but does not keep it awake on its own. Mice without norepinephrine were 10–20 % more sensitive at induction, but the largest difference was that they woke much later. Norepinephrine in the central thalamus hastened emergence from propofol without changing induction.
  • Orexin was the first sign that emergence is not a mirror image of induction. Blocking orexin did not change induction but delayed emergence from isoflurane and sevoflurane in rodents. Some patients with narcolepsy wake later after anaesthesia. High CO₂ hastens emergence, perhaps because orexin neurones are activated by CO₂.
  • Dopamine wakes, and the D1 receptor appears most important. Methylphenidate (Ritalin) and dextroamphetamine restored wake-like behaviour in animals during ongoing isoflurane, sevoflurane and propofol. The effect is mainly via dopamine, because the pure norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor atomoxetine did not rouse the rats. The source is the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
  • Sleep deprivation lowers the dose needed, and caffeine hastens emergence. Sleep deprivation lowered the dose needed for unconsciousness with propofol, sevoflurane and isoflurane in rats. Caffeine hastened emergence from isoflurane and propofol in rats, and from isoflurane in healthy volunteers in a double-blind crossover study.
  • Flumazenil may give faster or clearer emergence, even without benzodiazepines. In patients who had not received benzodiazepines, flumazenil produced EEG signs of arousal and faster emergence in one study with propofol and remifentanil. In another study it did not speed emergence but improved cognition in recovery.
  • None of the methods is clinically established. Narrative review, mostly animal studies. Effects in humans are small or uncertain. No conflicts of interest, NIH-funded.
Kelz, García, Mashour and Solt. Anesth Analg 2019;128:726–736

Dopamine and the VTA: emergence has its own circuits (Solt, Norwegian Autumn Meeting 2026)

At the Norwegian Autumn Meeting (Høstmøtet) 2026, Ken Solt (Massachusetts General Hospital) presented research from his group supporting the view that emergence is an active process in its own circuits, and that dopamine from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) in the midbrain is an important part of it. Almost everything is from rat experiments, where return of the righting reflex is used as a measure of consciousness.Source: Solt, lecture Høstmøtet 2026

  • Each anaesthetic acts on many targets. Each agent affects a range of receptors and ion channels, not a single target. This is one reason to look for shared circuits of consciousness rather than a shared site of action.Source: Alkire, Hudetz and Tononi 2008 (review in Science)
  • The old core network wakes first. 20 healthy volunteers were woken from dexmedetomidine or propofol in a PET scanner. At return of consciousness, the brainstem, thalamus, hypothalamus and anterior cingulate were active with both drugs, that is deep, evolutionarily old structures rather than the neocortex. The authors argue that a “primitive” level of consciousness must return before higher functions, and speculate that monitors measuring the cortex may miss this distinction.Source: Långsjö 2012
  • It is the VTA, not the substantia nigra, that wakes. Electrical stimulation of the VTA restored the righting reflex in 5 of 5 rats during ongoing isoflurane and 5 of 5 during propofol. Stimulation of the substantia nigra, which also contains dopamine neurons, woke none (0 of 5). The EEG shifted from delta towards theta. Small groups, and dopamine release was not measured.Source: Solt 2014
  • Dopamine wakes, noradrenaline alone does not. Dextroamphetamine 1 mg/kg woke 6 of 6 rats during ongoing sevoflurane (mean 160 seconds) and shortened emergence after propofol from 641 to 404 seconds. Atomoxetine, which raises noradrenaline, woke none, even though the EEG shifted towards theta. A D1 antagonist blocked the effect of dextroamphetamine. An EEG that looks more awake is therefore not the same as an awake animal.Source: Kenny 2015
  • Dopamine reverses dexmedetomidine, but not ketamine. After dexmedetomidine the rats woke after about 113 minutes with saline, but after 1.8 minutes with d-amphetamine 3 mg/kg. After ketamine the time was the same (19.7 versus 20.3 minutes). D1/D5 blockade abolished the effect after dexmedetomidine. Female rats woke 51 minutes later than males after dexmedetomidine with saline, but not with d-amphetamine.Source: Kato 2021
  • VTA stimulation works across agents, but not with ketamine. In 16 rats, VTA stimulation restored consciousness after sevoflurane, dexmedetomidine and fentanyl, but not after ketamine. D1 blockade weakened the effect after sevoflurane and fentanyl, but not after dexmedetomidine. Which receptors carry emergence thus depends on the agent.Source: Vincent 2024
  • Cognition returns in steps. 60 healthy adults, half under 3 hours of general anaesthesia and half awake controls. Abstract problem solving (prefrontal function) returned first, reaction time and attention later, and within about 3 hours the anaesthetised were at the level of the controls. Unpublished rat data also showed that activating dopamine neurons in the VTA gave faster cognitive recovery after high-dose dexmedetomidine.Sources: Mashour 2021; unpublished data shown by Solt in the lecture
  • Emergence is still mainly driven by elimination of the agent. Possible measures fall into three groups: altering pharmacokinetics, acting directly at the binding site, and using the brain's own arousal pathways. The first agents for speeding emergence are on their way, but no dopaminergic method is established in humans.Source: Vincent 2025 (review from the same group)
  • No region acts alone. Neuronal populations are not independent, and the network determines their activity.Source: McKinstry-Wu and Kelz, BJA editorial 2024 (shown in the lecture)
  • The EEG and consciousness can be separated (interpretation based on the sources). Atomoxetine changed the EEG without waking the animal, and ketamine could not be reversed with dopamine. This fits with the EEG and consciousness being separable, and with ketamine acting on other circuits and giving a different EEG from the GABA agents and dexmedetomidine. It also supports emergence not being induction in reverse (see the card on hysteresis above).
  • Patients taking Ritalin may need more during sedation and light anaesthesia. Methylphenidate woke rats under both isoflurane and propofol, but not during deep isoflurane with burst suppression. In humans there are only case reports: a child who was not sedated by usual doses of midazolam and ketamine, and two adults who needed more thiopental at induction but also took other psychotropic drugs. In 34 children there was no difference in BIS at 1 MAC sevoflurane.Sources: Solt 2011; Chemali 2012; Kenny 2016; Ririe 1997; Kasuga 2008; Chambers 2012
  • What does it mean in practice? At a high enough dose it probably matters little. If the patient has taken the drug the same day, the EEG gives a better picture of whether hypnosis is adequate than the dose and clinical signs. Whether the drug should be withheld before surgery has not been studied. (interpretation based on the sources)
  • None of this is clinical practice today. Rat experiments with small groups and the righting reflex as the measure of consciousness. Amphetamines raise blood pressure and heart rate.
Solt, lecture Høstmøtet 2026 Alkire 2008 Långsjö 2012 Solt 2014 Kenny 2015 Kato 2021 Vincent 2024 Mashour 2021 Vincent 2025

A brainstem switch for induction and emergence: the PPT and sevoflurane (Li 2024)

Animal study in mice of glutamatergic neurones in the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPT) of the brainstem. The PPT projects to, among others, the thalamus, hypothalamus, basal forebrain and the ventral tegmental area (VTA), which is important for wakefulness and reward.Source: Li 2024, Br J Anaesth 2024;132:320–333

  • Activity in the PPT follows consciousness. Neuronal activity fell before the mice lost the righting reflex under sevoflurane, stayed low while they were unconscious, and rose again as they woke.
  • Inhibition gives faster induction and slower emergence. When the neurones were inhibited chemogenetically, the mice lost consciousness faster (76 versus 121 seconds) and woke later (278 versus 145 seconds), and became more sensitive to sevoflurane. The EEG showed more delta.
  • Stimulation wakes during ongoing volatile anaesthesia. Light stimulation of the neurones, or of the pathway from the PPT to the VTA, produced awake-like behaviour during steady sevoflurane anaesthesia and activated the cortex. During sevoflurane-induced burst suppression, the suppression ratio fell from about 55 % to about 6 % during stimulation.
  • There are shared circuits for both transitions. Because both induction and emergence were affected, the authors interpret this as shared circuits for loss and recovery of consciousness. This nuances the finding that orexin delayed emergence without changing induction.Source for the orexin finding: Kelz 2019 (see the card above and Discrepancies)
  • The brainstem helps regulate consciousness (interpretation based on the sources). The finding supports that consciousness under anaesthesia is regulated by brainstem networks and not only by the cortex, and that emergence can be actively influenced. It is not clinically transferable today.
  • Caveats: few mice and sevoflurane only. Few animals per group (8–14). The authors do not know whether sevoflurane acts directly on the neurones or via their inputs. High-frequency light stimulation may also activate other pathways. No conflicts of interest, funded by Chinese research councils.
  • The PPT is one node among many. The finding supports the hypothesis that sleep and anaesthesia share circuits. But the PPT is only one of many neuronal populations in the forebrain, midbrain and brainstem that can promote or oppose anaesthesia, including the parabrachial nucleus, VTA, nucleus accumbens, thalamus, basal forebrain and preoptic area. If induction and emergence were mirror images, and the PPT were a master regulator, activity in the PPT should have recovered before emergence. It did not: it rose only as the mice woke. The next step is to understand how the network works together. Calling a neuronal population causal requires three things: its activity is altered by the anaesthetic, altering its activity changes the anaesthetic state, and it is connected to the rest of the network. Anaesthesia is no longer understood as a “wet blanket” that dampens the whole brain equally. No conflicts of interest; Kelz is also first author of the 2019 review above.Source: McKinstry-Wu and Kelz 2024, editorial “One node among many”
Li, Hu, Tan, Li, Huang and Wang. Br J Anaesth 2024;132:320–333 McKinstry-Wu and Kelz. Br J Anaesth 2024;132:220–223

Key points

  • Nociception is not pain. Nociception is the neural process that encodes noxious stimuli. Pain is a conscious experience. Anaesthesia can remove the experience without removing the process. That is why an unconscious patient can still develop tachycardia, hypertension and a stress response.See and “Pain and nociception: the definitions and the pathway”
  • Nociception can produce one of three EEG patterns. Beta arousal typically occurs in light anaesthesia with little opioid. Delta arousal occurs in deeper or balanced anaesthesia with too little opioid, especially with visceral stimulation. In alpha dropout, frontal alpha disappears transiently. The patterns do not always occur, and not all at once. Delta arousal and alpha dropout can make the index read the EEG as deeper anaesthesia, even though the patient is responding to stimulation.Source: García 2021. See
  • With delta arousal or alpha dropout, consider analgesia rather than less hypnotic. This applies when other signs of inadequate anaesthesia are absent. Concurrent autonomic signs such as heart rate, blood pressure and skin conductance point towards nociception. Weakened alpha alone has several possible causes.Source: García 2021. See and “Clinical example: alpha disappears with visceral pain (shared case)”
  • The signal continues under general anaesthesia. Volatile agents prevent movement at the spinal cord. The adrenergic response to incision is blocked only at doses well above those needed for unconsciousness. The nervous system thus processes the signal even though the patient does not experience it.See
  • The right dose, not the most. There is good reason to treat nociception to keep the circulation stable and dampen the stress response. Prevention of chronic pain in adults has not been shown. High intraoperative opioid doses, especially remifentanil, can cause somewhat more pain afterwards.See and “Neuroplasticity: when pain signals change the nervous system”
  • Remifentanil can cause hyperalgesia, especially at high doses and with abrupt withdrawal. The mechanism is probably central sensitisation via the NMDA receptor. Gradual tapering may prevent it, but this needs confirmation in larger trials. Ketamine spares opioid, but that it must be given before incision has not been shown.See
  • Caesarean section under general anaesthesia is a particularly vulnerable period. From induction until the baby is delivered, nociception is strong and the risk of awareness high (about 1 in 670). This argues for an adequate hypnotic dose. A short-acting opioid at induction may be considered according to local procedures and in consultation with the anaesthetist (interpretation based on the sources).Source: NAP5 (Pandit 2014). See

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

Hypnosis or analgesia? The pain pathway to heart and vessels

Hypnosis and analgesia are two different components and need different measures. If heart rate and blood pressure rise with surgical stimulation while the EEG is unchanged, and other causes are ruled out, analgesia is probably inadequate. Hypnosis may well be enough.Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)

Anaesthesia inhibits the transfer here
↑
heart rate and BP rise
↑
reflex movement
↑
↑
Tap a step to read briefly about it.
Sources: Yam 2018; D'Mello and Dickenson 2008; Sleigh et al. 2025; Brown et al. 2015
  • The pathway runs through the brainstem. The signal travels from the dorsal horn to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in the medulla. From there sympathetic output increases via the ventrolateral medulla and the sympathetic ganglia to the heart and vessels, and vagal output to the sinoatrial node is reduced via the nucleus ambiguus. The pathway is called the nociceptive-medullary-autonomic circuit.Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)
  • If hypnosis is adequate, the EEG will probably not change. The response runs through spinal cord and brainstem. Heart rate and blood pressure can therefore rise while the EEG and index are unchanged.Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)
  • Rule out other causes, then give analgesia. Consider bleeding, hypoxaemia, disconnection of the breathing circuit and inadequate neuromuscular block. Check relaxation, oxygen saturation and EEG. If it is still unexplained, the appropriate treatment is more analgesia.Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)
  • More hypnotic is a poor route. Blocking the adrenergic response to incision in half the patients required 1.45–1.60 MAC (halothane and enflurane with nitrous oxide), well above what is needed for unconsciousness. For movement under propofol, an opioid works better than more propofol.Sources: Roizen 1981; Sleigh et al. 2025
  • Other signs of inadequate analgesia. Sweating, lacrimation, dilated pupils and return of muscle tone and movement. The last two are not seen when the patient has received a neuromuscular blocker.Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)
  • When does the EEG change? If the stimulus is strong and hypnosis too light to keep the patient unconscious, the EEG and index may change and warn that consciousness is returning. Nociception can also produce its own EEG patterns (see the cards below).Source: Brown et al. 2015 (Miller 8th ed., ch. 50)

  • Anaesthesia can remove pain without removing nociception. Nociception is the neurophysiological process (receptor, peripheral nerve, dorsal horn, thalamus). Pain is a conscious experience that requires cortical processing. That is why an unconscious patient can still develop tachycardia, hypertension, a stress response and postoperative hyperalgesia.
  • EEG shows hypnotic level, but noxious stimulation leaves traces. An EEG that becomes “deeper” (more delta, less alpha) during surgery may therefore be a nociceptive phenomenon, not overdosing. The three patterns are described in the card below. See also the card on fentanyl and frontal theta in the Agents tab.Sources: García 2021, Balanza 2022
  • No monitor measures the experience of pain directly. EEG shows hypnosis. Nociception monitors (pupillometry, skin conductance, heart rate variability and the like) show the autonomic response. Haemodynamics show the circulation. The evidence that nociception-guided opioid dosing improves patient outcomes is still limited. The figure therefore describes a rationale, not a documented effect.
García 2021, Hight 2020, Balanza 2022

Three EEG reactions to a noxious stimulus: beta arousal, delta arousal and alpha dropout (García 2021)

This is a narrative review, not a systematic search. The authors started from key articles and their references. They grouped the literature into index studies, raw-EEG studies and animal studies.Source: García, Kreuzer, Hight, Sleigh. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:445–457

  • The nociceptive response has four dimensions, and EEG shows only one of them. The four are somatic (spinal reflexes, movement), autonomic (brainstem and hypothalamus: heart rate, respiration, vasoconstriction, pupil), cognitive arousal and memory (subcortical and midbrain, via forebrain and cortex), and endocrine, coagulation and immune responses. The EEG responses are more transient and do not always occur at the same time as the autonomic ones. They still show that the anaesthesia has not completely blocked the brain's response to tissue injury.
  • 1 Beta arousal: more activity at 12–25 Hz, and the index rises. It typically occurs at low dose (0.5–1.0 MAC without opioid), often together with movement. The mechanism is well known: aminergic and cholinergic activation from the brainstem depolarises the thalamus and inhibits the slow thalamocortical oscillations. The indices are designed to capture precisely this.Sources: Moruzzi and Magoun 1949, cited in García 2021
  • 2 Delta arousal (“paradoxical arousal”): more delta, which the index misreads as deeper anaesthesia. Power at 0.5–4 Hz increases. It occurs at higher doses or in balanced anaesthesia with too little opioid, especially with visceral stimulation. At incision, delta increased by 181% at 0.5 MAC isoflurane, while alpha was halved. Epidural blockade prevented the response completely. The mechanism is unclear, but the midbrain reticular formation appears to be involved. The response need not mean that the patient is heading towards consciousness. The problem is that the indices then “wrongly suggest that the hypnotic dose is too high”.Sources: Kochs; Kiyama and Takeda; cited in García 2021
  • 3 Alpha dropout: frontal alpha disappears suddenly, and opioid can bring it back. Alpha is lost in episodes, while delta often persists or increases. Alpha fell at incision and returned with fentanyl. Fentanyl given before incision prevented the fall, and a low opioid dose gave more alpha loss. The interpretation is that the thalamus switches from hyperpolarised “burst” mode (idling) to continuous firing. Thalamocortical communication thus resumes, while the cortex is still GABAergically depressed. That delta can increase while alpha falls shows that slow oscillations can be cortical and independent of the thalamus.Sources: Hagihira 2004; Mackay; cited in García 2021
  • With delta arousal or alpha dropout, do not reduce the hypnotic, but consider more analgesia. The exception is when there are other signs of inadequate anaesthesia. Analgesia can be opioid or a regional block. The authors propose titrating opioid to maximal frontal alpha power, with an individual reference (age, cognition, possibly a preoperative baseline or alpha at steady state before surgery). This is an unsolved problem for closed-loop dosing systems. Autonomic responses are linked to cardiovascular complications, but whether pure EEG responses matter for outcome is unknown.Source: García 2021
  • No monitor captures all three patterns. Most commercial “pain monitors” do not use EEG. They use heart rate variability, modelled opioid concentrations, the spinal flexor reflex, the plethysmographic pulse wave and heart interval, or a multivariable model. The multivariable model improved opioid titration and cardiovascular stability in two studies. A few monitors are EEG-based. The article does not mention skin conductance. It measures the number and amplitude of sympathetically triggered sweat fluctuations in the palm, and is thus an autonomic marker on a par with the others.Source: García 2021
  • Skin conductance reacts to airway stimulation, but is no better than heart rate at incision. In a prospective observational study of 49 patients (monitors blinded to staff), NOL and the skin conductance index SCA reacted to jaw thrust, laryngoscopy and intubation more often than heart rate did. They flagged two to three times as many patients as a 10% rise in heart rate. At skin incision neither was better than heart rate, and NOL flagged more patients than SCA. In a Norwegian pilot of 10 patients (HIPEC), SCA rose in 9 of 10 when core temperature rose from 36.2 to 38.4 °C, without other signs of pain. The method is therefore unreliable during rapid temperature changes. Neither study has outcome measures. The manufacturer's own claims about documentation are not reproduced here.Sources (outside the García article): Widarsson Norbeck 2025, BMC Anesthesiol 2025;25:51; Scand J Pain 2024
  • The evidence base is thin, and the benefit has not been tested. The review is narrative, not systematic. The studies are few and small, many from the 1990s, with different agents and stimuli. No randomised trials have tested whether EEG-guided analgesia improves outcome, which the authors themselves emphasise. No conflicts of interest; funded by the James S. McDonnell Foundation.
García, Kreuzer, Hight, Sleigh. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:445–457

Clinical example: alpha disappears during visceral pain (shared case)

Shared case from Norwegian clinical practice. It is not published and not peer reviewed. The description is based on one screenshot of a frontal EEG monitor with a skin conductance monitor alongside, and on information from the person who shared it. The screenshot is not reproduced here.

  • Alpha suddenly weakened, while delta remained. First there was a clear alpha band and strong slow-delta in both hemispheres. Around 14:00 the alpha band suddenly became much weaker in both hemispheres, while the power below about 4 Hz remained. Towards the end of the picture alpha partly returned. The spectral edge frequency (SEF) was about 10 Hz, and artefacts 0%.
  • At the same time, skin conductance, heart rate and blood pressure rose. This was reported by the person who shared the case. The stimulation was visceral.
  • The picture fits alpha dropout. Alpha falls suddenly while delta persists. Delta arousal (“paradoxical arousal”) is also seen particularly with visceral stimulation. Both patterns can make the indices read the EEG as deeper anaesthesia, even though the patient is responding to pain. The recommendation is then to consider more analgesia rather than reducing the hypnotic.Source: García 2021
  • It is the simultaneous autonomic signs that point towards nociception. Weakening of alpha alone has several possible causes, for example lower cardiac output (see the card on alpha and cardiac output in the Perfusion tab) or a changed dose.
  • Caveat: one case, one screenshot. It is not known which drugs and doses the patient received, whether anything was changed, or what was done afterwards.
Shared clinical example; García 2021

Pain and nociception: the definitions and the pathway

IASP (International Association for the Study of Pain) clearly distinguishes the two terms.

Anaesthesia inhibits the transfer here
↑
heart rate and BP rise
↑
reflex movement
↑
↑
Tap a step to read briefly about it.
Sources: Yam 2018; D'Mello and Dickenson 2008; Sleigh et al. 2025; Brown et al. 2015
  • Pain is an experience. IASP defines pain as “An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage”.Sources: IASP, revised 2020; Raja 2020
  • Nociception is a neural process. IASP defines nociception as “The neural process of encoding noxious stimuli.” The consequences may be autonomic (e.g. elevated blood pressure) or behavioural (a withdrawal reflex). Pain sensation is not necessarily implied.Source: IASP
  • Pain cannot be inferred solely from activity in sensory neurons. Pain and nociception are different phenomena. Inability to communicate does not negate the possibility that pain is experienced.Source: notes to the IASP definition
  • The signal first travels from the tissue to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Nociceptors convert noxious stimuli into nerve signals (transduction). Aδ fibres are myelinated and fast and give pricking pain. C fibres are unmyelinated and slow. Both end in the dorsal horn, which is the first relay site.Sources: Yam 2018; D'Mello and Dickenson 2008
  • From the dorsal horn the signal goes to the brainstem and thalamus. Nociceptive-specific cells lie mainly in laminae I–II, wide-dynamic-range cells deeper, in lamina V. Lamina I projects to the parabrachial nucleus and the PAG (periaqueductal grey) in the brainstem. Lamina V projects mainly to the thalamus via the spinothalamic tract.Source: D'Mello and Dickenson 2008
  • The brain itself regulates how much of the signal gets through. From the PAG, signals run via the RVM (rostral ventromedial medulla) down to the dorsal horn with serotonin and noradrenaline. This control can both inhibit and facilitate the signals.Sources: Yam 2018; D'Mello and Dickenson 2008

The brain’s own pain control

↓
↓
inhibits or facilitates
Tap a step to read briefly about it.
Sources: Yam 2018; D'Mello and Dickenson 2008
IASP terminology Raja 2020 D'Mello and Dickenson 2008 Yam 2018

Under general anaesthesia the signal still travels, even though the patient does not experience it

  • Volatile agents prevent movement via the spinal cord, below the cortex. When only the brain of goats received isoflurane, the dose that prevented movement had to be increased from 1.2 to 2.9%. Below 1 MAC, noxious stimuli still activated the midbrain reticular formation, the thalamus and the frontal EEG. At 1.1 MAC or more the activation was blunted.Sources: Antognini and Schwartz 1993; Antognini and Carstens 1999
  • The stress response needs more than unconsciousness. The dose that blocked the adrenergic response to incision in half of patients (MAC-BAR) was 1.45 MAC for halothane and 1.60 MAC for enflurane, with 60% nitrous oxide. That is well above what is needed for unconsciousness and immobility. Spinal anaesthesia blocked the response completely.Source: Roizen 1981
  • Nociception leaves traces in the EEG. It can give beta arousal, paradoxical delta arousal or alpha dropout (see the card above). Alpha dropout was seen in 31% of 237 patients, more often in abdominal or thoracic surgery and long procedures. It could perhaps measure nociception, but it is not validated.Sources: García 2021; Hight 2019
  • The patient does not experience pain, but the nervous system processes the signal. This happens in the spinal cord, brainstem and partly the thalamus and cortex. It shows up in circulation, hormones and the EEG.
  • Laryngoscopy under general anaesthesia is nociception and reflex, not pain. The blade and the tube stimulate nerves in the pharynx and larynx, and the signal travels to the brainstem. From there comes a reflex with increased sympathetic activity, higher blood pressure and heart rate, and protective reflexes such as gagging, coughing and laryngospasm. Pain is an experience, and that is absent under general anaesthesia. Intubation adds more than the blade: laryngoscopy with intubation gave higher blood pressure and heart rate than laryngoscopy alone of the same duration (randomised study, 80 patients).Sources: Khan and Ullah 2013; Smith 2008
  • In awake patients with good airway anaesthesia, laryngoscopy is mostly discomfort, but some feel pain. Awake laryngoscopy is performed with topical airway anaesthesia and sedation. With the right remifentanil dose, blood pressure and heart rate were stable and none recalled discomfort or pain. With nebulised lidocaine alone, 70% of healthy volunteers showed no reaction at all (two of the authors hold a patent on the nebuliser). Without adequate airway anaesthesia it is uncomfortable and triggers gagging and coughing. Pain is rarely the main outcome in the studies. In awake fibreoptic intubation with topical anaesthesia only, 54% felt no pain and 46% slight pain. Most patients found it acceptable, but some described it as very painful. Interpretation based on the sources: pain occurs particularly when the anaesthesia is incomplete. Direct laryngoscopy without anaesthesia has not been studied in awake people.Sources: Chin Med J 2009; Markerink 2024; Patil 2002, as described in Gostelow and Yeow 2023; Whited 2021
  • The drugs act at different points in the reflex. Topical anaesthesia stops the incoming signal, opioids dampen central processing, and beta-blockers only dampen the effect on heart and vessels. Beta-blockers, opioids, lidocaine and calcium channel blockers all reduced arrhythmias at intubation. Only lidocaine clearly reduced myocardial ischaemia, and then in one study. Interpretation based on the sources: when a beta-blocker dampens the rise in blood pressure, the signal to the brain is not gone. A calm blood pressure does not mean the nociception has been treated.Source: Khan and Ullah 2013 (Cochrane review)

The surgical stress response: what it does, how long it lasts and what blunts it

  • The stress response is started by nerve signals and inflammation. The nerve signals come from the injured area and are both somatic and autonomic. The inflammatory mediators come from the tissue.Source: Burton 2004
  • The hormones stay elevated for hours to days. Cortisol rises within 4–6 hours. ACTH and cortisol stay elevated for a period that depends on the size of the operation. ADH causes water retention that may last 3–5 days. Blood glucose above 12 mmol/L impairs wound healing and increases infection risk.Source: Burton 2004
  • Inflammation peaks within the first day. IL-6 peaks 12–24 hours after surgery.Source: Burton 2004
  • High-dose opioids and regional anaesthesia can blunt the hormonal response, but with limitations. High-dose opioids can abolish it in pelvic and abdominal surgery, but delay recovery and more often require postoperative ventilation. Regional anaesthesia abolishes it only when both the somatic and the autonomic nerve supply are blocked, and the inflammatory response is unchanged. Etomidate inhibits cortisol synthesis for up to 8 hours.Source: Burton 2004
  • That blunting improves outcome has not been shown consistently. This concerns the benefit of regional techniques.Source: Burton 2004
  • In newborns, fentanyl gave a smaller stress response and fewer complications. The study included 8 + 8 preterm infants undergoing surgery. Fentanyl also gave less protein breakdown in the first days. The study was very small, but it helped change the practice of operating on newborns without analgesia.Source: Anand 1987
  • The stress response fades over days. It is proportional to the size of the operation. Part of it is driven by inflammation, so even good analgesia cannot remove it completely.
Burton, Nicholson and Hall 2004 Desborough 2000 Anand 1987

Neuroplasticity: when pain signals change the nervous system

  • Pain signals can make the nervous system more sensitive. In peripheral sensitisation, nociceptors in the tissue respond more easily and have a lower threshold. In central sensitisation, nociceptive neurons in the central nervous system respond more strongly to normal or weak input.Source: IASP
  • The NMDA receptor is an essential step in central sensitisation. Its activation is needed both to start and to maintain the sensitisation. The phenomenon is prominent after surgical injury.Source: Latremoliere and Woolf 2009
  • Central sensitisation lasts minutes to hours, and the early phase passes. Wind-up, where repeated C-fibre input gives an ever stronger response, disappears within seconds. Central sensitisation lasts from tens of minutes to several hours, and the early phase is transient and reversible. The authors advise against calling it LTP in the spinal cord.Source: Latremoliere and Woolf 2009
  • Opioids can also cause hyperalgesia, so more is not automatically better. High intraoperative opioid doses gave somewhat more pain afterwards and higher morphine consumption at 24 hours, mainly linked to remifentanil. The effect was small.Source: Fletcher and Martinez 2014 (meta-analysis of 27 RCTs)
  • Ketamine spares opioid and gives slightly less pain. Opioid consumption was 19% lower and pain at rest 5 of 100 points lower at 24 hours. The effect on the area of hyperalgesia was uncertain.Source: Brinck 2018 (Cochrane review, 130 studies)
  • The immature brain may be affected, but the cause is unclear. Extremely preterm-born individuals had altered sensory function at 18–20 years, most after neonatal surgery. The study is observational and cannot separate pain signals from illness and other factors. About one hour of general anaesthesia in infancy gave no difference in IQ at 5 years compared with regional anaesthesia.Sources: Walker 2018; GAS, McCann 2019
Latremoliere and Woolf 2009 Fletcher and Martinez 2014 Brinck 2018 Walker 2018 McCann 2019

Why nociception should be treated properly, and how strong the evidence is

Reflection from the author of the app: the signal is sent even though the patient does not process it, and it gives a stress reaction. It should therefore be stopped. The points below show what the sources support in this.
  • Treatment keeps the circulation stable (strong evidence). Without enough antinociception, surgical stimulation raises blood pressure and heart rate. Nociception-guided remifentanil (NOL) gave fewer episodes of hypotension (5 versus 28%) and 30% less remifentanil.Sources: Roizen 1981; Meijer 2019
  • Treatment blunts the stress response (strong as a biological effect, weak for patient outcomes). Opioids and regional blocks blunt the hormonal response, but better outcomes in adults have not been shown consistently.Sources: Burton 2004; Anand 1987
  • Sensitisation is a known mechanism (strong in animal studies and as a mechanism, weak in clinical trials). Preventive analgesia before incision had an effect for epidural (effect size 0.38), wound infiltration and NSAIDs. For NMDA antagonists and opioids it was equivocal.Source: Ong 2005
  • Much pain after surgery is associated with chronic pain (moderate for association, weak for cause). Persistent pain occurs in 10–50% after common operations, severe in 2–10%. Nerve injury during surgery is probably the main cause. Each 10% more time in severe pain on day 1 gave a 30% higher incidence of chronic pain at one year. This concerns pain after surgery, not nociception during it.Sources: Kehlet 2006; Fletcher 2015
  • Nociception monitors reduce intraoperative opioid, but not pain afterwards. A meta-analysis of 21 RCTs found no difference in postoperative pain or opioid requirement. One small study found lower pain in recovery with NOL.Sources: Ma 2022; Meijer 2020
  • Conclusion (interpretation based on the sources): treat nociception, but with the right dose. There is good reason to treat nociception under general anaesthesia to keep the circulation stable and blunt the stress response, and because sensitisation is a known mechanism. That this in itself prevents chronic pain in adults has not been shown. The stress response fades over days. The aim is the right dose, not as much as possible, because high doses of remifentanil can cause hyperalgesia.
Roizen 1981 Meijer 2019, 2020 Ong 2005 Kehlet 2006 Fletcher 2015 Ma 2022

Hyperalgesia after remifentanil: why it happens, and what may prevent it

Opioid-induced hyperalgesia means that the patient becomes more sensitive to pain because of the opioid itself: the same stimulus gives stronger pain. Remifentanil is the opioid most clearly associated with the phenomenon. In short, the nervous system counter-regulates the strong opioid effect. When remifentanil disappears abruptly, the counter-regulation remains.Source: Santonocito 2018

  • High doses give slightly more pain afterwards, mostly with remifentanil. High intraoperative opioid doses gave somewhat more pain and higher morphine consumption after one day. The effect was small. There is no fixed dose threshold. Studies typically compare 0.05 with 0.3 µg/kg/min. The effect was greatest at high doses and in younger patients in cardiac surgery.Sources: Fletcher and Martinez 2014 (meta-analysis of 27 RCTs); Santonocito 2018
  • The main mechanism is central sensitisation via the NMDA receptor. Remifentanil increases phosphorylation of NMDA receptor subunits in the dorsal horn. More calcium flows in, and signalling pathways (PKC, CaMKII) amplify pain transmission. NMDA receptor activation is also a necessary step in central sensitisation after surgical injury (see the card on neuroplasticity).Sources: Zhu 2025; Latremoliere and Woolf 2009
  • Abrupt withdrawal appears to play a role of its own. In rats, abrupt withdrawal of remifentanil produced long-lasting potentiation of transmission in the dorsal horn. In volunteers, hyperalgesia followed abrupt withdrawal, appearing about 45 minutes after stopping and lasting less than 110 minutes. Gradual tapering did not have this effect, in either rats or volunteers. In patients, increased pain sensitivity is described from hours to days after stopping.Sources: Comelon, cited in Santonocito 2018; Zhu 2025
  • Several other mechanisms have been proposed, mostly from animal studies. Descending pathways from the brainstem shift from inhibiting to facilitating pain signals. Remifentanil downregulates μ receptors in the PAG. Glial cells and inflammatory mediators in the spinal cord are activated. How much each mechanism contributes is unclear. Doses and durations in animal studies are often higher than in clinical practice.Sources: Santonocito 2018; Zhu 2025
  • Gradual tapering is simple and inexpensive, but its benefit needs confirmation. It may prevent hyperalgesia, but only if confirmed in larger clinical trials. The most reasonable approach is to limit the intraoperative remifentanil dose.Source: Santonocito 2018
  • Ketamine spares opioid, whenever it is given. The effect on hyperalgesia is inconsistent: one study found less hyperalgesia with low-dose ketamine, two others found no effect on pain or opioid consumption. Overall, ketamine gave 19 % lower opioid consumption and 5 of 100 points lower pain at rest after one day. The results were similar whether ketamine was given before, during or after surgery.Sources: Joly 2005, cited in Santonocito 2018; Brinck 2018 (Cochrane review, 130 studies, 8341 adults)
  • What seems to matter most is ketamine being present through the painful period, not giving it before incision. The idea of giving ketamine before incision is to prevent sensitisation before it starts (“pre-emptive” analgesia). Analgesia before incision worked for epidural, wound infiltration and NSAIDs, but the effect was uncertain for NMDA antagonists and opioids. When asking instead whether the effect outlasted the drug itself (“preventive” analgesia), 58 % of ketamine studies found this, and none of four magnesium studies did.Sources: Ong 2005; McCartney 2004
  • Other drugs have some support, but from few studies. Dexmedetomidine reduced remifentanil hyperalgesia in animal studies and in one human study. Magnesium had an effect only at high remifentanil doses. Nitrous oxide reduced hyperalgesia in one human study.Source: Santonocito 2018
  • For practice (interpretation based on the sources): as little remifentanil as needed, and taper. Use as little remifentanil as needed to keep nociception under control. Consider tapering rather than stopping abruptly. Plan longer-acting analgesia before remifentanil is stopped. Ketamine has a documented opioid-sparing effect, but that it must be given before incision has not been shown.
  • Caveat: the mechanisms are shown almost only in rats and mice. The clinical effects are small and inconsistent. Zhu 2025 is a narrative review.
Santonocito 2018 Zhu 2025 Fletcher and Martinez 2014 Brinck 2018 Ong 2005 McCartney 2004 Latremoliere and Woolf 2009

Emergency caesarean section under general anaesthesia: before the baby is delivered

In general anaesthesia for caesarean section, opioid has traditionally been withheld until the baby is delivered, to avoid affecting the baby. The mother then has intubation and incision with only a hypnotic and a neuromuscular blocker.

  • Opioid at induction blunts the circulatory response. Remifentanil, alfentanil and fentanyl lowered peak systolic pressure, mean arterial pressure and heart rate compared with placebo. None of them changed the 1-minute Apgar. Fentanyl gave a lower 5-minute Apgar; remifentanil and alfentanil did not. The authors call for an adequately powered trial.Source: White 2019 (meta-analysis of 17 RCTs, 987 women)
  • The risk of awareness is high in caesarean section. It is about 1 in 670 for caesarean section, versus about 1 in 19,600 overall. The OAA and DAS guideline therefore stresses an adequate dose of induction agent.Sources: NAP5 (Pandit 2014); Mushambi 2015
  • The guidelines say little about opioid at induction. OAA/DAS 2015 gives no recommendation on it. A more recent review describes short-acting or low-dose opioids as safe. A separate “OAA/AAGBI 2018” guideline for general anaesthesia was not found.Sources: Mushambi 2015; Bone and Hoskins 2022
  • That untreated nociception before delivery gives lasting pain has not been shown. In a study where all had spinal anaesthesia, 11.4% had chronic pain at 3 months, associated with more postoperative pain. An earlier study linked general anaesthesia to more chronic pain than spinal (not read directly).Sources: Cançado 2012; Nikolajsen 2004, cited in Cançado 2012
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): enough hypnotic, and consider a short-acting opioid. The period from induction until delivery combines strong nociception with a high risk of awareness. That argues for enough hypnotic, and for considering a short-acting opioid at induction. The paediatrician should then be told. The choice must follow local procedures and be made with the anaesthetist.
White 2019 Pandit 2014 (NAP5) Mushambi 2015 Cançado 2012

The brain: perfusion, pressure and positioning

The point of this tab: during anaesthesia we must think perfusion, not just dose. The brain spends much of its energy on the electrical activity the EEG measures, so when blood supply fails it shows in the EEG, and it can look like anaesthesia that is too deep. Start with “Key message”. The other sub-tabs go into detail.

Why think perfusion during anaesthesia?

  1. The EEG shows whether the brain gets enough energy. About 60% of the brain's energy goes to the electrical signalling the EEG measures. When blood supply fails, it is this signalling that fails first. It shows in the EEG before the cells are damaged. Read more: .Sources: Patel et al. 2025; van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016
  2. Alpha and faster activity disappear first. In moderate ischaemia, alpha and beta fall. Then more delta appears, and finally suppression. In carotid surgery, a fall of more than 50% in 8–15 Hz is regarded as a sign of too little blood flow. A frontal alpha band that weakens without a change in dose may therefore be a perfusion signal.Sources: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016; Guay 2025
  3. Low perfusion can look like anaesthesia that is too deep. Too little oxygen to the brain gives the same picture as more hypnotic: lower frequencies, less power and burst suppression. Other causes of the same picture include hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, hypercapnia, anaemia and hypoxaemia.Source: Guay 2025
  4. Autoregulation is not guaranteed, so MAP 65 is not a safe target for everyone. The lower blood pressure limit of autoregulation varies from 40 to 90 mmHg in adults. In most it is around 70 mmHg. Chronic hypertension shifts the limit, and hypercapnia and sevoflurane can impair autoregulation. Read more: .Sources: Guay 2025; Patel et al. 2025
  5. Blood flow to the brain is about cardiac output, not just MAP. In Trendelenburg, cardiac output was the best predictor of blood flow to the brain. MAP mattered little within the autoregulatory range. Treating low blood pressure with a vasopressor alone can reduce cardiac output.Sources: Nordum 2024 (Ahus); Patel et al. 2025
  6. Positioning affects brain perfusion. Trendelenburg, sitting position, PEEP and head rotation change perfusion pressure and venous drainage from the brain. Read more: .Source: Patel et al. 2025; Breyer and Roth 2025
  7. Check perfusion before adjusting the hypnotic (interpretation based on the sources). When the EEG changes without a change in dose, first check blood pressure, cardiac output, CO₂, haemoglobin, temperature and position. Sometimes it is perfusion, not the anaesthetic dose, that needs optimising.

The physiology behind it, with normal values, energy use and CBF thresholds, is in .

Patel et al. 2025; Breyer and Roth 2025 van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 Guay 2025 Nordum 2024

Read the EEG and haemodynamics together

  • Low perfusion can mimic excessive anaesthetic depth. Too little oxygen to the brain produces lower frequencies, broadband power loss and burst suppression on the frontal EEG, just like deeper anaesthesia. Find the cause before the dose is changed.More in “Low perfusion can mimic excessive anaesthetic depth”
  • Cardiac output matters, not just MAP. Alpha can weaken when cardiac index falls at an unchanged dose, and the EEG can return to normal when it rises. In an 89-year-old the EEG normalised when the cardiac index rose from 1.3 to 2.7.More in “Low perfusion can mimic excessive anaesthetic depth”
  • One MAP threshold does not fit everyone. The lower MAP limit of autoregulation ranges from 40 to 90 mmHg in adults. In one patient the EEG was asymmetric until MAP was above 95 mmHg, and lost autoregulation may give alpha slowing (9.4 vs 10.5 Hz).More in “Autoregulation is individual”
  • The evidence on the blood pressure threshold is divergent. MAP below 55 mmHg or a 40% fall is linked to harm, but several studies find no association. In older patients a MAP target above baseline gave less delirium on day 1 (4% vs 16–22%).More in “How low can blood pressure go? The evidence is divergent”
  • No monitor proves hypoperfusion on its own. rSO₂ has a wide normal range and did not identify lost autoregulation in a pilot study. The frontal EEG has blind spots. So read the EEG and haemodynamics together before changing the dose.More in “What NIRS and frontal EEG can and cannot show”

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Low perfusion can mimic excessive anaesthetic depth

The frontal EEG cannot on its own distinguish too much hypnotic from too little oxygen to the brain. Both produce the same picture. The cause must therefore be clarified before the anaesthetic is adjusted.Source: Guay 2025

  • Same pattern, different causes. Too little oxygen to the brain produces a shift towards lower frequencies, broadband power loss, burst suppression and sustained suppression, as with deeper anaesthesia. With normal oxygen delivery the picture may be due to anaesthetic, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, hypercapnia, postictal suppression or noxious stimulation. With reduced delivery it may be due to shock, intracranial hypertension, venous congestion, hypoxaemia, hypocapnia, anaemia or stroke.Source: Guay 2025
  • The EEG followed the circulation. In three case reports the EEG changed with pressure and cardiac output. Loss of alpha and burst suppression appeared when the circulation failed (MAP below 70 mmHg with right heart failure), and the EEG returned to normal when the circulation improved, after adrenaline or when the cardiac index rose from 1.3 to 2.7. In one case the radial line showed MAP 80–90 while direct aortic pressure was 35 mmHg. A shared case shows the same: alpha weakened when MAP and cardiac index fell at an unchanged dose, and returned when the circulation improved.Sources: Guay 2025; shared case
  • It is unclear whether perfusion or concentration is at work. In a randomised trial, burst suppression disappeared in more than 50% when MAP was raised to the baseline value. The authors say it is unclear whether this is due to physiology, pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics. Shock and low cardiac output can also increase the propofol concentration and make the brain more sensitive.Sources: Georgii 2022, discussed in Guay 2025
  • The EEG does not prove hypoperfusion. Loss of alpha can also be caused by noxious stimulation. The case reports illustrate but do not validate. There is no threshold for which MAP or cardiac index produces EEG change in the individual patient. The schematic example is simulated and therefore shows no cause.Sources: Hight 2019; García 2021; Guay 2025

The studies in detail:

Guay 2025 Georgii 2022 Hight 2019 García 2021

Autoregulation is individual

The lower MAP limit of autoregulation ranges from 40 to 90 mmHg in adults, and autoregulation is impaired in many critically ill patients. The aim is therefore to find the patient’s own limit instead of using one number for everyone.Source: Guay 2025

  • EEG asymmetry can be a warning. In one patient with an occluded left and severely stenosed right internal carotid artery, the EEG became asymmetric at low pressure (SEF 10 Hz on the right and 25 Hz on the left). It became almost symmetric only at MAP above 95 mmHg, and the asymmetry returned when pressure fell to 75 mmHg. The authors argue that MAP alone cannot always be trusted when autoregulation is impaired. Caveat: a single case report without blood flow measurement, and ketamine and sevoflurane affect the EEG.Source: Nycz 2022
  • Lost autoregulation may give alpha slowing. In a pilot study with 36 analysed patients, the alpha peak frequency was lower with lost autoregulation (9.4 vs 10.5 Hz). Alpha power did not differ, and the groups were similar in MAP, PSI and SEF. Alpha frequency also falls with age and deeper propofol effect. The finding is therefore a hypothesis worth noticing, not something to act on alone.Source: Manquat 2022
  • Autoregulation can be measured. A Johns Hopkins protocol uses the correlation between MAP and flow velocity (Mx) to keep MAP above the patient’s own lower limit on cardiopulmonary bypass. The endpoint is postoperative delirium. Only the protocol is available, not results. Invasively, PRx and optimal CPP are used. With NIRS, TOx and COx can serve as surrogates, but with lower precision.Sources: Brown and Hogue (protocol); Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • Not validated for the individual (interpretation based on the sources). The EEG may be able to show when the patient’s limit is reached. But the suggestion about EEG asymmetry has not been tested, and the cut-off for lost autoregulation in the pilot study is not validated under anaesthesia.Sources: Nycz 2022; Manquat 2022

The studies in detail:

Guay 2025 Nycz 2022 Manquat 2022 Brown and Hogue (protocol) Lobo and Lamperti 2025

How low can blood pressure go? The evidence is divergent

The sources do not agree on a single blood pressure threshold, and the studies do not even define the baseline in the same way.

  • Low pressure is linked to harm. Expert consensus recommends MAP above 60–70 mmHg. Long cumulative time with low pressure, a fall of 40% from baseline and MAP below 55 mmHg are linked to cardiac and brain injury, including delirium, and to cognitive impairment and dementia within one year.Source: Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • But not everyone finds the association. A meta-analysis found no association between permitted MAP below 60 and mortality. Several studies also found no association between hypotension and postoperative neurocognitive impairment.Source: Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • A higher MAP target gave less early delirium. In a randomised trial of 150 older patients (65–80) undergoing hip arthroplasty, fewer had delirium on day 1 the higher the MAP target: 22%, 16% and 4% with targets 10–20% below, 0–10% below and 0–10% above baseline. On days 2 and 3 there was no difference. The group with the highest target had higher rSO₂, while BIS was similar. Caveat: a small, single-centre study that shows an association without testing the mechanism.Source: Xu 2020
  • The studies use different baselines, and “triple low” may not be a cause. One study uses the lowest measured MAP before anaesthesia as baseline, another an average before surgery. The studies therefore cannot be compared directly. “Triple low” may be a marker of vulnerable patients rather than a cause. Higher mortality with unintended burst suppression is likewise interpreted as a sign of underlying disease.Sources: Georgii 2022; Xu 2020; Lobo and Lamperti 2025; Guay 2025

The studies in detail:

Lobo and Lamperti 2025 Xu 2020 Georgii 2022 Guay 2025

What NIRS and frontal EEG can and cannot show

The EEG does not stand alone. Cerebral oximetry can add something, but both NIRS and the frontal EEG have weaknesses.

  • rSO₂ has a wide normal range. Normal is 55–80%. A fall of 15–20% from baseline, or values below 50%, is regarded as significant. In carotid surgery, a 20% fall after clamping has a high negative but low positive predictive value. Many therefore use rSO₂ more to guide haemodynamics than to decide on shunting.Source: Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • NIRS can miss. In a pilot study, rSO₂ did not distinguish lost from preserved autoregulation (minimum 50 vs 57%, p = 0.08). Possible reasons are extracranial contamination and vasoconstrictor.Source: Manquat 2022
  • The frontal EEG has blind spots. A frontal montage can miss focal temporal seizures and occipital strokes, and acute strokes rarely produce burst suppression frontally. Reduced blood flow can go unnoticed with high haemoglobin and high saturation, whereas anaemic and hypoxaemic patients tolerate less.Source: Guay 2025
  • Several monitors together gave less delirium. In a randomised trial of 255 patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy, guidance with EEG spectrogram, NIRS, transcranial Doppler and haemodynamics gave less delirium. In the shared case, it was the haemodynamic trend alongside that prevented the loss of alpha from being interpreted as nociception.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti 2025 (discusses the trial); shared case

The studies in detail:

Lobo and Lamperti 2025 Manquat 2022 Guay 2025

Schematic example: fall in cardiac output and loss of alpha

The image was made for teaching and is simulated. It is not patient data and not a printout from any equipment. It shows haemodynamics (arterial pressure, MAP and CI) above an EEG spectrogram for the left and right hemispheres. The fall in CI and the loss of alpha start at the same time.

  • What is simulated: CI goes from about 3.1 to about 1.7 l/min/m², stroke volume falls, and MAP and pulse pressure fall. Alpha (about 8–12 Hz) disappears in both hemispheres while delta (below 4 Hz) persists. The numbers were chosen to illustrate the pattern.
  • That the changes start together is a choice: Quantitative EEG captures changes in blood flow and metabolism within 28–104 seconds. The delay between a fall in cardiac output and EEG change will vary, and the image does not show it.Source: Foreman and Claassen 2012
  • Loss of alpha has several possible causes: Both an increase and a reduction in alpha have been reported with noxious stimulation. Sedatives and sleep can also confound the picture. Both noxious stimulation and low cardiac output are possible causes of such changes on frontal EEG. The image therefore shows no cause, and it cannot be used to distinguish perfusion from other causes.Sources: Sleigh et al. 2025; Foreman and Claassen 2012; Guay 2025
Foreman and Claassen 2012, Sleigh et al. 2025

Clinical example: alpha weakens when cardiac output falls (shared case)

One shared case from Norwegian clinical practice, from the author of the app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is included because it illustrates the same thing the sources describe.Sources: Guay 2025; Manquat 2022

  • What was seen: an adult during maintenance with an unchanged hypnotic dose, PSI 30, SR 0, EMG 0, SEF 10–11 Hz. On the same screen, a pulse contour monitor showed MAP and cardiac index falling for a few minutes (CI down towards about 1 l/min/m²). Over the same period the alpha band became weaker and drifted downwards in both hemispheres, and the spectrogram became “thinner” without suppression. When MAP was 83 mmHg and CI 3.5 again, the alpha band was back as before.
  • Why it is instructive: without the haemodynamic trend alongside, the picture would easily have been interpreted as nociceptive loss of alpha or as a dose that “drifts”. The timing with cardiac output, the unchanged dose and the complete return of alpha point to transient cerebral hypoperfusion. The same has been described in an 89-year-old in whom the EEG normalised when CI rose from 1.3 to 2.7.Sources: García 2021; Guay 2025
  • Caveat: one case, no measurement of CBF, NIRS or Doppler, and alpha weakening has several possible causes. The point is not that EEG “proves” hypoperfusion, but that EEG and haemodynamics should be read together. See image 17 in the image quiz.
Own clinical example; Guay 2025, Manquat 2022, Nycz 2022

The cards on burst suppression are collected in the tab.

The studies in detail: Guay, Manquat, Nycz, Xu, the Johns Hopkins protocol and two textbook chapters (7 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Frontal EEG as a perfusion marker in clinical practice (Guay 2025)

Review article from MGH and MIT (Anesthesiology 2025;143:1595–1618) on physiological EEG signatures in the critically ill, with three case reports.

  • Main point: signs of reduced cerebral oxygen delivery (CDO₂) during sedation or general anaesthesia resemble deeper anaesthesia on frontal EEG: a shift of power towards lower frequencies, broadband power loss, burst suppression and sustained suppression. The same applies to hypothermia and increased GABAergic effect. They must therefore be distinguished from one another before the anaesthetic is adjusted. CDO₂ is proportional to CBF, haemoglobin and SpO₂, and the authors emphasise the balance between CDO₂ and oxygen consumption (CMRO₂) more than the exact numbers.
  • Differential diagnosis for reduced neuronal activity: with normal CDO₂: anaesthetic effect, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, hypercapnia, postictal suppression and noxious stimulation. With reduced CDO₂: shock, intracranial hypertension, venous congestion, hypoxaemia, hypocapnia, anaemia and stroke. Primary brain injury can produce both.
  • Carotid surgery: the criteria for shunting (more than 50% power reduction in 8–15 Hz, more than 50% increase in slow-delta, more than 50% broadband reduction, or suppression) typically arise when global CBF falls to below 35–40% of normal (about 18–20 versus 50–55 ml/100 g/min).
  • CPP and autoregulation: CPP is MAP minus the greater of ICP and CVP. The lower MAP limit for autoregulation varies from 40 to 90 mmHg in adults, and autoregulation is impaired in many critically ill patients. Reduced CBF can go unnoticed with high haemoglobin and high saturation, whereas anaemic and hypoxaemic patients tolerate less.
  • Burst suppression: suppression is amplitude below 10 µV (typically below 5 µV), and electrocerebral inactivity is 2 µV or lower. In dogs with haemorrhagic shock (fentanyl and nitrous oxide), burst suppression appeared at MAP 31 ± 7 mmHg together with loss of diastolic transcranial Doppler flow (Werner 1995). A randomised trial (Georgii 2022) abolished burst suppression in more than 50% by raising MAP to the baseline value. The authors say it is unclear whether this is due to physiology, pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics. Shock can increase the propofol concentration and make the brain more sensitive.
  • Unintended burst suppression and “triple low”: sedation-induced burst suppression has been linked to lower mortality after traumatic brain injury, whereas unintended burst suppression is linked to higher mortality in intensive care. The authors interpret this as the patient's underlying disease, not burst suppression in itself, driving the risk.
  • Age and alpha: frontal alpha is weaker in old age, poor cognitive function, frailty and severe illness. In older patients without visible alpha, a broadband fall in power may be the first warning.
  • Loss of alpha can also occur with noxious stimulation under inadequate analgesia (Hight 2019), and unexpected beta and gamma during neuromuscular blockade should lead to more anaesthesia and analgesia.
  • Case reports (one patient each): (1) 39-year-old on propofol: burst suppression disappeared with lower propofol. Two days later, loss of alpha and burst suppression appeared when MAP fell below 70 mmHg with right heart failure and rising CVP, and the EEG normalised after adrenaline. The authors also mention that reduced cardiac output may have increased the propofol concentration. (2) 89-year-old after mitral valve surgery: broadband fall in power (slow-delta from 30–40 to 10–20 µV) and then burst suppression at a cardiac index of 1.3. The EEG normalised when CI increased to 2.7 after PVAD. (3) 65-year-old in LVAD surgery: burst suppression during weaning from cardiopulmonary bypass, while the radial artery showed MAP 80–90. Direct aortic pressure was 35 mmHg, probably due to vasoplegia and a fault in the radial line.
  • Limitations: a frontal montage can miss focal temporal seizures and occipital strokes, and acute strokes rarely produce burst suppression frontally. The case reports illustrate, but do not validate, and the article shows no EEG data from patients with raised ICP. They give no thresholds for which MAP or CI produces EEG change in an individual patient.
  • Caveat: Brown reports royalties from Masimo, and Guay reports travel support from Masimo.
Guay et al. Anesthesiology 2025;143:1595–1618

Alpha peak frequency as a marker of lost autoregulation under propofol (Manquat 2022)

Prospective pilot study from Lariboisière (Paris), BJA Open 2022;1:100004. The hypothesis was that frontal EEG can show whether cerebral autoregulation is preserved during propofol anaesthesia.

  • Patients and set-up: 56 included, 36 analysed (median age 57.5 years), elective interventional neuroradiology. Propofol TCI (Schnider, starting at 5 µg/ml) and remifentanil; noradrenaline for MAP above 65 mmHg. SedLine with four frontal channels (Fp1, Fp2, F7, F8; spectrum from Fp2), NIRS, transcranial Doppler in the middle cerebral artery during induction and 30 minutes after, and continuous MAP from a finger cuff (Clearsight).
  • Autoregulation: Mxa = correlation between 10-second averages of MAP and Doppler velocity over 30 epochs. Mxa ≥ 0.3 was regarded as lost autoregulation (CA−); the cut-off is taken from traumatic brain injury. The EEG was analysed only in stable windows (PSI 25–35, no burst suppression, SEF 8–15 Hz, MAP above 65, stable for at least 5 minutes).
  • Main finding: 18 CA+ and 18 CA−. The groups were similar in age (53 versus 57 years), MAP (71 mmHg), Doppler velocity, PSI and SEF. Alpha peak frequency was lower with lost autoregulation: 9.4 [9.0–9.9] versus 10.5 [10.1–10.9] Hz (p < 0.001), with a correlation of r = −0.556 against Mxa. Alpha, delta and total power did not differ. Univariate AUC 0.88; in a multivariate model OR 0.038 [0.004–0.409] per Hz (p = 0.007). Lower alpha peak frequency is also associated with postoperative delirium in the meta-analysis by Xu 2025 (Spectrogram tab) and in Gutiérrez 2019. Adding alpha peak frequency to age, ASA and noradrenaline dose increased the AUC from 0.76 to 0.93.
