  • What did not discriminate: NIRS (rSO₂ minimum 50 versus 57%, p = 0.08). The CA− group had a higher ASA class and more noradrenaline (0.06 versus 0.03 µg/kg/min). The authors consider NIRS to be insensitive here (extracranial contamination, vasoconstrictor), and that the indices hide the frequency information.
  • Interpretation: alpha frequency, not alpha power, tracks loss of autoregulation, and does so independently of age. Power loss and slow waves (Guay 2025, the carotid criteria) probably only appear with more severe ischaemia. A slower alpha may thus be an earlier and more subtle sign than the patterns described in the cards above. This is a hypothesis from a single pilot study.
  • Limitations: small, single centre, short Mxa window, static analysis (one time point), no clinical outcome measure, and the Mxa cut-off is not validated under anaesthesia. Alpha frequency also falls with age (Purdon 2015 BJA) and with deeper propofol effect, so a low value in an individual patient cannot simply be interpreted as loss of autoregulation. The authors call for a dynamic study. No conflicts of interest declared; funded by the AP-HP foundation.
  • Practical: The alpha peak frequency can be read approximately from the spectrogram, also where the monitor does not display it as a number. An alpha band sitting around 9 Hz in a middle-aged patient with stable PSI and MAP is worth noticing, not acting on alone.
Manquat et al. BJA Open 2022;1:100004

Hemispheric asymmetry on frontal EEG and blood pressure (Nycz 2022, case report)

  • Patient: one 65-year-old man with dialysis-dependent renal failure, complete left-sided ICA occlusion and severe (70–99%) right-sided ICA stenosis, for first rib resection and balloon dilatation of the subclavian vein. Preoperative MAP was 81 mmHg. Induction with fentanyl, lidocaine, propofol, suxamethonium, rocuronium and ketamine, then sevoflurane at 0.7 age-adjusted MAC guided by EEG. The EEG monitor was applied after induction, and the text mentions no EEG baseline before induction.
  • The event: after induction, hypotension occurred (MAP 50–60 mmHg, non-invasive 50–80), treated with noradrenaline boluses and later an infusion. The EEG showed asymmetry: spectral edge frequency (SEF) 10 Hz on the right and 25 Hz on the left, with a hot band at 20–30 Hz probably due to ketamine. When MAP was above 95 mmHg the spectrogram became almost symmetrical.
  • Reduced support: the authors set the lower MAP limit to above 70 mmHg (85% of baseline) and reduced the noradrenaline infusion. Within minutes, fast activity above 12 Hz disappeared in both hemispheres, most on the right (nadir 65 mmHg according to the figure legend). Symmetry returned at MAP above 95 mmHg. The pattern returned after a new fall to 75 mmHg (at 10:32) and did not recur after MAP was kept above 95. The patient was extubated on low-dose noradrenaline, had no new neurological deficits, and at 6 months the stenoses were unchanged.
  • The authors' interpretation: the pattern is “concerning for focal ischaemia”. They also mention possible intracerebral “steal” with exhausted vascular reactivity and increased venous pressure during manipulation of the superior vena cava, and that ketamine disturbs the EEG. They claim this is the first reported case of cerebral hypoperfusion captured by frontal EEG in a non-carotid procedure.
  • The authors' suggestion: MAP alone cannot always be relied on in patients with impaired autoregulation, and the lower MAP limit can be set from EEG symmetry on beat-to-beat arterial pressure. This is a suggestion from one case and has not been tested.
  • Limitations: case report. No CBF, NIRS, Doppler or imaging was measured to confirm ischaemia, the patient had no new deficits, and ketamine and sevoflurane affect the EEG. The edge frequency and asymmetry may have other explanations, and the authors point out that EEG interpretation is not a core skill in anaesthesia training.
  • Connection within the app: the pattern agrees with ischaemia first producing loss of fast activity (Foreman and Claassen) and with asymmetry as a sign of hemispheric involvement (BSI, Sheorajpanday). Guay 2025 describes other case reports in which pressure and cardiac output affect frontal EEG. All are single cases or reviews, not proof.
Nycz et al. Neurol Int 2022;14:1018–1023

Blood pressure targets and delirium (Xu 2020)

  • Design: randomised trial at a single hospital. 150 patients aged 65–80 years underwent hip arthroplasty and were divided into three groups by MAP target: 10–20% below baseline (D), 0–10% below (M) and 0–10% above (H). The anaesthetist could not be blinded.
  • Delirium day 1: 22% (D), 16% (M) and 4% (H), p = 0.031. On days 2 and 3 there was no difference.
  • Group H had higher rSO₂ from five minutes after incision, less emergence agitation (24%, 22% and 6%), a shorter stay in the recovery room (63 versus 92 minutes) and a shorter hospital stay (12 versus 15 days). BIS was similar between the groups.
  • The authors consider that higher rSO₂ may explain the effect. The study shows an association and does not test the mechanism.
  • Caveats: small sample, only one method for delirium, no blood markers, and discrepancies between text and tables (see Sources).
Xu et al. J Clin Anesth 2020;62:109730

Individual blood pressure targets from autoregulation monitoring: Johns Hopkins protocol (Brown and Hogue)

Protocol (version 2, 8 July 2014) for a randomised substudy nested in Hogue’s trial (NCT00981474), with Charles Brown as substudy lead. The file contains only the protocol, not the results.

  • Background: blood pressure targets are currently set empirically. In the elderly, hypertension, diabetes and vascular disease may shift the lower limit of autoregulation, and autoregulation is dynamic, influenced among other things by rewarming from hypothermia, inhaled agents (dose-dependently) and anaemia.
  • Patients: 55 years or older, surgery on cardiopulmonary bypass (coronary bypass, valve or ascending aorta), high risk of neurological complications, and with a TCD window.
  • Measurement: TCD over both middle cerebral arteries and NIRS on the forehead. MAP, flow velocity and rScO₂ are averaged in 10-second blocks. A moving correlation between MAP and flow velocity over 300 seconds (30 points) gives the mean velocity index (Mx), and the same with NIRS gives the cerebral oximetry index (COx). Values are sorted into 5 mmHg MAP bins. When autoregulation is intact, the correlation is near zero or negative; when lost, it approaches 1.
  • Intervention: MAP on bypass is kept above the patient’s own lower limit based on Mx. If MAP falls below the limit, phenylephrine 100 µg is given and isoflurane reduced (to a minimum of 0.5%), with vasopressin if needed. The control group is managed with standard MAP targets.
  • Endpoint: postoperative delirium, from 2014 defined by a consensus committee.
  • Caveats: this is a protocol, not results. Funded by the NIH.
Protocol, NCT00981474 (substudy), Johns Hopkins 2014

What is the blood pressure limit? The evidence is divergent

  • Chapter 11 in Lobo mentions that expert consensus recommends MAP above 60–70 mmHg. Long cumulative time with low pressure, a relative fall of 40% from baseline and MAP below 55 mmHg are linked to cardiac and brain injury, including delirium, and to cognitive impairment and dementia within one year.
  • A meta-analysis found no association between permitted MAP below 60 and mortality, and several studies found no association between hypotension and postoperative neurocognitive impairment.
  • Georgii defines baseline as the lowest measured MAP before anaesthesia. Xu uses an average of measurements before surgery. The definitions are not the same, so the studies cannot be compared directly.
  • “Triple low” (low pressure, low EEG index and low MAC) may be a marker of vulnerable patients rather than a cause. A randomised trial with alerts for such events did not affect 90-day mortality, but few alerts were acted on.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 11

Monitoring perfusion

  • rSO₂: the normal range is wide (55–80%). A fall of 15–20% from baseline, or values below 50%, is regarded as significant. Sensitivity 60–100% and specificity 94–98% for cerebral ischaemia.
  • Carotid surgery: a fall of 20% after clamping is linked to impaired consciousness with a high negative predictive value (about 2.6% develop neurological deterioration with smaller falls). The positive predictive value is low, and many use rSO₂ more to guide haemodynamics than to decide on shunting.
  • Preoperative rSO₂ of 60% or lower is linked to delirium in older patients after cardiac surgery, and below 50% to higher 30-day mortality.
  • Autoregulation: invasively, the pressure reactivity index (PRx) and optimal CPP (CPPopt) are used. With NIRS, the indices TOx and COx can be used as surrogates, with moderate to good correlation but lower precision. TCD requires an awake baseline.
  • The book refers to a randomised trial of 255 patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy in which multimodal guidance (EEG spectrogram, NIRS, TCD and haemodynamics) gave less delirium.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 1, 7 and 9

Positioning changes brain perfusion

  • Head height changes perfusion pressure. The head higher than the heart lowers cerebral perfusion pressure, and anaesthesia blunts compensation. In the “beach chair” position 80% had cerebral desaturation, even though arm pressure was the same as in the lateral position.See
  • In Trendelenburg, cardiac output matters. Cardiac output best predicted blood flow in the internal carotid artery. The largest fall came at induction (about 30%), not at tilt.See
  • End-tidal CO₂ becomes less reliable. Steep head-down position and pneumoperitoneum increase the gradient between arterial and end-tidal CO₂ and reduce compliance. Trendelenburg is contraindicated with raised intracranial pressure.See
  • The index can fall without a change in dose. Lower cardiac output can give a higher propofol concentration than the pump predicts, and hypercapnia gives less alpha and beta. Look at cardiac output, blood pressure, CO₂ and the raw EEG before reducing the dose (interpretation based on the sources).See
  • Positioning is also about eyes and air. Avoid pressure on the eyes, and assess vision when the patient is awake. In the sitting position air embolism can occur, and a patent foramen ovale carries a risk of paradoxical embolism.See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Head height and the pressure at the brain

The blood pressure in the arm is not necessarily the pressure in the brain. When the head is at a different height from the heart, the hydrostatic pressure must be taken into account.Source: Breyer and Roth 2025

  • The height difference matters. The head higher than the heart lowers cerebral perfusion pressure and can cause systemic hypotension. With invasive blood pressure measurement, the transducer should be zeroed at the level of the circle of Willis, and any pressure gradient should be documented. Anaesthesia blunts the baroreceptor reflex and sympathetic vasoconstriction. The changes with positioning are therefore larger.Source: Breyer and Roth 2025
  • In the “beach chair”, arm pressure can mislead you. 80.3% had cerebral desaturation in the “beach chair” position, versus 0% in the lateral position, even though arm pressure was the same in both groups. A mean arm pressure of 80 mmHg with a 38 cm height difference to the forehead corresponds to about 52 mmHg at the brain. Caveats: the surgeon chose the position, the study was not randomised, and no cognitive testing was done.Source: Murphy 2010 (cohort study, 124 patients undergoing shoulder arthroscopy)
  • Several mechanisms may contribute. Possible causes are reduced cardiac output, deliberate or permitted hypotension, lost compensation under anaesthesia, head height not being included in blood pressure management, narrowing of the vertebral artery with rotation, and air embolism. Hyperextension, hyperflexion and marked rotation of the neck are also implicated in cervical cord injury.Source: Breyer and Roth 2025
  • Measure blood pressure with the level of the brain in mind. Avoid hypotension and bradycardia, and treat them promptly. Avoid extreme head positions, and keep a distance between chin and chest.Source: Breyer and Roth 2025

The studies in detail:

Breyer and Roth 2025 Murphy 2010

Trendelenburg: blood flow follows cardiac output

Cerebral blood flow was maintained in steep Trendelenburg. Two studies of robot-assisted prostatectomy measured perfusion pressure in different ways and got different numbers, but the same main picture.Sources: Kalmar 2010, Nordum 2024

  • CPP was unchanged or fell, but blood flow did not fall further. At 40° (zero point at the external auditory meatus) both MAP and CVP rose, and CPP was unchanged (71 vs 70 mmHg). ICP was not measured. At 30°, CPP fell to 61–62 mmHg after one hour, but blood flow in the internal carotid artery did not fall further. According to the authors, this suggests that autoregulation was at least partly working.Sources: Kalmar 2010 (40°), Nordum 2024 (30°)
  • Induction gave the largest fall. Blood flow in the internal carotid artery fell about 30% after induction (483 to 344 ml/min). Tilt and pneumoperitoneum gave no further fall.Source: Nordum 2024
  • Cardiac output matters more than MAP. Cardiac output best predicted blood flow: 1 l/min/m² more gave 92 ml/min more. PaCO₂ had a small positive effect. MAP had a small negative effect within the classical autoregulatory range. The authors therefore consider monitoring cardiac output more important than MAP in this position.Source: Nordum 2024
  • Caveats. Both are small observational studies without a control group. Patients varied widely (CPP 49–99 mmHg during tilt), and 78% received vasopressor. None showed signs of cognitive dysfunction at 10 or 180 days. Neither study measured the EEG.Sources: Kalmar 2010, Nordum 2024

The studies in detail:

Kalmar 2010 Nordum 2024

Steep head-down position and pneumoperitoneum: CO₂, lungs and the index

Steep head-down tilt and CO₂ in the abdomen affect ventilation. This affects both how well end-tidal CO₂ reflects arterial CO₂ and what the index shows.

  • End-tidal CO₂ reflects arterial CO₂ less well. In all three studies the gradient between arterial and end-tidal CO₂ increased and compliance fell. The sources disagree on how much this matters. In one, the gradient increased from 1.06 to as much as 1.46 kPa, and the authors advise caution with end-tidal CO₂. In the other, the increase was smaller in healthy women (2.3 to 3.9 mmHg), and end-tidal CO₂ was judged still usable. The gradient is still larger in older patients, obese patients and with low cardiac output.Sources: Kalmar 2010, Pisitsak 2019
  • The lungs become stiffer. Plateau pressure rose from 14 to 26 cmH₂O, and compliance fell from 50 to 23 ml/cmH₂O. Plateau pressure predicted the CO₂ gradient. Oxygenation was still reduced at the end, probably due to atelectasis.Sources: Kalmar 2010, Pisitsak 2019
  • Pressure in the head and eyes rises. Trendelenburg increases intracranial and intraocular pressure and is contraindicated with raised intracranial pressure. Optic nerve sheath diameter increased from 5.8 to 6.4 mm during tilt.Sources: Breyer and Roth 2025, Nordum 2024
  • The index can change without a dose change. The lower the cardiac index, the higher the measured propofol compared with the pump prediction. In the knee–chest position BIS fell when cardiac output fell. Hypercapnia gave less alpha and beta and a lower SEF. A fall in the index during pneumoperitoneum should therefore prompt a look at cardiac output, blood pressure, CO₂ and the raw EEG before the dose is reduced (interpretation based on the sources, see the pneumoperitoneum card).Sources: Ogawa 2020, Chalo 2019, Kalkman 1991

The studies in detail:

Kalmar 2010 Pisitsak 2019 Nordum 2024 Breyer and Roth 2025 Ogawa 2020 Chalo 2019 Kalkman 1991

More than perfusion: air embolism and visual loss

Positioning affects more than cerebral perfusion. The sitting position carries a risk of air embolism. The prone position and long procedures carry a risk of visual loss.

  • In the sitting position, air can be drawn into the veins. When the surgical field is above the heart, air can be drawn into veins that are held open. Transoesophageal echocardiography detects it best. End-tidal CO₂ and pulse oximetry are much less sensitive. Treatment: stop further air entry, and give 100% oxygen, fluid and vasoactive drugs.Source: Breyer and Roth 2025
  • With a patent foramen ovale, many had air embolism, but none had paradoxical embolism. 33 of 82 patients (40.2%) had air embolism. Caveats: the figures come from four observational studies, and zero events among 82 does not rule out a risk of up to about 4%. The decision is made together with the patient, surgeon and anaesthetist.Source: Klein 2018
  • Visual loss is rare but serious. Ischaemic optic neuropathy occurs in about 1 in 60,000–125,000 anaesthetics, but more often in spinal and cardiac surgery. Central retinal artery occlusion is most often caused by external pressure on the eye.Source: Breyer and Roth 2025
  • The recommendations rest on weak evidence. The 2019 ASA advisory has no randomised studies behind it. It recommends the head level with or above the rest of the body when possible, a neutral position without pressure on the eyes, and assessment of vision when the patient is awake. Checking the eyes “about every 20 minutes” comes from Miller's, not from the ASA.Sources: ASA 2019, Breyer and Roth 2025

The studies in detail:

Breyer and Roth 2025 Klein 2018 ASA 2019

Pneumoperitoneum, cardiac output and ventilation: can the index fall without a change in dose?

A common explanation is that abdominal pressure compresses the liver, that propofol is then broken down more slowly, and that concentration and depth increase. The sources support parts of this, but no study shows the whole chain in patients.

  • Abdominal pressure can reduce liver blood flow, but the findings vary. In pigs, hepatic artery and portal vein flow fell clearly at 20 mmHg. Other animal studies found no change below 30 mmHg, or even increased liver clearance. In patients, 12 mmHg gave poorer liver perfusion than an individualised lower pressure.Sources: Diebel 1992, Gudmundsson 2001, Hoekstra 2013, Olmedilla Arnal 2023
  • Propofol clearance follows hepatic blood flow. This has been shown in intensive care patients.Source: Peeters 2008
  • During pneumoperitoneum, measured propofol was on average as predicted. In robot-assisted prostatectomy with CO₂ and head-down position, measured propofol was not higher than the TCI pump predicted (median error −1.5%). But the lower the cardiac index, the higher the measured concentration compared with the prediction.Source: Ogawa 2020
  • Measured propofol was higher than the models predicted. The measured concentration was a median 27–111% above the models (Eleveld 27%, Marsh 53%, Schnider 111%). The authors attribute this to the models being based on few severely obese patients and too short sampling, not to pneumoperitoneum. Pneumoperitoneum was not analysed. Some early samples were drawn during the bolus itself and may be artefactually high.Source: Braathen 2024, Oslo (69 patients, BMI 21.6–67.3, laparoscopic cholecystectomy or bariatric surgery; propofol 2 mg/kg, then 6 mg/kg/h for 30 minutes, then sevoflurane; 474 arterial samples)
  • Lower cardiac output gives higher propofol concentrations. This is the best documented mechanism. In animal studies, arterial propofol rose and clearance fell when cardiac output fell, and the BIS effect appeared at a much lower concentration. In patients in the knee–chest position, cardiac output fell from 5.6 to 3.9 L/min, measured propofol was about 74% higher than predicted, and BIS fell from 46.5 to 37.7.Sources: Upton 1999 (sheep), Johnson 2003 (pigs in haemorrhagic shock), Chalo 2019
  • In long procedures in steep head-down position, the EEG can change for reasons other than the drug. BIS and SEF were stable for hours with sevoflurane, while total EEG power fell, probably because of facial oedema. Case reports describe BIS falling to near 0 after several hours, also under desflurane. The authors suggest brain oedema or raised intracranial pressure as the cause, not drug concentration.Sources: Rubio-Baines 2026, Hoshi 2022
  • End-tidal agent concentration overestimates the arterial concentration during maintenance. The difference is about 15–30%. It is due to ventilation–perfusion mismatch in the lungs (alveolar dead space and shunt), not diffusion. For sevoflurane, arterial concentration was 2.09% versus 3.01% end-tidal during maintenance, but equal at emergence. During wash-out the relationship reverses: arterial concentration is then higher than end-tidal. How the patient is ventilated also affects the difference.Sources: Peyton 2020 and 2022, Lin 2015, Frei 1991, Enekvist 2010
  • High CO₂ can lower the index. Hypercapnia (PaCO₂ about 50 mmHg) gave less alpha and beta and a lower SEF, which reversed at normal CO₂. At very high PaCO₂ a marked fall in the index has been described, and end-tidal CO₂ may then underestimate the arterial value.Sources: Kalkman 1991, Ann 2017
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): In laparoscopy with a volatile agent, the brain probably receives somewhat less than the end-tidal concentration suggests, especially with atelectasis and shunt. With TIVA, propofol concentration can be higher than the pump shows when cardiac output falls. The index may therefore change without any change in dose. A fall in the index during pneumoperitoneum should prompt a look at cardiac output, blood pressure, CO₂ and the raw EEG before the dose is reduced.
Ogawa 2020 Braathen 2024 Chalo 2019 Upton 1999 Peyton 2020 Kalkman 1991 Rubio-Baines 2026
EEG is not covered in Breyer and Roth 2025. The EEG section above is based on Lobo and Lamperti and the studies. The evidence for EEG in raised ICP is sparse (see the card on ICP). Mean frequency falls when CPP is below 60 mmHg (Foreman and Claassen). Kalmar measured neither ICP nor EEG.
The studies in detail: Breyer and Roth 2025 on perfusion pressure, sitting position, air embolism and visual loss, Kalmar, Nordum, Pisitsak and ASA 2019 (8 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Positioning (Breyer and Roth 2025)

Perfusion pressure and head height

  • When the head lies at a different height from the heart, you must account for the hydrostatic pressure in the arteries and veins of the brain when estimating cerebral perfusion pressure. The chapter recommends documenting any pressure gradient.
  • Head above the heart lowers cerebral perfusion pressure and can produce systemic hypotension. With invasive blood pressure measurement the transducer should be zeroed at the level of the circle of Willis.
  • Trendelenburg increases intracranial and intraocular pressure, and the position is contraindicated in raised intracranial pressure.
  • General anaesthesia blunts the normal compensatory mechanisms (baroreceptor reflex, sympathetic vasoconstriction). Haemodynamic changes with positioning are therefore more pronounced.
Breyer and Roth 2025

Steep Trendelenburg and pneumoperitoneum (Kalmar 2010)

  • Design: observational study of 31 patients (age 62, range 49–76) undergoing robot-assisted prostatectomy in 40° Trendelenburg with CO₂ pneumoperitoneum at 10 mmHg. Mean time in the position was 159 minutes. Anaesthesia with propofol, sufentanil and sevoflurane (1 MAC).
  • Measurement of CPP: the pressure transducers were zeroed at the external auditory meatus, so CPP could be determined independently of position. CPP was calculated as MAP minus CVP, on the assumption that CVP is at least as high as ICP in this position. ICP was not measured.
  • Results: MAP rose from 79 to 95 mmHg and CVP from 8 to 26 mmHg, and CPP was unchanged (71 versus 70 mmHg in table 1). CPP stayed well above the lower limit of autoregulation. After return to the supine position MAP and CVP fell by the same amount, and CPP was briefly down at 61 mmHg before normalising within 3 minutes.
  • Cerebral oxygenation: SctO₂ (NIRS, second generation) rose from 70 to 73% (p < 0.001) and remained above 55% throughout, which the authors use as the limit below which ischaemia is very unlikely. The authors assume that higher CPP and higher PE′CO₂ increased blood flow and lowered oxygen extraction.
  • CO₂: PE′CO₂ rose from 4.12 to 4.79 kPa, and the gradient between arterial and end-tidal CO₂ increased from 1.06 to as much as 1.46 kPa. The authors recommend using PE′CO₂ with caution in this situation, because it underestimates PaCO₂ most at high values.
  • Lungs: plateau pressure rose from 14 to 26 cmH₂O, and compliance fell from 50 to 23 ml/cmH₂O. Compliance was still lower than baseline after return to the supine position.
  • The authors refer to earlier work describing intracranial hypertension with this combination, and lower SctO₂ in older patients and in patients with raised ICP. These groups were not the focus here. Raised CO₂ also increases intraocular pressure and may carry a risk of visual loss.
  • Limitations: small observational study, no control group, no ICP or EEG measurement, and only patients who tolerated the procedure. The findings cannot be transferred to patients with raised ICP.
Kalmar et al. Br J Anaesth 2010;104:433–9

What determines cerebral blood flow in Trendelenburg? Cardiac output, not MAP (Nordum 2024)

Prospective observational study from Ahus (Front Anesthesiol 2024;3:1395973): 44 men (mean 67 years) for robot-assisted prostatectomy in 30° Trendelenburg, propofol/remifentanil with BIS 40–60, deep neuromuscular blockade, PEEP 8 and tidal volume 6 ml/kg. 37 had intraoperative measurements at six time points: blood flow in the internal carotid artery (ICA) by ultrasound, cardiac output, CVP via the external jugular vein, optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) as a surrogate for ICP, and PaCO₂. Cognitive testing (CANTAB) before, and 10 and 180 days after.

  • Induction is the largest fall: ICA flow fell about 30% after induction (483 to 344 ml/min) and CPP from 98 to 73 mmHg. Tilt and pneumoperitoneum produced no further fall in ICA flow, even though CPP fell further to 61–62 mmHg after one hour and ONSD increased from 5.8 to 6.4 mm. After return to the supine position ICA flow rose to 407 ml/min.
  • Predictors: cardiac output was the strongest predictor of ICA flow (1 l/min/m² more gave 92 ml/min more), PaCO₂ had a small positive effect (1 kPa gave 49 ml/min), while MAP had a small negative effect (10 mmHg more gave 29 ml/min less) within the classical autoregulatory range. The authors consider monitoring of cardiac output more important than the traditional focus on MAP in this position.
  • Wide spread: during tilt CVP varied from 10 to 28 mmHg and CPP from 49 to 99 mmHg between patients. Vasopressor was used in 78% during tilt.
  • Cognition: no sign of postoperative cognitive dysfunction at 10 or 180 days; small improvements on several tests are consistent with a learning effect. None of the intraoperative measures predicted cognitive outcomes.
  • Versus Kalmar 2010: Kalmar found unchanged CPP at 40° with the zero point at the auditory meatus; Nordum found falling CPP at 30°, but preserved ICA flow, which argues for at least partly functioning autoregulation. Both found an increased CO₂ gradient and a fall in compliance.
  • Caveats: observational study without control group or power calculation, unilateral ICA measurement (the ICA supplies about 80% of cerebral blood flow), non-blinded ultrasound analysis, vasopressor at discretion, non-Scandinavian speakers excluded, and considerable dropout at 180 days (25 of 37). Publicly funded, no conflicts of interest.
Nordum et al. Front Anesthesiol 2024;3:1395973

How reliable is end-tidal CO₂ in Trendelenburg? (Pisitsak 2019)

20 healthy women (mean 42 years) for laparoscopic gynaecological surgery in 30° Trendelenburg with pneumoperitoneum 13 mmHg, thiopental/sevoflurane/nitrous oxide, PEEP 5 (J Med Assoc Thai 2019;102:122–128).

  • The gradient increases, but only a little: PaCO₂–PETCO₂ rose from 2.3 to 3.9 mmHg after 45 minutes of pneumoperitoneum (p = 0.02) and returned to 2.85 after desufflation. The correlation between ETCO₂ and PaCO₂ was maintained (r about 0.5). Static compliance fell from 32 to 22 ml/cmH₂O. Minute ventilation had to be increased about 14% to keep ETCO₂ at 28–35 mmHg.
  • Predictor: plateau pressure during pneumoperitoneum predicted the gradient (R² 0.40). Oxygenation (PaO₂/FiO₂) fell from 516 to 415 and was still reduced (398) at the end, probably atelectasis.
  • Conclusion: ETCO₂ remains usable with pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg in healthy patients, but the gradient is larger in older patients, obese patients and with low cardiac output. The authors recommend higher PEEP and recruitment. Small sample, only healthy women.
Pisitsak et al. J Med Assoc Thai 2019;102:122–128

Sitting and “beach chair”

  • Hypotension is common. Mean arterial pressure, systolic pressure and cardiac index fall in the sitting position, and the chapter recommends gradual positioning with fluid and vasopressor ready.
  • Possible mechanisms of cerebral ischaemia: reduced cardiac output, deliberate or permitted hypotension, lost compensation under general anaesthesia, failure to account for head height in blood pressure management, dynamic narrowing or occlusion of the vertebral artery on rotation, and air embolism.
  • Cerebral oximetry: in an observational study of 124 patients undergoing shoulder arthroscopy, 80% in the “beach chair” position had cerebral desaturation, versus none in the lateral position. The chapter says there is no gold standard for threshold values, and that trends should be interpreted with stable ventilation and position. Murphy 2010: prospective cohort study with 61 patients in the “beach chair” position and 63 in the right or left lateral position, where the surgeon chose the position (not randomised). All received standardised anaesthesia with sevoflurane, BIS 40–60 and blood pressure within 20% of baseline. Cerebral desaturation (CDE) was defined as a fall of at least 20% from baseline or SctO₂ below 55% for 15 seconds, measured with FORE-SIGHT and treated according to a fixed protocol (increased blood pressure, increased EtCO₂ or increased FiO₂). 80.3% (49 of 61) in the “beach chair” position had CDE versus 0% in the lateral position, with a median of 4 episodes per patient (0–38). SctO₂ fell from about 80% to about 70% within 9 minutes and stayed between 66 and 70%, even though brachial blood pressure did not differ between the groups. Eight patients had 12 episodes below 55%, all in the “beach chair” position. After the first treatment SctO₂ rose in 61%. The authors calculate that a brachial mean pressure of 80 mmHg with a 38 cm height difference to the forehead corresponds to about 52 mmHg at the brain, which may have been too low for some. No obvious neurological deficits were seen, but no cognitive testing was done. Among patients without an interscalene block, nausea was 50.0% versus 6.7% and vomiting 27.3% versus 3.3% in those with CDE, but the CDE group consisted only of “beach chair” patients (none in the lateral position), so position and CDE cannot be separated. The probes were supplied at cost by CAS Medical Systems, and the first author has received honoraria from CASMED.
  • Recommendation in the chapter: measure blood pressure with the level of the brain in mind, avoid and treat hypotension and bradycardia promptly, and avoid extreme head positions.
  • The neck: hyperextension, hyperflexion and forceful rotation are implicated in cervical cord injury. The chapter mentions quadriplegia and spinal infarction. It is recommended to examine range of motion preoperatively and to keep a gap between chin and chest (classically two finger breadths).
Breyer and Roth 2025 (Murphy 2010, Hindman 2011)

Venous air embolism (VAE)

  • The surgical field lies above the heart, and the dural veins lack valves and are held open by the skull. VAE can cause arrhythmias, desaturation, pulmonary hypertension, circulatory collapse and cardiac arrest.
  • With a patent foramen ovale there is a risk of paradoxical arterial embolism with stroke or myocardial infarction. A more recent review in the chapter found no paradoxical emboli in patients with known patent foramen ovale, even though VAE was detected in 40%. The decision is made together with the patient, surgeon and anaesthetist. Klein 2018: systematic review of four observational studies published after 2007 (Ammirati 2013, Ganslandt 2013, Hervías 2014 and Feigl 2014). Among 82 patients with known patent foramen ovale (PFO), 33 (40.2%) had air embolism, and none had paradoxical embolism. The figure of 82 counts only the 4 of 10 PFO patients in Ammirati who were operated on sitting (6 were operated on prone because the shunt was judged to be significant). Most come from Feigl (52 patients, 29 with air embolism detected by transoesophageal echocardiography, without clinical deterioration) and Ganslandt (24 patients, 4 with air embolism). An earlier review (Fathi 2009) reported nine clinically relevant paradoxical emboli in 2866 operations (0.3%), and an estimated 2.5% in presumed PFO patients among those not examined. The authors consider that surgery in the semi-sitting position is justifiable at experienced centres even with PFO, but that closure before surgery can be considered for a large PFO (over 4 mm) or a permanent right-to-left shunt in patients who have had paradoxical embolism. Limitations: only four observational studies, no controlled studies, and patients with a large shunt may have been operated on in another position (selection bias). Zero events among 82 patients does not rule out a risk of up to about 4% (own calculation with exact 95% confidence interval, not given in the article).
  • Transoesophageal echocardiography is the most sensitive (down to about 0.02 ml/kg of air), transcranial Doppler almost as sensitive, and transthoracic Doppler is the most sensitive non-invasive method (about 0.05 ml/kg). End-tidal CO₂ and pulse oximetry are much less sensitive.
  • Treatment: stop further air entry (flood the field with saline, bone wax), 100% oxygen, fluid and vasoactive agents, and consider left lateral position and Trendelenburg if possible.
  • Pneumocephalus is almost always found on imaging after surgery in the sitting position. Tension pneumocephalus is very rare.
Breyer and Roth 2025 (Mirski 2007, Klein 2018)

Perioperative visual loss (POVL)

  • Causes: central or branch retinal artery occlusion, anterior and posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, cortical blindness, acute glaucoma and gas expansion after retinal surgery.
  • Ischaemic optic neuropathy occurs in about 1 in 60,000–125,000 anaesthetics, but more often in spinal surgery and cardiac surgery. After spinal fusion a case-control study found increased risk with male sex, obesity, Wilson frame, long anaesthesia time, large blood loss and a low colloid fraction in replacement fluid.
  • Central retinal artery occlusion is most often caused by external pressure on the eye. The chapter recommends a foam head rest with the eyes in a cut-out and checking the head and eyes about every 20 minutes.
  • The American advisory (2012, confirmed in the 2019 edition) says there is no evidence that facial oedema or ocular compression causes ischaemic optic neuropathy. Direct pressure on the eye should nevertheless be avoided to prevent central retinal artery occlusion.
  • High-risk patients should have the head level with or above the heart when feasible. Vision should be assessed when the patient is awake, and if there is suspicion, prompt ophthalmological assessment is required.
  • Nitrous oxide must not be used in patients who have recently received a gas bubble (for example perfluorocarbon) after vitrectomy, because the bubble expands and can cause visual loss.
Breyer and Roth 2025 (ASA 2012 and 2019, Shen 2009, Rubin 2016)

ASA Practice Advisory for perioperative visual loss in spinal surgery (2019)

  • What it is: updated advisory from the ASA, the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society and the Society for Neuroscience in Anesthesiology and Critical Care (Anesthesiology 2019;130:12–30). It applies to adults and children over 12 years undergoing spinal surgery in the prone position under general anaesthesia and covers posterior and anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, retinal artery occlusion, cortical blindness and PRES. “High-risk patients” are defined as prone position with procedures over 4 hours, blood loss over 800 ml, or both.
  • Evidence: no randomised studies. The recommendations are based on observational studies, case reports (82 articles in total) and surveys among experts and members of the professional societies. They are not standards and cannot guarantee any outcome.
  • Before surgery: review risk factors (anaemia, hypertension, diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, coronary disease, previous stroke, carotid stenosis, smoking and obesity) and inform high-risk patients of the increased risk. The literature is insufficient for glaucoma and for the optic disc “cup-to-disc” ratio.
  • Blood pressure and blood loss: assess baseline blood pressure, monitor blood pressure continually in high-risk patients (the advisory distinguishes “continual”, meaning repeated regularly and frequently, from “continuous”, without interruption) and treat prolonged significant falls. Hypotension as a cause is uncertain in the literature. Controlled hypotension should be considered case by case and used only if anaesthetist and surgeon agree that it is necessary, with higher pressures in hypertensive patients. Hb or Hct should be measured regularly with large blood loss, but there is no documented lower Hb limit linked to visual loss, and a transfusion threshold that removes the risk cannot be stated. Crystalloid or colloid may be used, and vasopressors may be used when needed.
  • Positioning: the head should be level with or above the rest of the body when possible, in a neutral position, without pressure on the eyes, and the eyes should be checked regularly. The literature is insufficient to recommend any particular head rest equipment or a particular frequency for checking the eyes. Staged surgery can be considered case by case, but the effect has not been studied.
  • After surgery: assess vision when the patient is awake and request immediate ophthalmological assessment if there is suspicion. CT or MRI can be used to rule out intracranial causes. Optimise Hb, haemodynamics and oxygenation. There is no evidence for steroids, antiplatelet agents or pressure-lowering agents in ischaemic optic neuropathy (14 case reports without improvement and two with improvement).
  • Note: the Task Force writes that there is no mechanism by which facial oedema causes ischaemic optic neuropathy, and that there is no evidence that ocular compression causes isolated neuropathy of this kind. The recommendation to check the eyes “about every 20 minutes” appears in the chapter in Miller's, not in this advisory.
  • Conflicts of interest: three of the authors have served as expert witnesses in cases concerning perioperative visual loss.
ASA Task Force et al. Anesthesiology 2019;130:12–30

Ischaemia shows in the EEG before cells are damaged

  • Synapses fail first, and this is reversible: In mild to moderate ischaemia (15–35 ml/100 g/min) alpha and beta fall, then delta increases, while neurons survive. Below about 10 ml/100 g/min the rhythms disappear permanently. (see “Ischaemia in the EEG, step by step”)
  • The EEG responds within seconds: During carotid clamping, changes appear within about 20 seconds, whereas diffusion-weighted MRI shows changes only after about 30 minutes. The mean frequency falls when CPP is below 60 mmHg, also in sedated patients. (see “Ischaemia in the EEG, step by step”)
  • Loss of fast activity is the first sign: In carotid surgery, preserved cortical rhythms are regarded as a reliable sign of adequate blood flow, and asymmetry measures such as the BSI can quantify the difference between the hemispheres. (see “Carotid surgery and asymmetry: when one hemisphere gets too little”)
  • The EEG has prognostic value, with caveats: A continuous EEG at 12 hours indicated good outcome after cardiac arrest, and an isoelectric EEG or burst suppression with identical bursts at 24 hours indicated poor outcome. In cerebral infarction the predictive value is low to moderate. (see “EEG and prognosis after cerebral infarction, SAH and cardiac arrest”)
  • Much can mimic ischaemia, so check the raw EEG: Sedatives, opioids, ICP changes and sleep confound interpretation, and processed algorithms do not detect suppression until it reaches about 40%. (see “What can mimic ischaemia, and the vulnerable brain”)
  • The vulnerable brain tolerates less: The risk of burst suppression rises with age and impaired neurological status. The evidence for EEG in raised ICP is very sparse. (see “What can mimic ischaemia, and the vulnerable brain”)

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Ischaemia in the EEG, step by step

Synaptic signalling uses a lot of energy, and it fails first when blood flow falls. That is why ischaemia shows in the EEG before cells are permanently damaged.Source: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016

As blood flow falls (ml/100 g/min)

reversible
↓
↓
lasting damage
Tap a step to read briefly about it.
Sources: Foreman and Claassen 2012; van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016
  • Fast activity disappears first, and this can reverse. In mild to moderate ischaemia (15–35 ml/100 g/min) the synapses fail, but the neurons survive. The EEG shows less alpha and beta, then more delta. Even an isoelectric EEG may then be reversible. Below 10 ml/100 g/min the rhythms disappear permanently.Source: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016
  • The sources give the same order, with slightly different numbers. Fast frequencies disappear at about 25–35 ml/100 g/min, slow frequencies increase at about 17–18, and at 10–12 and below the EEG becomes silent and the damage irreversible.Source: Foreman and Claassen 2012
  • The EEG changes within seconds, not minutes. In circulatory arrest the EEG becomes isoelectric within 10–40 seconds. During carotid clamping, reversible changes appear within about 20 seconds. Diffusion-weighted MRI shows changes only after about 30 minutes.Sources: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016; Foreman and Claassen 2012
  • Low perfusion pressure shows too. The mean EEG frequency falls when CPP is below 60 mmHg, also in comatose or sedated patients. In focal ischaemia, relative delta percentage correlates most robustly with blood flow and metabolism.Sources: Diedler 2009, discussed in Foreman and Claassen 2012

The studies in detail:

van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 Foreman and Claassen 2012 Diedler 2009

Carotid surgery and asymmetry: when one hemisphere gets too little

In carotid surgery, the EEG under anaesthesia is best studied as a perfusion monitor. The key is the difference between the hemispheres.

  • Loss of fast activity at clamping suggests too little blood flow. More slow activity often follows. The EEG does not see deep structures, but preserved cortical rhythms are regarded as a reliable sign of adequate blood flow, also at depth.Source: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016
  • When to shunt is debated. Moderate EEG changes did not cause stroke, whereas major changes caused stroke in 2 of 22 (57 patients). The stroke rate was 1.4% with routine shunting, 1.6% with EEG-guided shunting, 2% without shunting and 4.8% with shunting guided by transcranial Doppler.Sources: Blume 1986; AbuRahma 2011
  • Which measure works varied with the anaesthetic. Spectral edge frequency captured ischaemia on isoflurane. Relative delta percentage was accurate on propofol.Source: Foreman and Claassen 2012
  • Asymmetry can be quantified. The brain symmetry index (BSI) measures the difference between the hemispheres from 0 to 1, and a change of 0.05 is regarded as significant. The pdBSI variant tracked NIHSS and infarct volume and distinguished infarction from TIA and controls. The study was small, done in awake patients, and required manual artefact removal by an expert.Sources: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016; Sheorajpanday 2009

The studies in detail:

van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 Blume 1986 AbuRahma 2011 Foreman and Claassen 2012 Sheorajpanday 2009

EEG and prognosis after cerebral infarction, SAH and cardiac arrest

Outside the operating theatre, the EEG is used to follow and predict the course after brain injury. Its value varies widely between conditions.

  • In cerebral infarction the EEG predicts only low to moderately well. Even so, outcome at one year was predicted correctly in 85% with the EEG, versus 60% with clinical criteria. In one study, delta power fell 100 minutes before clinical improvement after thrombolysis.Sources: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016; Foreman and Claassen 2012
  • In subarachnoid haemorrhage the EEG may warn of delayed cerebral ischaemia, but the evidence is weak. This concerns changes in the alpha/delta ratio. All the studies are small, and the authors themselves call for prospective validation.Source: Foreman and Claassen 2012
  • After cardiac arrest, the EEG at 12 and 24 hours says a lot about outcome. A continuous EEG at 12 hours, normal or diffusely slowed, predicted good outcome (specificity 91%). An isoelectric, low-amplitude EEG or burst suppression with identical bursts at 24 hours predicted poor outcome (specificity 100%, sensitivity 42%). Mild hypothermia barely affects the EEG, and usual propofol doses keep the EEG continuous. After anoxic injury, bursts are identical with abrupt transitions. With sedation they are heterogeneous.Source: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016
  • In dying patients the index may rise just before death. Processed EEG does not distinguish non-specific activation, seizures and EMG from organised activity. The findings concern dying patients, not prognosis in survivors.Source: Mashour 2024

The studies in detail:

van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 Foreman and Claassen 2012 Mashour 2024

What can mimic ischaemia, and the vulnerable brain

An EEG that looks ischaemic is not always ischaemia. Some brains show the patterns more easily than others, and more faintly.

  • Much can mimic ischaemia, so the raw EEG remains the gold standard. Seizures, changed intracranial pressure, systemic illness, sedatives, opioids and antipsychotics can confound interpretation. Normal slow-wave sleep can resemble ischaemia. Automatic artefact removal can mix ischaemic delta with slow activity from eye movements and drowsiness.Sources: Foreman and Claassen 2012; Sheorajpanday 2009
  • The algorithms lag behind. Processed BSR algorithms do not detect suppression until it reaches about 40%. Look at the raw EEG.Source: Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • The vulnerable brain develops burst suppression more easily. The risk rises with age and impaired neurological status, and in older patients the pattern is harder to detect. In septic encephalopathy, EEG slowing is the earliest finding. A metabolic theory, in which falling ATP causes burst suppression, fits with low perfusion producing the pattern, but is unproven.Source: Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • Raised ICP is poorly documented. A systematic review found only 4 studies that met the criteria. That the index may mistake raised ICP for deeper anaesthesia is a reasonable assumption, not a demonstrated finding (see the card on raised intracranial pressure).Source: Lenstra 2026

The studies in detail:

Foreman and Claassen 2012 Sheorajpanday 2009 Lobo and Lamperti 2025 Lenstra 2026

EEG and raised intracranial pressure: sparse evidence

  • Raised ICP probably affects the EEG through perfusion: Increased ICP lowers CPP and thereby CBF, and the cortex gets less oxygen and energy. The EEG changes are thus assumed to arise via CPP, CBF and metabolism (and possibly herniation), not from ICP itself. Neurogenic mechanisms may then dominate over vasomotor, chemical and metabolic ones in the regulation of CBF.Source: Lenstra 2026
  • The evidence is very sparse: Of 873 hits, only 4 studies met the criteria (adults with moderate to severe traumatic brain injury and ICP measured via ventricular drain or parenchymal probe). Three concerned post-traumatic seizures, one the direction between EEG and ICP. Larger studies are needed. The review does not say that a validated pattern is lacking, but that personalised EEG-ICP thresholds must be developed. Case reports, series, children and invasive EEG were excluded.Source: Lenstra 2026 (systematic review)
  • The EEG may precede ICP: In 21 patients (15 TBI, 6 SAH, a total of 1055 hours), changes ran from EEG to ICP on average 38% of the time (Granger causality), with a delay of 25–50 seconds, most often in relative alpha (12 patients). In one patient the direction was reversed. The authors interpret this as possible neurovascular coupling. The EEG was not examined during the intracranial hypertension episodes themselves, and sedation boluses did not change the finding.Source: Sanz-García 2018, cited in Lenstra 2026
  • Not everyone finds changes: In 17 intensive care patients with acute ICP rise, quantitative EEG showed no changes during the ICP peaks. There were only 30 minutes of EEG per patient, so late changes may have been missed.Source: McNamara 2003, cited in Lenstra 2026
  • Small series suggest the EEG can warn of deterioration: Cyclic patterns, varying degrees of slowing and attenuated fast activity often preceded clinical deterioration in intracranial hypertension. In presumed plateau waves, generalised rhythmic delta activity and loss of fast activity appeared about 30 minutes before clinical change (seven non-traumatic neurocritical patients, retrospective). In two patients with herniation, increased low-frequency power and asymmetry in the spectrogram appeared roughly an hour before clinical deterioration. These fall outside the review's criteria.Sources: Sheikh 2022 (J Clin Neurophysiol); Alsallom 2022
  • In an animal study, EEG power tracked ICP: The median cross-correlation between total EEG power and ICP was 0.7, and 0.55 for CPP. A model with only three variables had accuracy 0.70, sensitivity 0.53 and specificity 0.79. The direction of the correlation is not stated.Source: Pose (pilot study)
  • No source tests indices and the spectrogram with raised ICP under general anaesthesia: ICP changes, sedatives and sleep can confound EEG interpretation. Intracranial hypertension is one of the causes of reduced cerebral oxygen delivery, and such changes can resemble deeper sedation on frontal EEG, but Guay 2025 shows no data from patients with raised ICP. That processed indices may confuse them with deeper anaesthesia is therefore a reasonable assumption, not a demonstrated finding for ICP.Sources: Foreman and Claassen 2012; Guay 2025
Lenstra 2026, Sheikh 2022, McNamara 2003 and Pose
The studies in detail: van Putten and Hofmeijer, Foreman and Claassen, Sheorajpanday, Mashour 2024 and Lobo and Lamperti (9 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

What ischaemia does to the EEG (van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016)

  • Energy: the brain accounts for about 20% of the body's energy requirement. In the cortex about 40% of ATP goes to the resting membrane potential and action potentials, and about 35% to synaptic transmission. The rhythms in the EEG arise from summed postsynaptic current in the pyramidal cells, and action potentials contribute little.
  • Normal blood flow is about 750 ml/min, 15–20% of cardiac output, or 50–54 ml/100 g/min.
  • Mild to moderate ischaemia (15–35 ml/100 g/min): it is primarily synaptic transmission that fails. The neurons retain their membrane potential, and CT and MRI are normal. The EEG shows less alpha and beta, then more delta, depending on severity and duration. In severe cases the EEG can become isoelectric, and even an isoelectric EEG can be due to isolated synaptic failure and be reversible.
  • Below 10 ml/100 g/min: the membrane potential shifts towards the Donnan potential (about −15 to −20 mV), and cytotoxic oedema and cell death follow. The EEG rhythms then disappear permanently. Lack of energy for more than 5–8 minutes produces such changes.
  • How fast: a few minutes without blood flow produce synaptic failure with full recovery when perfusion returns. In circulatory arrest the EEG becomes isoelectric within 10–40 seconds. In figure 1 (syncope), slower rhythms appear after a few seconds and clear slowing around 20 seconds after the arrest.
  • Inhibitory neurons are probably more vulnerable than excitatory ones. This may explain increased synchronisation and generalised periodic discharges in severe hypoxic injury.
van Putten and Hofmeijer. J Clin Neurophysiol 2016;33:203–210

EEG in carotid surgery

  • During test clamping of the internal carotid artery, reduced fast activity (often followed by more slow activity) reflects reduced blood flow. In figure 3, loss of fast activity alone corresponds to a CBF in the ipsilateral hemisphere of about 25–35 ml/100 g/min, and loss of fast activity plus more delta to about 15. These figures are taken from Foreman and Claassen and were not measured in the study.
  • Which changes require a shunt is debated. In a study of 57 patients (Blume 1986), moderate changes (8–13 Hz retained, but an amplitude fall of 50% or more and increased delta above 1 Hz) did not lead to postoperative stroke. Major changes (8–13 Hz reduced to minimal or absent, and a doubling of delta) led to stroke in 2 of 22. Most neurophysiologists nevertheless recommend a shunt for any change, and the authors consider that a fall in alpha/beta amplitude of about 10% can probably be accepted.
  • Perioperative stroke rate in a review (AbuRahma 2011): 1.4% with routine shunting, 1.6% with selective shunting guided by EEG and 2% without shunting. With shunting guided by transcranial Doppler it was 4.8% versus 1.6% with EEG. In the authors' own hospitals a shunt was used in about 3–5%.
  • EEG is not sensitive to deep structures, but preserved cortical rhythms are regarded as a reliable indicator of adequate blood flow deep down as well. This is because reduced flow usually produces a corresponding fraction in cortex and deep structures, and because the cortex has the greatest energy requirement.
  • Quantitative: the brain symmetry index (BSI) measures spectral asymmetry between the hemispheres on a scale from 0 to 1, with normal values of 0.05–0.08. A change of 0.05 is regarded as significant and agrees well with visual assessment. Temporal BSI captures global changes over time.
van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 (Blume 1986, AbuRahma 2011)

EEG in acute cerebral infarction

  • The predictive value of EEG for outcome after cerebral infarction is low to moderate. In a study of 110 patients, pdBSI and the (delta + theta)/(alpha + beta) ratio correlated with mRS at 6 months with a Spearman rho of about 0.46–0.47.
  • Continuous quantitative EEG with BSI correlated well with NIHSS in hemispheric infarction and was used to follow the effect of thrombolysis.
  • Spreading depolarisation occurs in acute infarction and may contribute to growth of the injury, but is difficult to measure through an intact skull. So far it has only been demonstrated reliably with electrocorticography.
van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016

EEG after cardiac arrest

  • About half of comatose patients after cardiac arrest have a poor outcome. SSEP and pupillary and corneal reflexes at 72 hours capture only about 20% of those who do not recover.
  • Continuous, normal or diffusely slowed EEG at 12 hours predicted good outcome (CPC 1–2) with specificity 91%, sensitivity 55%, PPV 84% and NPV 70%. Isoelectric, low-voltage (below 20 μV) or burst suppression with identical bursts at 24 hours predicted poor outcome (CPC 3–5) with specificity 100%, sensitivity 42%, PPV 100% and NPV 55%. The figures are based on two prospective cohorts with a total of 377 patients, all treated with mild therapeutic hypothermia and sedated.
  • Evolution towards continuous physiological EEG within 12 hours gives a very good prognosis. The patient's further prognosis then depends on injury to other organs, and the patients with favourable EEG and poor outcome died of failure of other organs, particularly the heart. Deep coma in the first hours does not rule out full recovery.
  • The authors call it a persistent misconception that EEG cannot be used during hypothermia or sedation. Mild hypothermia to 32 °C barely affects the EEG. At usual propofol doses the EEG remains continuous with anteriorisation of alpha, and isoelectricity does not occur.
  • Sedation-induced versus pathological burst suppression: in a relatively healthy brain the bursts are heterogeneous, and they come and go gradually. In postanoxic injury the bursts are identical, the intervals between them are flat, and the transitions between suppression and burst are abrupt. The latter has a poor prognosis.
  • The cerebral recovery index (CRI) combines five quantitative features (mean amplitude, alpha/delta ratio, entropy, coherence and continuity) into one number between 0 and 1. In the patient with good outcome CRI was about 0.7 at 24 hours, and in the patient with poor outcome about 0.3. In the first hours the EEG was almost identical in both.
  • The authors point out that recent guidelines do not include early EEG for prognostication, and expect EEG to be included in future guidelines. Interpretation of reactivity is not simple, and inter-rater agreement is only moderate.
van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016

Consciousness and the dying brain (Mashour 2024)

Narrative review (Anesthesiology 2024;140:1221–1231; Mashour, Lee, Pal and Li) on near-death experiences and EEG around cardiac arrest and death.

  • Incidence: 10–20 % of survivors of in-hospital cardiac arrest report near-death experiences. In AWARE II, 21.4 % of 28 interviewed patients had a “transcendent recalled experience of death”.
  • The indices just before death: in seven critically ill patients without brain injury, BIS and SedLine values rose to levels consistent with consciousness just before death, after withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment. In a follow-up, 13 of 28 (46 %) had such a surge, while none of seven brain-dead patients did. Other series have not found this.
  • Why the indices cannot be read as consciousness: processed EEG cannot distinguish non-specific activation (for example glutamate release as hypoxic neurones die) from organised activity, cannot distinguish wakefulness from seizures, has only frontal electrodes, and EMG is hard to exclude completely.
  • Animal studies: in rats, a brief surge of gamma and theta with increased coupling between cortical regions occurred within 30 seconds of cardiac arrest. During asphyxia, release of many neurotransmitters increased; serotonin rose more than 20-fold within 2 minutes.
  • Humans: in 2 of 4 dying comatose patients, beta and gamma increased after the ventilator was disconnected. Both had a history of seizures, so seizure activity cannot be excluded. In a study of 8 patients, EEG ceased a median 78 seconds before circulatory arrest. None of the findings is linked to an actual experience.
  • During CPR: in AWARE II, SedLine gave interpretable EEG in 53 of 85 during ongoing CPR, and near-normal activity was seen up to 35–60 minutes into CPR. Detailed analysis has not been published.
  • Isoelectric is not always final: in animal models the isoelectric phase can be reversed by rapid reoxygenation, and the authors do not exclude that experiences may arise while the brain recovers.
  • Relevance and caveats: anaesthesia staff take part in CPR, organ donation and withdrawal of treatment. The authors reject non-neurobiological explanations. Funded by NIH, no competing interests. Note that the findings concern dying patients, not prognosis in survivors.
Mashour, Lee, Pal and Li. Anesthesiology 2024;140:1221–1231

Quantitative EEG, CBF and CPP (Foreman and Claassen 2012)

  • Thresholds: when CBF falls to about 25–35 ml/100 g/min, the EEG first loses fast frequencies. At about 17–18 slow frequencies increase gradually, and the authors call this a critical ischaemic threshold at which neurons begin to lose transmembrane gradients. At 10–12 ml/100 g/min and below the EEG becomes silent, and the cell injury is irreversible.
  • How fast: during carotid clamping the changes occur within about 20 seconds and are reversible. Infarction may only appear after hours at this flow level. Quantitative EEG (qEEG) captures changes in blood flow and metabolism within 28–104 seconds. Diffusion-weighted MRI detects changes at CBF 35–40 after about 30 minutes, whereas EEG detects them within seconds.
  • CPP: the mean frequency in the EEG falls when CPP is below 60 mmHg, also in comatose or sedated patients (Diedler 2009, according to the review). More slow activity (delta and theta) and less fast activity (alpha and beta) follow reduced cerebral oxygen metabolism (CMRO₂).
  • Which measure works: in carotid surgery, spectral edge frequency (SEF) captured ischaemic changes in patients on isoflurane, whereas relative delta percentage (delta/total power) was accurate in patients on propofol. Overall, relative delta percentage gives the most robust correlation with CBF and metabolism in focal ischaemia.
  • Confounding factors: seizures and periodic discharges, changes in intracranial pressure (for example acute hydrocephalus), systemic disease, sedatives, opioids and antipsychotics. Normal slow-wave sleep can resemble ischaemic changes. Raw EEG remains the gold standard, and any qEEG algorithm should be checkable against the raw EEG by someone who knows EEG.
  • The spectrogram (compressed spectral array) gives, according to the authors, the highest ratio of pixels to data and is easy to read, compared with raw EEG.
  • The review does not discuss the operating room beyond carotid surgery. Most of the review concerns intensive care patients. The suggestion of use after high-risk vascular and cardiac surgery, in refractory hypotension and in sepsis is the authors' own, and not documented in studies.
Foreman and Claassen. Crit Care 2012;16:216

EEG in cerebral infarction and subarachnoid haemorrhage

  • Infarction: in the early subacute phase the EEG correlates well with CBF while oxygen extraction increases (“misery perfusion”). Later it correlates more with CMRO₂ (“luxury perfusion”). Loss of reactivity and absent sleep-wake cycling suggest a poor prognosis. Absence of delta or presence of faster frequencies within 24 hours belongs to good outcome. Regional attenuation of fast frequencies without delta (RAWOD) suggests severe early CBF loss (mean 8.6 ml/100 g/min), and in one series mortality was up to 67%.
  • One year after infarction, functional outcome was predicted correctly in 60% of cases with clinical criteria. With EEG this increased to 85%.
  • After thrombolysis, delta power fell 100 minutes before clinical improvement in one study.
  • Delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) after SAH: occurs in 20–40%. Daily transcranial Doppler is about 60–70% sensitive. In the table of studies: in 34 comatose patients, a change of 10% in the alpha/delta ratio over 6 minutes gave sensitivity 100% and specificity 76%, and a change of 50% over one minute gave 89% and 84%. In 12 patients, sensitivity for predicting neurological deterioration increased from 40% with clinical assessment alone to 67% with qEEG (specificity 73%). In one study, relative alpha variability fell in all 19 with vasospasm, on average 2.9 days before vasospasm was confirmed, but also in 7 without vasospasm, mainly because of infarction or increased ICP.
  • All the studies are small, and the authors themselves point out that the findings must be validated prospectively and in randomised trials.
Foreman and Claassen 2012

Asymmetry and reproducibility in ischaemia (Sheorajpanday 2009)

  • Design: exploratory, methodological study in 41 patients: 21 with cerebral infarction (median NIHSS 11, mean DWI volume 79 ml), 10 with TIA and 10 controls aged 55 years or more with subjective memory complaints and normal MRI. One EEG per patient, awake with eyes closed for at least 10 minutes, 19 electrodes with impedance below 5 kΩ. 128 seconds free of artefacts were analysed after visual artefact removal. The study was not done under anaesthesia.
  • pdBSI: a variant of the brain symmetry index that compares the power spectrum between homologous channel pairs (8 pairs, 1–25 Hz), instead of the average for the whole hemisphere.
  • Reproducibility: minimum Cronbach's alpha was 0.95–0.99 for standard spectral measures and 0.96–0.99 for pdBSI, both within the same recording and between and within raters. The authors say that visual artefact removal by a skilled person is a critical first step that cannot be replaced by automatic artefact removal. Automation can confuse ischaemic delta with slow activity from eye movements and drowsiness.
  • Clinical correlation: pdBSI correlated with NIHSS (rho 0.64–0.70) and with DWI volume (rho 0.79–0.84). Standard measures such as relative alpha and the delta/alpha ratio correlated moderately with NIHSS, but not significantly with DWI volume after adjustment for multiple testing.
  • Group difference: pdBSI distinguished infarction from TIA and controls. The standard measures did not after adjustment. Neither pdBSI nor the standard measures could distinguish TIA from controls.
  • Broad frequency bands: pdBSI over 1–25 Hz was better than narrower bands, and 1–3 Hz alone was not significant. The authors interpret this as the whole frequency range being affected in acute ischaemia.
  • Relative measures: the authors used relative power, because absolute power is affected by skull thickness. The skull is on average about 80 times less conductive than brain and scalp, and a 10% thinner skull can produce a change of 800% in amplitude.
  • Caveats: small study, one recording per patient, and no ambition of diagnostic value for individual patients. Asymmetry measures are not specific for ischaemia, and pdBSI will not detect equal injury on both sides of a channel pair.
Sheorajpanday et al. Clin Neurophysiol 2009;120:845–855

EEG in pathology, age and the vulnerable brain

  • Septic encephalopathy: EEG slowing is the earliest finding and can be seen even with a normal neurological examination. The chapter also mentions increased theta, dominant delta, triphasic waves, periodic epileptiform discharges and suppression.
  • Burst suppression: the risk increases with age and with impaired neurological status. In older patients the bursts and suppression phases are less distinct, and the pattern is difficult to detect.
  • High-dose ketamine does not itself produce burst suppression, but can lower the threshold. Pain and nociceptive input can also lower the threshold.
  • Processed BSR algorithms do not pick up suppression until it is around 40%. The chapter therefore recommends assessing the raw EEG.
  • Two theories explain burst suppression: cortical hyperexcitability, and a metabolic theory in which falling ATP opens ATP-gated potassium channels. The metabolic theory fits with findings that low perfusion can produce burst suppression, but it is not proven.
  • ENGAGES did not change the incidence of delirium, but found lower 30-day mortality in the EEG group. The book calls this an observation that should be investigated further.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 1, 5 and 11

The physiology behind perfusion and the EEG

  • The EEG reflects the brain’s energy use: About 60% of the brain’s energy goes to the signalling the EEG measures, and most anaesthetic drugs suppress only this part. Once the EEG is flat, more drug does not lower energy use further and gives no further protection. (see “The EEG reflects the brain’s energy use”)
  • The Lassen curve is outdated: The autoregulatory plateau is narrower than assumed, and the lower limit in healthy people ranged from 57 to 91 mmHg. Without an autoregulation monitor, 70 mmHg is a reasonable limit in most people. (see “Autoregulation: narrower and more individual than the Lassen curve”)
  • Autoregulation can be impaired: Hypercapnia impairs it, and during hypercapnia propofol preserves it whereas sevoflurane impairs or abolishes it. The reserve is reduced with CNS injury, an incomplete circle of Willis and hypertension. (see “Autoregulation: narrower and more individual than the Lassen curve”)
  • Optimise volume before vasopressor, and account for head height: Low cardiac output probably adds to low MAP in hypotension, and bolus phenylephrine can lower cardiac output. With the head raised, MAP at the heart must be about 85 mmHg to keep CPP at 60–65 mmHg. (see “What governs blood flow: CO₂, cardiac output, vasopressors and head height”)
  • Physiological control matters more than deeper anaesthesia: EEG signs of ischaemia appear from about 20 ml/100 g/min, and inducing burst suppression to protect the brain is not supported in anaesthetised patients. (see “Thresholds and neuroprotection: physiology before depth”)

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

The EEG reflects the brain’s energy use

The brain uses energy for two things: signalling between nerve cells, which is the electrical activity the EEG measures (about 60%), and “housekeeping” that keeps the cells alive. This is why the EEG and energy use track each other under anaesthesia.Source: Patel et al. 2025

  • Anaesthetic drugs suppress only the signalling. Barbiturates, isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane, propofol and etomidate lower oxygen consumption as the EEG becomes quieter. Once the EEG is flat, signalling is already switched off. More drug then does not lower energy use further. Ketamine and nitrous oxide do not follow this pattern.Source: Patel et al. 2025
  • Cold lowers energy use even after the EEG is flat. For every degree the temperature falls, energy use falls by 6–7%. Cold also lowers “housekeeping”. Anaesthetic drugs do not.Source: Patel et al. 2025
  • The drugs affect blood flow differently. Propofol lowered regional blood flow by 53–79% at surgical depth, and autoregulation and CO₂ response were preserved even during burst suppression. Ketamine is the only one that increases both energy use and blood flow. Volatile agents lower energy use but are also direct vasodilators: at 0.5 MAC blood flow falls, at 1 MAC it is unchanged, and above 1 MAC it rises.Source: Patel et al. 2025
  • Burst suppression is not the same with all drugs. At full suppression oxygen consumption is about the same. Barbiturates lower it evenly throughout the brain, whereas isoflurane and sevoflurane lower it most in the neocortex. The choice of drug can also affect whether SSEP monitoring works (interpretation based on the sources).Source: Patel et al. 2025

The studies in detail:

Patel et al. 2025

Autoregulation: narrower and more individual than the Lassen curve

The classical picture is that blood flow is held constant at MAP between about 60 and 160 mmHg. This picture, the old Lassen curve, is now regarded as outdated (“outmoded”).Sources: Lobo and Lamperti 2025; Patel et al. 2025

  • The plateau is narrower than assumed. It is short and slopes slightly. With rapid pressure changes it can be as short as 10 mmHg or absent altogether. With slow changes it is at least ±20 mmHg. Autoregulation is best described as a family of curves, not one.Source: Patel et al. 2025
  • The lower limit varies widely, but 70 mmHg is a reasonable limit. In awake, healthy people the mean lower limit was 57–91 mmHg, with enormous variation. The authors' assessment is that in most people the limit is not below 70 mmHg. Without an autoregulation monitor, 70 mmHg is therefore a reasonable limit.Source: Patel et al. 2025 (seven studies)
  • Brief hypotension is usually tolerated; a sustained fall is not. The brain can increase oxygen extraction. Blood flow can therefore fall by 50–60% before compensation fails. In awake people, symptoms of ischaemia appear only when blood flow has fallen by 35–40%.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti 2025; Patel et al. 2025
  • Autoregulation can be impaired. Hypercapnia impairs it. During hypercapnia propofol preserves it, whereas sevoflurane impairs or abolishes it. The reserve is reduced with CNS injury, an incomplete circle of Willis (35–40% of the population) and hypertension. In hypertensive patients autoregulation is nevertheless preserved, and treatment to normal pressure does not lower blood flow.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti 2025; Patel et al. 2025

The studies in detail:

Patel et al. 2025 Lobo and Lamperti 2025

What governs blood flow: CO₂, cardiac output, vasopressors and head height

Blood pressure is only one of several factors that determine how much blood the brain receives. CO₂, oxygen, cardiac output, choice of vasopressor and head height all play a part.

  • CO₂ changes blood flow a lot; oxygen only when it is low. Blood flow changes by 1–2 ml/100 g/min per mmHg PaCO₂ between 25 and 70 mmHg, but hypotension impairs the CO₂ response. Hypocapnia widens the autoregulatory range, hypercapnia narrows it. PaO₂ has little effect between 60 and 300 mmHg, but below 60 blood flow rises rapidly.Source: Patel et al. 2025
  • Optimise volume first. Low cardiac output probably adds to low MAP in hypotension. Whether cardiac output affects blood flow independently of MAP and PaCO₂ is uncertain: one estimate is that a 30% fall in cardiac output gives about a 10% fall in blood flow, but a meta-analysis does not confirm an independent association.Sources: Patel et al. 2025; Meng
  • A vasopressor alone can lower cardiac output. Phenylephrine and noradrenaline do not change global blood flow when autoregulation is intact. Bolus phenylephrine can lower cardiac output further and slightly lowered the NIRS value in several studies. Ephedrine did not. Outcome studies are lacking.Sources: Patel et al. 2025; Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • With the head raised, a higher MAP is needed at the heart. Pressure at the brain falls by about 2 mmHg per 2.5 cm the head is above the heart. To keep CPP at 60–65 mmHg with the head raised, MAP at the heart must be about 85 mmHg. Intracranial pressure is also affected by positioning, by head rotation that compresses the jugular veins, and by PEEP that impedes venous drainage.Sources: Patel et al. 2025; Lobo and Lamperti 2025

The studies in detail:

Patel et al. 2025 Meng Lobo and Lamperti 2025

Thresholds and neuroprotection: physiology before depth

The blood flow thresholds explain when the EEG changes. Deeper anaesthesia is not a shortcut to brain protection.

  • The EEG shows ischaemia from about 20 ml/100 g/min. Normal blood flow is about 50 ml/100 g/min. Symptoms appear in awake subjects at about 30, EEG signs of ischaemia from about 20, and the cortical EEG becomes isoelectric at about 15. The SSEP amplitude also changes at about 15. Between 10 and 20 the dysfunction is reversible if blood flow is restored. The data are mainly from animal studies and vary with drug and species.Sources: Patel et al. 2025; Lobo and Lamperti 2025 (SSEP)
  • A suppressed EEG is not always perfusion or depth. At a blood glucose around 2.2 mmol/L the EEG shows slowing: it shifts from alpha and beta towards delta and theta. Below about 1.1 mmol/L it becomes flat.Source: Patel et al. 2025
  • Burst suppression does not protect. Anaesthetic drugs protect in animal models, but only in mild ischaemia and not lastingly. In patients, neither drugs given to EEG suppression nor general anaesthesia (versus local anaesthesia in carotid surgery) improved outcome. Physiological control of CPP, oxygenation, normocapnia, temperature, glucose and seizures matters more.Sources: Patel et al. 2025; IHAST; GALA
  • Seizures increase energy demand, and the EEG may be the only sign. Seizure activity can increase energy use by up to 400%. In a paralysed patient the EEG is the only way to detect it. Sevoflurane at high concentrations can cause seizures at induction in children.Source: Patel et al. 2025

Figure: where on the CBF scale EEG and the cells fail

Patel et al. 2025 · van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 · Foreman and Claassen via van Putten
The studies in detail: Lobo and Lamperti and Patel et al. 2025 on normal values, autoregulation, CO₂ and cardiac output, anaesthetic drugs, epileptogenic drugs, thresholds and SSEP (8 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Perfusion, CPP and autoregulation

  • Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is MAP minus intracranial pressure (ICP). Blood flow (CBF) is CPP divided by cerebrovascular resistance.
  • ICP is affected by volume inside the skull (tumour, oedema, haemorrhage, increased CSF volume), by positioning (for example Trendelenburg), by rotation of the head that compresses the jugular veins, and by high intrathoracic pressure and PEEP that impede venous drainage.
  • With intact autoregulation, MAP between approximately 60 and 160 mmHg does not affect CBF, which is kept at around 50 ml/100 g/min. When autoregulation fails, blood flow follows pressure passively.
  • CBF can fall by 50–60% before compensation fails, because the brain then increases oxygen extraction.
  • Cerebrovascular resistance is affected by vasopressors and vasodilators, by PaCO₂, and can be shifted by chronic hypertension. Treating low blood pressure with a vasopressor alone can reduce cardiac output.
  • Hypercapnia impairs autoregulation, and the anaesthetic agents play a part: propofol preserves it during hypercapnia, whereas sevoflurane at a corresponding PaCO₂ impairs or abolishes it.
  • The brain is about 2% of body weight, but receives 12–15% of cardiac output and uses up to 20% of the oxygen. Approximately 75–80% of oxygen consumption goes to restoring the membrane potential.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 1, 2 and 7

Patel et al. 2025: cerebral physiology and the anaesthetic drugs (Patel, Drummond and Lemkuil)

Normal values, energy use and why EEG and CMR go together

  • Normal values (Miller's box 10.1): the brain is only about 2% of body weight but receives 12–15% of cardiac output. The values below are for adults. “Per 100 g” means per 100 grams of brain tissue.
    MeasureWhat it isNormal
    CBF, whole brainCerebral blood flow45–55 ml/100 g/min
    CBF, cortexGrey matter uses most energy and receives most blood75–80 ml/100 g/min
    CBF, below the cortexLess active tissue receives less blood8–20 ml/100 g/min
    CMRO₂Cerebral oxygen consumption3–3.5 ml O₂/100 g/min
    rSO₂Regional oxygen saturation in brain tissue, measured with NIRS on the forehead55–80%
    SjVO₂Oxygen saturation of venous blood leaving the brain (jugular bulb)60–70%
    ICPPressure inside the skull, supine8–12 mmHg
  • The brain uses energy for two things: about 60% goes to signalling between neurons, that is, the electrical activity the EEG measures. The rest goes to keeping the cells alive and maintained (“housekeeping”).
