Anaesthetic drugs such as barbiturates, isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane, propofol and etomidate dampen only the signalling. The quieter the EEG becomes, the less oxygen the brain uses. When the EEG is flat, signalling is already switched off, and more drug does not lower energy use further (fig. 10.2). Ketamine and nitrous oxide do not follow this pattern.
  • Cooling acts on both parts: for every degree the body temperature falls, the brain's energy use falls by 6–7%. The EEG becomes flat at about 18–20 °C, and at 18 °C oxygen consumption is below 10% of normal. Because cold also lowers “housekeeping”, cooling reduces energy use further even after the EEG is flat. Anaesthetic drugs do not.
  • Burst suppression is not the same with all drugs: when the EEG is completely suppressed, cerebral oxygen consumption is about the same whichever drug is used, but it is distributed differently. Barbiturates lower blood flow and energy use evenly throughout the brain, while isoflurane and sevoflurane lower it most in the outer cortex (neocortex). The burst-suppression pattern just before the EEG becomes completely flat also varies from drug to drug.
  • Relevance for neuromonitoring: SSEPs (somatosensory evoked potentials) are the cortex's response to stimulation of a nerve in an arm or leg, and are used to monitor the spinal cord and brain during surgery. With thiopental, SSEPs can still be recorded at doses far beyond those giving a flat EEG, but with isoflurane in burst suppression (about 1.5 MAC) they are hard to elicit. The choice of agent can therefore affect whether neuromonitoring works (interpretation based on the sources).
  • What it means for EEG interpretation: a very low index or a flat EEG means the drug has already lowered the brain's energy use as much as it can. More dose gives no more protection of the brain. That is the background for the cards on overdose and burst suppression in the Spectrogram and Agents tabs.
Patel et al. 2025, box 10.1 and fig. 10.2

Autoregulation: the Lassen curve is outdated, the lower limit is around 70 mmHg in most people

  • The classical picture (CBF constant at 50 ml/100 g/min from MAP 50 to 150) was built on a heterogeneous sample with single measurements, and the chapter calls it “outmoded”. Newer analyses give a narrower plateau with a gentle upslope, so pressure-passive CBF applies over a wider MAP range than assumed. With rapid pressure changes (dynamic autoregulation) the plateau may be as short as 10 mmHg or absent; with slow changes over about 10 minutes (static) the plateau is at least ±20 mmHg.
  • Lower limit (LLA): across seven studies in awake, healthy subjects the mean LLA ranged from 57 to 91 mmHg, with enormous inter-subject variability. The authors (Drummond) hold that the LLA in the majority is not below 70 mmHg, which with normal ICP (5–10) gives a CPP of 60–65 mmHg, and that 70 mmHg is a prudent threshold without an autoregulation monitor. Upper limit: about 90 mmHg on cardiopulmonary bypass, probably above 140 in hypertensives. Autoregulation is best described as a family of curves (fig. 10.5), not one.
  • Reserve: symptoms of ischaemia appear only when CBF has fallen 35–40% in awake subjects. This cerebrovascular reserve means that brief hypotension below the LLA is usually tolerated; sustained falls are not. Reserve is reduced with CNS injury (autoregulation impaired for about 2 weeks, restored after 1–3 months), raised local tissue pressure (ICP, retractors, cervical stenosis), an incomplete circle of Willis (35–40% of the population) and hypertension.
  • Hypertension: both dynamic and static autoregulation are preserved in hypertensives, and treatment to normal pressure does not reduce CBF. The intraoperative question is hypotension: the authors limit the MAP fall to no more than 20% below baseline measured at head level in the sitting position, in the section on chronic hypertension they give 30–35%, and state that a 25% fall brings both normo- and hypertensive patients to the LLA. See the discrepancy list.
  • Hydrostatic gradient: 2 mmHg per inch (2.5 cm) the head is above the heart; 12 inches give about 24 mmHg. To keep CPP at 60–65 with the head elevated, MAP at heart level must be about 85. The siphon model (closed loop) is rejected: gravity does affect CPP. See the card on perfusion pressure and head height.
  • Practical MAP target: in patients without acute ischaemia and with normal or well-controlled pressure the chapter regards an intraoperative MAP of about 75 mmHg as adequate, and table 10.2 lists subspecialty targets in brain injury (for example SBP above 100–110 in traumatic brain injury depending on age, MAP above 65 after cardiac arrest).
Patel et al. 2025, fig. 10.3–10.5, table 10.2

CO₂, O₂, cardiac output and vasopressors

  • PaCO₂: CBF changes 1–2 ml/100 g/min per mmHg within 25–70 mmHg; the response is attenuated below 25 and above 75–80. Moderate hypotension (MAP fall under 33%) attenuates the CO₂ response markedly, severe hypotension (about 66%) abolishes it. Hypocapnia widens the autoregulatory range, hypercapnia narrows it. The effect of a changed PaCO₂ wanes over 6–8 hours as CSF pH normalises; abrupt normalisation after prolonged hyperventilation gives CSF acidosis and increased CBF/ICP.
  • PaO₂: little effect between 60 and 300 mmHg; below 60 CBF rises rapidly, linearly with falling saturation. Haemodilution gives a smaller CBF rise than hypoxaemia for the same fall in O₂ content. 1 atm oxygen lowers CBF by about 18%.
  • Cardiac output: Meng estimates that a 30% fall in CO gives about a 10% fall in CBF independent of MAP and PaCO₂; a newer study found that a 10% fall in MAP and a 20% fall in CO gave the same fall (about 5%) in MCA velocity. A meta-analysis nevertheless does not confirm an independent relationship, because CO cannot be changed without changing MAP and PaCO₂. The chapter still concludes that low CO probably adds to low MAP in hypotension, that volume should be optimised first, and that bolus phenylephrine may lower CO further. See the Nordum 2024 card (Trendelenburg) and the clinical example with alpha and cardiac output.
  • Vasopressors: α₁-agonists (phenylephrine, noradrenaline) do not change global CBF in humans when autoregulation is intact; they act via MAP. Bolus phenylephrine slightly lowered NIRS-measured SCO₂ in several studies, ephedrine did not, probably because ephedrine maintains CO; extracranial contamination of NIRS exceeds this difference. Koch found that ephedrine, not phenylephrine, increased local CBF, tissue oxygenation and microcirculation in brain-tumour patients. Outcome studies are lacking. Dexmedetomidine lowers CBF 25–30% via CMR; dopamine up to 100 µg/kg/min does not cause cerebral vasoconstriction; dobutamine increased CBF and CMR by 20 and 30%.
Patel et al. 2025, fig. 10.8–10.10, table 10.3

What the anaesthetic drugs do to CBF and CMR

  • Intravenous agents preserve flow–metabolism coupling, autoregulation and CO₂ responsiveness. Propofol lowered regional CBF 53–79% and whole-brain glucose metabolism 48–58% at surgical depth in volunteers; autoregulation and CO₂ response are preserved even at burst suppression. Etomidate 0.2 mg/kg: CBF −34%, CMR −45%. Midazolam 0.15 mg/kg: CBF −30 to −34% (−12% globally with PET). Opioids: small reductions in the unstimulated brain; sedative remifentanil can increase CBF regionally; a bolus with a MAP fall can raise ICP through autoregulatory vasodilation. Flumazenil can give an overshoot in CBF/ICP in patients with poor intracranial compliance.
  • Ketamine is the only one that increases CMR and CBF: subanaesthetic doses (0.2–0.3 mg/kg) increased global CMR by about 25%, most in frontal and anterior cingulate cortex; S-ketamine increases CMR, R-ketamine lowers it. CBF rose 14% (subanaesthetic) and 36% (anaesthetic) without a change in CMRO₂ in one study; CBV +50%. Propofol, benzodiazepines and isoflurane blunt or abolish the ICP rise, and systematic reviews find no ICP rise in head injury. See the ketamine cards in the Agents tab for the EEG pattern.
  • Volatile agents: lower CMR dose-dependently but are also direct vasodilators. Net: at 0.5 MAC CBF falls, at 1 MAC it is unchanged, above 1 MAC it rises (“luxury perfusion”), and autoregulation to rising pressure is impaired. Vasodilating potency: halothane ≫ enflurane > desflurane ≈ isoflurane > sevoflurane. At 1 MAC sevoflurane and desflurane lowered CBF by 38 and 22% and CMR by 39 and 35% (Kety–Schmidt, cortical measurement); PET shows about 50% for both. Maximal CMR reduction is reached at EEG suppression, at 1.5–2 MAC. Sevoflurane lowers regional CBF but not CBV; propofol lowers both. If CMR is already suppressed (for example by propofol), the vasodilation is unmasked: adding a volatile agent then clearly increases CBF.
  • Entropy and sevoflurane: in a dose-escalation study in humans the largest reduction in entropy was at 1 MAC sevoflurane, with smaller reductions at higher concentrations. This fits with CMRO₂ falling sharply with the onset of the anaesthetic EEG pattern and more slowly thereafter.
  • Nitrous oxide increases CBF, CMR and ICP, most alone or with a volatile agent (0.75 MAC isoflurane + 65% N₂O gave 43% higher CBF than 1.5 MAC isoflurane); with intravenous agents the effect is blunted. CBV is little affected.
  • Lidocaine: 5 mg/kg over 30 min + 45 µg/kg/min lowered CBF 24% and CMR 20% in awake volunteers; membrane stabilisation is thought to lower the energy needed for membrane integrity. A 1.5 mg/kg bolus was as effective as thiopental 3 mg/kg against the ICP rise at pin placement, with less MAP fall. After a 2 mg/kg bolus peak concentrations are 6.6–8.5 µg/mL, below the seizure threshold (above 5–10 µg/mL in awake subjects); lidocaine seizures have not been reported in anaesthetised patients. See the card on multimodal anaesthesia in the Agents tab.
  • Neuromuscular blockers have no direct cerebrovascular effect beyond histamine release; succinylcholine can raise ICP by about 5 mmHg as an arousal phenomenon under light anaesthesia, blocked by deep anaesthesia or defasciculation.
Patel et al. 2025, fig. 10.12–10.19

Epileptogenic drugs according to Patel et al. 2025

  • Sevoflurane: seizures at induction with high concentrations in children, also without a known predisposition. In two healthy volunteers burst suppression at 2 MAC was accompanied by epileptiform discharges with a clear CBF increase (coupling preserved). In patients with temporal lobe epilepsy 1.5 MAC produced widespread paroxysmal activity that was not confined to the focus and did not help localisation. Tonic–clonic movements at emergence have been reported in healthy patients. No sequelae documented; caution in epilepsy. See the card on epileptiform activity and images 19–20 in the Spectrogram tab.
  • Etomidate often causes myoclonus without epileptiform EEG, but can trigger generalised epileptic activity in epileptics; 0.1 mg/kg is used to activate a quiescent focus intraoperatively. Methohexital activates foci. Ketamine can trigger seizures in predisposed patients, with subcortical activity not always seen in surface EEG, but is also used for refractory status (effective in 56%). Propofol is not confirmed as proconvulsant and shortens ECT seizures; high-amplitude beta is described. Opioids: high-dose fentanyl produced electrical seizure activity in 8 of 9 patients with partial complex seizures during temporal lobe surgery; alfentanil 50 µg/kg augmented spikes in temporal lobe epilepsy. Isoflurane gives spikes and myoclonus but is not regarded as epileptogenic and is used for refractory status. Enflurane is epileptogenic, potentiated by hypocapnia.
  • Why it belongs in an EEG app: seizure activity can raise CMR by up to 400%, and in a paralysed patient the EEG is the only way to detect it.
Patel et al. 2025, section Epileptogenesis

CBF thresholds (fig. 10.20), hypoglycaemia and neuroprotection

  • Thresholds: normal CBF about 50 ml/100 g/min. Symptoms of hypoperfusion in awake subjects only at about 30. EEG evidence of ischaemia from about 20. Isoelectric cortical EEG at about 15. Penumbra 10–20: reversible dysfunction, but cell death if flow is not restored. Signs of irreversible membrane failure (extracellular potassium, lost direct cortical response) only at about 6–10 (the legend says 6–12). The data are from the cortex of barbiturate-anaesthetised baboons and awake monkeys, and the levels vary with drug and species; in humans under halothane and N₂O the threshold for the first EEG change matched the animal data. The thresholds are drawn into the figure “Where on the CBF scale EEG and the cells fail” alongside van Putten and Foreman and Claassen.
  • Completeness: with complete global ischaemia (cardiac arrest) energy supply fails within minutes; with incomplete (focal) ischaemia residual flow keeps ATP production going longer, which is why focal ischaemia is apparently better tolerated.
  • Hypoglycaemia in the EEG: with a gradual fall to about 40 mg/dL (about 2.2 mmol/L) the EEG shifts from alpha and beta towards delta and theta; below 20 mg/dL (about 1.1 mmol/L) the EEG becomes flat. Persistence at that level gives seizures and hippocampal injury. Hyperthermia above 42 °C gives an abrupt fall in oxygen consumption (protein denaturation).
  • Neuroprotection: barbiturates, propofol, ketamine, volatile agents and xenon protect in animal models, but only with mild ischaemia and not durably. In humans: in IHAST thiopental, etomidate or propofol to EEG suppression gave no better outcome; in GALA general anaesthesia gave no advantage over local anaesthesia for carotid surgery. Conclusion: inducing burst suppression for brain protection is not supported in anaesthetised patients, and physiological control (CPP, oxygenation, normocapnia, temperature, glucose, seizures) matters more. Etomidate can worsen tissue hypoxia during temporary vessel occlusion. Hypothermia 32–36 °C after cardiac arrest: TTM and TTM2 showed no benefit of lower targets; guidelines keep 32–36 °C and strict avoidance of hyperthermia.
  • Deferring elective surgery after stroke: the risk of death within 30 days was highest in the first 3 months and only stabilised after 9 months; the chapter recommends deferring elective surgery for 9 months, with an exception for early carotid surgery in small infarcts.
Patel et al. 2025, fig. 10.20–10.24

SSEP, ICP and falling blood flow (Lobo and Lamperti ch. 6)

  • The text states that SSEP amplitude changes at a CBF fall to about 15 ml/100 g/min and disappears below 18.
  • Increased ICP changes the SSEP classically: amplitude decreases and latency is prolonged. With herniation, subcortical responses may disappear first.
  • The book does not directly describe how the EEG changes with raised ICP. CBF thresholds for EEG are given in the van Putten and Hofmeijer card and in the figure “Where on the CBF scale EEG and the cells fail”.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 6

Burst suppression

Burst suppression is not needed for unconsciousness, amnesia or immobility during general anaesthesia or sedation, and when it appears unintentionally it is a signal to look for the cause. The most common is more anaesthetic or sedative than the patient needs, especially in older patients. Also check blood pressure, oxygenation, haemoglobin and temperature. Here you will find why the pattern arises, when it is wanted as treatment, what it means for outcome, and why the suppression ratio should always be checked against the raw EEG.

Key points

  • Burst suppression is not needed for general anaesthesia or sedation. Propofol produces burst suppression at about 4.9 µg/ml, while unconsciousness occurs at far lower concentrations. Unintended burst suppression is a signal to look for the cause, not a sign of adequate anaesthetic depth (interpretation based on the sources).See
  • The pattern reflects the energy balance of the cortex. Too much drug and too little energy (hypothermia, ischaemia) end in the same mechanism: falling ATP opens ATP-gated potassium channels. The suppression ratio rises gradually until the EEG becomes isoelectric.See
  • Older patients get it most easily, but in them it is hardest to see. The risk rises with age and impaired neurological status. In older patients the bursts are weaker and the suppression shallower and shorter.See
  • Confirm on the raw EEG and look for the cause. Confirm the pattern on the raw EEG and assess symmetry. Reduce the dose if suppression is symmetrical and the dose is high. If it persists at a low dose, look for hypotension, hypoxaemia, anaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and hypocapnia.Source: Gruenbaum 2026. See
  • The suppression ratio is an estimate that can be wrong in both directions. EMG and low bursts can give a falsely low SR. Poor electrode contact and artefacts can give a falsely high SR. Use the number as a warning to check against the raw EEG, not as the answer.See
  • There is no single documented target for therapeutic depth. Expert practice describes pauses of about 10 seconds, but no target has been tested against outcome. The content of the bursts distinguished successful from failed weaning; pause length did not. The target should be agreed with a neurologist or neurointensivist for each patient (interpretation based on the sources).See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

When is burst suppression wanted, and when is it not needed?

A synthesis of the cards in this tab. Sources are given under each point.

  • It can be a deliberate treatment. Burst suppression is induced in refractory status epilepticus, raised intracranial pressure and aneurysm surgery with temporary clipping, to lower metabolism and ICP. It should be individualised and time-limited, with concurrent attention to perfusion, oxygenation and temperature. In status epilepticus it is part of third-line treatment (Intensive care tab).Source: Gruenbaum 2026
  • Whether it protects the brain is uncertain. The rationale is that oxygen consumption and blood flow fall together. But this coupling weakens with age, vascular disease and anaesthesia. In aneurysm surgery the evidence is mixed, and animal studies suggest that protection does not require burst suppression. After cardiac arrest, a protective down-regulated state is a hypothesis.Sources: Gruenbaum 2026, Jegarl 2026, Forgacs 2020
  • It is not needed for general anaesthesia. Propofol produces burst suppression at about 4.9 µg/ml, whereas movement to incision is prevented only at about 15 µg/ml. Unconsciousness occurs at much lower concentrations (Components tab). A «silent second» is too deep for clinical anaesthesia. Excessive cortical silencing gives no additional protection against awareness but may carry a cognitive cost.Sources: Pilge 2014, Gruenbaum 2026
  • It is not needed during ICU sedation. Burst suppression was associated with higher mortality (HR 2.04), and more time in burst suppression gave higher odds of delirium (OR 4.16). Nobody had burst suppression as a goal. Burst suppression is mostly a marker of how ill the patient is, but titrating to the lowest necessary dose may have a modest effect.Sources: Watson 2008, Andresen 2014, Hogan 2020
  • If it appears unintentionally, look for the cause. Check blood pressure, oxygenation, haemoglobin, glucose and temperature before increasing or accepting the dose. In one study burst suppression disappeared in 55 % of cases simply by raising MAP to the patient's baseline.Sources: Gruenbaum 2026, Georgii 2022
  • If it is the goal, it must be verified. A flat EEG is not the same as the intended burst suppression (the herniation case under Clinical examples). Unilateral suppression may mean focal ischaemia or a technical fault.Sources: Gruenbaum 2026, the ECMO case in the Intensive care tab
  • Interpretation based on the sources: burst suppression can have a place as a deliberate, time-limited treatment. It is not needed for unconsciousness, amnesia or immobility during anaesthesia or sedation. Unintended burst suppression is a signal to look for the cause, not a sign of adequate anaesthetic depth.

What it is and why it occurs

What burst suppression is: a sign of cortical energy balance

Burst suppression is alternating periods of almost absent activity and high-amplitude bursts. It is never seen in natural sleep. The sources explain the pattern slightly differently, but meet in one common mechanism.Source: Lobo and Lamperti 2025

  • Falling ATP is the common point. Two mechanisms have been proposed: cortical hyperexcitability (extracellular calcium and a refractory period after the burst) and a metabolic theory. In the metabolic theory, falling ATP opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels and the neurones hyperpolarise. A computational model builds on this theory. The model has only 14–20 cells, and the KATP channel is a hypothesis. It explains but does not prove, and other channels and extracellular calcium may act together.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti 2025, Ching 2012, Gruenbaum 2026
  • The pattern can mean too much agent or too little energy. Anaesthetic agents reduce firing and thereby CMRO₂ secondarily. Hypothermia and ischaemia reduce metabolism directly. One process is down-regulation (excessive dose, hypothermia), the other is metabolic failure from insufficient substrate or oxygen (hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, ischaemia). Both end in the same mechanism.Sources: Ching 2012, Gruenbaum 2026
  • It is a continuum, not a separate state. The suppression ratio rises gradually with deeper inactivation, until the EEG is completely isoelectric. In the model, 50 % of normal ATP production gave a suppression ratio of about 0.5, and 30 % gave about 0.75. With severe hypoperfusion or anoxic injury the EEG can become isoelectric.Sources: Ching 2012, Gruenbaum 2026
  • The bursts repeat the pattern from just before suppression started. Under propofol this is often alpha and slow-delta. If the EEG had already become mostly slow-delta, that is what the bursts contain. Deeper anaesthesia mainly gives longer suppression periods and fewer bursts. True bursts have organised spectral content, whereas artefacts give broadband spikes.Sources: Ching 2012, Gruenbaum 2026
  • Ketamine is the exception. Ketamine does not usually produce classic burst suppression, even at high doses, but affects the threshold. Ketamine increases CMRO₂.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti 2025, Ching 2012

The studies in detail:

Lobo and Lamperti 2025 Ching 2012 Gruenbaum 2026

Who gets it, and what to do when it appears?

Burst suppression is common, age increases the risk, and its meaning depends on the patient. The sources agree on this, and there is a practical approach.Sources: Gruenbaum 2026, Lobo and Lamperti 2025

  • It is common, and most common in older patients. In a retrospective study of more than 38,000 adults nearly half had burst suppression. Likelihood and duration increased with age. The risk also rises with impaired neurological status. In older patients the pattern is less distinct: weaker bursts and shallower, shorter suppression. The most vulnerable are thus those in whom it is hardest to detect.Sources: Gruenbaum 2026, Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • Reserve matters more than minutes. Young, healthy people may tolerate burst suppression without measurable consequences. In vulnerable patients, recurrent or persistent burst suppression more often reflects exhausted reserve. Meta-analyses show about 1.5 times higher risk of postoperative delirium. ENGAGES was inconclusive, but has been criticised for the lack of standardised analgesia and for not taking age and cognitive frailty into account.Sources: Gruenbaum 2026, Lobo and Lamperti 2025
  • Pain and opioids shift the threshold. Opioids do not produce burst suppression directly, but can unmask or accentuate it together with propofol or volatile agents. Pain and nociception can lower the threshold. Nociception can produce beta or delta arousal that is misread as too-light hypnosis. Giving more hypnotic then increases the risk.Sources: Lobo and Lamperti 2025, Gruenbaum 2026
  • Look at the raw EEG, not just the index. The indices are affected only when suppression dominates the analysis window. Acceptable index values can therefore coexist with clear discontinuity. Automated detection missed burst suppression in about 14 % of cases.Source: Gruenbaum 2026
  • Four steps. (1) Confirm on the raw EEG. (2) Assess symmetry: unilateral suppression may mean focal ischaemia or a technical fault, so keep the dose unchanged and assess perfusion. (3) With symmetric suppression and a high dose: reduce by 0.1–0.2 MAC or propofol by 10–20 %. (4) If it persists at a low dose: look for hypotension, hypoxaemia, anaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and hypocapnia. Caveat: the source is a narrative review without a systematic search, focused on surgery.Source: Gruenbaum 2026

The studies in detail:

Gruenbaum 2026 Lobo and Lamperti 2025

Measurement: the suppression ratio is an estimate

How deep should therapeutic burst suppression be? Pauses, bursts and SR

When burst suppression is used as treatment, the sources describe pauses of about 10 seconds and as little epileptiform activity in the bursts as possible. None of the targets has been tested against outcome, and the evidence is weak.

  • SR below 5 % (Rasulo) does not concern therapeutic depth. The statement “If burst suppression is used, the suppression ratio should be kept at < 5%” (strong consensus in a Delphi panel) sits under the question of whether burst suppression should be avoided. Read in context, it means that SR during sedation should be kept below 5 %, in practice without burst suppression. The figure is not justified. The article notes that burst suppression is still part of many treatment algorithms for refractory status epilepticus, but gives no depth for it.Source: Rasulo 2023
  • Pauses of about 10 seconds are expert opinion, with weak evidence. Experts consider an interburst interval of about 10 seconds for 24 hours reasonable in refractory status epilepticus. In retrospective data burst suppression was achieved in only about 40–60 % of patients. One quantitative study of 17 patients found no association between suppression ratio and outcome.Source: review 2022 (doi 10.1007/s10309-022-00539-z)
  • The target is rarely reached in practice. In 35 patients with refractory status epilepticus, the target was a burst suppression probability of 0.8 ± 0.15. Patients were within the target for a median of only 8 % of treatment time, and below it 84 % of the time. The same weight-adjusted dose gave different suppression in different patients, and some drifted without any change in infusion.Source: An 2018 (Massachusetts General Hospital)
  • The content of the bursts matters more than the pauses. In 19 patients (37 weaning attempts) the amount of epileptiform activity in the bursts was the only feature that separated successful from failed weaning (p = 0.008). Interburst interval, suppression ratio and burst length did not. A maximum burst amplitude below 125 µV had a sensitivity of 84.6 % and specificity of 61.1 % for successful weaning.Source: Johnson 2016
  • SR below 5 % is far below the definition of burst suppression. ACNS 2021 defines burst suppression as suppression in 50–99 % of the record. A scoping review divides it into incomplete (20–49 %) and complete (50–99 %) burst suppression. This fits with the Rasulo statement being about avoiding burst suppression.Sources: ACNS 2021, Fisch 2026
  • SR 40–60 % as a treatment target has no known source. The author of the app has heard it but does not remember the source. It has not been found in peer-reviewed literature, and the 2026 scoping review gives no SR treatment target.Source: Fisch 2026
  • Burst suppression has not been shown to improve outcome. All patients with refractory status epilepticus received continuous intravenous anaesthesia, and the question was how deep. In a nine-year cohort of 102 patients without anoxic brain injury, reaching burst suppression was not associated with lasting seizure termination, in-hospital survival or return to previous function (adjusted analyses). The scoping review concludes that the evidence does not support burst suppression over seizure cessation as the target for most patients.Sources: Fisch 2023 and 2026
  • The guideline accepts seizure cessation on the EEG as a target. The dose is titrated to cessation of electrographic seizures or burst suppression (very low evidence, strong recommendation). A period of 24–48 hours of electrographic control is then recommended before slow withdrawal (very low evidence, weak recommendation). Burst suppression is therefore not required.Source: NCS guideline, Brophy 2012
  • Older studies on depth and outcome:
    • Deep suppression gave fewer breakthrough seizures, but more hypotension. Titration to background suppression (burst suppression or an isoelectric EEG) gave breakthrough seizures in 4 versus 53 % with titration to seizure suppression, and hypotension in 76 versus 29 %. The goal did not affect withdrawal seizures, early treatment failure or change of agent. Mortality was 48 % and was not associated with agent or goal. Large caveats: nearly all with background suppression received pentobarbital, and all on midazolam were titrated to seizure suppression, so agent and goal cannot be separated. Only 27 % on pentobarbital had continuous EEG, versus 78 % on midazolam or propofol. The authors write that this “may very likely explain” the fewer breakthrough seizures, because seizures without clinical signs are easily missed without continuous EEG.Source: Claassen 2002 (systematic review of case series 1970–2001, 28 studies, 193 patients)
    • A flat EEG more often gave lasting seizure control than burst suppression. Lasting seizure control after tapering in 17 of 20 with a flat EEG versus 6 of 12 with burst suppression as the deepest level. Isolated epileptiform discharges during the infusion did not correlate with outcome. Recurrent electrographic status after tapering predicted relapse.Source: Krishnamurthy and Drislane 1999 (35 patients on pentobarbital)
    • Outcome was the same with and without burst suppression. Burst suppression was reached in 20 of 33 monitored episodes (61 %). The authors consider the cause of the status to be the main determinant of outcome.Source: Rossetti 2005 (49 episodes of refractory status epilepticus in Boston)
  • What has been shown, and what has not? (interpretation based on the sources): In small, retrospective data, deeper suppression is associated with fewer breakthrough seizures and relapses, but causes more hypotension. The difference may partly be because patients with deep suppression less often had continuous EEG, and therefore fewer detected seizures. Lower mortality or better function has not been shown. The content of the bursts predicted successful weaning, not the length of the pauses. No randomised trial has compared burst suppression with seizure cessation.Sources: Claassen 2002, Krishnamurthy 1999, Rossetti 2005, Fisch 2023, Johnson 2016
  • 24–48 hours and repeated cycles rest on usual practice, not studies. The Shorvon and Ferlisi review is among the most cited references in Norwegian guidelines and procedures. There are no controlled or randomised studies, so treatment has to be based on case reports and opinion.
    • Depth: “It is usual” to keep anaesthesia at burst suppression, because this usually stops all electrographic seizure activity. Whether it is needed in all cases is unclear, and what little evidence there is conflicts. As a compromise against hypotension, it is common to aim for burst suppression first and lighten anaesthesia in prolonged episodes.
    • Duration: “It is usual practice” to try to reverse anaesthesia every 24–48 hours and re-establish it if seizures recur. After a few weeks, each cycle is often extended to 5 days. How long anaesthesia should continue has not been studied.
    • Monitoring and weaning: EEG at least once a day, and slow weaning over days. No interburst interval, bursts per minute, BIS or SR is given.
    Interpretation based on the sources: the 24–48-hour and 5-day cycles in the Sørlandet procedure correspond to what Shorvon and Ferlisi describe as usual practice, not a result from studies.Source: Shorvon and Ferlisi 2011 (Brain), citing Krishnamurthy 1999 and Rossetti 2005
  • The origin of the target is unclear. The pattern was described in 1936 and named burst suppression in 1949. It later became a treatment target in refractory status epilepticus, but the evidence for putting the brain into burst suppression is “inconclusive”. The origin of a specific number of seconds for the pauses has not been found in the sources.Source: Hawkes 2024
  • Norwegian review: burst suppression is a practical goal. General anaesthesia should be started as soon as possible, most often with propofol. Full burst suppression is “hardly strictly necessary”, but “burst suppression for 12 to 24 hours can be a practical goal”. The right depth of anaesthesia based on the EEG is “not fully clarified”, and the EEG is the most important monitoring tool. The need for continued propofol should be reassessed after two to three days because of the risk of propofol infusion syndrome.Source: Heuser 2024 (Journal of the Norwegian Medical Association, status epilepticus in adults)
  • “Practical” because continuous EEG is often unavailable. Duration and depth are controversial. “Common practice” is burst suppression for 24–48 hours, but the rationale is “limited”. Whether burst suppression is necessary can be discussed, but all epileptic activity must be suppressed for a period. Most hospitals do not have continuous EEG around the clock, so burst suppression can be a practical way of ensuring that anaesthesia is deep enough. Propofol should be restricted to 48 hours and tapered over 24 hours. BIS, SR and bursts per minute are not mentioned.Source: Heuser 2022 (book chapter by the neurologists behind the Norwegian review)
  • The national guideline gives no EEG target. Anaesthesia is step 3, with propofol for up to 48 hours or midazolam. A barbiturate is considered for persistent convulsive status. Neither burst suppression, seizure cessation, SR nor BIS is given as a target.Source: NevroNEL, Norwegian status epilepticus network (updated 2026)
  • Example of a local procedure (Sørlandet Hospital, ICU Arendal, 2026): an openly published ICU procedure shows how one hospital has translated the sources.
    • Target: it is uncertain whether the target should be seizure cessation or burst suppression, and seizure cessation is “probably sufficient”. Burst suppression with 10-second pauses, “i.e. 3–5 bursts per min”, is called a common target. The procedure nevertheless states that no association has been shown between pause length and effect.
    • Monitor: adequate depth is stated as BIS 7–15 and SR 60–80 %, without a reference in the text, but the figures match Musialowicz 2010 (see below). BIS below 30 corresponded to burst suppression in one study. Continuous EEG is recommended, but availability is uncertain. BIS is an alternative that only measures frontally.
    • Duration and weaning: anaesthesia for 24 (–48) hours, then slow weaning over 24 hours, for example propofol by 20 % every 3 hours. If seizures recur, a new round of 24–48 hours is given the first time, then 5–7 days.
  • What do the studies of BIS and burst suppression show?
    • BIS and SR closely tracked the number of bursts. In 12 adults on pentobarbital for raised intracranial pressure (11 after head injury, none with seizures), the dose was titrated by the raw EEG to 3–5 bursts per minute. This corresponded to BIS 15 (95% CI 10–20) and SR 71% (61–80), with a strong correlation (r = 0.90 and −0.89). The authors suggest BIS 10–20 and SR 60–80% as a possible initial target for barbiturates in this setting, but it needs further testing. Caveats: vasopressors were given on 81% of days, and BIS was lower on days with vasopressors (15 versus 33). Bursts per minute ignore burst length: three bursts of 5 seconds are deeper suppression than three of 15 seconds. The study received an equipment grant from the manufacturer of BIS.Source: Riker 2003
    • BIS below 30 showed burst suppression, but did not separate epileptic bursts from ordinary ones. In 10 patients with refractory status epilepticus (propofol titrated to burst suppression for at least 12 hours, guided by full EEG), BIS below 30 separated burst suppression from other EEG (sensitivity 99 %, specificity 98 %). 3 bursts per minute corresponded to BIS 7 and SR 80 %, and 5 bursts per minute to BIS 15 and SR 61 %. There is no consensus on the number of bursts per minute, but the target is “usually” 3–5, citing studies of barbiturates for raised intracranial pressure (Riker 2003, Cottenceau 2008). Neuromuscular blockade was given only at induction in three patients, signal quality was good, and all received noradrenaline. Limitations, according to the authors themselves:
      • BIS could not distinguish epileptic bursts from ordinary ones: with spikes in the bursts, BIS was 23 and SR 44 % at 3 bursts per minute, versus BIS 7 and SR 81 % during ordinary burst suppression.
      • In two patients, full EEG showed regional epileptic discharges that BIS did not capture, because it only measures frontally.
      • If BIS rises suddenly, it may be lighter anaesthesia or new seizures, and only EEG can tell. Muscle activity, rigidity and movement can cause artefacts.
      The conclusion is that continuous EEG is the primary method. BIS can be used to maintain burst suppression with propofol when continuous EEG is not available.Source: Musialowicz 2010 (Kuopio)
    • The monitor's numbers tracked the EEG well. In 4 patients, BIS, SR and bursts from the monitor correlated strongly with bursts on the EEG.Source: Arbour 2015 (4 patients, 1,972 measurements over 33 hours)
    • Overall, these are small observational studies. SR can help maintain depth when continuous EEG is not available. But a frontal monitor cannot rule out non-convulsive status, and the raw EEG from BIS missed periodic discharges in about 75 % of cases in one study.Source: Gimson and Smith 2021
  • What the numbers mean (interpretation based on the sources): BIS below 30 shows that the EEG is in burst suppression, not how deep it should be. None of the studies tested a BIS or SR target against outcome. The numbers also do not quite fit together: 10-second pauses give 4–5 bursts per minute, whereas 3 bursts per minute give pauses of almost 20 seconds. BIS 7–15 and SR 60–80 % from Sørlandet match the Musialowicz table for 3–5 bursts per minute and resemble Riker. The target of 3–5 bursts per minute itself comes from barbiturates for raised intracranial pressure after head injury, not status epilepticus. BIS and SR are also algorithms: EMG from the forehead and noise above the amplitude threshold can give a falsely low SR and a falsely high BIS, and poor contact can give a falsely high SR. A BIS or SR number therefore cannot stand alone as a treatment target, but must be checked against the raw EEG.Sources: Musialowicz 2010, Riker 2003, Sørlandet Hospital 2026. See
  • The arithmetic (interpretation based on the sources): SR is the proportion of time spent in suppression. Pauses of 10 seconds with bursts of 1–3 seconds give an SR of about 75–90 %. An SR of 40–60 % means bursts and pauses last about equally long. An SR below 5 % means an almost continuous EEG, in other words no burst suppression, as Rasulo recommends during ordinary sedation.
  • What it means (interpretation based on the sources): there is no single documented target. Follow the raw EEG and the content of the bursts (epileptiform activity), not just SR. SR from a frontal monitor is an estimate that can be wrong in both directions (see the card below). The target should be agreed with a neurologist or neurointensivist for each patient.
Rasulo 2023, An 2018, Johnson 2016, Fisch 2023 and 2026, Heuser 2024, Brophy 2012, Claassen 2002, Krishnamurthy 1999, Rossetti 2005, Hawkes 2024, Shorvon and Ferlisi 2011, Heuser 2022, NevroNEL 2026, Sørlandet Hospital 2026, Riker 2003, Musialowicz 2010, Arbour 2015, Gimson and Smith 2021, review 2022 (doi 10.1007/s10309-022-00539-z)

Suppression ratio and ‘suppression time’: an algorithm that can be wrong in both directions

Many studies and much teaching emphasise minutes in suppression. The number comes from the monitor's algorithm, not from someone reading the raw EEG.

  • The number is the proportion of time below an amplitude threshold. The monitor calculates what proportion of a time window (BIS: the last 63 seconds) lies below the threshold and calls it suppression. It does not recognise bursts, only low amplitude. «Minutes in suppression» in studies is this proportion multiplied by time.Sources: Andresen 2014, Kratzer 2020
  • SR can be falsely low. Noise above the threshold prevents the algorithm from seeing suppression, and EMG is the most common source. In image 2 of the image quiz (shared case) SR was 0 and BIS 64 while the EEG was almost flat. After a neuromuscular blocker, with no change in dose, SR rose to 82 and BIS fell to 8. In older patients low bursts can fall below the threshold, and SR underestimates suppression compared with visual reading. Automated detection missed burst suppression in about 14 % of cases.Sources: Muhlhofer 2017 (cited in Kratzer 2020), Gruenbaum 2026
  • SR can be falsely high. Poor electrode contact or high impedance can produce a low-amplitude signal that resembles suppression. Electrocautery, suction and movement can produce large transients followed by signal dropout that resemble bursts and pauses. On visual reading, low-amplitude but continuous EEG in older patients can be misread as suppression if the scale is not adjusted.Source: Gruenbaum 2026
  • Small changes cause large swings. SR is highly sensitive to the amplitude threshold and to noise. Small changes in amplitude or artefacts can cause large fluctuations in low-amplitude EEG.Source: Gruenbaum 2026
  • Measurement error may explain conflicting research findings. In a study of 41 patients, visually determined suppression duration was associated with delirium (p = 0.039), whereas duration from the monitor's SR was not (p = 0.275). Such measurement limitations probably explain why strong associations in observational studies have not translated into benefit in randomised EEG-guided trials. The data are also coarse in several studies: values read from screenshots every 5 minutes and interpolated, or BIS recorded for only 10–20 minutes per day.Sources: Jegarl 2026, Gruenbaum 2026, Fritz 2016, Watson 2008
  • A separate suppression time number does not make documentation more precise. Many ask for a suppression time (ST) number for documentation. Some monitors give a separate suppression time, others only SR as a percentage of time, and the manufacturer does not always describe the time window and calculation. Interpretation based on the sources: an ST number rests on the same amplitude threshold as SR and inherits the same sources of error, so it is no more precise than the raw-EEG assessment behind it.
  • In practice: read SR together with the raw EEG at the right scale, the EMG bar, signal quality and the spectrogram. The first step is to confirm the pattern on the raw EEG before anything else.Source: Gruenbaum 2026
  • Interpretation based on the sources: ‘suppression time’ in studies and on the monitor is an algorithmic estimate that can be too low (noise, EMG, low bursts) or too high (poor contact, artefacts, low-amplitude continuous EEG). The number should be used as a warning to be checked, not as ground truth.
The studies in detail: mechanisms and age, the Ching model, four steps (3 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Burst suppression: mechanisms, age and delirium (Lobo and Lamperti, ch. 5)

  • What it is: alternating periods of almost absent activity and high-amplitude bursts. Never seen in natural sleep. The bursts are thought to reflect brief periods of thalamic disinhibition.
  • Two proposed mechanisms: cortical hyperexcitability (extracellular calcium and a refractory period after the burst) and a metabolic theory in which falling ATP opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels.
  • Who gets it most easily: the risk increases with age and with impaired neurological status. In older patients the pattern is less distinct: weaker bursts and shallower, shorter suppression, which makes it harder to detect in the most vulnerable (fig. 5.2).
  • Thresholds: high-dose ketamine does not usually produce burst suppression, but affects the threshold; opioids do not produce it directly, but pain and nociception can lower the threshold.
  • Delirium: several groups have found an association, but ENGAGES was inconclusive and has been criticised for the lack of standardised analgesia and for not taking age and cognitive frailty into account. See ENGAGES in the Components tab.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 5

Why burst suppression? A neurophysiological-metabolic model (Ching 2012)

Computational model from MGH, MIT and Boston University (PNAS 2012;109:3095–3100; Ching, Purdon, Vijayan, Kopell and Brown). It attempts to explain why anaesthesia, hypothermia, hypoxic-ischaemic coma and early infantile encephalopathy (Ohtahara) produce the same EEG pattern.

  • The idea: the common denominator is reduced cerebral metabolism. In the model (10 pyramidal neurons and 4 interneurons, Hodgkin-Huxley type), neuronal firing is coupled to ATP production via ATP-gated potassium channels (KATP). When ATP production is reduced, ATP is depleted during a burst, the KATP channels open, the cells hyperpolarise and fall silent; ATP slowly builds up again, and the next burst can start. 50% of normal ATP production gave a suppression ratio of about 0.5, 30% gave about 0.75; bursts and pauses lasted 4–10 seconds.
  • A continuum: burst suppression is not a separate state, but a gradually increasing suppression ratio with deeper inactivation, ending in a completely isoelectric EEG. The authors show an example of rewarming after cooling to 18 °C in which the suppression ratio gradually falls until the EEG is continuous again.
  • The bursts carry the old pattern: during propofol-induced burst suppression the alpha rhythm lives on inside each burst; the spectrogram looks “as if it has been multiplied by a sequence of zeros and ones”. The model predicts that the spectral content of a burst should be the same as just before burst suppression started, regardless of agent. It also predicts a slow frequency drift within each burst (about 11 to 8 Hz) and that fast activity is limited by metabolism, not by GABA inhibition; these two have not been confirmed experimentally.
  • Why it is relevant to perfusion: anaesthetic agents reduce firing and thereby CMRO₂ secondarily, whereas hypothermia and ischaemia reduce metabolism directly without changing the synapses. Both end in the same KATP mechanism. This is the basis for suppression being able to mean either too much agent or too little energy (Guay 2025, Georgii 2022). Ketamine, which increases CMRO₂, does not produce classic burst suppression at clinical doses.
  • The authors' interpretation: each burst is “an attempt to restore basal cortical dynamics”, and suppression is an energy-saving protection. In severe ischaemia even complete isoelectricity cannot preserve ATP, and injury follows. They suggest that the character of the bursts could be used to detect ischaemia during surgery and to distinguish burst suppression from seizures, and that the difference between a low suppression ratio and full isoelectricity should be clarified before “burst suppression” is used as a target in neuroprotection.
  • Limitations: a model with 14–20 cells, without spatial extent, and the KATP channel is a hypothesis; other channels and extracellular calcium (Kroeger and Amzica 2007) may act together. The model explains, but does not prove. No conflicts of interest declared.
Ching et al. PNAS 2012;109:3095–3100

Burst suppression during anaesthesia: a four-step clinical approach (Gruenbaum 2026)

Narrative review (Br J Anaesth 2026;136:1843–1854; Gruenbaum, Safavynia and Bilotta). The authors describe burst suppression as a context-dependent marker of cortical energy balance, neither a therapeutic target nor a pure dose phenomenon.

  • Two processes: down-regulation by anaesthetics (excessive dose, hypothermia) and metabolic failure from insufficient substrate or oxygen (hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, ischaemia). When ATP falls, ATP-gated potassium channels open and neurones hyperpolarise. Astrocytes supply lactate to neurones, and this works less well with age and vascular disease. Low ATP can also weaken the blood–brain barrier and admit inflammatory mediators; the injury markers S100B and GFAP are linked to delirium. With severe hypoperfusion or anoxic injury the EEG can become isoelectric.
  • Who tolerates it: burst suppression may be tolerated in young, healthy people without measurable consequences, whereas recurrent or persistent burst suppression in vulnerable patients more often reflects exhausted reserve. The authors argue that its meaning depends more on the brain's metabolic reserve than on its duration.
  • Raw EEG over the index: The indices are affected by suppression only when it dominates the analysis window, so acceptable index values can coexist with clear discontinuity. Automated detection underestimated duration compared with visual scoring and missed burst suppression in about 14 % of cases. On the spectrogram, burst suppression produces a «checkerboard» pattern with dark horizontal stripes. Electrocautery and poor electrode contact can mimic burst suppression: true bursts have organised spectral content, whereas artefacts give broadband spikes.
  • Numbers: in a retrospective study of more than 38,000 adults nearly half had burst suppression, and both likelihood and duration increased with age. Sevoflurane produces burst suppression at about 2.9 % (above 1 MAC), propofol at about 4.9 µg/ml, whereas more than 15 µg/ml is needed to prevent movement. Meta-analyses show about 1.5 times higher risk of postoperative delirium.
  • Four steps: (1) confirm on the raw EEG: electrode contact and impedance, artefacts, and the lowest scale that shows the trace without clipping. (2) Assess symmetry: unilateral suppression may mean focal ischaemia or a technical fault; keep the dose unchanged and assess perfusion. (3) With symmetric suppression and a high dose: reduce by 0.1–0.2 MAC or propofol by 10–20 %. (4) If it persists at a low dose: look for hypotension, hypoxaemia, anaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and hypocapnia.
  • Pain and opioids: nociception can produce beta or delta arousal that is misread as too-light hypnosis, and more hypnotic then increases the risk of burst suppression. Opioids can unmask or accentuate burst suppression together with propofol or volatile agents.
  • Caveats: narrative review without a systematic search, focused on surgery rather than cardiac arrest or intensive care. No conflicts of interest. The authors state that a language model from OpenAI was used for editing. Safavynia is a co-author both here and of Jegarl 2026.
Gruenbaum, Safavynia and Bilotta. Br J Anaesth 2026;136:1843–1854

Key points

  • A ‘silent second’ is too deep for clinical anaesthesia. EEG suppression occurred at about 2.9 vol % sevoflurane, 1.5 vol % isoflurane and 4.85 µg/ml propofol. For the gases, that is above MAC. The endpoint cannot be used for ketamine, which does not produce burst suppression.See
  • Bursts become weaker with age. In older patients the first burst had lower amplitude (13.1 versus 20.3 µV in the young) and was more irregular. Normalised alpha was unchanged. It is the amplitude, not the architecture, that disappears.See
  • The monitor may underestimate suppression in older patients. The indices look for EEG below an amplitude threshold, not for bursts. Low bursts in older patients can therefore themselves fall below the threshold.See
  • After burst suppression, the same concentration gives a deeper effect. After a brief period of suppression, the measured index was consistently below the model-predicted value at the same calculated effect-site concentration. The difference lasted for the rest of the operation.See
  • Models do not replace continuous EEG. The authors consider that the anaesthetised brain behaves as a non-linear system, and recommend continuous EEG monitoring, especially in vulnerable patients. The study had no control group.See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Dose and age

Burst suppression lies far above what is needed

A “silent second” means EEG suppression for at least 1 second. The dose needed for it shows how deep burst suppression is compared with ordinary anaesthesia.Source: Pilge 2014

  • For the gases, suppression only comes above MAC. Sevoflurane produced suppression at about 2.93 vol%, over 1.4 times MAC. Isoflurane produced suppression at 1.51 vol%, over 1.3 times MAC.Source: Pilge 2014
  • For propofol, suppression comes below the dose that prevents movement. Propofol produced suppression at 4.85 µg/ml (the article states “mg/ml”, probably micrograms/ml). That is under a third of the concentration that prevents movement at incision (15.2 µg/ml). Movement mostly reflects the spinal cord, whereas a “silent second” is meant to measure the effect on the brain.Sources: Pilge 2014; Smith 1994 (movement at incision)
  • Consciousness is lost much earlier. With slow induction, patients lost response at a calculated effect-site concentration of 2.0 µg/ml on average. That is a large gap from loss of response to burst suppression for propofol (interpretation based on the sources). A “silent second” is too deep for clinical anaesthesia.Sources: Sepúlveda 2026; Pilge 2014
  • The agents are not alike. Ketamine does not produce burst suppression, so the measure cannot be used for ketamine. Both the pattern and the shape of the burst vary between agents.Sources: Pilge 2014; Fleischmann 2018, discussed in Kratzer 2020
  • The figures rest on small samples. The studies had 55 patients divided into three groups and 23 healthy patients under 60 years. The confidence intervals may be too wide, particularly for propofol.Sources: Pilge 2014; Sepúlveda 2026

The studies in detail:

Pilge 2014 Smith 1994 Sepúlveda 2026 Fleischmann 2018

Older patients: weaker bursts that the monitor can miss

This concerns the first burst after burst suppression appeared during propofol induction (102 of 408 patients). The finding ties in with other age-related changes in the EEG and with how monitors measure suppression.Source: Kratzer 2020

  • The amplitude disappears, not the architecture. In older patients the burst was lower (maximum amplitude 13.1 µV versus 20.3 µV in the young) and more irregular (higher permutation entropy). Absolute alpha power fell linearly with age, while normalised alpha was unchanged.Source: Kratzer 2020
  • The bursts are low because the EEG is already low-amplitude before suppression. The same age-related change is seen during maintenance without burst suppression. The spectral content of the burst is also predicted to mirror the EEG just before suppression started. The bursts in older patients are thus low because the EEG in older patients is low-amplitude even before suppression (interpretation based on the sources).Sources: Purdon 2015; Kreuzer 2020; Ching 2012, discussed in Kratzer 2020
  • The monitor looks for silence, not for bursts. The indices detect burst suppression by looking for EEG below an amplitude threshold for a certain time. Low, flat bursts can themselves fall below the threshold. The suppression ratio therefore underestimates suppression compared with visual reading. The authors argue that burst information should be used as a plausibility check, but age-adjusted.Sources: Kratzer 2020; Muhlhofer 2017
  • Caveats. Retrospective analysis of frontal EEG, only propofol-induced bursts and no adjustment for comorbidity. The midazolam subgroup among the older patients was small.Source: Kratzer 2020

The studies in detail:

Kratzer 2020 Purdon 2015 Kreuzer 2020 Ching 2012 Muhlhofer 2017

The dose alone does not predict the effect

A TCI pump displays a calculated effect-site concentration. The question is whether the same calculated concentration gives the same EEG effect before and after a brief period of suppression.Source: Sepúlveda 2026

  • Same concentration, deeper effect. In 23 healthy patients propofol was increased until BIS showed a 1% suppression ratio. The effect-site concentration was then set back to the level at loss of response. Before the perturbation, observed and predicted BIS were the same. Afterwards, observed BIS lay consistently below predicted BIS (largest bias −17.5), with lower alpha power and stronger delta–alpha coupling (Kmod 0.21 versus 0.16). The difference persisted for the rest of the operation.Source: Sepúlveda 2026
  • The models are built on other conditions. Slow induction gave loss of response at about 2.0 µg/ml, versus an EC50 of about 3 µg/ml in the Eleveld model for the same age. The explanation may be that the models were built on bolus and rapid-infusion data without equilibrium between plasma and effect site.Source: Sepúlveda 2026
  • The brain behaves non-linearly. The same dose does not give the same effect, and the effect does not return to the starting point. Linear PK/PD models therefore cannot predict the effect after a disturbance, whether experimental or clinical, such as haemorrhage or an altered infusion rate. The authors recommend continuous EEG monitoring, especially in vulnerable patients.Source: Sepúlveda 2026
  • Caveats. There was no control group without perturbation, so time alone cannot be excluded. “The same concentration” is defined by the model being tested, and there were no plasma measurements. Nociception could explain the lower alpha, but the stronger delta–alpha coupling argues against it.Source: Sepúlveda 2026
  • Taken together: read the EEG directly, not just the dose figure (interpretation based on the sources). The threshold for suppression lies high on average, the bursts look different with age, and the same calculated concentration can give a different effect in the same patient over time.Sources: Pilge 2014; Kratzer 2020; Sepúlveda 2026

The studies in detail:

Sepúlveda 2026 Pilge 2014 Kratzer 2020
The studies in detail: Pilge 2014, Kratzer 2020, Sepúlveda 2026 (3 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

Burst suppression MAC and CP50 (Pilge 2014)

  • What it is: a study proposing the “silent second” (EEG suppression for at least 1 second) as a measure of the anaesthetic agent's effect on the brain, instead of movement at incision (MAC, which mostly reflects the spinal cord).
  • Design: 55 unpremedicated ASA I–II patients for elective surgery were randomised to sevoflurane (16), isoflurane (21) or propofol (18). The concentration was held constant for 15 minutes and EEG analysed in the 16th minute, and the next patient received a 10% lower concentration if suppression occurred and 10% higher if not (Dixon's “up-and-down” method, six independent crossover pairs per group). The values were calculated with logistic regression.
  • Result: sevoflurane 2.93 vol% (95% CI 2.80–3.15), isoflurane 1.51 vol% (1.45–1.60) and propofol 4.85 (CI 4.25–5.40; the article states “mg/ml”, probably micrograms/ml). That is over 1.4 times MAC for sevoflurane (2.05 vol%), over 1.3 times MAC for isoflurane (1.15 vol%) and under a third of the propofol concentration that prevents movement at incision (15.2 µg/ml, from Smith 1994).
  • Reservations: the starting concentrations were above the population value, and the authors write that the confidence intervals may therefore be too wide, particularly for propofol. The sample is small. Burst suppression does not occur with ketamine, so the measure cannot be used for ketamine. The pattern also differs between agents, and the authors write that a “silent second” is too deep for clinical anaesthesia.
  • What the article does not say: it does not state that fentanyl reduces the propofol concentration by about 80%. That figure comes from Smith 1994 via Miller's.
  • Conflicts of interest: none declared. Funded by departmental funds.
Pilge et al. Br J Anaesth 2014;112:1067–1074

The bursts become weaker and more irregular with age (Kratzer 2020)

Retrospective analysis from TU Munich and Columbia (Front Syst Neurosci 2020;14:599962) of the first burst after burst suppression appeared during propofol induction. The data are from Hesse 2019 (Atlanta), recorded with SedLine (Legacy) and analysed by an independent university group.

  • Method: 102 of 408 patients had a distinct first burst after a “silent second” (at least 1 s below 10 µV). Only the first 1.5 seconds of the burst were analysed, so that differing duration and dose would not affect the result. Median age 56 years; 16 patients under 45 years (YOUNG) and a group over 65 years (OLD). Fentanyl equivalents did not differ with age.
  • Findings: older patients had lower absolute power in 1–15 Hz and relatively more power above 15 Hz within the burst. Absolute alpha power fell linearly with age (AUC 0.86 for young versus old), while normalised alpha did not change: it is the amplitude, not the architecture, that disappears. Maximum amplitude was 20.3 µV in the young versus 13.1 µV in the older patients (AUC 0.84), steepest slope 1.22 versus 0.86 µV/ms, and permutation entropy was higher in the older patients (more irregular signal). Subanalysis of the 83 who received midazolam premedication gave the same result.
  • Why it matters for the monitor: The indices detect burst suppression by looking for suppression, that is EEG below an amplitude threshold for a certain time, not by recognising the bursts. When the bursts in older patients are lower and flatter, they can themselves fall below the threshold, and Muhlhofer 2017 showed that the suppression ratio underestimates suppression compared with visual reading. The authors argue that burst information should be used as a plausibility check, but then age-adjusted. This is the mechanism behind Image 6 and 13 in the image quiz: in older patients both normal EEG and bursts can look “weak”.
  • Connection in the app: the same age-related change that Purdon 2015 (BJA) and Kreuzer 2020 described for maintenance without burst suppression, and which Ching 2012 predicts: the spectral content of the burst mirrors the EEG just before the suppression started. Obert 2024 (Older patients and delirium sub-tab) shows that slow induction can avoid burst suppression in older patients in the first place.
  • Limitations: frontal EEG, only propofol-induced bursts (Fleischmann 2018 showed that the agent affects the shape of the burst), no adjustment for comorbidity, and the midazolam subgroup among the older patients was small. Funded by the James S. McDonnell Foundation (García); no conflicts of interest declared.
Kratzer et al. Front Syst Neurosci 2020;14:599962

After burst suppression the brain is not the same: non-linear pharmacodynamics (Sepúlveda 2026)

Prospective, non-randomised dose–response study from Osorno (Anesth Analg 2026;143:261–270, NCT06417645): 23 healthy patients under 60 years received slow induction (10 mg/kg/h) to loss of response, then Eleveld TCI, remifentanil 4.5 ng/ml and rocuronium. After intubation, propofol was increased to 15 mg/kg/h until BIS showed a 1% suppression ratio (“perturbation”), and the effect-site concentration was then set back to the level at loss of response. Observed BIS was compared with BIS predicted by the Eleveld model (TIVA Trainer), and the EEG spectrum and delta–alpha phase-amplitude coupling were analysed.

  • Before the perturbation: observed and predicted BIS were the same (no significant difference).
  • After the perturbation: with the same calculated effect-site concentration as before, observed BIS lay consistently below predicted BIS (largest bias −17.5 in the phase after the perturbation), and the difference persisted for the rest of the operation. Alpha power (absolute and relative) was lower than before, and the delta–alpha modulation (Kmod) was stronger (0.21 versus 0.16, p = 0.01), which the authors interpret as deeper thalamocortical synchronisation. Same concentration, deeper effect.
  • Slow induction gives a lower Ce at loss of response: on average 2.0 µg/ml, versus an EC50 of about 3 µg/ml in the Eleveld model for the same age. The authors believe the models were built on bolus and rapid-infusion data without plasma–effect equilibrium (“front-end” kinetics), and that ke0 is a mathematical device to collapse the hysteresis loop.
  • Interpretation: the brain under anaesthesia behaves as a non-linear system (the same dose does not give the same effect, no return to the starting point). Linear PK/PD models therefore cannot predict the effect after a disturbance, whether experimental (brief burst suppression) or clinical (haemorrhage shrinking V1, altered infusion rate). The conclusion is continuous EEG monitoring, especially in vulnerable patients. The authors discuss nociception as an alternative explanation for the lower alpha (surgery was under way after the perturbation), but consider that the stronger delta–alpha coupling argues against it.
  • Caveats: no control group without perturbation, so time alone cannot be excluded; circularity because “the same concentration” is defined by the model being tested; no plasma measurements; only healthy subjects under 60; the BIS prediction from Eleveld is itself debated (Coetzee 2024). The numbers in the abstract and the results section do not agree (see discrepancies). No conflicts of interest, public funding (ANID).
Sepúlveda, Barra, Baloian, Gutiérrez. Anesth Analg 2026;143:261–270

Key points

  • Burst suppression is associated with delirium and death in observational studies. More minutes of suppression during surgery gave a higher incidence of delirium. Burst suppression during ICU sedation was associated with higher mortality at 6 months (HR 2.04).See
  • More time in burst suppression during coma gave more delirium. About one hour versus one minute in burst suppression gave four times higher odds of delirium after coma. The delirium was also less likely to resolve.See
  • Burst suppression is mostly a marker of vulnerability. Severity of illness drove both burst suppression and mortality. Burst suppression mediated only about 10 % of the effect of critical illness on death. Titrating to the lowest necessary dose may nevertheless have a modest effect.See
  • EEG guidance has not reduced delirium in the large randomised trials. ENGAGES and ENGAGES-Canada gave less burst suppression, but no difference in delirium.See
  • Measurement and definitions diverge. Definitions vary, and the suppression ratio underestimates suppression compared with visual interpretation. The suppression phase looks the same whatever the cause. Incidence and duration alone therefore cannot distinguish oversedation from ischaemia, hypothermia or hypoglycaemia.See
  • Raise the blood pressure before simply reducing the dose. In patients over 60, burst suppression fell to 0 in 55 % of cases simply by raising MAP to baseline. Burst suppression can also be limited by avoiding hypothermia and ensuring oxygenation.See

The theme cards below tell the story with references to the studies. The summaries of each study are collected under “The studies in detail” at the bottom.

Burst suppression and outcomes

The association with delirium and death in observational studies

Three observational studies from the operating theatre and the ICU find that burst suppression is associated with worse outcomes. They are widely cited, but can only show association, not cause.Sources: Fritz 2016; Watson 2008; Andresen 2014

  • During surgery: more suppression, more delirium. In 727 adults, 86 % undergoing cardiac surgery, more minutes of suppression gave a higher incidence of delirium, also after adjustment (OR 1.22 per log unit of minutes of suppression). Suppression time predicted delirium better than time with BIS below 20, but both were weak predictors on their own.Source: Fritz 2016
  • In the ICU: burst suppression is associated with death and delirium. 39 % of 125 ventilated patients had burst suppression, although nobody had it as a goal. 59 % of them died within 6 months versus 33 % without (adjusted HR 2.04). In comatose patients who later woke, about one hour versus one minute in burst suppression gave four times higher odds of delirium (OR 4.16), and the delirium took longer to resolve.Sources: Watson 2008; Andresen 2014
  • The dose explains only part of it. During surgery, higher end-tidal concentration and lower opioid dose gave more suppression, but it is unclear which was cause and which was effect. In the ICU the lorazepam dose in the last 24 hours was higher before burst suppression, but none of the agents differed when the dose was adjusted for weight.Sources: Fritz 2016; Watson 2008
  • The studies are small and the measurements short. One study was a post hoc analysis with only 10–20 minutes of EEG per day, one had 69 patients, and in one nearly everyone had some suppression (548 of 619), so the comparison group was small. The authors of the two ICU studies themselves caution against firm conclusions.Sources: Watson 2008; Andresen 2014; Fritz 2016
  • After cardiac surgery too, those who developed delirium had more burst suppression. The patients were 60 years or older and received isoflurane (about 0.7 MAC) and sufentanil. Of 81, 26 (32 %) developed delirium, most often quiet (hypoactive) delirium. They had a median of 107 minutes of burst suppression during surgery, against 44 minutes in the others. Burst suppression was read from the monitor, not assessed in the raw EEG. The authors themselves write that it is not known whether burst suppression causes delirium or is only associated with it. Two of the authors have received lecture fees from the monitor manufacturer.Source: Soehle 2015 (observational study, full text read)

The studies in detail:

Fritz 2016 Watson 2008 Andresen 2014 Soehle 2015

Cause or marker?

There are two possibilities. Either excessively deep anaesthesia is the cause, or suppression occurs more easily in patients with subclinical brain pathology, so that anaesthesia acts as a “neural stress test”. Later studies point mostly towards the latter, but not entirely.Source: Fritz 2016

  • Severity of illness drives both. In 471 ICU patients, severe versus mild illness gave 39 % more burst suppression burden and 35 % higher mortality. Burst suppression mediated only 10 % of the effect of critical illness on death. A high versus low cumulative propofol dose gave only 6 % more burst suppression. Unintended burst suppression is therefore primarily an effect of critical illness and a marker of vulnerability.Source: Hogan 2020
  • A small contribution nevertheless exists. 100 % versus 0 % burst suppression burden gave 12 % higher mortality. Individual titration to the lowest necessary dose may have a modest effect. The difference in effect size from the earlier ICU study may be due to different methods and populations.Sources: Hogan 2020; Watson 2008
  • The randomised trials: less burst suppression, but mostly no less delirium. ENGAGES (n = 1232) and ENGAGES-Canada (n = 1140) gave less burst suppression in the EEG group, but no difference in delirium. Balanced (n = 655) gave 17 versus 29 % delirium, but with greater dose separation and differing anaesthetic sensitivity between centres. A blood pressure intervention study also reduced burst suppression without any difference in delirium in the recovery room. Of 27 healthy volunteers given 3 hours of isoflurane at 1.3 MAC, 93 % had burst suppression and none developed delirium.Sources: Jegarl 2026; Georgii 2022
  • Context decides (interpretation based on the sources). Burst suppression in healthy people need not cause delirium. In ill and vulnerable patients it mostly says something about the patient’s reserve. The causal analysis was nevertheless retrospective, with selection towards patients with brain injury, and the associations outside the randomised trials are observational.Sources: Hogan 2020; Jegarl 2026

The studies in detail:

Fritz 2016 Hogan 2020 Watson 2008 Jegarl 2026 Georgii 2022

Measurement and definition explain some of the discrepancy

Why do the observational studies find an association that the randomised trials do not confirm? Part of the answer lies in what was actually measured.Source: Jegarl 2026

  • Burst suppression is defined differently. ACNS 2021 requires burst suppression to make up 50–99 % of the record and distinguishes suppression (below 10 µV) from attenuation. The anaesthesia literature uses the term more loosely and measures with 1–4 frontal channels. Some studies counted any BSR above 0 as burst suppression.Sources: Jegarl 2026; Watson 2008
  • The monitor underestimates. The proprietary suppression ratio underestimates burst suppression compared with visual interpretation. In one study (41 patients), visually determined suppression duration was associated with delirium (p = 0.039), whereas SR-based duration was not (p = 0.275). The same caveat about processed BSR applies in the blood pressure study.Sources: Jegarl 2026; Georgii 2022
  • Time in burst suppression is often crudely measured. Duration has been calculated as the mean suppression ratio multiplied by time in coma, read from screenshots every 5 minutes and interpolated (141 patients), or only recorded for 10–20 minutes per day as yes/no without duration.Sources: Andresen 2014; Fritz 2016; Watson 2008
  • The pattern looks the same whatever the cause. The suppression phase looks the same in oversedation, ischaemia, hypothermia and hypoglycaemia, so incidence and duration alone cannot distinguish them. The content of the bursts (intraburst spectrum, preburst activity, spatial distribution) may be more informative.Source: Jegarl 2026

The studies in detail:

Jegarl 2026 Georgii 2022 Andresen 2014 Fritz 2016 Watson 2008

What can be done: more than turning down the dose

If burst suppression can mean either too much agent or too little energy, the dose is only one of several levers.

  • Blood pressure first. In patients over 60, MAP at the start of the episodes was lower than baseline. When MAP was raised to the patient’s baseline, BSR fell to 0 in 55 % of cases (24 of 44) without other measures. The intervention group had shorter suppression (5.9 versus 10.1 minutes). The effect came at induction; during maintenance the difference was not significant. The study does not prove causation, and the sample is small.Source: Georgii 2022
  • Temperature and oxygen matter too. Burst suppression can be limited not only with the dose, but by raising blood pressure, avoiding hypothermia and ensuring oxygenation. CMRO2 falls by about 6 % per °C, and the EEG becomes isoelectric at 18–20 °C.Source: Jegarl 2026
  • The lowest necessary dose. In ENGAGES and ENGAGES-Canada, lower MAC gave less burst suppression. Avoiding overdosing probably has little effect on mortality, but individual titration to the lowest necessary dose may have a modest effect.Sources: Jegarl 2026; Hogan 2020
  • When it is intended. In aneurysm surgery with temporary clipping, the evidence for barbiturate-induced burst suppression is mixed. Animal studies suggest that protection does not require burst suppression.Source: Jegarl 2026

The studies in detail:

Georgii 2022 Jegarl 2026 Hogan 2020
The studies in detail: delirium, mortality, causal analysis, context and blood pressure (6 cards)

Summaries of each article and chapter, with numbers and caveats. The theme cards above build on these.

EEG suppression during surgery and subsequent delirium (Fritz 2016)

Observational study from Washington University (Anesth Analg 2016;122:234–242), a sub-study of the SATISFY-SOS registry. This is the study most often cited for the association between burst suppression during anaesthesia and delirium.

  • Patients: 727 adults (mean 62 years, 63% men) for general anaesthesia with planned intensive care stay, 86% cardiac surgery. Induction with propofol, maintenance with a volatile agent. Suppression ratio from one BIS channel (Fp1–F7), recorded once a minute, summed to minutes with suppression. In 141 patients the values were read from screenshots every 5 minutes and interpolated. Delirium was assessed with CAM-ICU twice daily on days 1–5 in 619 patients.
  • Findings: median suppression 4.5 minutes (IQR 0.7–17.4). 162 (26%) developed delirium, 73% of them hypoactive. More minutes in suppression gave a higher incidence of delirium across quartiles (p < 0.0001), and the association held after adjustment for age, ASA, comorbidity, type of surgery, opioid, ketamine, transfusion and end-tidal concentration: OR 1.22 per log unit of minutes of suppression (99% CI 1.06–1.40). Suppression time predicted delirium better than time with BIS below 20 (c-statistic 0.62 versus 0.57), but both are weak predictors on their own.
  • What produced suppression: higher end-tidal concentration (OR 1.5 per 0.5 MAC) and lower opioid dose (OR 0.5 per 1 morphine equivalent/kg). The authors cannot say whether less opioid led to more suppression, or whether deeply anaesthetised patients without signs of nociception simply received less opioid.
  • Interpretation, the authors' two possibilities: either too deep anaesthesia as the cause, or that suppression arises more readily in patients with subclinical brain pathology, so that anaesthesia acts as a “neural stress test”. The study cannot separate the two; see Hogan 2020 and Jegarl 2026 below.
  • Limitations: observational study without causal inference, delirium measured as part of routine care (low sensitivity), no preoperative Barthel measurement, only planned intensive care patients, and mostly cardiac surgery. Almost all (548 of 619) had some suppression, so the comparison group without suppression was small (71). No conflicts of interest reported. The follow-up ENGAGES (Wildes 2019) from the same group found that EEG-guided anaesthesia reduced suppression time without reducing delirium.
Fritz et al. Anesth Analg 2016;122:234–242

Burst suppression during sedation and mortality (Watson 2008)

Post hoc analysis of a prospective cohort (Crit Care Med 2008;36:3171–3177) from the medical ICU at Vanderbilt: 125 adult ventilated patients without known neurological disease, APACHE II 27, 98% received sedation (lorazepam, midazolam, diazepam, propofol, fentanyl, morphine), titrated to the Ramsay scale. BIS (A1050, 2-channel frontal) was recorded for 10–20 minutes daily together with RASS and CAM-ICU. Burst suppression was defined as BSR above 0.

  • How common: burst suppression in 49 of 125 (39%), and in almost half of the comatose patients (46 of 93). 54% of the episodes occurred in the first 72 hours. None had burst suppression as a goal in the chart.
  • Mortality: 59% (29 of 49) died within 6 months versus 33% (25 of 76) without burst suppression. Adjusted for age, comorbidity, dementia, APACHE II, SOFA, coma and delirium: HR 2.04 (95% CI 1.12–3.70, p = 0.02).
