ICU mortality 37% versus 18% and hospital mortality 49% versus 24% were not significant individually. Length of stay on the ward after the ICU was longer (HR 1.84).
  • Drugs: the lorazepam dose in the preceding 24 hours was higher before burst suppression (27.8 versus 7.5 mg/day, p = 0.004). Propofol, morphine and fentanyl did not differ, and none of the agents differed when the dose was adjusted for weight. The groups were similar at inclusion.
  • The authors' main point: once the patient is unresponsive, no sedation scale can capture that the sedation is becoming deeper. Burst suppression is an EEG sign of deep sedation that can be read without EEG expertise, and which is probably less affected by encephalopathy than the index value itself. They propose that pEEG should be evaluated alongside sedation and delirium scales.
  • Sources of error they describe: EMG can give a falsely high index in intensive care patients, while hepatic and renal encephalopathy give slower, higher-amplitude EEG that resembles sedation and can give a falsely low index.
  • Caveats: post hoc, hypothesis-generating, 125 patients, only 10–20 minutes of EEG daily (burst suppression probably underestimated), yes/no classification without duration, and the sensor was applied just before recording, which may have stimulated the patient. Aspect provided monitors and partial salary for a research nurse; Ely and Watson report honoraria or support from Aspect, Hospira, Pfizer and Lilly. The authors themselves warn against firm conclusions.
Watson et al. Crit Care Med 2008;36:3171–3177

Time in burst suppression during coma and subsequent delirium (Andresen 2014)

Prospective observational cohort nested in BRAIN-ICU (Crit Care Med 2014;42:2244–2251), Vanderbilt, medical, surgical and cardiovascular intensive care. 124 ventilated patients had continuous BIS for up to 7 days; 69 were comatose (RASS −3 or deeper) and later awoke, and were included in the analysis. RASS twice daily, CAM-ICU twice daily when not comatose. Staff were blinded to burst suppression with a cover over the monitor. None received neuromuscular blocking agents.

  • Main finding: 42 of 69 (61%) developed delirium after coma. Most had burst suppression, but briefly: median 6.4 minutes (IQR 1–58). Adjusted for time with BIS below 40 and a component of APACHE II and cumulative doses of benzodiazepine, opioid and propofol during coma, more time in burst suppression gave higher odds of delirium (OR 4.16, 95% CI 1.27–13.62, p = 0.02) and later resolution of delirium (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.53–0.98, p = 0.04).
  • In practice: about 1 hour of burst suppression (75th percentile) versus 1 minute (25th percentile) gave four times higher odds of delirium and a 22% lower probability of it resolving during follow-up.
  • How time was calculated: BIS recorded the suppression ratio every minute (proportion of the last 63 seconds that was isoelectric); the mean was multiplied by time in coma. Minutes with low signal quality were excluded.
  • The authors' interpretation: sedation scales “lose their usefulness” when the patient is comatose, and pEEG can reveal the deepest sedation. The findings support lighter sedation strategies, but the authors themselves say that no firm conclusions can be drawn until larger studies have been done.
  • Caveats: small sample (69), monitoring did not always start at the onset of coma, maximum 7 days, eight patients would have dropped out with RASS −4 as the coma threshold, and no adjustment for hypoxia, hypotension, sleep or diagnosis. Watson reports research support from Aspect; several authors fees from Hospira and Orion.
Andresen et al. Crit Care Med 2014;42:2244–2251

Is burst suppression cause or marker? Causal analysis (Hogan 2020)

Retrospective observational study from Massachusetts General Hospital (Neurocrit Care 2020;33:565–574): 471 ventilated patients from seven intensive care units (2014–2017) with continuous EEG for at least 18 hours, after excluding anoxic encephalopathy after cardiac arrest and intentional burst suppression (raised ICP, status epilepticus, neuromuscular blockers). Median age 61 years, 27% died in hospital, half had unintentional burst suppression, and 63% had structural brain injury. The authors applied prediction models and causal inference (counterfactual “randomised” comparison, mediation, E-values) to the observational data.

  • Severity of illness drives both: going from mild to severe illness (10th versus 90th percentile) gave 39% (95% CI 8–66) more burst suppression burden and 35% (29–41) higher mortality.
  • Burst suppression contributes, but little: 100% versus 0% burst suppression burden gave 12% (7–17) higher mortality, and burst suppression mediated 10% (2–21) of the effect of critical illness on death.
  • Propofol matters less than assumed: high cumulative dose (1316 mg/kg) versus low (284 mg/kg) gave only 6% (0.8–12) more burst suppression, and propofol had no direct effect on mortality; the whole effect went via burst suppression.
  • The authors' interpretation: unintentional burst suppression is “primarily an effect of critical illness, not iatrogenic propofol use”, either because the illness itself produces the pattern (as in sepsis) or because it alters the brain's sensitivity so that ordinary doses produce burst suppression. Burst suppression thus becomes a marker of vulnerability. Avoiding overdosing will probably have little effect on mortality, but individual titration to the lowest necessary dose may still have a modest effect.
  • Versus Watson 2008: the authors consider that the difference in effect size may be due to differing methods and differing populations, and that intensive care versus operating theatre may be an effect modifier.
  • Caveats: selection (continuous EEG is obtained when brain dysfunction is suspected, hence 63% brain injury), coarse burden calculation in 8–12-hour windows, arbitrary distinction between mild and severe illness, in-hospital mortality only, cumulative dose without time course, binary clinical variables, no adjustment for unit, and seizure burden as an explicitly stated possible confounder. No conflicts of interest reported. Code is openly available.
Hogan et al. Neurocrit Care 2020;33:565–574

Burst suppression: good, bad or indifferent? Context decides (Jegarl 2026)

Narrative review from Weill Cornell (Anesth Analg 2026;142:1169–1179) that attempts to explain why observational studies find an association between burst suppression and postoperative delirium, while the large randomised trials do not.

  • The definitions diverge: ACNS 2021 distinguishes attenuation (≥ 10 µV, but below 50% of background) from suppression (below 10 µV), requires that “burst-suppression” makes up 50–99% of the recording, and that a burst lasts ≥ 0.5 s with ≥ 4 phases. The anaesthesia literature uses the term more loosely, calls suppression “isoelectric”, and measures with 1–4 frontal channels and a proprietary suppression ratio that underestimates burst suppression compared with visual interpretation. In one study (41 patients), visually determined suppression duration was associated with delirium (p = 0.039), but SR-based duration was not (p = 0.275).
  • The Ching model: a neurophysiological-metabolic model in which falling ATP opens ATP-gated potassium channels, hyperpolarises the neurons and produces burst suppression at about a 50% fall in ATP production, with suppression duration proportional to the ATP deficit. The model unifies deep anaesthesia, hypoxia/ischaemia, hypoglycaemia (below 50 mg/dl), the postictal state and hypothermia (CMRO2 falls about 6% per °C, isoelectric at 18–20 °C). Ketamine, dexmedetomidine and xenon do not produce burst suppression.
  • The trials: ENGAGES (n = 1232) and ENGAGES-Canada (n = 1140) gave lower MAC (0.69 versus 0.8 and 0.66 versus 0.8) and less burst suppression (7 versus 13 and 4 versus 12 minutes) in the EEG group, but no difference in delirium (26.0 versus 23.0% and 18.2 versus 18.1%). Balanced (n = 655, BIS 50 versus 35) gave 17 versus 29% delirium and longer suppression in the delirious (7 versus 2 minutes), but with greater dose separation and differing anaesthetic sensitivity between centres. 27 healthy volunteers with 3 hours of isoflurane at 1.3 MAC: 93% developed burst suppression, none developed delirium.
  • When burst suppression is used deliberately: in aneurysm surgery with temporary clipping the evidence for barbiturate-induced burst suppression is mixed, and animal studies suggest that protection does not require burst suppression. In hypothermic circulatory arrest, temperature below 12.5 °C and cooling for more than 50 minutes were the only reliable predictors of isoelectric EEG (only 60% were isoelectric at 18 °C), and each degree above the temperature at which the EEG became continuous again gave RR 1.56 for neurological injury.
  • Protective down-regulated state: the painted turtle survives months of anoxia with burst suppression-like EEG and 80 times higher GABA. The authors (via Schiff and Brown) propose a corresponding “protective down-regulated state” in humans after cardiac arrest and severe covid-19, where prolonged unconsciousness without structural injury may be protective. In 795 intubated covid patients, time to recovery of consciousness increased from 9 to 22 days with the degree of hypoxaemia.
  • Conclusion: the suppression phase looks the same regardless of cause, so incidence and duration alone cannot distinguish oversedation from ischaemia, hypothermia or hypoglycaemia. The burst content (intraburst spectrum, preburst activity, spatial distribution) may be more informative. In any case, burst suppression can be limited not only by the dose, but by raising the blood pressure, avoiding hypothermia and ensuring oxygenation.
  • Caveats: narrative review without a systematic search. Goldstein is a co-inventor on patents for alkylphenols against neuropathic pain.
Jegarl et al. Anesth Analg 2026;142:1169–1179

Burst suppression and blood pressure (Georgii 2022)

  • Design: randomised trial at a single clinic. Patients ≥60 years, at least 60 minutes of surgery under general anaesthesia, without neuropsychiatric disease. 104 were analysed, and 68 had a burst suppression ratio (BSR) above 0 (control 32, intervention 36).
  • Intervention: when BSR was above 0, MAP was first raised to the patient's baseline (lowest measured MAP before anaesthesia, mainly with catecholamines). If BSR was still positive, the anaesthetic concentration was reduced. The control group received standard anaesthesia with the EEG concealed.
  • Result: cumulative BSR was 433 versus 1385 (p = 0.002), duration 5.9 versus 10.1 minutes (p = 0.002) and maximum BSR 35 versus 50 (p = 0.027). The effect occurred at induction. During maintenance the difference was not significant.
  • MAP at the start of the BSR episodes was significantly lower than baseline in both groups. When MAP was raised to baseline (44 cases), BSR was reduced, and in 55% (24 of 44) it went to 0 without other measures. During maintenance this happened in 7 of 11.
  • Delirium: no one developed postoperative delirium on days 1–3. 28% developed delirium in the recovery room, with no difference between the groups.
  • The authors' caveats: the study does not prove a causal relationship between hypotension, hypoperfusion and burst suppression. Processed BSR may underestimate suppression, and 57% had a maximum state entropy of 80 or more. The sample is small.
Georgii et al. Front Syst Neurosci 2022;16:786816

Key points

  • Burst suppression after cardiac arrest is not on its own a sign of poor prognosis. Three patients with short time to ROSC and little cortical injury woke after 17–37 days and became functionally independent. All had prominent burst suppression with theta in the bursts.Source: Forgacs 2020 (see “Burst suppression with theta in the bursts after cardiac arrest: a recovery marker? (Forgacs 2020)”)
  • The content of the bursts may separate good from poor outcome. With a good outcome there was a persistent theta peak in the bursts, and the peak frequency rose over time. With a poor outcome the spectrum was flat, the theta only transient or the frequency falling. This requires full EEG and spectral analysis.Source: Forgacs 2020 (see “Burst suppression with theta in the bursts after cardiac arrest: a recovery marker? (Forgacs 2020)”)
  • One patient woke after 5 weeks of burst suppression. A 71-year-old with a short time to ROSC had burst suppression even after sedation had stopped, and met the criteria for a poor prognosis. The family declined withdrawal of treatment. He woke after about 5 weeks and returned to an active life.Source: Becker 2017 (see “Case report: 5 weeks of burst suppression after cardiac arrest, and the patient woke up (Becker 2017)”)
  • The shape of the bursts matters. Identical bursts after 24 hours are regarded as a sign of poor prognosis. Burst suppression in which the bursts vary and come and go gradually is distinguished from this.Source: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 (see “Clinical example: young patient with prolonged burst suppression after cardiac arrest who woke with good brain function (shared case)”)
  • Prognosis should rest on several criteria over time. The shared case, a young patient with short anoxia time who woke with good brain function, fits the profile in Forgacs 2020. Withdrawal of treatment after cardiac arrest usually happens within 5–7 days. The literature is therefore coloured by self-fulfilling prophecy. (interpretation based on the sources)Sources: shared case and Forgacs 2020 (see “Clinical example: young patient with prolonged burst suppression after cardiac arrest who woke with good brain function (shared case)”, “Burst suppression with theta in the bursts after cardiac arrest: a recovery marker? (Forgacs 2020)”)
  • The brain can show fast activity just before it stops. Two of four comatose patients had a brief increase in gamma activity when ventilator support was withdrawn. The study is small and says nothing about experience.Source: Xu 2023 (see “What happens in the brain when the circulation stops? (Xu 2023)”)

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

After cardiac arrest

Burst suppression with theta in the bursts after cardiac arrest: a recovery marker? (Forgacs 2020)

Three patients who awoke from coma 17–37 days after cardiac arrest and became functionally independent. In addition, a prospective cohort of 53 cardiac arrest patients, of whom 17 had burst suppression on the acute EEG.Source: Forgacs, Devinsky and Schiff. Ann Neurol 2020;87:618–632

  • The three woke late, long after the drugs had worn off. They had a short time to ROSC (10–20 minutes), therapeutic hypothermia to 33 °C and minimal cortical injury on CT or MRI. Two had preserved SSEP. Eye opening came 23–26 days and command following 37–67 days after all sedation had been stopped, far beyond the half-lives of the drugs. All had prominent burst suppression with a theta peak (about 4–7 Hz) in the bursts.
  • In the cohort, everyone with a good outcome had a persistent theta peak in the bursts. Of the 17 with burst suppression, 3 had a good outcome (CPC 2) and 14 a poor one (13 died). In the three with a good outcome, the peak frequency rose over time. In the 14 with a poor outcome, the spectra were flat or without lasting features (7), had only transient theta or falling frequency (5), or a shallow peak around 4 Hz (2).
  • Prolonged burst suppression may mean the neurons are alive but have impaired metabolism. This is the authors' hypothesis. They propose maintaining nutrition and fluids during the observation period and considering a time-limited trial of amantadine. Withdrawal of treatment after cardiac arrest usually occurs within 5–7 days, so the literature is marked by self-fulfilling prophecy.
  • Caveats: three case reports and a small cohort, and no causal test. Analysis of burst content requires full EEG and spectral analysis. No conflicts of interest, NIH-funded.
Forgacs, Devinsky and Schiff. Ann Neurol 2020;87:618–632

What happens in the brain when the circulation stops? (Xu 2023)

“Surge of neurophysiological coupling and connectivity of gamma oscillations in the dying human brain”.Source: Xu, Mihaylova, Li et al. and Borjigin. PNAS 2023, doi 10.1073/pnas.2216268120

  • Two of four dying patients had a brief increase in gamma activity. There were four comatose patients whose ventilator support was withdrawn. In two of them gamma activity briefly increased, and the heart rate rose.
  • The brain can display organised, fast activity just before it stops functioning. This is why the finding is interesting.
  • Caveats: four patients, and only two showed the finding. The study says nothing about what the patients may have experienced.
Xu et al. PNAS 2023

Case report: 5 weeks of burst suppression after cardiac arrest, and the patient woke up (Becker 2017)

One patient, described in full text. The authors are from the same group as Forgacs 2020.Source: Becker, Schiff, Devinsky and colleagues. Epilepsy Behav Case Rep 2017;7:1–5

  • The patient: 71 years old, with coronary artery disease, bypass surgery, hypertension, diabetes and atrial fibrillation. Found pulseless at the bottom of a pool, shockable rhythm, pulse back within 10 minutes. CT showed minimal loss of grey–white differentiation. Treated with hypothermia.
  • Burst suppression continued without sedation. During rewarming he developed status epilepticus, followed by generalised periodic discharges. Burst suppression was induced with propofol on day 5, with pauses of up to 30 seconds and 1-second bursts of sharp theta and delta. Propofol and lorazepam had been weaned off by day 13, but burst suppression continued. Burst suppression and a discontinuous EEG alternated for about 5 weeks in total.
  • He met the criteria for a poor prognosis. GCS 3, absent brainstem reflexes, no corneal reflex 19 days after the arrest and no motor response after 7 days. The neurologists suggested withdrawing treatment, but the family declined.
  • Even so, he woke and returned to an active life. Spontaneous eye opening on day 37, following commands on day 50 and discharged to rehabilitation on day 79. He has mild lasting difficulties with attention, executive function, naming and short-term memory, but speaks in public and travels. The EEG was reactive early in the course.
  • Burst suppression may perhaps protect neurons. The authors' hypothesis is that burst suppression continuing without sedation may protect neurons close to cell death, and that hypothermia may extend this effect. Prognostic criteria from before hypothermia may therefore be less valid.
  • Caveats: one patient. Case reports with a good outcome are more readily published than the many with a poor outcome.
  • Interpretation based on the sources: the patient was not young, but had a short time to ROSC and little injury on CT, like the patients in Forgacs 2020. The bursts contained theta and were not described as identical.
Becker et al. Epilepsy Behav Case Rep 2017

Clinical example: young patient with prolonged burst suppression after cardiac arrest who woke up with good brain function (shared case)

Shared with the author of this app. Young patient with a short anoxic time after cardiac arrest. The EEG showed prolonged burst suppression without other criteria for a poor prognosis. The patient survived with good brain function.

  • The term “burst suppression” is not enough on its own – the shape of the bursts matters. Identical bursts after 24 hours are regarded as a sign of poor prognosis. Burst suppression in which the bursts vary and come and go gradually is distinguished from this.Source: van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016 (Perfusion tab)
  • Everyone with identical bursts died without waking. Bursts were regarded as identical when the first 500 milliseconds were alike. Among comatose patients after cardiac arrest, 20 had identical bursts between 12 and 36 hours after the arrest, and all 20 died (specificity 100 %, sensitivity 40 %). Of the 28 with burst suppression without identical bursts, 18 (64 %) had a good outcome.Source: Hofmeijer 2014
  • Identical bursts look different from bursts caused by propofol. With identical bursts the pauses were flat and the transitions abrupt. With propofol the bursts vary and come and go gradually. The pattern was not seen in any of 183 patients with anaesthesia-induced burst suppression. But most with identical bursts were receiving low-dose propofol at the same time, and some had no sedation at all.Source: Hofmeijer 2014
  • The study has caveats. A single centre, some died of causes other than the brain injury, and reactivity and brainstem reflexes were not recorded. The EEG was not used in treatment decisions.Source: Hofmeijer 2014
  • A later finding from the same group points the same way. 34 of 179 comatose patients after cardiac arrest had identical bursts, and all had a poor outcome. Identical bursts were always bilaterally synchronous and had higher amplitude.Source: van Putten 2014 (conference abstract)
  • Those who woke late shared a profile. In Forgacs 2020 (above), the three who woke late and became independent had a short time to ROSC (10–20 minutes), little cortical injury on imaging and prominent burst suppression with theta in the bursts. One hypothesis is that the brain is then in a «protective down-regulated state».Sources: Forgacs 2020, Jegarl 2026
  • Young, healthy people may tolerate burst suppression. Its meaning depends on the brain's metabolic reserve.Source: Gruenbaum 2026
  • Interpretation based on the sources: the case fits the profile in Forgacs 2020: young patient, short anoxic time and no other signs of severe injury. Whether the bursts contained theta is not known. The case illustrates that burst suppression alone should not be read as a poor prognosis, and that prognostication should rest on several criteria over time.
  • Caveats: a single case. Sedation, timing of the EEG and burst morphology are not described here.
Shared case

Key points

  • Unexpected suppression can be caused by haemorrhage. In a shared case, burst suppression disappeared after transfusion and the EEG became continuous again. Reduced oxygen delivery to the brain can produce the same pattern as deep anaesthesia.Source: shared case (see “Clinical example: burst suppression during haemorrhage that resolves after transfusion (shared case)”)
  • Look for the cause before simply reducing the dose. Haemorrhage and anaemia, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia and hypnotic overdose can produce the same pattern. The EEG does not prove hypoperfusion, but unexpected suppression should prompt a search.Source: shared case (see “Clinical example: burst suppression during haemorrhage that resolves after transfusion (shared case)”)
  • A flat EEG is not the same as the intended burst suppression. In a neurosurgical patient where burst suppression was the goal, the EEG was completely flat when connected. The cause was herniation. An unexpectedly flat EEG must not be taken to mean the target has been reached.Source: shared case (see “Clinical example: burst suppression wanted, but the EEG was flat because of herniation (shared case)”)
  • Connect the EEG early to obtain a baseline. EEG from arrival, preferably before deep sedation, makes it possible to see when the pattern changes. Before titrating towards burst suppression, one should know that the brain can produce bursts. Processed EEG is recommended as early as possible in patients who need deep sedation. (interpretation based on the sources)Sources: shared case, Rasulo 2023 (see “Clinical example: burst suppression wanted, but the EEG was flat because of herniation (shared case)”)

The cards below summarise the articles and chapters these points are based on.

Clinical examples

Clinical example: burst suppression during bleeding that resolves after transfusion (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is described from two screenshots of a frontal EEG monitor taken about 20 minutes apart. The screenshots are not reproduced here.

  • During the bleeding, the EEG moved towards suppression. PSI was first around 35–40 and then fell to 10. The suppression ratio (SR) was 44%, EMG 0% and artefacts 0%, and the spectral edge frequency (SEF) was not calculated. In the spectrogram, power lay mostly below about 10–12 Hz without a clear alpha band, followed by increasingly frequent suppression periods in both hemispheres. The raw EEG was almost flat and low-amplitude. Electrode impedances were acceptable.
  • After transfusion, the EEG became continuous again. The suppression periods became shorter and disappeared. PSI was 44, SR 0% and SEF 15.8 Hz on the left and 16.4 Hz on the right. The raw EEG showed high-amplitude slow waves with faster activity superimposed, and the spectrogram showed power from slow-delta up to about 15 Hz.
  • Too little oxygen to the brain can look like deep anaesthesia on the EEG. During the bleeding, power shifted to lower frequencies, then came power loss and then burst suppression. Reduced cerebral oxygen delivery (CDO₂) produces exactly this pattern, and anaemic patients tolerate falls in blood flow less well.Source: Guay 2025
  • Bleeding hits oxygen delivery in two ways. CDO₂ depends on blood flow, haemoglobin and saturation. Bleeding can lower both blood pressure and haemoglobin, and transfusion can improve both. Burst suppression often resolved when MAP was raised to the patient’s baseline.Sources: Guay 2025, Georgii 2022
  • The screenshots do not show what mattered most. We do not know blood pressure, haemoglobin, temperature, the patient’s age or whether anaesthetic doses were changed. It therefore cannot be determined whether blood pressure, haemoglobin or both mattered most, or whether other factors contributed. Hypothermia, hypoglycaemia and hypnotic overdose can produce the same pattern.Sources: Patel et al. 2025, Guay 2025
  • Caveats: a single case without measurement of CBF, NIRS or Doppler. The point is not that the EEG «proves» hypoperfusion, but that unexpected suppression should prompt a search for the cause, including bleeding and anaemia, before the dose is simply reduced.
Own clinical example; Guay 2025, Georgii 2022, Patel et al. 2025

Clinical example: burst suppression was the goal, but the EEG was flat because of herniation (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed, and it is described from verbal information.

  • The course: a neurosurgical patient was transferred from another hospital, with no complications expected. The goal was burst suppression. When the EEG was connected, it was completely flat, and this turned out to be due to herniation.
  • Without a baseline, a flat EEG is hard to interpret. When the EEG is connected only after the patient is deeply sedated, there is nothing to compare with. A flat EEG may then be due to the drugs, but also to a brain that has stopped functioning.
  • Patterns persisting without sedation should be investigated as primary neurological disease. Electrocerebral inactivity is defined as 2 µV or lower. The suppression in burst suppression is below 10 µV.Source: Guay 2025
  • The spectrogram can give early warning of herniation. In two patients with herniation, increased low-frequency power and asymmetry in the spectrogram appeared roughly an hour before clinical deterioration.Source: Alsallom 2022
  • Start processed EEG early in deep sedation. It is recommended to start as early as possible and monitor continuously in patients who need deep sedation. Burst suppression should only be used to control raised intracranial pressure. Whether earlier EEG would have changed the course for this patient, one case cannot say.Source: Rasulo 2023
  • What it may mean in practice (interpretation based on the sources): EEG from arrival, preferably before deep sedation, gives a baseline and makes it possible to see when the pattern changes. If burst suppression is the goal, you should know that the brain can produce bursts before titrating towards it. An unexpectedly flat EEG should not be read as the goal having been reached.
  • Caveats: one case without screenshots. The diagnosis, drugs and time course are not known. Frontal EEG sees only part of the cortex.
Shared clinical example Guay 2025, Rasulo 2023, Alsallom 2022
